associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: The assessed Pu-Ta phase diagram is shown in the figure. The diagram is based on the earlier work and on the present thermodynamic modeling. The solubility of Ta in liquid Pu was measured at selected temperatures between 700 and $950^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ . The solubility of Ta in liquid Pu at 1000 and $2000^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ was reported, referring to unpublished work at Los Alamos National Laboratory. It was proposed that the phase diagram was a simple eutectic although it was noted that no eutectic microstructure was observed in Pu-Ta alloy samples after solidification and that the slight lowering of the melting temperature of Pu (which would be indicative of a eutectic reaction close to pure Pu) could have been the result of the presence of small amounts of impurities. Recently the Pu-Ta system was reviewed and also assessed to be a simple eutectic reaction very close to $100\%$ Pu and at $640^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ . We have attempted a theoretical calculation of the phase boundaries in the Pu-Ta system by utilizing the Miedema model to estimate the enthalpies of formation in the liquid and in the solid (bcc) phases, and assuming ideal entropy of mixing in both phases. Calculation of the phase boundaries at and below the melting point of Pu reveals greater solubility of Ta in (εPu) than in liquid Pu, thus suggesting that the Pu-Ta system is actually of a simple peritectic type. However, the liquidus trend calculated using the values for the enthalpies of formation obtained from the Miedema model turned out to be slightly displaced towards higher Ta content when compared with the experimental data. Hence, the values for the enthalpies of formation obtained from the Miedema model were adjusted to fit the liquidus data. The resulting fit is very good for all the data points except one at $2000^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ . The liquidus and solidus obtained from the revised values of the enthalpy of mixing are indicated by the dashed lines. The actual assessed liquidus has been drawn as a smooth curve interpolated between the calculated liquidus trends near pure Ta and Pu and passing through the data point at 16 at.% Ta and $2000^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ . The remaining phase boundaries indicated are those calculated using the revised values for the enthalpy of formation. The calculated peritectic reaction $[\mathbf{L} + (\mathbf{T}\mathbf{a})\leftrightarrow (\varepsilon \mathbf{P}\mathbf{u})]$ occurs at 0.782 at.% Ta and $658^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ . In addition, invariant reactions may be expected in connection with each of the allotropic transformations of $\mathbf{Pu}$ . Our calculation suggests that the eutectoid reaction $[( \varepsilon \mathbf{P}\mathbf{u})\leftrightarrow \delta^{\prime}\mathbf{P}\mathbf{u} +$ (Ta)] is at 0.235 at.% Ta and $477^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ . The calculations also suggest a pronounced retrograde solidus for the (Ta) phase. The invariant reactions below $400^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ have not been modeled. It was necessary to adjust the values of the enthalpy of formation because an estimate of the magnitude of the excess entropy of mixing was not possible without making assumptions regarding the (Ta) solidus.

associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: In a recent paper, the authors studied this system near the $\mathrm{Ni}_3\mathrm{Al}$ composition using two experimental techniques: (a) diffusion couple experiments and (b) directional solidification plus quenching to preserve the microstructures at the freezing interface. The results of this study supported the Schramm diagram and are shown in the figure. The solid circles were determined by the diffusion couple experiments, and the open circles were determined by the directional solidification studies. The quenched interface studies preserved the eutectic structure and gave conclusive evidence that the eutectic phases could not be the $\gamma + \gamma'$ required by the ASM diagram because the $\beta$ phase was clearly one of the eutectic phases. The solidification studies were limited to experiments done at the relatively rapid solidification rate of $61~{\mu\mathrm{m}}/\mathrm{s}$ , and it was concluded that the eutectic phases observed were $\beta + \gamma'$ as required by the Schramm type diagram of the figure. Subsequent experiments at slow solidification rates, to less than $1~{\mu\mathrm{m}}/\mathrm{s}$ , found that the phase diagram of the figure correctly described the general phase equilibria in this system, but the eutectic observed in our early study was, in fact, a metastable eutectic between the $\beta$ and $\gamma$ phases. This paper presents results of the experiments at slow growth rates, which find minor modifications of the diagram of the figure, and it presents evidence showing that in this system it is possible to form a metastable eutectic between the $\beta$ and $\gamma$ phases under certain growth conditions and compositions. According to the figure, one would expect that with a plane front interface, hypoeutectic alloys will begin to solidify with single phase $\gamma$ . When the fraction solidified becomes large enough, the liquid will become sufficiently enriched in Al to reach the liquid eutectic composition, and a coupled growth eutectic solid will form, provided a divorced eutectic reaction does not dominate at the slow growth conditions. And, for hypereutectic alloys, one would expect the final liquid to again form a eutectic solid after initially forming a $\beta$ phase alloy. The sequence of phase formation and the chemical compositions provide confirmation for the general form of the phase diagram given in the figure. This sequence of phase formation in the hypereutectic alloys is consistent with the phase diagram of the figure. It is seen from the equilibrium diagram of the figure that at any isotherm below the eutectic temperature, extrapolation of the liquidus lines requires $C_3 > C_2$ , which is opposite to the requirements for mass transport and presents strong evidence that coupled three-phase growth should not be occurring in the binary Ni-Al system. Therefore, one would expect the composition of the interdendritic liquid here to be close to the eutectic value of $24.5\%$ Al seen in the figure. Hence, the appearance of the metastable $\beta +\gamma$ eutectic only at compositions of $24.5\%$ Al in this study is consistent with its appearance at interdendritic locations.

A peritectic type of reaction was reported between the liquid, the Pt-rich solid solution, and the Ag-rich solid solution. The solid solubilities from X-ray studies near the peritectic are in agreement with the boundaries in the figure. Furthermore, the maximum volume change in sintered Ag-Pt alloys at about 40 at.% Pt also may be interpreted as the result of the invariant reaction. The assessed peritectic is between liquid with 20.1 at.% Pt and fcc solid solutions of 40.6 at.% Pt and 77.9 at.% Pt at $1186^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ . Below $965^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , there are several reports of intermetallic phases based on electrical conductivity, X-ray, mechanical property, and metallographic studies of alloys annealed for extended periods. At lower temperatures, just above $600^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , the authors claimed that the $\gamma$ phase has another modification identified as $\gamma'$ . Evidence for the existence of the $\delta$ phase at about 90 at.% Pt has been disregarded. The thermodynamic properties of Ag-Pt alloys in liquid or solid phases are not available in the literature. In this evaluation, thermodynamic modeling of the liquid phase and the solid solutions was performed to obtain the smooth and self-consistent phase boundaries shown by solid lines in the figure. Emphasis was given to the liquidus points and the X-ray data for the solid solubilities. The intermetallic phases $\alpha^{\prime}$ , $\beta$ , and $\gamma$ were not included in the modeling because of controversy over their existence. The much less divergent solidus and liquidus are consistent with the thermodynamic requirement. All of the phase boundaries above $965^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ were calculated using the coefficients. associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration:
General Features. The Fe-V system is a relatively simple system with an azeotropic minimum in its melting behavior, continuous solid solution at elevated temperatures, a closed $\gamma$ loop on the Fe-rich side, and an intermediate phase that forms congruently from the high-temperature solid solution near equiatomic stoichiometry. The assessed phase diagram is shown in the figure. This diagram is a composite of available information. The solidus and liquidus are a combination of the calculated results of Hack et al. and of Andersson. The boundaries associated with the $\gamma$ loop are based on the experimental work of Fischer et al. and of Kirchner and have been corroborated by the calculations of Andersson. The boundaries associated with the $\sigma$ phase are taken from the work of Inden and Buth. The temperatures for the Fe transformations are taken from the review of Swartzendruber, and the melting temperature of V is taken from the review of Smith. 
Liquidus and Solidus. It is well established that there is an azeotropic melting minimum in the Fe-V system, and there is remarkably good agreement with regard to the temperature and composition associated with this azeotropic minimum. Vogel and Tammann initially reported the minimum at 34 at.% V and $1435^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , Wever and Jellinghaus at 33 at.% V and $1468^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , Hellawell and Hume-Rothery at 30.5 at.% V and $1473.5^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , Furukawa and Kato at 32 at.% V and $1470^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , and Oswald Kubaschewski et al. at 35 at.% V and $1468^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ . Because the minimum tends to be relatively flat, the spread between 30.5 and 35 at.% V is not significant, and the calculated value of 31 at.% V can be considered as quite satisfactory agreement. Furthermore, if one discounts the early value of $1435^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ from Vogel and Tammann because of purity, the calculated temperature of $1468^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ is in very good accord with the experimental values. Therefore, the experimental liquidus and solidus points of Hellawell and Hume-Rothery in the composition range 0 to 40 at.% V and of Furukawa and Kato in the composition range 32 to 82 at.% V, as well as the thermodynamic curves of Kubaschewski et al., are all in close accord with the liquidus and solidus curves of the figure. 
Within the past two decades, V of higher purity has become available. Within this more recent period, studies of the boundary of the $\gamma$ loop show considerably less scatter, with the three most recent reports all showing the maximum V content as occurring near $1150^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , with values of 1.41 at.% V, 1.39 at.% V, and 1.40 at.% V. Beyond the $\gamma$ maximum, these same investigators found the $\alpha + \gamma$ two-phase field extending, respectively, to 1.81, 1.8, and 2.0 at.% V. Andersson quoted unpublished results of Kirchner and Gemmel, which are in accord with the results of these investigations. For the figure, values of 1.40 at.% V for the $\gamma$ maximum and 2.0 at.% V for the upper limit of the two-phase field were taken from the work of Fischer et al.; this selection was made because of the purity of the alloys of Fischer et al. and because the magnetic technique which was employed allowed good resolution of the respective contributions of the ferritic and austenitic fractions in the two-phase field. 
Variations in metal purity undoubtedly contribute to the diversity of results. The kinetics of the $\alpha \rightleftharpoons \sigma$ transformation also play a role in defeating precise determination of the temperature-composition coordinates of the $\sigma$ and $\alpha +\sigma$ phase fields. The boundaries that are shown in the figure are the calculated boundaries of Inden and Buth and are based upon thermodynamic data with inclusion of effects from atomic and magnetic ordering. These calculated boundaries thus represent the prognosis for the temperature-composition coordinates after attainment of strain-free equilibrium in the pure binary system. 
Magnetic Aspects ( $\alpha$ Phase). The Curie temperature of the $\alpha$ phase has been measured as a function of composition by a number of investigators and, with a single exception that can be attributed to poor metal purity, there is agreement that V additions to Fe cause the Curie temperature of the $\alpha$ phase to pass through a maximum above $800^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and below 20 at.% V. The maximum in the figure between 13 and 14 at.% V near $840^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ is a compromise among the composite data. From studies at higher temperatures in the paramagnetic region, Arajs et al. placed the maximum of the paramagnetic Curie temperature at $880^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and 10 at.% V; the difference between the ferromagnetic Curie maximum and the paramagnetic Curie maximum results from the neglect of curvature in the reciprocal susceptibility vs temperature plots immediately above the temperature intercept. The reasons for this curvature are not understood. 
Hack et al. did not develop relationships for describing the $\alpha/\gamma$ phase equilibria, because Hack's formulation of the Gibbs energies of phase formation neglected magnetic contributions. Recently, Andersson, starting with essentially the same thermodynamic input as Hack et al., added expressions for the magnetic contributions to the Gibbs energies of phase formation and recalculated the entire diagram with fewer adjustable parameters. He used a three-sublattice model for the $\sigma$ phase. The details of his calculation are too involved for inclusion in the present review, but it may be noted that the compositions associated with the $\alpha/L$ and V-rich side of the $\alpha/\sigma$ equilibria are not much affected by introduction of the magnetic energy. However, addition of the magnetic energy causes the compositions associated with the $\alpha/\sigma$ equilibria on the Fe-rich side to have a significantly different temperature trend. Inden and Buth's evaluation of the entire system takes into account both chemical and magnetic ordering; however, Buth's complete thesis is not yet available to this reviewer, so that explicit analytical expressions for the Gibbs energy functions are not given here.

The calculated and experimental liquidus data at various temperatures are compared. The overall agreement between Ga-In-Sb phase diagrams calculated in the present work and previous experimental data is generally very satisfactory. The Ga-In-Sb phase diagram was previously calculated by Gratton and Woolley, Miki et al., Blom and Plaskett, Szapiro, Liao et al., and Brebrick et al. Further, the regular solution model for the liquid phase used by them is inconsistent with the experimental thermodynamic data of Ga-Sb and In-Sb binary systems, as is clear from the work of Sharma et al. Miki et al. also used the regular solution model for the liquid phase and a complicated modified delta lattice parameter (MDLP) model for the solid compound, obtaining good agreement with the liquidus data and with the tie-line data. associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: On the other hand, no compound has been reported to transform congruently on cooling. Even if extended solid solution phases are also considered, a congruent transformation on cooling is not common. However, it is very easy to construct a hypothetical phase diagram with a compound transforming to a continuous solid solution phase on cooling. For example, the figure shows a hypothetical Ag-Au phase diagram with an equiatomic compound "AgAu," where, for simplicity, the liquid and solid phases are assumed to be ideal solutions. The relationship between the liquidus and solidus as calculated for this situation is essentially identical to that of the published assessed phase diagram. According to the criterion, the magnitude of the Gibbs energy of AgAu is quite normal. Then, why don't we see the congruent transformation on cooling? The answer is in the entropy term. The entropy of an ordered phase is smaller than that of a disordered phase making the $-TS$ term of the disordered phase overwhelm that of the ordered phase at high temperatures. Therefore, the disordered phase is always more stable at higher temperatures. In the present model, the structure of "AgAu" was not considered. The transformation as shown in the figure could occur when the compound has a simple structure while that of the solid solution phase is relatively complex, e.g., in organic systems. However, it may be safe to conclude that a congruent transformation of a compound phase to a solid solution will not occur on cooling, especially when the structure of the solid solution phase is relatively simple, as in metallic systems.

associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: The liquidus and solidus surface projections prepared in the figure are based on SEM analyses of the microstructures, EMPA, and x-ray data. Three-phase equilibria in the figure are denoted by letters and may guide the readers through the reaction scheme. Eutectic structures extending over large areas enabled EMPA area scans to allocate position of the lines of joint crystallization on the liquidus surface. Composition of the solid phases measured in as-cast samples was accepted to correspond to solidus temperatures. Locations of the monovariant lines of crystallization of $\tau_{1}$ with Al-Ti based phases and composition of the solid phase on the solidus surface are compatible with data on the existence of a eutectic invariant reaction between $\tau_{1}$ and $\gamma$ . Both ternary compounds ( $\tau_{1}$ and $\tau_{2}$ ) crystallize from the liquid but both form incongruity. The observation is compatible with the peritectic formation of $\tau_{1}$ , $\mathrm{L} + \delta = \tau_{1}$ , along the monovariant line $\mathrm{U}_{1} - \mathrm{U}_{4}$ , which contains a maximum invariant point $\mathfrak{p}_3$ . The exact position of the tie-line corresponding to this invariant reaction was not established, but from comparison of the lattice parameters and composition of $\tau_{1}$ in the as-cast and annealed states, as well from composition of the coexisting solid phases and finally crystallized eutectic structures, we can conclude that this tie-line is located close to the Al-rich end of $\tau_{1}$ . In both cases, the composition of the fine eutectic was found to be within the triangle $\tau_{1} + \tau_{2} + \mathrm{RuAl}_{2}$ close to the tie-line $\tau_{2} - \mathrm{RuAl}_{2}$ . This eutectic was accepted to be invariant $\mathrm{E}_{2}$ and is connected with the quasibinary eutectic $\mathbf{e}_{2}$ . The latter corresponds to the maximum on the liquidus and solidus surfaces separating the equilibria, which involve $\tau_{1}$ phases from the remaining Al-rich portion of the diagram. In combination with EMPA data of the finally crystallized liquids, one may conclude that $\tau_{2}$ forms in a peritectic reaction $\mathrm{p}_{10}:\mathrm{L} + \mathrm{Ti}_{1 - x}\mathrm{Al}_{1 + x} = \tau_{2}$ . Arguments for the construction of the liquidus surface can be found from the crystallization of sample 72Al-8Ru-20Ti. After primary crystallization of the $\tau_{2}$ phase, the remaining liquid meets the monovariant line of joint crystallization of $\tau_{2}$ and $\mathrm{Ru}_4\mathrm{Al}_{13}$ , and finally crystallizes in an invariant ternary eutectic $\mathrm{E_3: L} = \tau_2 + \mathrm{TiAl}_3 + \mathrm{Ru}_4\mathrm{Al}_{13}$ . Similar to $\mathrm{E}_2$ , this invariant eutectic is located very close to the tie-line with a maximum temperature on the solidus surface (see $\max_4$ ). Additional corrections due to literature data were made to comply with thermodynamic rules for proper connection of phase regions and for a smooth change of phase boundaries with temperature. Phase equilibria that derive from the proposed solidus surface and reaction scheme were introduced. Dashed lines mark phase equilibria still uncertain. Although there is no doubt about these isothermal reactions, there was no experimental proof for the two-phase equilibrium $\alpha_{2} + \delta$ in alloys annealed at $950^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ : the equilibrium, however, exists in alloys annealed at $770^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and $800^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ . BINGSS uses a least-squares method for simultaneously optimizing thermodynamic functions for each phase in a system, and the temperature-composition phase diagram. The six optimized Redlich-Kister polynomial constants utilized for the liquid excess free energy equation (five enthalpy terms and one entropy term) are also listed in the table. The liquidus curve was calculated using the data in the table, and is in quite good agreement with that of the assessed phase diagram, except for the metal-rich and boron-rich portions of the diagram. The optimized values of these coefficients are given in the table. The optimized formation enthalpies for the compounds are in excellent agreement with the reported values discussed earlier, and the formation entropies are relatively small, as one would predict for a solid state formation reaction.

$$
\alpha \left(1 - X _ {\mathrm {T a}}\right) ^ {2} + \Delta_ {\text {f u s}} G _ {\mathrm {T a}} + R T \ln X _ {\mathrm {T a}} = 0
$$

obtained by substituting $\Delta G_{\mathrm{Ta}}^{\mathrm{ex}} = -\Delta_{\mathrm{fus}}G_{\mathrm{Ta}} - RT\ln X_{\mathrm{Ta}}$ in the previous equation. The equation was solved by the Newton-Raphson method at different temperatures, and the results are shown in the figure. The liquidus compositions calculated in this work are in good agreement with the reported measured data.

The monotectic temperatures and compositions were calculated in the present work. The equation has three real solutions instead of a single value of $X_{\mathrm{Ta}}$ above a certain temperature for each system. The minimum temperature at which the equation has three solutions corresponds to the monotectic temperature of the system. The two $X_{\mathrm{Ta}}$ values out of the three solutions at the monotectic temperature will be common corresponding to the monotectic composition, and the third value represents the RE-rich liquidus composition at this tempera ture. The results are shown in the figure. The monotectic reactions for the Sm-Ta, Eu-Ta, Dy-Ta, Ho-Ta, Ta-Tm, and Ta-Yb systems were found to occur above the boiling pints of the pure RE metals and, therefore, were not shown in the respective phase diagrams.

The Clausius-Clapeyron equation representing the liquidus curve for equilibrium between a pure solid RE and a liquid solution of Ta in the RE can be given as:

$$
\ln \left(1 - X _ {\mathrm {T a}}\right) = - \Delta_ {\mathrm {f u s}} H _ {\mathrm {R E}} \left(T _ {\mathrm {m}} - T\right) / R T _ {\mathrm {m}} T
$$

where $\Delta_{\mathrm{fus}}H_{\mathrm{RE}}$ and $T_{\mathrm{m}}$ are, respectively, heat of fusion and melting point of the pure RE and $X_{\mathrm{Ta}}$ is the liquidus composition at temperature $T$. Raoult's law has been assumed for the solvent in the RE-rich liquid solution. A simultaneous solution of the equations for $T$ and $X_{\mathrm{Ta}}$ gives eutectic temperature and composition, respectively. The results are shown in the figure.

associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: The thermodynamic calculation of phase equilibria in the system under consideration was performed within the framework of a modified quasi-chemical model, assuming a linear temperature dependence of the interaction parameters of the atomic pairs $(W_{ij}^{f})$. This model is advantageous for its simplicity as well as for the fact that its parameters have a meaning of interaction energies between all kinds of atom pairs and thus can be determined by various methods including the ab initio calculations. Optimization of parameters was done by recurrent calculation of the binary boundary systems Al-Mg, Al-Si, and Mg-Si together with experimental data for the position of univariant eutectic $\mathrm{L}\Leftrightarrow \alpha\text{-Al} +\mathrm{Mg}_2\mathrm{Si}$ in the ternary system. Our interaction parameters have values similar to those used by other authors at given temperatures, thus implying that a rather simple quasi-chemical model is applicable for description of phase equilibria in the Al-Mg-Si system. The results established that variation of $W_{ij}^{f}$ within wide limits preserves the characteristic features of the equilibria of the fusion diagram under consideration, $\nu iz$ . noncoincidence of the quasibinary section $(\alpha \text{-Al} + \mathrm{Mg}_2\mathrm{Si})$ with the corresponding stoichiometric section of the ternary system and its displacement to the area of alloys enriched in magnesium. It is known that the maximum in the concentration dependence of the eutectic transformation temperature is determined by the condition of contact of two respective liquidus surfaces $(\mathrm{L} \Leftrightarrow \alpha \text{-Al}$ and $\mathrm{L} \Leftrightarrow \mathrm{Mg}_2\mathrm{Si})$ , whereas the actual coordinates of the unvariant eutectic transformation $\mathrm{L} \Leftrightarrow \alpha \text{-Al} + \mathrm{Mg}_2\mathrm{Si}$ are defined by the condition of their crossing. The $\mathrm{L} \Leftrightarrow \alpha \text{-Al}$ surface is asymmetric with respect to the stoichiometric section $\mathrm{Al - Mg_2Si}$ , which is induced by different solubility of magnesium and silicon in the aluminum melt. As a result, the point $e^o$ , which is a contact point between the respective isotherms of liquidus $(\mathrm{L} \Leftrightarrow \alpha \text{-Al}$ and $\mathrm{L} \Leftrightarrow \mathrm{Mg}_2\mathrm{Si})$ , is displaced to the area of alloys enriched in magnesium. The contact of the two liquidus curves $(\mathrm{L} \Leftrightarrow \alpha \text{-Al}$ and $\mathrm{L} \Leftrightarrow \mathrm{Mg}_2\mathrm{Si})$ occurs at $591^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , while the ratio of the components $C_{\mathrm{Mg}} / C_{\mathrm{Si}}$ in the alloy equals 2.51. The quasi-binary section $(\alpha \text{-Al} + \mathrm{Mg}_2\mathrm{Si})$ of the phase diagram is shown in the figure. The experimental investigation of the position of liquidus surfaces $(\mathrm{L} \Leftrightarrow \alpha$ -Al and $\mathrm{L} \Leftrightarrow \mathrm{Mg}_2\mathrm{Si})$ allows determination of the volumetric fraction of $\mathrm{Mg}_2\mathrm{Si}$ in the eutectic alloy on the quasi-binary section (having the maximum melting temperature and zero melting range) with high accuracy. Such studies established that the eutectic contains about $13.10\%$ $\mathrm{Mg}_2\mathrm{Si}$ on the quasi-binary section. The direct comparison provides evidence of large informative capabilities of the quasichemical phase model for the description of the fusion diagrams of aluminum alloys.

Thus the intersection of the miscibility gap with the solidus gives rise to a peritectic-type diagram in the Cu-Ir system. The peritectic invariant temperature as obtained by DTA measurements is $1138 \pm 5^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , and the corresponding reported compositions of the liquid, (Cu), and (Ir) phases are $\sim 4$ , $\sim 8$ , and $\sim 97$ at.% Ir, respectively. The liquidus and the (Ir) phase boundaries were calculated as shown by a solid line in the figure. In the absence of any experimental results for the liquid, the calculated diagram was compared for reproducibility against the solidus for the (Ir) phase, part of which (up to $1600^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ ) is known from experimental work. The calculated solidus shows satisfactory agreement with the latter. Incorporation of an additional entropy term in the $G^{\mathrm{ex}}(\mathrm{fcc})$ expression does not improve further the reproducibility of the phase diagram. On the other hand, if the $G^{\mathrm{ex}}(\mathrm{fcc})$ is represented by a combination of one enthalpy and an entropy term, or if the liquid was allowed to assume nonregularity, the resultant calculated solidus differs considerably from the diagram. The resultant liquidus boundaries also exhibit large deviations from those shown experimentally. Thus, the expressions are considered most appropriate and are accepted in this evaluation to represent the thermodynamic properties of the liquid and the fcc phase, respectively. As expected, the calculated solvus boundaries show better agreement with the experimental boundaries than do calculated boundaries based on a single expression for the $G^{\mathrm{ex}}$ for both (Cu) and (Ir). The three-phase equilibria data at $1138^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ were utilized to derive the $G^{\mathrm{ex}}$ for the liquid for a regular solution model. The liquidus and the (Ir) solidus are shown by plus $(+)$ marks at selected temperatures in the figure. The above calculations indicate good internal consistency in the liquidus derived from the thermodynamic analysis of the experimental phase diagram. The calculated liquidus shows an inflection point, which indicates the likelihood that the liquid develops a metastable miscibility gap at lower temperatures. The metastable gap of the liquid was calculated and is shown in the figure, with the critical temperature at $\sim 1350^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ . The symmetric shape of the gap is a consequence of the liquid being approximated as a regular solution. The figure also shows the metastable miscibility gap of the fcc phase. associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: Another series of isothermal sections in the temperature range from $770 - 1250^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ was constructed for the composition range 30-100 at.% Ti. Both research groups used for their investigations x-ray powder diffraction (XPD), light optical microscopy (LOM), and electron microprobe analyses (EMPA); in addition scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) were used. All authors were in agreement (1) on the existence of continuous solid solutions between the isostructural compounds, TiRu and RuAl, and (2) on a wide homogeneity region wherein occurs the $\mathrm{Th}_{6}\mathrm{Mn}_{23}$ type structure. In the isothermal sections this region is labeled $\tau$ though it was originally called G. In the present work evidence will be presented to show that two ternary compounds, $\tau_{1}$ and $\tau_{2}$ , exist. The Ru content of the $\tau_{1}$ -phase holds for the entire homogeneity region extending from 36.7-50.8 at.% Al and equals about 23.5 at.% Ru. These data agree with the Ru content in the G-phase, as defined by various authors at 24.2 at.%, 25 at.%, and 19-28 at.%. Based on an uncertainty in the determination of the Ru content on Ru-rich and Ru-poor sides of the $\tau_{1}$ -phase, the authors presented this phase boundary in dashed lines. There are no contradictions on the Al content in the Al-rich part of the $\tau_{1}$ -phase. Values from 50-52 at.% Al at $800^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ are reported in fair accord with 52 at.% Al established at $1250^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ . Composition of the Ti-rich side of the $\tau_{1}$ -phase is uncertain: a content of 33 at.% Al is reported, a value of 36 at.% Al can be read from the $800^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ isothermal section, and aluminum contents of about 38 at.% at $770^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and 40 at.% at $1250^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ are claimed. The general tendency in the change of the $(\beta \mathrm{Ti})$ homogeneity region on lowering of temperature can be seen from a comparison of the isothermal sections at $1100^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and $1050^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ . Only one inconsistency in the $1050^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ isothermal section has to be noted—the homogeneity region of $(\beta \mathrm{Ti})$ meets the Al-Ti diagram two times in disagreement with the binary system. Therefore, phase equilibria for the Al-rich part of $(\beta \mathrm{Ti})$ have to be read as in the isothermal section at $1100^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ . No optimization of the $1050^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ section is given in this article. The isothermal section at $950^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ differs significantly from the equilibrium proposed by the same authors at $1100^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ . For the temperature range 950-1100 °C, the existence of two invariant reactions was suggested: $\beta + \gamma = \alpha_{2} + \tau$ ( $\mathrm{U}_{15}$ ) and $\beta + \tau = \alpha_{2} + \delta$ ( $\mathrm{U}_{17}$ ), which yield equilibrium between $\alpha_{2}$ and $\delta$ at $950^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ . A further argument to improve the Ti-rich portion of the isothermal section at $950^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ concerns the curvature of the homogeneity regions of $(\beta \mathrm{Ti})$ in the two-phase equilibrium with $(\alpha \mathrm{Ti})$ and $\alpha_{2}$ , which is strongly concave at $1100^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , but appears as convex in the isothermal section at $950^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ . The extension of the $\tau_{2}$ single-phase field is compatible with the trend of its decrease with decreasing temperature as seen in samples annealed at $1100^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and lower. Furthermore, the structural transformation from bcc $\beta \mathrm{Ti}$ to CsCl-type (denoted as $\beta^{\prime}\mathrm{Ti}$ ) was included in the isothermal sections at $1250^{\circ}$ and $1100^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ by dotted lines following the data of Khataee et al. (although these authors did not include $\beta^{\prime}\mathrm{Ti}$ , probably due to lack of information about corresponding ordering in the Al-Ti binary system). Dashed lines mark phase equilibria still uncertain. Decreasing the temperature from $1250^{\circ}\mathrm{C} - 1100^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ results in the phase equilibria changing due to the appearance of $\mathrm{Ti}_{3}\mathrm{Al}\left(\alpha_{2}\right)$ , which results in a strongly decreasing aluminum content in $(\alpha \mathrm{Ti})$ and $(\beta \mathrm{Ti})$ . The isothermal section at $1100^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ reveals two three-phase equilibria $(p)$ $\beta +\alpha +\alpha_{2}$ and $(q)$ $\beta +\alpha_{2} + \mathrm{TiAl}(\gamma)$ , which were not observed at $1250^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ . These equilibria are the product of an invariant equilibrium, $\alpha +\gamma = \beta +\alpha_{2}$ (U14), which is connected to the binary eutectoid reaction $\alpha = \gamma +\alpha_{2}$ at $1114^{\circ}\mathrm{C},$ and to the three-phase region $\alpha +\beta +\gamma$ at $1250^{\circ}\mathrm{C}.$ The alternative reaction $(\alpha +\gamma +\beta = \alpha_{2})$ was rejected because it would suggest a significant solubility of Ru in $\alpha_{2}$ for which there is no evidence from the experimental data. This fact is revealed from combined x-ray, SEM, and EMPA data for samples in the as-cast state and those annealed at $1100^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ . $\tau_{2}$ was found to be perfectly homogenized, in contrast to as-cast conditions, and it forms equilibria with $\tau_{1}$ and $\mathrm{RuAl_2}$ . In such a case, a Ru-poor composition would correspond to the high temperature modification, because heat treatment of as-cast samples at $1100^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ results in complete homogenization of $\tau_{2}$ and annealed samples contain only the phase at the Ru-rich composition.

A projection of a proposed liquidus surface is shown in (a). The phase equilibria data substantiating these projections are described in this paper. Four phases are considered in the present section: a Nb-Ti-Si solid solution, $\mathrm{Nb}_{3}\mathrm{Si}$ , $\mathrm{Nb}_{5}\mathrm{Si}_{3}$ , and $\mathrm{Ti}_{5}\mathrm{Si}_{3}$ . $\mathrm{Nb}_{5}\mathrm{Si}_{3}$ and $\mathrm{Ti}_{5}\mathrm{Si}_{3}$ are not isomorphous and have tI32 and hP16 crystal structures, respectively. There are two options for the liquidus surface. In option 1, shown in (a), the first transition reaction (at higher Si concentration) is described by:

$$
\mathrm {L} + \mathrm {N b} (\mathrm {T i}) _ {5} \mathrm {S i} _ {3} \rightarrow (\mathrm {N b}, \mathrm {T i}) _ {3} \mathrm {S i} + \mathrm {T i} (\mathrm {N b}) _ {5} \mathrm {S i} _ {3}
$$

The above reaction occurs at the intersection between the peritectic ridge that descends from the first transition reaction and the $(\mathrm{Nb},\mathrm{Ti})_3\mathrm{Si} - (\mathrm{Nb},\mathrm{Ti},\mathrm{Si})$ eutectic groove, as shown in (a), at a temperature of $\sim 1350^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ . The data that are discussed subsequently indicate that this is the correct version of the liquidus surface. However, the steep nature of the peritectic ridge between the two transition reactions, and the small composition interval between them, make it very difficult to determine unequivocally that option 1 is indeed correct. The second option for the liquidus surface is shown in (b) and has the following first transition reaction (at higher Nb concentration):

$$
\mathrm {L} + \mathrm {N b} (\mathrm {T i}) _ {5} \mathrm {S i} _ {3} \rightarrow (\mathrm {N b}, \mathrm {T i}) _ {3} \mathrm {S i} + (\mathrm {N b}, \mathrm {T i}, \mathrm {S i})
$$

There are two other possible options in addition to the two described so far, with the second transition reaction being a class I ternary eutectic. However, there was no evidence for the formation of a ternary eutectic in any of the structures that were examined. There are no previous data on the compositions or temperatures at which the above transition reactions occur. These results are summarized in (c) and indicate that the first of the above options is the correct version. (d) shows a partial Scheil reaction scheme for the Si-lean region of the Nb-Ti-Si ternary. Thus, the locus of the eutectic groove shown in (c) is consistent with the microstructures for compositions as high as 16Si and as high as 44Ti. Thus, the first phase to solidify was primary $\mathrm{Ti(Nb)_3Si_3}$ . This suggests that this composition is from the $\mathrm{Ti}_5\mathrm{Si}_3$ -rich region, as shown in (c). It is also evidence for the second transition reaction. No ternary eutectic was observed in this composition. The microstructure also suggests that the Nb-70Ti-20Si composition is close to the $\mathrm{L} + \mathrm{Ti(Nb)}_5\mathrm{Si}_3 \rightarrow (\mathrm{Nb},\mathrm{Ti})_3\mathrm{Si}$ peritectic ridge. Thus, the liquid composition shifted during solidification and met the peritectic ridge just below the first transition reaction (at higher Si concentration) and led to solidification of peritectic $(\mathrm{Nb},\mathrm{Ti})_3\mathrm{Si}$ on the primary $\mathrm{Ti(Nb)_5Si_3}$ . However, the liquid composition only followed the peritectic ridge for a short distance, and it dropped off this ridge into the lower hypereutectic corner of the eutectic $(\mathrm{Nb},\mathrm{Ti},\mathrm{Si})$ $(\mathrm{Nb}, \mathrm{Ti})_{3} \mathrm{Si}$ valley. This led to solidification of cells of the latter eutectic. The liquid composition continued to move down the eutectic $(\mathrm{Nb}, \mathrm{Ti}, \mathrm{Si}) - (\mathrm{Nb}, \mathrm{Ti})_{3} \mathrm{Si}$ valley, and it eventually reached the second transition reaction (at lower Si concentration) where the remaining liquid in the intercellular regions solidified as $\mathrm{Ti}(\mathrm{Nb})_{5} \mathrm{Si}_{3} - (\mathrm{Nb}, \mathrm{Ti}, \mathrm{Si})$ eutectic. The microstructures also suggest that the reaction between $\mathrm{Nb}(\mathrm{Ti})_{5} \mathrm{Si}_{3}$ and $\mathrm{Ti}(\mathrm{Nb})_{5} \mathrm{Si}_{3}$ is not a eutectic; if it were, it seems likely that at least some $\mathrm{Nb}(\mathrm{Ti})_{5} \mathrm{Si}_{3}$ and $\mathrm{Ti}(\mathrm{Nb})_{5} \mathrm{Si}_{3}$ eutectic would have been observed between the primary $\mathrm{Ti}(\mathrm{Nb})_{5} \mathrm{Si}_{3}$ dendrites. The structure is consistent with the existence of the peritectic ridge between the two transition reactions, and it also provides evidence for the second transition reaction $\mathrm{L} + (\mathrm{Nb}, \mathrm{Ti})_{3} \mathrm{Si} \rightarrow (\mathrm{Nb}, \mathrm{Ti}, \mathrm{Si}) + \mathrm{Ti}(\mathrm{Nb})_{5} \mathrm{Si}_{3}$ , but it does not provide direct evidence for the first transition reaction. The regions close to the Nb-Si and Ti-Si binary eutectics are straightforward. The loci of the peritectic ridge from the $\mathrm{L} + \mathrm{Nb}_{5}\mathrm{Si}_{3} \rightarrow \mathrm{Nb}_{3}\mathrm{Si}$ peritectic, the Ti- $\mathrm{Ti}_{5}\mathrm{Si}_{3}$ eutectic groove, and the locations of the two transition reactions that occur are more complex, and particular emphasis is placed on these features in this section. Here, a peritectic $(\mathrm{L} + \mathrm{Nb}(\mathrm{Ti})_{5}\mathrm{Si}_{3} \rightarrow \mathrm{Ti}(\mathrm{Nb})_{5}\mathrm{Si}_{3})$ is assumed between $\mathrm{Nb}(\mathrm{Ti})_{5}\mathrm{Si}_{3}$ and $\mathrm{Ti}(\mathrm{Nb})_{5}\mathrm{Si}_{3}$ ; a eutectic is also possible, but the evidence that will be discussed subsequently suggests a peritectic. However, either a eutectic or a peritectic reaction between $\mathrm{Nb}(\mathrm{Ti})_{5}\mathrm{Si}_{3}$ and $\mathrm{Ti}(\mathrm{Nb})_{5}\mathrm{Si}_{3}$ provides a groove or ridge that falls toward the valley between the binary eutectics.

From a study of the solidification of several Al-Li-Si alloys, it was shown that invariant transformations take place at a temperature approximately $8^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ lower than that of the Al-Si eutectic $(577^{\circ}\mathrm{C})$. The presence of a ternary compound was also reported, as an extension of AlLi up to the formula $\mathrm{Al_2Li_3Si_2}$ (11.2 wt.% Li and 45.2 wt.% Si). The phase equilibria and phase relationships at the Al-rich corner of the Al-Li-Si system were studied using high-purity alloys with up to 12 wt.% Li and Si and employing thermal analysis (under controlled heating and cooling conditions) and microscopy. From polythermal sections with constant contents of 2.0, 5.0, 7.0, and 11.5 wt.% Si; 3.0 and 5.0 wt.% Li; 92 wt.% Al and sections with a Si-to-Li ratio of 2.7, the liquidus projection was constructed. From their microstructural examination and thermal analysis results for the polythermal sections, they established the eutectic reactions:

$$
\begin{array}{l} E _ {1}: L (1 1. 5 w t. \% S i a n d 0. 5 w t. \% L i) \leftrightarrow (A l) \\ + (\mathrm {S i}) + \mathrm {T a t} 5 6 5 \pm 3 ^ {\circ} \mathrm {C} \\ \end{array}
$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{array}{l} \mathrm {E} _ {2}: \mathrm {L} (2.0 \mathrm {wt} . \% \mathrm {Si} \text {and} 9.2 \mathrm {wt} . \% \mathrm {Li}) \leftrightarrow (\mathrm {Al}) \\ + \mathrm {A l L i} + \mathrm {T a t} 5 9 5 \pm 2 ^ {\circ} \mathrm {C} \\ \end{array}
$$

where $\mathbf{T}$ is the ternary compound with the approximate chemical formula $\mathrm{Al}_{2}\mathrm{Li}_{3}\mathrm{Si}_{2}$. associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: The figure shows the calculated Fe-Ni phase diagram at low temperatures. The dashed lines show the calculated metastable equilibria. Chamberod et al. studied four (Fe,Ni) alloys at 30, 32, 35, and $40\%$ Ni using Mössbauer spectroscopy. These alloys were annealed at $800^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and cooled to room temperature. The same alloys were subsequently subjected to $3\mathrm{meV}$ electron irradiation with $4\times 10^{19}$ electron/cm² at $80^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. The Mössbauer spectra of the four alloys with and without irradiation treatments clearly show that the $30\%$ Ni alloys without irradiation is paramagnetic. The same alloy after irradiation shows the presence of at least one other phase. These results can be explained readily in terms of the phase diagram shown in the figure. Heating to $723\mathrm{K}$ converts some of the L10 phase to $\gamma_{2}(\mathbf{F})$. It is difficult to account for the results obtained from the shock wave experiments, except that there might have been an abrupt rise in temperature associated with the shock wave. Thus, the shock wave would yield similar results as temperature, i.e., decreasing the amount of L10 with a corresponding increase in $\gamma_{2}(\mathbf{F})$. These results are consistent with the stable and metastable phase diagrams presented in the figure. The metastable phase equilibria were obtained in the following manner. According to Reuter et al. and others, the ordered FeNi phase $(\mathrm{L}1_{0})$ transforms to the fcc phase at $320^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ (593 K). Their data are shown in the figure. They also determined the compositions of phases present in meteorite samples by means of analytical electron microscopy. According to their calculations, there would be no diffusion below $150^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ (423 K), even over geological time. Accordingly, the chemical compositions obtained by them must correspond to this temperature of $423\mathrm{K}$, as shown in the figure. Chuang took $593\mathrm{K}$ to be the transformation temperature of L10 to fcc and $\sim 430\mathrm{K}$ to be the peritectoid temperature for the formation of $\mathrm{Fe_3Ni(L12)}$. The solution models he used for the L10 and L12 phases are those developed by our research group. As shown in the figure, the calculated phase equilibria involving the $\mathrm{Fe_3Ni(L12)}$ and L10 phases are consistent with the results of Reuter et al. Nevertheless, a word of caution is in order. Although we are reasonably confident of our calculated miscibility gap below $662\mathrm{K}$, the monotectoid temperature, the calculated equilibria involving the $\mathrm{Fe_3Ni(L12)}$ and L10 phases are based on two data points mentioned above. Furthermore, the models consider only the nearest neighbor interaction and take no other effect into consideration, which is obviously an over-simplification of the real situation. Additional and undoubtedly very difficult experimental investigations on well-controlled irradiated samples and meteorites are needed before a more definitive phase diagram is available at low temperatures. Scorzelli and Danon made a detailed analysis of the Mössbauer spectra for the Santa Catharina meteorite. According to their analysis, this meteorite has the following three phases, $38 \pm 5\% \gamma_{1}(\mathbf{P})$, $12 \pm 5\% \gamma_{2}(\mathbf{F})$ and $50 \pm 5\% \mathrm{FeNi(L1_0)}$. After heating the meteorite to $450^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ (723 K) for $15\mathrm{h}$ and subjecting it to shock waves with pressures of 100 and 200 kbar, the relative amount of $\gamma_{1}(\mathbf{P})$ remains essentially the same, that of L10 decreases with a corresponding increase in $\gamma_{2}(\mathbf{F})$.

associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: No data are available on the $\alpha/\gamma$ equilibrium boundaries below $912^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. The boundaries were constructed using the $\gamma \rightarrow \alpha$ and $\alpha \rightarrow \gamma$ transformation temperatures. The measured transformation temperatures do not represent equilibrium phase boundaries. As with many Fe alloys with an expanded $\gamma$ field, the $\alpha \rightleftharpoons \gamma$ transformations become sluggish and often have a martensitic nature. The equilibrium lines were drawn using the regular solution model described below and with the assumption that the equal $G$ values ( $T_{0}$ curves) should be approximately midway between the $\mathbf{A}_{\mathrm{s}}$ and $\mathbf{M}_{\mathrm{s}}$ transformations and the equilibrium lines should straddle $T_{0}$. The calculated boundaries are shown along with the $\mathbf{M}_{\mathrm{s}}, \mathbf{M}_{\mathrm{f}}$ and $\mathbf{A}_{\mathrm{s}}, \mathbf{A}_{\mathrm{f}}$ lines. The Curie temperature and magnetic moment of the $\alpha$ phase as a function of Os content was measured, reporting a decrease in Curie temperature of $11^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ per atomic percent Os added and a decrease in average moment of approximately 0.02 Bohr magnetons per atomic percent Os. The Curie temperature results are shown in the figure. Up to about 5 at.% Os, the $\mathbf{A}_{\mathrm{s}}^{\alpha \rightarrow \gamma}$ temperature lies above the Curie temperature, permitting the metastable extension of the measured results into the $\alpha + \gamma$ field. The known equilibrium phases of Fe-Os are (1) the liquid, L; (2) the $\alpha$ solid solution based on the low-temperature bcc phase of Fe; (3) the $\delta$ solid solution based on the high-temperature bcc phase of Fe; (4) the $\gamma$ solid solution based on the fcc phase of Fe; and (5) the $\varepsilon$ phase based on cph Os.

associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: Starting metal powders of purity of $99.99\%$ were used. The powder mixtures were initially melted and then annealed at $450^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ for $15\mathrm{d}$. In the figure, the ternary phase labeled $\Gamma_{1}^{\prime}$ is not continuous with the isostructural Fe-Zn binary phase $\Gamma_{1}$. This result can be interpreted as a miscibility gap existing at this temperature, rather than the existence of a true ternary compound as suggested. The continuous solid solution is apparently metastable and breaks up into two phases of differing composition with the much-longer annealing times (15 days), as compared with $30\mathrm{min}$. A thermodynamic assessment of this ternary system was presented, deriving for the first time the ternary interaction parameters and calculated isothermal sections at 450, 465, and $480^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. Several isothermal sections have been reported for Zn rich alloys of this system in the galvanizing temperature range. For a composition range of Ni and Fe of 20 at.% or more, there are two versions of the isothermal section at $450^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. Fe of $\sim 99.9\%$ purity was used with a galvanizing time of $30\mathrm{min}$.

associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration:
The assessed phase diagram for the Cd-Na system is based principally on the thermal analysis measurements and the sampling and analysis measurements. Melting points of the elements are from literature. The phase diagram was calculated from the thermodynamic analysis. The thermodynamic properties of this system have been measured several times. The A.D. Pelton, 1988. Experimental points from the thermal analysis measurements are shown in the figure. The latter authors also reported preliminary measurements in an earlier article. The two studies are in essential agreement, although that of the latter authors appears to be more careful and complete. A small liquid-liquid immiscibility gap extending from 60 to 70 at.% Na at a monotectic temperature of about $331^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ was reported. However, from the measured thermodynamic properties, it is now certain that no such gap exists in this region. A compound Cd5Na with a congruent melting point of $360^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ was proposed. From their more extensive measurements, a maximum of the liquidus was placed at $363^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ at the composition Cd6Na. However, as shown in the figure, the maximum is very flat so that their results are also consistent with the formula $\mathrm{Cd}_{11}\mathrm{Na}_2$ , which on the basis of crystal structure deter minations is now known to be correct. As discussed below, the formula $\mathrm{Cd_{11}Na2}$ is also more consistent with the thermodynamic analysis. It was reported that the stoichiometry $\mathrm{Cd_{11}Na2}$ was verified by "thermogravimetric analysis". However, no details were given. On the basis of their failure to observe a eutectic halt near $350^{\circ}C$ for compositions between 14.25 and 17.0 at.% Na, it was proposed that the compound exists over a range of compositions extending to higher Na contents. However, given that the stoichiometry is $\mathrm{Cd_{11}Na2}$, this conclusion is based on only two experimental composition points, at 16.0 and 17.0 at.% Na. The thermodynamic analysis argues against significant nonstoichiometry of $\mathrm{Cd_{11}Na2}$ . For Na content above 87 at.%, the liquidus was determined by sampling and analysis, which is the preferred technique when the liquidus is very steep. Their results are in excellent agreement with the present thermodynamic analysis. For temperatures below $210^{\circ}C$ , the points fall on the line:
$$
\log 10(\text {at.}\%) \mathrm{Cd}) = 2.59 - 1035 / T 
$$
where (at.% Cd) is the solubility of Cd in liquid Na, and $T$ is temperature in K. The liquidus calculated from the thermodynamic analysis falls within 0.2 at.% of the line for temperatures below $210^{\circ}C$ . Freezing-point depressions of Cd caused by Na additions of 1.3 at.% or less were measured. The observations agree well with the limiting freezing-point depression for no solid solubility calculated thermodynamically with the enthalpy of fusion of Cd. Measurements of the Na activity in the liquid phase in the composition range near pure Cd indicate quite strong negative deviations from ideality. Furthermore, the activity coefficient of Na does not approach a constant value, even in extremely dilute solutions. It is thus clear that the activity coefficient of Cd in the liquid decreases quite rapidly with small Na additions. For this reason, the calculated Cd liquidus drops quickly at Na content above 2 at.% Liquidus points reported at 3.5 and 4.7 at.% Na lie several degrees above the calculated liquidus. However, it is not possible for the liquidus to pass through these experimental points and then drop very rapidly to the eutectic reported by the same authors (5.5 at.% Na at $291^{\circ}C$ ), which is close to the calculated eutectic. As part of the present evaluation, a simultaneous optimizational analysis of the phase diagram data and the thermodynamic data was carried out. All experimental phase diagram data were considered, along with the liquid activity data, liquid partial enthalpy data $\Delta H(\mathrm{Na},\mathrm{L})$, and integral enthalpy of liquid mixing data. The Gibbs energies of fusion of the pure elements were taken as:
$$
\Delta f u s G ^ {0} (C d) = 6 2 0 1 - 1 0. 4 3 4 4 T J / m o l 
$$
$$
\Delta \mathrm {f u s} G ^ {0} (\mathrm {N a}) = 2 5 9 8 - 7. 0 0 3 5 T \mathrm {J / m o l} 
$$
where $T$ is temperature in K. The compounds $\mathrm{Cd}_{11}\mathrm{Na}2$ and $\mathrm{Cd}_2\mathrm{Na}$ were considered stoichiometric, and zero solid solubility was assumed. The results of the analysis are the following expressions for the integral enthalpy and excess entropy of mixing of the liquid and the Gibbs energies of fusion of the two compounds:
$$
\begin{array}{l} \Delta H = X _ {C d} X _ {N a} (- 4 1 5 3 6. 7 + 7 5 4 8 5. 6 X _ {N a} \\ - 3 4 8 5 4. 4 X N a ^ {2}) J / m o l \\ \end{array}
$$
$$
\begin{array}{l} \mathbf {S} ^ {\mathrm {e x}} (\mathrm {L}) = X _ {\mathrm {C d}} X _ {\mathrm {N a}} (- 3 9. 5 7 8 + 6 3. 8 8 8 X _ {\mathrm {N a}} \\ - 2 6. 7 8 3 X _ {N a} ^ {2} - 8. 9 7 8 X _ {N a} ^ {3}) \\ \end{array}
$$
$$
\begin{array}{l} \Delta \mathrm {f u s} G (1 / 1 3 \mathrm {C d} _ {1 1} \mathrm {N a} _ {2}) = 6 8 1 6 - 1 0. 7 2 4 T J / \mathrm {m o l} \\ \Delta f u s G (1 / 3 C d _ {2} N a) = 8 3 6 8 - 1 2. 7 3 7 T J / m o l \\ \end{array}
$$
where $X_{\mathrm{Cd}}$ and $X_{\mathrm{Na}}$ are the atomic fractions, and $T$ is temperature in K. By differentiation of the expressions, the partial enthalpy of Na, $\Delta H(\mathrm{Na},\mathrm{L})$ as well as the activity coefficient of Na, $\gamma \mathrm{Na}$ may be calculated. associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: The Al-Re phase diagram shown in the figure was proposed on the basis of results obtained using a combination of techniques: melting points, thermal, microstructural, and x-ray analysis as well as hardness and microhardness measurements. Four intermetallic phases were reported: (1) a $\chi$ phase of $\alpha \mathrm{Mn}$ structure at 57 at. $\%$ Re, (2) a phase $\mathrm{Al}_{\chi}\mathrm{Re}$ of unknown structure with a composition close to the equi-atomic ratio, (3) a phase $\mathrm{Al}_2\mathrm{Re}$ of unknown structure at 33 at. $\%$ Re, and (4) a phase $\mathrm{Al}_{12}\mathrm{Re}$ isotopic with $\mathrm{Al}_{12}\mathrm{W}$ at 7.7 at. $\%$ Re. For alloys with 30 to 90 at. $\%$ Re, the melting points were measured using an optical pyrometer, and with the help of microstructural analysis and hardness measurements, the invariant melting reactions at 2273, 1863, and $1758\mathrm{K}$ were determined to be the incongruent melting points of the $\chi$ , $\mathrm{Al}_x\mathrm{Re}$ , and $\mathrm{Al}_2\mathrm{Re}$ phases, respectively. The uncertainties of the measurements were estimated to be at least $\pm 25\mathrm{K}$ . Thermal analysis data of Al-rich alloys indicated a reaction at $963 \pm 7\mathrm{K}$ , which was interpreted to be the peritectic reaction, L + $\mathrm{Al}_2\mathrm{Re} = \mathrm{fcc}$ . Decomposition of $\mathrm{Al}_{12}\mathrm{Re}$ to fcc and $\mathrm{Al}_2\mathrm{Re}$ occurred at about $873\mathrm{K}$ . Based on microstructural analysis, the maximum solubility of Re in the fcc phase and that of Al in hcp phase were reported to be 0.26 at.% Re and 2.8 at.% Al, respectively. The existence of these phases was confirmed, but the $\chi$ phase was reported to be at 63.5 at.% Re instead of 57 at.% Re, using the alloys prepared originally. Compared to the figure, the phase diagram has the liquidus compositions at much higher Re contents, so that they are not consistent with the experimental data. For example, the composition of the liquid phase at the invariant reaction $\mathrm{L} + \mathrm{Al}_{11}\mathrm{Re}_4 = \mathrm{Al}_4\mathrm{Re}$ is about 15 at.% Re, in contrast to 2.5 at.% Re (15 wt.% Re) shown in the figure. The original phase diagram was in weight percent while that by others was in atomic percent of Re. The phase diagram from the present work is in accordance with the melting data. It was suggested that $\mathrm{Al}_{12}\mathrm{Re}$ was formed from the liquid instead of via a solid-state reaction according to the original work. Therefore, it was suggested that the invariant reactions at 873 and 963 K reported originally might correspond to the invariant reactions: $\mathrm{L} = \mathrm{fcc} + \mathrm{Al}_{12}\mathrm{Re}$ , and $\mathrm{L} + \mathrm{Al}_4\mathrm{Re} = \mathrm{Al}_6\mathrm{Re}$ , respectively. Thus, the invariant reaction at the extreme Al-rich end is eutectic instead of peritectic according to the original work. The other part of the phase diagram combined the melting data with x-ray analysis. $\mathrm{AlRe}_2$ was believed to be the $\chi$ phase and $\mathrm{AlRe}$ the $\mathrm{Al}_{\chi}\mathrm{Re}$ phase reported originally. A new phase diagram was proposed by including all six intermetallic compounds, with $\mathrm{Al}_2\mathrm{Re}$ replaced by $\mathrm{Al}_{11}\mathrm{Re}_4$ . Because $\mathrm{AlRe}$ was observed in alloys annealed at $1273\mathrm{K}$ but not at $1373\mathrm{K}$ , a peritectoid reaction, $\mathrm{Al}_{11}\mathrm{Re}_4 + \mathrm{AlRe}_2 = \mathrm{AlRe}$ , was placed between 1272 and $1373\mathrm{K}$ , instead of the melting of $\mathrm{AlRe}$ at $1863\mathrm{K}$ according to the original work. The decomposition temperature of $\mathrm{Al}_{11}\mathrm{Re}_4$ was placed at $1863\mathrm{K}$ , which was the decomposition temperature of $\mathrm{AlRe}$ according to the original work. Because the $\mathrm{Al}_4\mathrm{Re}$ phase was found to exist above $1273\mathrm{K}$ , its decomposition temperature was placed at $1758\mathrm{K}$ , which was the decomposition temperature of $\mathrm{Al}_2\mathrm{Re}$ (now $\mathrm{Al}_{11}\mathrm{Re}_4$ ) according to the original work. At the Al-rich side of the system, neither the proposed peritectic reaction at $963 \pm 7\mathrm{K}$ nor the eutectic reaction at $873\mathrm{K}$ involving the fcc and liquid is plausible. $\mathrm{Al}_{12}\mathrm{Re}$ forms at $873\mathrm{K}$ by a solid-state reaction, $\mathrm{fcc} + \mathrm{Al}_6\mathrm{Re} = \mathrm{Al}_{12}\mathrm{Re}$ . They argued that an attempt to make a correlation between the melting point data and more recent x-ray results could not be justified, because there were discrepancies on the total number of phases, their crystal structures, and their stoichiometries. The four phases reported originally were essentially confirmed, except that AlRe was found to decompose at about $1323\mathrm{K}$ instead of melting at $1863\mathrm{K}$ . With regard to the phase diagram, there were large uncertainties indicated with dashed lines due to the experimental difficulties discussed earlier. Moreover, the melting point data were not well characterized, and the structures for two out of the four compounds were not determined. The calculated phase diagram is consistent with the thermal arrests obtained originally.

associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: The Ge-Ru system was investigated by Raub and Fritzsche and by Susz. They established the existence of GeRu, a compound melting congruently at $1475^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, and of $\mathrm{Ge}_3\mathrm{Ru}_2$, formed by a peritectic reaction: liquid + GeRu $\leftrightarrow$ $\mathrm{Ge}_3\mathrm{Ru}_2$ at $1460^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. Poutcharovsky et al., by crystallographic investigations, and Susz et al., by high-temperature resistivity measurements, observed an allotropic transformation in $\mathrm{Ge}_3\mathrm{Ru}_2$ at approximately $440^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. Previous structural studies in the system are summarized, including Wallbaum's work on $\mathrm{Ge}_2\mathrm{Ru}$, which was later identified as $\mathrm{Ge}_3\mathrm{Ru}_2$ by Raub and Fritzsche. The phase diagram assessed by Massalski shows that the liquidus lines are unknown, particularly in the composition range that includes GeRu and $\mathrm{Ge}_3\mathrm{Ru}_2$. In order to obtain a steeper liquidus, it was necessary to have a more negative enthalpy of mixing for the liquid at the eutectic temperature. This is compatible with the measured $\Delta H^{\mathrm{liq}}(x)$ if the enthalpy of mixing is temperature dependent. The enthalpy of mixing was measured at three different temperatures, but no temperature dependence of $\Delta H$ was reported. $\mu$ values of liquid alloys are also known as a function of temperature and concentration. The analytical expression used for the liquid phase must be able to describe all these properties. Because $\Delta H$ and $\mu$ have both been measured, $a$ and $b$ coefficients are independently adjustable, and the asymmetric nature of the $\Delta H$ curve requires that at least two $a$ coefficients, $a_0$ and $a_1$ , be used. associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: A metastable miscibility gap of the liquid exists below the liquidus in this system. The presence of impurities has been known to stabilize such miscibility gaps above the equilibrium liquidus, giving rise to a monotectic transformation. The thermal analysis data are reminiscent of such a monotectic transformation, which could conceivably arise from impurity contamination effects. The calculated liquidus agrees to within $7^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ of the assessed liquidus and is displaced above the latter, except above 90 at.% Bi where the two liquidus curves essentially coincide. The calculated eutectic temperature and composition values obtained were $270.5^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and 99.5 at.% Bi, in excellent agreement with the experimental values. In the other calculation using the data of 81Tas, the $Q$ vs composition expression was accepted as given by the author, and the corresponding expression for $\beta$ was calculated from optimization with the experimental liquidus data. The composition variation of $\Delta H$ , as given by 81Tas, was retained here in order to study its effect on the shape of the liquidus being calculated. The calculated liquidus indicates a deviation from the assessed liquidus much larger than that obtained with the previous calculation. The rms deviation of the optimization fit of the data reported by Hultgren; Binary is three times lower than that of 81Tas. Thus, Hultgren's thermodynamic data are more consistent with the experimental Cu-Bi phase diagram than are those of 81Tas. This was done to evaluate the comparative appropriateness of the thermodynamic parameters from these two sources in relation to the measured phase diagram. The latter, in fact, shows very close agreement with the experimental liquidus, comparable to the optimization calculation results in the midcomposition ranges. Thus, the results demonstrate that the thermodynamic parameters of the liquid Cu-Bi alloys given by Hultgren; Binary, including the near-symmetric parabolic variation of $\Delta H$ with composition, agree quite satisfactorily with the phase diagram data. The moderately high positive values of $\Delta H$ for the liquid at $1200\mathrm{K}$ and the gentle slope of the liquidus, having an inflection point in the midcomposition range, suggest the possible development of a miscibility gap in the liquid at temperatures not far removed from the liquidus. This metastable miscibility gap was calculated using the optimized thermodynamic parameters of the liquid based on Hultgren and is shown in the figure. The gap shows an asymmetric shift in composition, with the critical point at $\sim 28$ at.% Bi and $\sim 650^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ . The corresponding ${}^{E}\Delta S$ values, however, show much greater asymmetry and are mainly responsible for the asymmetry in the miscibility gap. The resultant metastable miscibility gap of the liquid, shown in the figure, has a shape very similar to the corresponding $^E\Delta S$ curve. The shifts of the calculated liquidus based on these data with respect to the assessed experimental liquidus also bear resemblance to the contour of the $^E\Delta S$ curve. Thus, the $^E\Delta S$ of the liquid has a pronounced effect on the shape of both the liquidus and the metastable miscibility gap in the Cu-Bi system. To judge if the above shift in the $\Delta H$ values is significant and to ascertain which of these representations best represent the measured phase diagram, the following thermodynamic calculations were performed. The $Q$ $(= \Delta H / X(1 - X))$ and $\beta (= {}^E\Delta S / X(1 - X))$ values derived from the data tabulated by Hultgren; Binary were fitted into polynomial expressions parabolic in com position, analogous to the similar fit of the data given by 81Tas. Hultgren's thermodynamic data, in combination with the accepted liquidus data from the phase diagram determinations, were utilized in a computer program to arrive at a set of optimized expressions for the composition dependence of $Q$ and $\beta$ for the liquid alloys.

An upper limit is set by the maximum point $e_{0}$ of the eutectic trough $\mathrm{L} \leftrightarrow \delta + (\mathrm{Ni})$ , at very high pressure. It might be reasonable to assume a local pressure of about $5\mathrm{Pa}$ . This corresponds to $1351^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ for reaction $U_{1}^{\prime}(5\mathrm{Pa})$ , and corresponds well with the measured $1353^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ . Using this assumption on the local pressure, all the related data can be quantitatively understood from the thermodynamic model. However, the actual liquid participating in that reaction, $\mathrm{L} + \mathrm{gas} \leftrightarrow (\mathrm{Ni}) + \delta$ , is not located on that section, but virtually in the binary Ni-Ti edge system 89.1Ni-10.9Ti- $10^{-3}\mathrm{N}$ (at.%) at $U_{1}^{\prime}$ . The liquid phase involved is the very same virtually binary Ni-Ti liquid at $U_{1}^{\prime}$ . After sintering at $1500^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ in vacuum, a reaction between Ni and TiN and a eutectic microstructure of $\delta + (\mathrm{Ni})$ was observed . This can be clearly understood from the calculated phase diagrams. Upon cooling L shifts toward $U_{1}^{\prime}$ and the first solid solution (Ni) appears. As long as $\mathbf{L} + \mathbf{gas}$ can react, the eutectic-like $\delta + (\mathrm{Ni})$ structure can be formed in $U_{1}^{\prime}$ . Even with an excess amount of gas, this solidification will be complete. For an insufficient amount of gas, or once the gas supply to the liquid is cut off, further solidification will occur virtually in the binary Ni-Ti system according to the path $U_{1}^{\prime} - E_{1}$ . associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: If the liquid is denser, as in the system ice/water, the result illustrated in the figure is obtained. The diagram illustrates that the two changes of $T$ agree with Le Chatelier's principle. The second change of $T$ is opposite to, but smaller than, the first one, as required by the equation. On the other hand, the two changes in $P$ do not agree with the principle. Even though the second change of $P$ is opposite to the first one, it is larger, and $dP$ under equilibrium $(D = 0)$ would be of opposite sign to $dP$ under constant $\xi$ . Evidently, we should not attempt to apply the principle to $P$ unless the disturbance is caused by a change of $V$ . In the present case, it is caused by a change in $U$ . Notice that the dashed line in the figure shows an impossible case because it predicts that the second change in $T$ would be opposite to, but larger than, the initial change. Thus, $dT$ under equilibrium $(D = 0)$ would be of opposite sign to $dT$ under constant $\xi$ , which would disagree with the equation. Note that the primary disturbances were represented by the same arrow in the figure in order to emphasize that it does not depend on the difference in density between the solid and the liquid. First, suppose we disturbed the internal, two-phase equilibrium by adding a certain amount of heat to a solid/liquid system under constant volume. Then $dU = dQ - PdV = dQ$ . Thus, we would have increased $U$ by $dQ$ and should ask what would happen to the conjugate potential to $U$ , which is $-1 / T$ according to the equation. For small changes of $T$ , we could just as well examine $T$ , which may be more convenient. Before there is time for a phase transformation, $T$ will increase, and due to the volume being kept constant, $P$ will also increase to eliminate the thermal expansion. The slope of the arrow representing the initial disturbance would be $dP / dT = \alpha / \kappa$ where $\alpha$ and $\kappa$ are the thermal expansion and isothermal compression coefficients, averaged over the phases present. Due to the increased temperature, the system would thus move into the liquid region of the phase diagram, and part of the solid should melt in order to bring the system back to the line representing the two-phase equilibrium. The enthalpy of melting would be taken from the remaining parts of the system, and the system should move back along the first arrow. However, the two phases usually have different densities; that would give rise to an additional change of $P$ if $V$ is kept constant. It would be positive or negative depending upon what phase is denser. However, that same fact also determines the slope of the two-phase line in the phase diagram.

Later, a number of alloys were prepared using $99.99 + \%$ Sb and doubly sublimed Te, and the phase equilibria were reinvestigated by thermal analysis and XRD. There were two major findings of their investigation: (a) The liquidus minimum, between (Sb) and $\mathrm{Sb}_2\mathrm{Te}_3$ , is not a eutectic but is, in fact, an azeotropic minimum. (b) There are two intermediate phases, $\delta$ and $\gamma$ , between (Sb) and $\mathrm{Sb}_2\mathrm{Te}_3$ with extended ranges of solid solubility. The powder diffraction patterns of these two intermediate phases were given, but their structures were not determined. The eutectic reaction at $\sim 33$ at.% Te reported in the earlier investigations is probably due to the rapid cooling of the melt, which prevented peritectic formation of the $\delta$ and $\gamma$ phases. The azeotropic minimum and the two peritectic reactions are shown in the figure. The phase diagram in the range of 0 to 60 at.% Te was reinvestigated by XRD only. The alloys were prepared by agitation of liquid-solid mixtures near the solidus. The presence of the azeotropic liquidus minimum was confirmed but only one intermediate phase that ex tends from 10 to 60 at. $\%$ Te was reported. This is at variance with previous results, and a very recent study confirmed all the results. Also contrary to the report, an XRD study of an Sb-33.3 at. $\%$ Te alloy proved that the structure of the $\delta$ phase is not that of a solid solution based on $\mathrm{Sb}_2\mathrm{Te}_3$ . The structure is, however, related to that of $\mathrm{Sb}_2\mathrm{Te}_3$ . The phase equilibria in the range of Sb and $\mathrm{Sb}_2\mathrm{Te}_3$ were investigated with thermal analysis, metallography, and XRD techniques. They confirmed the presence of a peritectic reaction at $560^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ . However, they reported the existence of eleven discrete phases in this composition range and did not observe the $\gamma$ phase. Their results are at variance with previous results.

It was reported earlier that three solid phases take part in the phase equilibria in the Ti-rich region of the Ti-Si-Ga system (below 38 at.% Ga and above 62 at.% Ti) at $1350^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ . These phases are the $\beta$ Ti solid solution ( $\beta$ ), the compound $\mathrm{Ti}_5\mathrm{Si}_3$ with Ga in solid solution denoted as $\mathrm{Ti}_5(\mathrm{Si},\mathrm{Ga})_3$ , or z in this article and the compound $\mathrm{Ti}_2\mathrm{Ga}$ designated as $\chi$ . The same phases were found in the as-cast alloys. Therefore, these phases are involved in the solidification processes. Data on the constitution of the as-cast samples and those annealed at $1350^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ are listed in Tables 2 to 5. These data, which were obtained by means of metallography, XRD, EPMA, and DTA techniques, are considered in more detail below. They were used to construct the Ti-Si-Ga phase diagram presented as the solidus and the liquidus surface projections, the isothermal section at $1350^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , and the isopleth at 68 at.% Ti; these are shown in the figure. 
The homogeneity range of the $\beta$ solid solutions was found to extend along the Ti-Ga side of the ternary Ti-Si-Ga phase diagram in accord with the high Ga solubility in $\beta \mathrm{Ti}$ in the binary Ti-Ga system (up to 27 at.% Ga at $1420^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ ). The maximum Si solubility in $(\beta \mathrm{Ti})$ is accepted to be 4.7 at.% in the binary Ti-Si system at $1355^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ . It decreases with increasing Ga content and changes insignificantly with lowering of temperature as shown by EPMA (see the figure). It should be noted that the $\beta$ phase with the bcc W-type structure was never observed during this investigation, because the high-temperature $\beta$ phase disappeared during cooling to room temperature after undergoing a number of phase transforma tions depending on composition. Thermal effects at $\sim 900$ to $925^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ corresponding to the $\alpha \leftrightarrow \beta$ transformation were observed on the DTA curves during both heating and cooling. Precipitation of $\mathrm{Ti}_{2}\mathrm{Ga}$ as a result of decreasing Ga solubility with decreasing temperature was shown to occur by microstructural analysis (MSA) and XRD for those alloys that contained $\beta$ phase with more than $\sim 18$ at.% Ga. The lattice parameters of the $\alpha$ phase, formed as a result of the phase transformations of the $\beta$ phase, decrease with increasing Ga content owing to the substitution of smaller Ga atoms for larger Ti atoms. Solution of Si in Ti shows a similar effect. Besides the thermal effect resulting from the $\alpha \rightarrow \beta$ transformation, the DTA curves for the as-cast alloys containing a Ga-rich Ti phase were found to show an additional thermal effect at 1000 to $1035^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ due to the occurrence of the $\mathrm{Ti}_3\mathrm{Ga}(\alpha_2)$ phase. This last effect was not observed for those alloys annealed at $1350^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ . 
With the aim of defining the $\mathrm{Ti}_{5}(\mathrm{Si},\mathrm{Ga})_{3}$ apex of the $(\beta + \mathrm{Ti}_{5}(\mathrm{Si},\mathrm{Ga})_{3} + \mathrm{Ti}_{2}\mathrm{Ga})$ tie-triangle, an additional experiment was carried out. In the as-cast eutectic alloys 75Ti-5Si-20Ga and 75Ti-3Si-22Ga, the $\mathrm{Ti}_{5}(\mathrm{Si},\mathrm{Ga})_{3}$ phase is present only or almost only as very fine particles in a eutectic matrix, and they grow during annealing. The $\mathrm{Ti}_{5}(\mathrm{Si},\mathrm{Ga})_{3}$ grains formed during annealing are at equilibrium, whereas the large grains of the primary crystallized silicide phase do not reach an equilibrium state even during a long annealing time. The additional EPMA investigation of these alloys provides more reliable data concerning the position of the apex point of $\mathrm{Ti}_{5}(\mathrm{Si},\mathrm{Ga})_{3}$ of the tie-triangle (Table 3, the figure). 
The phase equilibria observed at $1350^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and reported recently apply up to the solidus temperatures. The phase equilibria in the region of investigation are characterized by the absence of any ternary compounds and involve only the pseudobinary phases. The $\mathrm{Ti}_{5}(\mathrm{Si},\mathrm{Ga})_{3}(\mathrm{z})$ is a phase based on the $\mathrm{Ti}_{5}\mathrm{Si}_{3}$ binary compound. It extends up to $\sim 25$ at.% Ga and coexists with the Ti-Ga-base phases ( $\beta$ , $\mathrm{Ti}_{2}\mathrm{Ga}(\chi)$ , $\mathrm{Ti}_{5}\mathrm{Ga}_{3}(\mathrm{g}))$ . It forms an extended ( $\beta + \mathrm{Ti}_{5}(\mathrm{Si},\mathrm{Ga})_{3}$ ) two-phase field, a ( $\mathrm{Ti}_{2}\mathrm{Ga} + \mathrm{Ti}_{5}(\mathrm{Si},\mathrm{Ga})_{3}$ ) narrow two-phase field, and two three-phase regions: ( $\mathrm{Ti}_{5}(\mathrm{Si},\mathrm{Ga})_{3} + \mathrm{Ti}_{2}\mathrm{Ga} + \mathrm{Ti}_{5}\mathrm{Ga}_{3}$ ) and ( $\beta + \mathrm{Ti}_{5}(\mathrm{Si},\mathrm{Ga})_{3} + \mathrm{Ti}_{2}\mathrm{Ga}$ ).

associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: The thermodynamic calculation of phase equilibria in the system under consideration was performed within the framework of a modified quasi-chemical model, assuming a linear temperature dependence of the interaction parameters of the atomic pairs $(W_{ij}^{f})$ . This model is advantageous for its simplicity as well as for the fact that its parameters have a meaning of interaction energies between all kinds of atom pairs and thus can be determined by various methods including the ab initio calculations. Optimization of parameters was done by recurrent calculation of the binary boundary systems Al-Mg, Al-Si, and Mg-Si together with experimental data for the position of univariant eutectic $\mathrm{L}\Leftrightarrow \alpha	ext{-Al} +\mathrm{Mg}_2\mathrm{Si}$ in the ternary system. It is of interest to compare the values of thermodynamic parameters used by different authors in the calculation of phase boundaries in this system. For this purpose, we present the values of the interaction parameters at two different temperatures (555 and $595^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ ). As can be seen, our interaction parameters have values similar to those used by other authors at given temperatures, thus implying that a rather simple quasi-chemical model is applicable for description of phase equilibria in the Al-Mg-Si system. We have also varied values of interaction parameters within the wide limits.
