Based on the structural and chemical results of this study, the Fe-rich regions of the Fe-Ni-S isothermal phase diagrams at 700, 600, 500, 400, and $300^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ are plotted in Fig. 8. The measured phase boundaries at 900 and $800^{circ}\mathrm{C}$ are consistent with previous results and are not plotted in Fig. 8. All the tie-line data used for constructing the phase diagrams are listed in Table 2. The small crosses at $10\mathrm{wt.}\%$ S in Fig. 8 are the nominal alloy compositions and the thin lines are the measured tie lines from this study. The bold lines are the new phase boundaries that are compared with the phase boundaries measured previously (dashed lines) at 700, 600, 500, and $400^\circ\mathrm{C}$. The radius of the circle that encloses each tie-line end point corresponds to the error associated with the measurement of that point. There is a statistical error for the measurement of Ni and S for each tie-line composition. The largest error (for Ni or for S) was used to determine the size of the circles; that is, the error for Ni dominates the composition error of the Fe-Ni phases, and the error for S dominates the composition error of FeS. The Ni content of the $\alpha$ , $\alpha + \gamma$ , $\gamma$ , $\gamma'$ and $\gamma'$ shown in Fig. 8 is only for the S-saturated phases. The Ni content of the $\alpha$ , $\alpha + \gamma$ , $\gamma$ , and so forth phase fields along the binary Fe-Ni axis in Fig. 8 is not shown. As an example of the effect of low S on the composition of the phase fields, an expanded region of the $700^\circ\mathrm{C}$ phase diagram between 0 and $0.1\mathrm{wt.}\%$ S is shown in Fig. 8(b).
The measured Ni solubility limit in FeS (Table 2) is related to the temperature and the alloy composition. For a given alloy, the Ni solubility decreases with temperature, which causes Ni depletion from the FeS. For a given temperature, the Ni solubility decreases with the Ni content. The S content in the $\alpha$ and $\gamma$ phases (Table 2) is relatively independent of aging temperature and composition. Some higher-S data points might be in error due to the presence of small FeS precipitates in the Fe-Ni. Because the S solubility in $\alpha$ and $\gamma$ is essentially independent of Ni content, the $\alpha / \alpha + \mathrm{FeS}$ , $\alpha + \gamma / \alpha + \gamma + \mathrm{FeS}$ , and $\gamma / \gamma + \mathrm{FeS}$ phase boundaries are parallel to the Fe-Ni side of the ternary isotherm. These boundaries are shown in Fig. 8(b).
The measured phase boundaries in this study are consistent with previous results at 900, 800, and $700^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Because all the $900^\circ\mathrm{C}$ data fall in the $(\gamma +\mathrm{FeS})$ field of the previous work, no isotherm is shown. Similarly, at 800 and $700^\circ\mathrm{C}$ , the $(\gamma +\mathrm{FeS})$ tie lines all fall within the $(\gamma +\mathrm{FeS})$ phase field of the previous work. However, the three-phase field $(\alpha +\gamma +\mathrm{FeS})$ is narrower in Ni content than that given in the 800 and $700^\circ\mathrm{C}$ isotherms, as is clear from Fig. 8(a).
The measured $(\alpha + \gamma + \mathrm{FeS})$ phase boundaries at 600 and $500^\circ\mathrm{C}$ are also close to those of previous results. Again, the $(\alpha + \gamma + \mathrm{FeS})$ field is narrower in Ni content than that given at $600^\circ\mathrm{C}$ (Fig. 8c), but at $500^\circ\mathrm{C}$ , the $(\alpha + \gamma + \mathrm{FeS})$ field extends to slightly higher Ni content than that given at $500^\circ\mathrm{C}$ previously (Fig. 8d). It was not possible to define the $(\alpha + \gamma + \mathrm{FeS})$ field at 400 or $300^\circ\mathrm{C}$ (see Fig. 8e and f and Table 2).
The major discrepancy between this and previous Fe-Ni-S phase diagram studies is the measurement of two new three-phase fields, $(\gamma + \gamma' + \mathrm{FeS})$ and $(\gamma + \gamma' + \mathrm{FeS})$ at or below $600^\circ\mathrm{C}$ . At 500 and $400^\circ\mathrm{C}$ , these three-phase fields occupy the region of the diagram where the $(\gamma + \mathrm{FeS} + (\mathrm{Fe}, \mathrm{Ni})_9 \mathrm{~S}_8)$ three-phase field is located (Fig. 8d and e).
At $600^\circ\mathrm{C}$ , the $(\gamma'' + \mathrm{FeS})$ boundary of the $(\gamma + \gamma'' + \mathrm{FeS})$ field is drawn tentatively as a bold dashed line (Fig. 8c). As discussed above, the $\gamma''$ phase was too small for EPMA analysis. The tie-line composition for $\gamma''$ at $600^\circ\mathrm{C}$ was $47.0 \pm 1.5$ wt.% Ni (Table 2). In addition, the extent of the $(\gamma'' + \mathrm{FeS})$ field was not measured. Note that there is no indication of $\gamma' (\mathrm{Ni}_3\mathrm{Fe})$ at high Ni contents in the previous diagram and that neither $\gamma''$ nor $\gamma'$ is present in the binary Fe-Ni diagram at $600^\circ\mathrm{C}$.
A previous study measured the presence of a three-phase field, $(\gamma +$ FeS $^+$ (Fe,Ni)9S8) at $600^\circ\mathrm{C}$ . This observation conflicts with that of the other previous work (Fig. 8c). The $\gamma$ phase contained $64.9\mathrm{wt.}\%$ Ni, similar to $\gamma^\prime$ observed at $400^\circ\mathrm{C}$ in this study. The extent of the $(\gamma +\mathrm{FeS} + (\mathrm{Fe,Ni})_9\mathrm{S}_8)$ phase field was not measured at $600^\circ\mathrm{C}$ because the experimental alloys in this study were too iron-rich.
At $500^\circ\mathrm{C}$ , we have measured the boundaries of the $(\gamma + \gamma'' + \mathrm{FeS})$ field. Although no $(\gamma + \mathrm{FeS})$ tie lines were measured, the extent of this two-phase field is defined by the surrounding three-phase fields, $(\alpha + \gamma + \mathrm{FeS})$ and $(\gamma + \gamma'' + \mathrm{FeS})$ , (Fig. 8d). At $500^\circ\mathrm{C}$ the $(\gamma + \gamma'' + \mathrm{FeS})$ field now occupies part of the region of the previous diagram where the $(\gamma + \mathrm{FeS} + (\mathrm{Fe}, \mathrm{Ni})_9 \mathrm{~S}_8)$ field and the $(\gamma + (\mathrm{Fe}, \mathrm{Ni})_9 \mathrm{~S}_8)$ fields are located (Fig. 8d). To accommodate the newly established $(\gamma + \gamma'' + \mathrm{FeS})$ phase field, the $(\gamma + \mathrm{FeS} + (\mathrm{Fe}, \mathrm{Ni})_9 \mathrm{~S}_8)$ field (Fig. 8d) must be redefined as the $(\gamma'' + \mathrm{FeS} + (\mathrm{Fe}, \mathrm{Ni})_9 \mathrm{~S}_8)$ field with $\gamma'$ at the stoichiometric FeNi composition. The $(\gamma + (\mathrm{Fe}, \mathrm{Ni})_9 \mathrm{~S}_8)$ two-phase field must also be redefined as the $(\gamma'' + (\mathrm{Fe}, \mathrm{Ni})_9 \mathrm{~S}_8)$ field with $\gamma'$ at the FeNi composition. These changes are not shown in Fig. 8d. The boundaries of other phase fields at compositions $>50$ wt.% Ni in the $500^\circ\mathrm{C}$ diagram will need to shift as well.
A previous study measured the presence of a three-phase field, $(\gamma +$ FeS $^+$ (Fe,Ni)9S8) at $500^\circ\mathrm{C}$ The $\gamma$ phase contained 65.1 wt.% Ni, similar to $\dot{\gamma}^\prime$ observed at $400^\circ\mathrm{C}$ in this study. The $(\gamma^{\prime} + \mathrm{FeS}$ $^+$ $(\mathrm{Fe,Ni})_9\mathrm{S}_8)$ phase field is not plotted on the $500^\circ\mathrm{C}$ isotherm (Fig 8d). Pentlandite, $(\mathrm{Fe,Ni})_9\mathrm{S}_8,$ would be in equilibrium with $\gamma^\prime$ as shown previously and not with $\gamma ''$ . Again, the alloys in this study were too Fe-rich to confirm the presence of this threephase field or to establish the phase relations among $\dot{\gamma}^{\prime},\gamma^{\prime \prime}$ ,and $(\mathrm{Fe,Ni})_9\mathrm{S}_8.$
At $500^\circ\mathrm{C}$ , $\gamma^{\prime}(\mathrm{Ni}_{3}\mathrm{Fe})$ is stable and appears in the previous diagram at high Ni contents. The $\gamma^\prime$ phase is in equilibrium with $\mathrm{Ni}_3\mathrm{S}_2$ at this temperature. Both the Kullerud diagram and the $500^\circ\mathrm{C}$ isotherm of the previous work indicate the presence of a three-phase field $(\gamma^{\prime} + (\mathrm{Fe},\mathrm{Ni})_{9}\mathrm{S}_{8} + \mathrm{Ni}_{3}\mathrm{S}_{2})$ . At $500^\circ\mathrm{C}$ , $\gamma^\prime$ $(\mathrm{Ni}_{3}\mathrm{Fe})$ is stable and appears in the binary Fe-Ni diagram. However $\gamma''$ (FeNi) only appears in the binary diagram below $500^\circ\mathrm{C}$ . Figure 8(d) only shows the S-saturated portion of the Fe-Ni-S $500^\circ\mathrm{C}$ isotherm.
At $400^\circ\mathrm{C}$ , the tie lines of the $(\alpha + \gamma + \mathrm{FeS})$ field were not measured. However, tie lines for the adjacent S-saturated $(\alpha + \mathrm{FeS})$ and $(\gamma + \mathrm{FeS})$ fields were measured. These two-phase fields define the maximum extent of the $(\alpha + \gamma + \mathrm{FeS})$ field (Fig. 8e). At $400^\circ\mathrm{C}$ , $\gamma'$ is the stable phase, and $\gamma''$ is not observed. However, as shown in the Ni profile across the $\gamma/\gamma'/\mathrm{FeS}$ interface, metastable $\gamma''$ at 52 wt.% may be present, decomposing into $\gamma$ and $\gamma'$ . The $\gamma'$ at $400^\circ\mathrm{C}$ is in equilibrium with the lower-Ni $\gamma$ phase.
The boundaries of the $(\gamma + \gamma' + \mathrm{FeS})$ field were measured (Table 2) and are shown in Fig. 8(e). A previous study measured a $(\gamma + \mathrm{FeS} + (\mathrm{Fe}, \mathrm{Ni})_9 \mathrm{~S}_8)$ field at $400^\circ\mathrm{C}$ . The $\gamma$ contained 62.5 wt.% Ni, similar to the $\gamma'$ composition of $64.9 \pm 4.0$ wt.% Ni measured at $400^\circ\mathrm{C}$ . In redrawing the previous $400^\circ\mathrm{C}$ isotherm, the $(\gamma + \mathrm{FeS} + (\mathrm{Fe}, \mathrm{Ni})_9 \mathrm{~S}_8)$ field should be drawn as $(\gamma' + \mathrm{FeS} + (\mathrm{Fe}, \mathrm{Ni})_9 \mathrm{~S}_8)$ . This field is separated from the $(\gamma + \gamma' + \mathrm{FeS})$ field by a new $(\gamma' + \mathrm{FeS})$ field, not shown in Fig. 8(e). The $(\gamma + (\mathrm{Fe}, \mathrm{Ni})_9 \mathrm{~S}_8)$ field of the $400^\circ\mathrm{C}$ previous isotherm (Fig. 8e) should be eliminated. In the binary Fe-Ni diagram at $400^\circ\mathrm{C}$ , $\gamma' (\mathrm{Ni}_3 \mathrm{Fe})$ is stable and $\gamma'' (\mathrm{FeNi})$ is metastable.
At $300^\circ\mathrm{C}$ , there are little data available to establish the phase regions between $(\alpha + \mathrm{FeS})$ and the $(\gamma + \mathrm{FeS} + (\mathrm{Fe,Ni})_9\mathrm{S}_8)$ region (see Fig. 8f). The metal phase of the $300\mathrm{FeNi}20\mathrm{S}10$ sample contained either $\gamma'$ or $\gamma''$ at $57.4 \pm 3$ wt.% Ni. The phase was $\sim 10$ nm in size. It is probable that equilibrium between $\alpha$ and $\gamma'$ or $\gamma''$ occurs at this temperature at very low S contents, probably below the S solubility of 0.05 wt.% in the $\gamma$ . This two-phase region is consistent with that observed in the Fe-Ni binary phase diagram. A previous study found that $\gamma$ was unreactive at less than $400^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and could not establish the three-phase field boundaries at $300^\circ\mathrm{C}$ .
Figures 8(a) to (f) display the S-saturated $\alpha / (\alpha + \gamma)$ and $\gamma / (\alpha + \gamma)$ boundaries of the $\alpha + \gamma$ field of the Fe-Ni-S ternary isotherms. As noted above, these figures, except for Fig. 8(b), do not show the Fe-Ni binary phase boundaries. Table 3 gives the $\alpha / (\alpha + \gamma)$ and $\gamma / (\alpha + \gamma)$ boundaries of the $(\alpha + \gamma)$ field for Fe-Ni and for S- and P-saturated Fe-Ni-S and Fe-Ni-P. Both S and P increase the Ni content in the $\alpha$ phase and decrease the Ni content in the $\gamma$ with respect to the binary system. The addition of S or P decreases the size of the $(\alpha + \gamma)$ field. The effect of adding only $\sim 0.05$ wt.% S is comparable to the effect of adding $>1.0$ wt.% P to saturate the $\alpha$ and $\gamma$ phases.

associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: Fig. 2 compares both the calculated Fe-C-Mn orthoequilibrium phase diagram (solid line) and the corresponding quasi-binary paraequilibrium phase diagram (dashed line) at $u_{\mathrm{Mn}} = 0.03$ in austenite, ferrite, and cementite. The applied compositional constraints reduce the degrees of freedom of the ternary system by one, and the $\gamma + \alpha +$ cementite three-phase field, introduced by manganese addition, degenerates to a straight line in the quasi-binary (Fe/Mn)-C system (line (d)). Generally, any higher order multi-component system with only $N$ independently variable (mobile) components (here, C) can be treated as a system with $N + l$ compositional degrees of freedom if all compositionally constrained components are treated as a homogeneous lump compound (here, $\mathrm{Fe} + \mathrm{Mn}$). On quenching a very low-carbon Fe-C-Mn alloy with $u_{\mathrm{Mn}} = 0.03$ and $w_{C} = 0.005$ wt.% from point A to point B, as indicated in Fig. 2, one can expect the transformation of $\gamma$ into $\alpha$ to begin after passing the orthoequilibrium phase region boundary $\gamma / \gamma + \alpha$ indicated by (a). As long as the temperature remains above the corresponding paraequilibrium boundary (b), any transformation of austenite into ferrite is thermodynamically possible only with partitioning of both manganese and carbon. As the temperature decreases below the paraequilibrium boundary (b), growth of $\alpha$ by rapid C-diffusion without partitioning of manganese becomes thermodynamically feasible.

associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: A detailed view of the Mn-rich part of the Cr-Mn phase diagram is shown in the figure; it is based primarily on the work of [71Lug]. The results of the various investigations are in general agreement concerning the Cr-rich region of the phase diagram, but vary considerably for the Mn-rich region. It appears that the conflicts are due to the appearance of metastable phase regions in quenched alloys. For this reason, the results of [71Lug] are accepted, based on studies of the phase relations in the Mn-rich region, using high-temperature X-ray techniques. The liquidus and solidus curves shown in the figure are based on the work of [49Car1], who carried out the most comprehensive study. The melting points of Cr and Mn, given by [49Car1] as 1863 and $1246^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, respectively, are identical to the presently accepted values. The liquidus temperatures reported by [49Zwi] in the region from 60 to 100 at.% Mn agree with the selected curve within $\pm 50^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. However, the eutectic reaction reported by [49Zwi] at $\sim 90$ at.% Mn does not exist. Numerous investigations have firmly established the existence of another intermediate phase at approximately 75 at.% Mn. The phase has the $\sigma$-type structure; it exhibits three modifications, $\sigma(\mathrm{HT})$, $\sigma'$ (MT), and $\sigma''$ (LT), corresponding to different states of order. The $\sigma$ phase forms peritectically at $1312^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$; it transforms at approximately $1000^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ to $\sigma'$. At about $800^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, the low-temperature modification $\sigma''$ is formed. In contrast to the very fast $\sigma \rightleftharpoons \sigma'$ transformation, the $\sigma' \rightleftharpoons \sigma''$ transformation is sluggish. The solid-state phase equilibria in the Mn-rich region, which are adopted in this evaluation, are based primarily on the work of [71Lug], who investigated this region by means of high-temperature X-ray techniques. The considerable differences between the results of [71Lug] and the diagrams presented in earlier reviews are probably due to the appearance of metastable phase regions in quenched alloys. It appears that the $(\delta \mathrm{Mn})$ and the $\sigma$ phases transform rapidly on cooling to the $(\gamma \mathrm{Mn})$ and the $\sigma^{\prime}$ phases, respectively; the high-temperature forms cannot be retained by quenching. On the other hand, the transformations of the $(\gamma \mathrm{Mn})$ and $\sigma^{\prime}$ phase to their respective low-temperature allotropes appear to be very slow. Apparently, the very fast quenching of liquid alloys in the composition region near $\sim 75$ at.% Mn prevents the formation of the equilibrium $\sigma$ phase, which requires at least partial ordering, and leads to a metastable extension of the equilibrium ( $\delta \mathrm{Mn}$ ) solid solution toward higher Cr concentrations. In fact, it is possible that ( $\delta \mathrm{Mn}$ ) and ( $\mathrm{Cr}$ ) may form a continuous solid solution in the metastable state because the equilibrium ( $\mathrm{Cr}$ ) field extends as far as $\sim 71$ at.% Mn. More work is needed to establish a reliable phase diagram, particularly in the region from 75 to 100 at.% Mn above $800^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. The investigations should be carried out by means of high-temperature X-ray and neutron diffraction techniques in order to determine the true stable equilibria.

The phase designated herein as $\mathrm{Al}_{7}\mathrm{Sr}_{8}$ has also been reported as “$\mathrm{AlSr}$” and “$\mathrm{Al}_{2}\mathrm{Sr}_{3}$” by several investigators (see “Crystal Structures” section). Table 1 summarizes the special points of the assessed Al-Sr phase diagram.

The experimental points shown in Fig. 1 were taken from a small illustration given in [74Vak]. Numerical information was provided on the melting temperature of $\mathrm{Al_4Sr}$ - $1000\pm 20^{\circ}C$ and on the eutectic points in the system - $630\pm 5^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and 3.2 at.%

[75Bru] studied the system by thermal analysis, X-ray diffraction (XRD), and metallographic methods. Three compounds were reported—$\mathrm{Al_4Sr}$, $\mathrm{Al_2Sr}$, and “$\mathrm{Al_2Sr_3}$”. The first melts congruently at $1040^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and the second and the third decompose by peritectic reactions at 936 and $666^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, respectively. “$\mathrm{Al_2Sr_3}$” and $(\beta \mathrm{Sr})$ form a eutectic reaction at 81.75 at.% Sr and $590^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$; no information was given about a eutectic reaction between (Al) and $\mathrm{Al_4Sr}$, except a line drawn at $660^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. The results obtained from thermal analysis are shown in Fig. 1.

[85Sat] studied the Al-rich part of the diagram up to 7.2 at.% Sr by thermal analysis, XRD, and optical microscopy. [85Sat] found a eutectic at 0.85 at.% Sr and $654 \pm 1^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$.

[86Clo] performed a new investigation of the Al-Sr diagram with DTA, XRD, and optical microscopy. Their experimental points are shown in Fig. 1. The results confirmed the general features of the diagram of [75Bru]. However, some values given in [86Clo] are quite different from those of [75Bru]. For example, the authors of [86Clo] confirmed the eutectic reaction on the Al side (reported at $654^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and 0.75 at.% Sr). The melting point of $\mathrm{Al_4Sr}$ was given as $1025^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, the peritectic reaction of formation of $\mathrm{Al_2Sr}$ at $920^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, and "AlSr" (instead of the "Al$_2$Sr$_3$" in [75Bru]) at $664^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. The eutectic reaction on the Sr side was shown at $580^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and 73.5 at.% Sr. The authors of [86Clo] mentioned that they had difficulties with detection of thermal arrests in alloys containing more than 73.5 at.% Sr. Judging by the scatter of the data, the problems started at smaller Sr concentrations—at about 40 at.% Sr. Therefore, the liquidus line at higher-Sr concentrations seems to be less reliable than in [75Bru].

The temperatures of the peritectic reactions of formation of $\mathrm{Al_2Sr}$ and $\mathrm{Al_7Sr_8}$ and the temperature of the congruent melting of $\mathrm{Al_4Sr}$ were adopted from [75Bru]. The compound $\mathrm{Al_7Sr_8}$ is shown in Fig. 1, instead of the previously reported "Al$_2$Sr$_3$" or "AlSr" (see "Crystal Structures" section). It should be noted that none of the above investigations mentioned the allotropic transformation in Sr at $547^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, which should influence the shape of the phase diagram. This transformation is included in the phase diagram as a dashed line.

[39Now] did not observe any solubility of Sr in (Al). They concluded that $\mathrm{Al_4Sr}$ possesses a homogeneity range from about 15 to 25.7 at.% Sr at $700^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, and that "AlSr" dissolves some Sr. The solubility in the intermetallic phases was not confirmed in subsequent publications. [75Bru] did not mention any mutual solubility of the components or homogeneity ranges in the intermetallics, and they are shown as line compounds in Fig. 1.

[87Man] prepared an alloy with 40 at.% Sr by melting components in an arc furnace under Ar and annealed it for 700 h at 500 °C. A single crystal was selected from this alloy and studied with XRD. The crystal had a new hybrid structure Al9Sr5 with space group $R\overline{3}m$ and consisted of alternating layers of $\mathrm{RX}_2$ (of $\mathrm{MgZn_2}$ type) and $\mathrm{R}_3\mathrm{X}_5$. The conditions of formation and stability of this phase at different temperatures is uncertain. It was not shown in Fig. 1 and Table 1.

The confirmation of the results of [75Bru] in subsequent publications has lead to the adoption of most of the features of their diagram. However, the temperature of the eutectic reaction on the Al side—(654 °C) was taken from [85Sat] and [86Clo]. The composition of the eutectic point was estimated on the basis of the properties of Al: $T_{\mathrm{fus}} = 660.45^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, $\Delta_{\mathrm{fus}}H = 10.7\mathrm{kJ / mol}$, and the assumption that the Al activity coefficient in liquid alloys with up to 1 at.% Sr is equal to 1. The estimated position of the eutectic point at about 1 at.% Sr does not contradict the data of [83Han], [85Sat], and [86Clo]. Therefore, the position of the calculated L/[L + (Al)] boundary is accepted, rather than the experimental result of [83Han], [85Sat], or [86Clo].

A two-dimensional phase diagram is obtained by projecting the three-dimensional equilibria onto the $c-T$ plane. So, it is not an isobaric section. Figure 4 shows the Fe-O binary phase diagram as a function of temperature and composition. The partial pressure of $\mathrm{O}_2$ is superposed on the diagram as isobars, which are analogous to the isotherms on the liquidus projection of a ternary system. The isobars coincide with the horizontal tii-lines in the two-phase region. Unlike the first category, in the single-phase region for any composition and temperature the pressure is fixed and cannot be selected by free choice. The phase rule is readily applied by taking the partial pressure and the vapor phase into consideration. For example, in the two-phase region of wustite and magnetite $F = 2 - 3 + 2 = 1$. Among the variables (temperature, the compositions of the two solid phases, and the partial pressure in the vapor phase), only one can be chosen independently. A phase diagram of the Fe-O system determined at constant (atmospheric) pressure cannot strictly be called an equilibrium diagram. For all practical purposes, such a diagram may coincide with the one determined by taking the variation in the partial pressure into account; significant differences, however, can arise in regions where the partial pressure is appreciable, for example, in the high-temperature equilibrium between magnetite and hematite in Fig. 4.

The assessed Au-Cd phase diagram has been composed from several sources, and it includes a number of features that remain to be clarified, as discussed below. The phases included are: (1) the liquid, L; (2) the fcc Au terminal solid solution, (Au), with a maximum solubility of 32.5 at.% Cd in (Au) at $627^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$; (3) the phases $\alpha_{1}$, $\alpha_{2}$, and a series of long-period superlattices in the composition range between $\alpha_{1}$ and $\alpha_{2}$; (4) the CsCl-type $\beta$ phase, with several forms of martensitic modifications at low temperatures; (5) a succession of related phases, $\delta$, $\delta'$, and $\delta''$, at temperatures above approximately $305^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$; (6) the $\mathrm{Au}_{3}\mathrm{Cd}_{5}$ phase, below $340^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$; (7) the $\varepsilon$ phase, with a possible martensitic transformation at $\sim 270^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$; (8) the closely related $\eta$ and $\eta'$ phases; and (9) the cph Cd terminal solid solution, (Cd), with a maximum solubility of 3.5 at.% Au in (Cd) at $309^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. The structural details of these phases are given in Table 1. The nomenclature adopted in Table 1 may be different from the various symbols used by different investigators in the literature. The $\beta$ phase region is especially confusing in this respect (Table 2). Invariant reactions and points are listed in Table 3.

Au Terminal Solid Solution, (Au). The (Au) solidus boundary is based on a thermodynamic assessment by Filby and Pratt (Table 10) (see "Thermodynamics"), which is in agreement with the experimental values of [62Riv]. The $(\mathrm{Au}) / [(A u) + \alpha_{2}]$ and $(\mathrm{Au}) / [(A u) + \alpha_{1}]$ solvus boundaries were determined by Owen and Roberts (Table 11) and by Hirabayashi and Ogawa (Table 7).

$\alpha_{1}$ Phase. The $(\mathrm{Au}) + \alpha_{2} \rightleftharpoons \alpha_{1}$ peritectoid reaction was reported to occur at $425^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ from lattice parameter measurements, and at $415^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ (Table 12) from thermal measurements. Subsequently, [62Riv] considered that the thermal effect at $412^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ observed by [61Hir], also corresponded to the above reaction. The order-disorder like transition at $422^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ in a 25 at.% Cd alloy is apparently the result of a peritectoid reaction. The form of the $[(A u) + \alpha_{1}] / \alpha_{1}$ boundary remains controversial. X-ray studies show this boundary to pass through $\sim 24$ at.% Cd at $250^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ or 20 at.% Cd at $300^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. The $(\mathrm{Au}) + \alpha_{2} \rightleftharpoons \alpha_{1}$ peritectoid temperature at $412^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and the phase boundary of the $\alpha_{1}$ phase on the Au-rich side have been based tentatively on the results of [61Hir]. [78Hus] found a transition (reported to be an order-disorder type) in a 25 at.% Cd thin film sample at $300^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, more than $100^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ lower than the corresponding reaction temperature in bulk materials.

$\alpha_{2}$ Phase. According to [62Riv], the $\mathrm{L} + (\mathrm{Au}) \rightleftharpoons \alpha_{2}$ peritectic temperature and the $\mathrm{L} \rightleftharpoons \alpha_{2} + \beta$ eutectic temperature are 627 and $626.6^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, respectively. The lattice parameter measurements of [40Owe] suggested the form of the $[(A u) + \alpha_{2}] / \alpha_{2}$ phase boundary, as shown in the assessed diagram. The $\alpha_{2} / [\alpha_{2} + \beta]$ boundary is also from the work of [40Owe], whose redetermined values are in [41Owe] (Table 11). [57Mas] placed the Cd-rich side of the $\alpha_{2}$ phase boundary at $439^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, in agreement with [40Owe].

$\pmb{\beta}$ Phase. The $\beta$ liquidus and solidus were examined by many investigators. Earlier reports on the $(\mathbf{L} + \beta)$ two-phase field, in the composition region of less than $\sim 50$ at.% Cd, indicated wider temperature ranges between the liquidus and solidus $(\sim 10^{\circ}\mathrm{C})$ than the more recent reports $(\sim 1^{\circ}\mathrm{C})$. The results of [73Kom] have been accepted tentatively in the assessed diagram. The results of [62Riv] and [68Was] are not in agreement with [73Kom] when compared in detail. The data of [68Was] suggested the existence of two L $\neq \beta$ congruent points at $\sim 47.5$ and $\sim 50.5$ at.% Cd, which is unlikely from the thermodynamic point of view. The volatility of Cd in this temperature range $(\sim 630^{\circ}\mathrm{C})$ makes the experimental work particularly difficult.

$\varepsilon$ and $\varepsilon'$ Phases. The phase boundaries of the $\varepsilon$ and the possible $\varepsilon'$ phases are based on the few data points available at this writing. Thus, the phase field is, at best, only tentative. The transition $\varepsilon \rightarrow \varepsilon'$ was reported to be an order to disorder type at $267^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ (Table 12). However, [77Ala1] did not observe any allotropic transformations corresponding to the $\varepsilon \rightarrow \varepsilon'$ transition. More recently, [82Ahm] reported that the $\varepsilon \rightarrow \varepsilon'$ transition is martensitic, occurring at $269^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ (Table 12).

Liquidus. The melting points of Au and Cd are 1064.43 and $321.108^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, respectively. The (Cd) liquidus was investigated in the 1800's by [1889Tam] and [1892Hey] (Table 4). The overall form of the liquidus and solidus boundaries was established by Vogel and Saldau (Table 5). More recent investigations covered only partial composition ranges, as follows: 51.4 to 98.0 at.% Cd, Durrant (Table 6); 10.4 to 54.22 at.% Cd, Rivlin, Hume-Rothery, and Rader (Table 7); 28 to 51.9 at.% Cd, Wasilewski (Table 5); 60 to 90 at.% Cd, Komarek and Stummerer (Table 8); and 60.5 to 82 at.% Cd, Alasafi and Schubert (Table 9). The agreement among these investigations generally is good. The scatter of individual data points generally is about $\pm 2^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ within smoothed curves representing the phase boundaries, except for some sporadic anomalous points found in early experiments. The $\beta$ liquidus is discussed below (see "Phase").

$\delta, \delta', \delta''$, and $\mathbf{Au}_3\mathbf{Cd}_5$ Phases. The experimentally determined phase boundaries of the $\delta$ and $\delta'$ phases from various sources are in very good agreement. The form of the $\delta''$ phase field at low temperatures is based on the work of [79Ala]. This phase corresponds to the $\gamma$ phase reported in [Hansen]. The $\mathrm{Au}_3\mathrm{Cd}_5$ phase, originally referred to as the $\gamma^\prime$ phase, because it was considered to be a low-temperature allotropic form of the $\gamma$ (present $\delta ''$) phase, was shown by [79Ala] to be unrelated to the $\delta ''$ phase.

associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: The assessed Zr-Fe phase diagram is based primarily on the work of [51Hay], [62Sve], [63Sve], [81Mal], [82Mal], [85Aub], and [85Stu], and includes: at $1673^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, and has a composition-dependent ferromagnetic transition in the range 300 to $470^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. The phase diagram differs from those given in previous evaluations [Hansen, Elliott, Shunk, Metals, 76Kub] in various details of the intermediate phases and of the invariant reactions. The eutectoid reaction $(\beta \mathrm{Zr})\leftrightarrow (\alpha \mathrm{Zr}) + \mathrm{Zr3Fe}$ was studied by [51Hay], [59Tan], [63Sve], [81Mal], and [82Mal]. Clearly, reasonable agreement exists concerning the composition of $(\beta Zr)$ at the eutectoid reaction, for which we took the value 4.0 at.% Fe. On the other hand, a $\sim 60^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ discrepancy regarding the temperature of the eutectoid reaction exists between the earlier results by [51Hay] and [59Tan] and those of [63Sve], [81Mal], and [82Mal]. The value of $730^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ given by [81Mal] has been adopted because this work is based on data from several alloy compositions obtained using better (general) experimental methods. For the compositions of $(\alpha \mathrm{Zr})$ and $\mathrm{Zr}3\mathrm{Fe}$ in the eutectoid reaction, we take, respectively, the maximum solubility of Fe in $(\alpha \mathrm{Zr})$, 0.03 at.% Fe, and the composition of the lower boundary of $\mathrm{Zr}3\mathrm{Fe}$, 24.0 at.% Fe. The boundaries of the $(\alpha Zr) + (\beta Zr)$ two-phase region are consistent with the temperature of $863^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ for the $\alpha \leftrightarrow \beta$ equilibrium in pure Zr and with the assessed temperature and $(\alpha Zr)$ and $(\beta Zr)$ compositions for the eutectoid reaction $(\beta Zr) \leftrightarrow (\alpha Zr) + Zr_3Fe$. The eutectic reaction $\mathrm{L} \leftrightarrow (\beta \mathrm{Zr}) + \mathrm{Zr}_2\mathrm{Fe}$ was studied by [51Hay], [59Tan], [62Sve], [81Mal], and [82Mal]. The values given in the more recent work by [82Mal] have been adopted. It turns out that the chosen values are essentially an average of all the values listed in Table 3. The melting point of pure $\mathbf{Zr}$ is $1855^{\circ}C$. No experimental data exist for the $(\beta Zr) + L$ two-phase field, and consequently, the corresponding boundaries shown are merely tentative. [85Aub] pointed out that the possible existence of $\mathrm{Zr_4Fe}$ intermediate phase should be rejected, because the appearance of this phase is due solely to contamination effects. Therefore, $\mathrm{Zr_4Fe}$ is not included. The liquid shown is taken from a figure in [63Sve]. The melting point of Fe is $1538^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and the temperatures of the $\delta \leftrightarrow \gamma$ and $\gamma \leftrightarrow \alpha$ equilibria in pure Fe are 1394 and $912^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, respectively. The temperature of the catalytic reaction ($\delta\mathrm{Fe}$) $\leftrightarrow$ L + ($\gamma\mathrm{Fe}$) is assessed to be $1357^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, with a tentative composition of $\sim 95.5$ at.% Fe for the intervening ($\delta\mathrm{Fe}$) phase. For the eutectic reaction L $\leftrightarrow$ ZrFe3 + ($\gamma\mathrm{Fe}$), the temperature is assessed to be $1337^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, with compositions of 90.2 and $\sim 99.3$ at.% Fe for the L and ($\gamma\mathrm{Fe}$) phases, respectively. Very good agreement exists between [63Sve] and [70Fis] regarding the temperature of the peritectoid reaction ZrFe3 + ($\gamma\mathrm{Fe}$) $\leftrightarrow$ ($\alpha\mathrm{Fe}$), so the value adopted is $925^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. The composition of ($\alpha\mathrm{Fe}$) in the last reaction is $\sim 99.90$ at.% Fe. Using a thermodynamic model, [70Fis] calculated both the interrupted $\gamma$ loop and the metastable $\gamma$ loop extension. However, the resulting Zr composition for $(\delta \mathrm{Fe})$ in the $(\delta \mathrm{Fe}) \leftrightarrow \mathrm{L} + (\gamma \mathrm{Fe})$ reaction is $\sim 0.4$ at.% Zr, clearly lower than the value shown. Further experimental investigation would be in order to solve this important discrepancy. [73Gus] reported the existence of a stable intermediate phase with C14 Laves structure, near the composition 77 at.$\%$ Fe and in the temperature range of 1220 to $1480^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, but this phase has not been observed by anybody else. Because [74Lys] reported the existence of a ternary $\mathbf{Zr2Fe3Si}$ compound with C14 Laves structure, we tend to think that the C14 structure in [73Gus] was probably stabilized by Si impurities or by other impurities such as oxygen or nitrogen; therefore, we have not included this C14 phase. [85Alt] found that amorphous Zr-Fe alloys in the composition range of 24.0 to 42.5 at.% Fe transform into the metastable cubic Fe3W3C-type structure by means of a crystallization process that could be explosive. Subsequently, the samples evolve into the structures indicated by the assessed Zr-Fe equilibrium phase diagram.

associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: The boundaries between $\alpha$ and $\gamma$ are compared in Fig. 3 with the $\gamma \rightarrow \alpha$ and $\alpha \rightarrow \gamma$ transformation temperatures measured by [37Fal], [38Mar], and [65Bla]. These measured transformation temperatures do not represent equilibrium phase boundaries. As with many Fe alloys with an expanded $\gamma$ field (e.g., Fe-Ni), the $\alpha \rightleftarrows \gamma$ transformations become sluggish and often have a martensitic nature. The $M_{s}, M_{f}$ and $A_{s}, A_{f}$ lines as given by [37Fal] are reproduced in Fig. 3. The experimental work necessary to determine the equilibrium phase boundaries in this region has not been performed for Fe-Ru. However, in analogy with the Fe-Ni work, where extensive experiments were performed to determine the equilibrium boundaries [81Smi], and paralleling the analysis of [71Bre], the $\alpha \rightleftarrows \gamma$ transformations can be used to place some restriction on the equilibrium boundaries. At temperatures between about 800 and $900^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, the equal $G$ values ($T_0$ curves) should be approximately midway between the $\mathbf{A}_{\mathrm{f}}$ and $\mathbf{M}_{\mathrm{f}}$ transformations, and the equilibrium lines should straddle $T_0$. The calculated boundaries shown in Fig. 3 fulfill this requirement, whereas the construction of [60Rau] falls too close to the Fe side. Combining this with the $\gamma/\varepsilon$ equilibrium shifts the eutectoid temperature to a much higher value $(\sim 650^{\circ}\mathrm{C})$ than that given by [60Rau] $(\sim 500^{\circ}\mathrm{C})$. Because of a lack of true equilibrium studies, a very high uncertainty must be placed on this eutectoid temperature. The Curie temperature of the $\alpha$ phase as a function of Ru content was measured by [38Mar], [37Fal], and [65Bla] up to about 9 at.% Ru, with good agreement among the various authors. The results of [38Mar] are shown in Fig. 3. Up to 9 at.% Ru, the $A_{s}^{\alpha \rightarrow \gamma}$ temperature lies above the Curie temperature, permitting the metastable extension of measured results into the $\alpha + \gamma$ field. The magnetic moment as a function of Ru content also was measured by [37Fal] and is essentially constant up to about 8 at.% As pointed out by [71Bre], the observed rapid drop in the moment above about 8 at.% Ru probably is due to the increasing content of the $\varepsilon$ phase in the alloys. As can be seen in Fig. 1, 2, and 3, the resulting model of Table 3 does provide an assessment that will represent the currently available data on this system.

associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: Fig. 4 presents the zero-phase fraction boundaries of the calculated paraequilibrium phase diagram for 3 at.% manganese and carbon concentrations up to 1 wt.%. Lines $(b)$ through $(d)$ are the corresponding boundaries in paraequilibrium, where line $(b)$ corresponds to the zero-phase fraction boundary of ferrite and lines $(c)$ and $(d)$ to zero-phase fractions of cementite and austenite, respectively. The applied compositional constraints reduce the degrees of freedom of the ternary system by one, and the $\gamma + \alpha +$ cementite three-phase field, introduced by manganese addition, degenerates to a straight line in the quasi-binary (Fe/Mn)-C system (line (d)). Generally, any higher order multi-component system with only $N$ independently variable (mobile) components (here, C) can be treated as a system with $N + 1$ compositional degrees of freedom if all compositionally constrained components are treated as a homogeneous lump compound (here, $\mathrm{Fe} + \mathrm{Mn}$). The equilibrium phase diagrams reveal much of the information necessary for a treatment of possible phase transformation reactions in the alloying system under consideration. Depending on the location of the start and end points of a reaction in the phase diagram, information on the reaction products and possible intermediate reaction paths can be derived. It must be emphasized, however, that a phase diagram can only represent the thermodynamic limits for phase transformations. Whether any such transformation reaction actually occurs depends on kinetic constraints such as the availability of potential nucleation sites or sufficient driving force for nucleation and for the maintenance of the phase boundary movement. As the temperature decreases below the paraequilibrium boundary (b), growth of $\alpha$ by rapid C-diffusion without partitioning of manganese becomes thermodynamically feasible.

The assessed Zr-Al phase diagram (Fig. 1) is based primarily on the work of [39Fin], [54Mcp], [60Eds], [62Eds], [62Pot], [83Sch], and [84Kem], and includes: (1) the liquid, L; (2) the bcc terminal solution, $(\beta \mathrm{Zr})$, in which Al has a maximum solubility of 26 at.% at $1350^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$; (3) the cph terminal solid solution, $(\alpha \mathrm{Zr})$, which shows a maximum solubility of 10.5 at.% Al at $940^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$; (4) the intermediate compound $\mathrm{Zr}_3\mathrm{Al}$ with the cubic $\mathrm{AuCu}_3$-type structure, stable up to the peritectic temperature of $988^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$; (5) the hexagonal $\mathrm{InNi}_2$-type intermediate compound $\mathrm{Zr}_2\mathrm{Al}$, stable up to the peritectic temperature of $1250^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$; (6) the tetragonal compound $\mathrm{Zr}_{5}\mathrm{Al}_{3}$, isostructural with $\mathrm{Si}_3\mathrm{W}_5$, stable in the temperature range from $\sim 1000$ to $1400^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ where it decomposes peritectically; (7) the tetragonal compound $\mathrm{Zr}_3\mathrm{Al}_2$ stable up to the peritectic temperature of $1480^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$; (8) the hexagonal compound $\mathrm{Zr}_4\mathrm{Al}_3$, stable up to the peritectoid temperature of $\sim 1030^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$; (9) the hexagonal $\mathrm{Ga}_4\mathrm{Ti}_5$-type intermediate compound $\mathrm{Zr}_{5}\mathrm{Al}_{4}$ stable from ${\sim}1000^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ to $1550^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ where it melts congruently; (10) the intermediate compound ZrAl with the orthorhombic BCr-type structure, stable up to the peritectoid temperature of $1275^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$; (11) the orthorhombic compound $\mathrm{Zr}_{2}\mathrm{Al}_{3}$, which decomposes peritectically at $1590^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$; (12) the hexagonal $\mathrm{MgZn_2}$-type intermediate compound $\mathrm{ZrAl}_2$, stable up to the congruent melting temperature of $1660^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$; (13) the tetragonal compound $\mathrm{ZrAl}_3$, which melts congruently at $1580^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$; (14) the fcc terminal solid solution, (Al), with a maximum solubility of 0.083 at.% $\mathrm{Zr}$ at its peritectic temperature of $660.8^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$.

Figure 1 differs from [Massalski1] mainly in some details of the intermediate phases in the range 35 to 45 at.% Al. The melting points of elemental Al and Zr are accepted from [Massalski1] as $660.452^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and $1855^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, respectively. The temperature $863^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ for the $\alpha \leftrightarrow \beta$ equilibrium in pure Zr was also adopted from [Massalski1].

The addition of Al stabilizes $(\alpha Zr)$ relative to $(\beta Zr)$. The solubility of Al in $(\alpha Zr)$ was studied by [54Mcp] (metallography) and [70Tiw] (lattice parameters). The results of [54Mcp] and [70Tiw] agree around $850^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. However, below this temperature, [70Tiw] found that Al is significantly more soluble in $(\alpha Zr)$ than indicated by [54Mcp]. The reasons for this discrepancy are not clear. Nevertheless, since we estimate that the contamination levels with interstitial impurities in the samples of [70Tiw] are lower than those of [54Mcp] samples, we accept the results of [70Tiw] in Fig. 1. [76Kub] made the same choice when assessing the $\mathbf{Zr}$-Al system. The $(\alpha Zr)/[(\alpha Zr) + \mathbf{Zr}_3\mathbf{Al}]$ boundary (see Fig. 1) can be described by the semi-empirical expression:

$$
\ln \left[ X _ {\mathrm {A l}} (1 - X _ {\mathrm {A l}}) ^ {3} \right] = 1. 8 8 8 8 - 5 4 2 8. 7 T ^ {- 1}
$$

where $T$ is in kelvin and $X_{\mathrm{Al}}$ indicates mole fraction. The values we adopt for the temperature of the peritectoid reaction $(\beta Zr) + Zr_3\mathrm{Al} \leftrightarrow (\alpha Zr)$, $940 \pm 10\mathrm{K}$, and the composition of $(\alpha Zr)$ at this reaction, $10.5 \pm 0.5$ at.% Al, agree with [54Mcp].

No experimental information exists concerning the shape of the two-phase $(\alpha + \beta)$ field except for some results presented by [54Mcp]. However, these results are particularly affected by contamination as demonstrated by the width of the $\alpha \leftrightarrow \beta$ transition $(\sim 20^{\circ}\mathrm{C})$ observed by [54Mcp] even in the case of their pure $\mathbf{Zr}$ metal. The tentative $(\alpha + \beta)$ boundaries indicated in Fig. 1 were drawn primarily to be consistent with the assessed temperature and $(\alpha Zr)$ composition at the peritectoid reaction $(\beta Zr) + Zr_{3}Al \leftrightarrow (\alpha Zr)$ as well as with the van't Hoff relation with the value $3888\mathrm{J / mol}$ for the latent heat of the $\alpha \leftrightarrow \beta$ transformation in pure $\mathbf{Zr}$ [76Alc]. Hence, the composition obtained for $(\beta Zr)$ at the peritectoid reaction is 8.1 at.% Al.

The $(\beta \mathrm{Zr}) / [(\beta \mathrm{Zr}) + \mathrm{Zr}_3\mathrm{Al}]$, $(\beta \mathrm{Zr}) / [(\beta \mathrm{Zr}) + \mathrm{Zr}_2\mathrm{Al}]$ and $(\beta \mathrm{Zr}) / [(\beta \mathrm{Zr}) + \mathrm{Zr}_5\mathrm{Al}_3]$ boundaries were investigated by [54Mcp] (metallography). The assessed $(\beta \mathrm{Zr}) / [(\beta \mathrm{Zr}) + \mathrm{Zr}_2\mathrm{Al}]$ boundary given in Fig. 1 can be described by the semi-empirical expression:

$$
\ln \left[ X _ {\mathrm {A l}} \left(1 - X _ {\mathrm {A l}}\right) ^ {2} \right] = - 0. 3 4 3 3 - 2 5 2 6 T ^ {- 1}
$$

where $T$ is in kelvin and $X_{\mathrm{Al}}$ is again the mole fraction. The solubility of Al in $(\beta Zr)$ at the eutectic reaction $\mathbf{L} \leftrightarrow (\beta Zr) + Zr_5\mathrm{Al}_3$ was estimated by [54Mcp] to be approximately 26 at.%

Because experimental results are not available, the shape of the $(\beta Zr) + L$ two-phase region shown in Fig. 1 is merely tentative; however, it satisfies the van't Hoff relation when the value 18814 J/mol is used for the latent heat of melting of pure Zr [76Alc].

The existence of this phase was reported by [54Mcp] (metallography) who also estimated the temperature of the peritectoid reaction $(\beta \mathrm{Zr}) + \mathrm{Zr}_{5}\mathrm{Al}_{3} \leftrightarrow \mathrm{Zr}_{2}\mathrm{Al}$ to be within the limits 1200 to $1300^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$; the value adopted in Fig. 1 is $1250 \pm 40^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. For the composition of $(\beta \mathrm{Zr})$ at this reaction we take the value 22.5 at.% Al from the expression given above for the $(\beta \mathrm{Zr}) /[(\beta \mathrm{Zr}) + \mathrm{Zr}_{2}\mathrm{Al}]$ boundary.

A discrepancy existed regarding the crystal structure of $\mathrm{Zr}_{5}\mathrm{Al}_{3}$. [59Wil2] suggested a hexagonal $\mathrm{Mn}_{5}\mathrm{Si}_{3}$-type structure for this compound. However, [60Eds] and [62Pot] agreed that the crystal structure of $\mathrm{Zr}_{5}\mathrm{Al}_{3}$ is of the tetragonal $\mathrm{Si}_{3}\mathrm{W}_{5}$-type and, moreover, [60Eds] proved that the contamination with interstitial impurities stabilizes the $\mathrm{Mn}_{5}\mathrm{Si}_{3}$-type structure. More recently, [83Sch] (X-rays) confirmed the tetragonal structure for the $\mathrm{Zr}_{5}\mathrm{Al}_{3}$ phase at temperatures $>800^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ but proposed the hexagonal structure for lower temperatures. Hence, according to Fig. 1, the hexagonal $\mathrm{Mn}_{5}\mathrm{Si}_{3}$-type structure would be a low-temperature, metastable form of pure $\mathrm{Zr}_{5}\mathrm{Al}_{3}$. [83Sch] also mentioned that this hexagonal form of $\mathrm{Zr}_{5}\mathrm{Al}_{3}$ seems to be strongly stabilized by interstitial impurities. Contrary to these conclusions, [88Kim] (X-rays) reported the hexagonal structure in the range 800 to $1100^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and suggested that this is the true stable structure of $\mathrm{Zr}_{5}\mathrm{Al}_{3}$; however, their results might have been affected by the superficial contamination of their samples.

The existence of this intermediate compound was established by [54Mcp] by means of the metallographic analysis of as-cast samples. These authors used thermal analysis to determine that $\mathrm{Zr}_3\mathrm{Al}_2$ forms peritectically at $1480 \pm 10^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. [54Mcp] evaluated the composition of L at this peritectic reaction to be $\sim 39$ at.% Al. These values are those shown in Fig. 1. The crystal structure of the $\mathrm{Zr}_3\mathrm{Al}_2$ compound was reported to be tetragonal by [60Wil1] and [62Pot].

[54Mcp] (metallography, thermal analysis) proposed the existence of an intermediate compound whose composition is close to $\mathrm{Zr_4Al_3}$ and which melts congruently at $1530\pm 10^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. This composition was later investigated by [62Pot] (X-rays, metallography) who concluded from crystal structure determinations that the correct composition for this compound is $\mathrm{Zr}_{5}\mathrm{Al}_{4}$ with a hexagonal crystal structure isotypic to that of $\mathrm{Ga}_4\mathrm{Ti}_5$. However, [60Wil2] confirmed the existence at low temperatures of a stable hexagonal structure with the composition $\mathrm{Zr_4Al_3}$. This last intermediate phase was also observed by [62Pot] who investigated the structural changes of alloys close to the composition $\mathrm{Zr}_{5}\mathrm{Al}_{4}$ upon annealing around $1000^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. The later authors then tentatively rationalized the available experimental information by suggesting the existence of (1) a peritectoid reaction $\mathrm{Zr_3Al_2 + Zr_5Al_4\leftrightarrow Zr_4Al_3}$ at $\sim 1030^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, and (2) a $\mathrm{Zr_5Al_4\leftrightarrow Zr_4Al_3 + ZrAl}$ eutectoid reaction at $\sim 1000^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ (see Fig. 1).

The assessed temperature of $1550^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ for the congruent melting of $\mathrm{Zr}_{5}\mathrm{Al}_{4}$ shown in Fig. 1 is consistent with the upper thermal arrests found by [54Mcp] for alloys of composition 42.7 and 49.1 at.% Al.

[54Mcp] (metallography, thermal analysis) indicated the existence of a eutectic reaction $\mathrm{L} \leftrightarrow \mathrm{Zr}_{5} \mathrm{Al}_{4} + \mathrm{Zr}_{2} \mathrm{Al}_{3}$ which occurs at 1485 $\pm 10^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ with a L composition of $\sim 49$ at.$\%$ Al ($\mathrm{Zr}_{5} \mathrm{Al}_{4}$ is designated as $\mathrm{Zr}_{4} \mathrm{Al}_{3}$ in [54Mcp]). However, [54Mcp] reported one and two thermal arrests for alloys containing 51 and 49 at.$\%$ Al, respectively. Therefore, in Fig. 1 we adopt the value 51 at.$\%$ Al for this eutectic composition; the same choice was made by [62Pot].

[54Mcp] (metallography, thermal analysis) examined alloys of composition close to 50 at.% concluding that a compound ZrAl forms at $1250 \pm 50^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ through the peritectoid reaction $\mathrm{Zr}_{5}\mathrm{Al}_{4} + \mathrm{Zr}_{2}\mathrm{Al}_{3} \leftrightarrow \mathrm{ZrAl}$. Later work by [62Pot] (metallography, X-rays), [83Sch] (X-rays), [84Kem] (X-rays), and [85Kem] (X-rays) confirmed the peritectoid formation of ZrAl. Because the results of [83Sch] suggested that $\mathbf{ZrAl}$ should remain stable up to $1300^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, in Fig. 1 we adopt for the peritectoid temperature the value $1275\pm 25^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ as a compromise between the works of [54Mcp] and [83Sch]. The crystal structure of $\mathbf{ZrAl}$ was determined by [62Spo] to be of the orthorhombic BCr-type.

The existence of this compound was reported by [54Mcp] (metallography, thermal analysis). These authors also reported the existence of the peritectic reaction $\mathrm{L} + \mathrm{ZrAl}_2 \leftrightarrow \mathrm{Zr}_2\mathrm{Al}_3$ which occurs in the temperature range 1585 to $1605^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ with a L composition of $\sim 59$ at.$\%$ Al. The peritectic temperature shown in Fig. 1 is $1590^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. [61Ren] and [62Pot] established that the structure of $\mathrm{Zr}_2\mathrm{Al}_3$ is orthorhombic. [83Sch], [84Kem], and [85Kem] confirmed this result as well as the high temperature stability of $\mathrm{Zr}_2\mathrm{Al}_3$.

This intermediate compound was reported by [54Mcp] (metallography, thermal analysis) to melt congruently at $1645 \pm 10^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. However, this temperature strictly corresponds to the thermal arrest shown by a 68.8 at.% Al sample. Therefore, we slightly modify the assessed melting temperature of $\mathrm{ZrAl_2}$ and take in Fig. 1 the value $1660^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$.

[54Mcp] determined the existence of a eutectic reaction $\mathrm{L} \leftrightarrow \mathrm{ZrAl}_2 + \mathrm{ZrAl}_3$ which occurs in the temperature range 1480 to $1500^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ with a L composition of $\sim 73.5$ at.% Al. However, these values impose a steep slope on the $\mathrm{L} /(\mathrm{L} + \mathrm{ZrAl}_3)$ boundary at the eutectic temperature, which implies special characteristics for the thermodynamic properties of the L phase. In turn, this steep slope also constrains the slope of $\mathrm{L} /(\mathrm{L} + \mathrm{ZrAl}_2)$ to be steep at the eutectic temperature. In order to minimize this feature of the Zr-Al phase diagram, and be compatible with the presently available experimental information [54Mcp], we tentatively place in Fig. 1 the temperature of the $\mathrm{L} \leftrightarrow \mathrm{ZrAl}_2 + \mathrm{ZrAl}_3$ eutectic reaction at $1500^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and take for the L composition the more symmetrical value of 72 at.% Al. This last composition value is consistent with the single thermal arrest observed by [54Mcp] in a sample containing 71.3 at.% Al. Further experimental investigation of this feature of the Zr-Al phase diagram is necessary.

Consistent with the observations of [54Mcp] (metallography) and [76Sch] (metallography, microhardness), the temperature of the peritectoid reaction $(\beta Zr) + Zr_{2}Al \leftrightarrow Zr_{3}Al$ is assessed to be 988 $\pm 12^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. For the composition of $(\beta Zr)$ at this reaction, we adopt the value 12.5 at.% Al from the numerical expression given above for the $(\beta Zr) / [(Zr + Zr_{2}Al]$ boundary.

The existence of the eutectic reaction $\mathrm{L} \leftrightarrow (\beta \mathrm{Zr}) + \mathrm{Zr}_{5} \mathrm{Al}_{3}$ was established by [54Mcp] who, from thermal analysis and incipient melting, determined its temperature to be $1350 \pm 10^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. From metallographic examination of as-cast alloys, the same authors proposed that the composition of the L phase at this eutectic reaction should be $\sim 29.5$ at.% Al. However, from the eutectic microstructure and the single thermal arrest reported by [54Mcp] for alloys with compositions 30.7 and 31.4 at.% Al, respectively, we adopt the value 31 at.% Al for this eutectic composition.

For the composition of the L phase at the $\mathrm{L} + \mathrm{Zr}_3\mathrm{Al}_2 \leftrightarrow \mathrm{Zr}_5\mathrm{Al}_3$ peritectic reaction, [54Mcp] suggested the approximate value 37 at.$\%$ Al. However, this value implies a large difference between the $\mathrm{Zr}_3\mathrm{Al}_2$ and $\mathrm{Zr}_5\mathrm{Al}_3$ liquidus slopes, a feature which is thermodynamically implausible. To attend this point, and compatible with the experimental observations made by [54Mcp], we finally select $1400^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ for this peritectic temperature and tentatively adopt 35 at.$\%$ Al for the corresponding composition of the L phase.

associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: [1992Ali3] also gave an isothermal section of the Cu-Ni-Ti system at $600^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ (Fig. 7). No experimental details for arriving at the $600^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ isothermal section are available from their report. Figure 7 indicates that the $\Delta$ phase is in equilibrium with all the phases existing in the Cu-Ti and Ni-Ti systems up to 50 at.% Cu or Ni. The $\beta$ phase was shown to extend from the Ni-Ti binary up to $\sim 20$ at.% Cu. The $\Phi ((\mathrm{Cu},\mathrm{Ni})_3\mathrm{Ti}_2)$, $\Psi (\mathrm{Cu}_{25}\mathrm{Ni}_{50}\mathrm{Ti}_{25})$, and $\Gamma (\mathrm{Cu}_{10}\mathrm{Ni}_{65}\mathrm{Ti}_{25})$, the ternary phases found at 870 and/or $800^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ by other investigators, does not appear to exist at $600^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and the $\Delta$ phase is rather restricted at $600^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. The phase equilibria at $600^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, given in Fig. 7, however, are not consistent with the binary data. For example, Cu-Ti binary shows the $\mathrm{Cu}_{2}\mathrm{Ti}$ phase only at higher temperatures (above $870^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$). Thus at $600^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, the $\Delta$ phase cannot be in equilibrium with the $\mathrm{Cu}_{2}\mathrm{Ti}$ phase. Moreover, because $\mathrm{Cu - Ni}$ is an isomorphous system, only a single solid solution phase fcc $\gamma$ exists. Only at $T < 350^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ is the $\gamma$ phase suggested to undergo a spinodal decomposition. Hence, at $600^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ it is not possible to have three two-phase regions $\Delta + \gamma (\mathrm{Cu},\mathrm{Ni})$ and $\Delta + \gamma (\mathrm{Ni},\mathrm{Cu})$, and $\Delta + \gamma$.

associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: Fig. 3 presents the zero-phase fraction boundaries of the calculated orthoequilibrium phase diagram for 3 at.% manganese and carbon concentrations up to 1 wt.%. Line $(a)$ corresponds to the zero-phase fraction boundary of ferrite and lines $(e)$ and $(f)$ to zero-phase fractions of cementite and austenite, respectively, in orthoequilibrium. The equilibrium phase diagrams reveal much of the information necessary for a treatment of possible phase transformation reactions in the alloying system under consideration. Depending on the location of the start and end points of a reaction in the phase diagram, information on the reaction products and possible intermediate reaction paths can be derived. It must be emphasized, however, that a phase diagram can only represent the thermodynamic limits for phase transformations. Whether any such transformation reaction actually occurs depends on kinetic constraints such as the availability of potential nucleation sites or sufficient driving force for nucleation and for the maintenance of the phase boundary movement. Equilibrium phase diagrams consist of multiple zero-phase fraction boundaries. These boundaries have been evaluated for the binary Fe-C and the ternary Fe-C-Mn systems with $u_{\mathrm{Mn}} = 0.03$ under both unconstrained and constrained equilibrium conditions. The $u$-fraction variable denotes the fraction of an element with respect to the substitutional elements only. Addition of manganese shifts the $\gamma/\gamma + \alpha$ phase boundary to lower temperatures and decreases the size of the $\alpha$ single-phase field. The eutectoid reaction $\gamma \Leftrightarrow \alpha +$ cementite in binary Fe-C is represented by the straight line $(h)$. Addition of manganese adds one degree of freedom to the system and allows for the existence of a three-phase field $\gamma + \alpha +$ cementite (between lines $(e)$ and $(f)$).

associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: An enlarged region from 15 to 45 at.% Te is shown in Fig. 2. The equilibrium phases of the Pd-Te system include: (3) Pd$_{17}$Te$_4$ (tentative); (4) high-temperature, bcc Pd$_3$Te; (5) rhombohedral Pd$_{20}$Te$_7$; (6) orthorhombic Pd$_8$Te$_3$; (7) monoclinic Pd$_7$Te$_3$; (8) monoclinic Pd$_9$Te$_4$; (9) orthorhombic Pd$_3$Te$_2$. Although the crystal structure of Pd$_{17}$Te$_4$ could not be determined, its XRD pattern was definitely different from that reported for "Pd4Te," and the existence of single-phase "Pd4Te" could not be confirmed. Because the Pd$_{17}$Te$_4$ (19.0 at.% Te) stoichiometry satisfies most of the above observations, it is accepted tentatively. However, further studies, especially crystallographic studies, are needed for confirmation. The reaction type and temperature of formation of this phase also were reported variously: the peritectoid formation temperature of "β" is 770°C according to one work, and the peritectic melting point of Pd$_{17}$Te$_4$ is 760°C according to another. The phase relationship proposed with the peritectoid formation at 770°C is accepted. The peritectic melting point of "Pd$_4$Te" was given as about 1000°C, which is probably the liquidus temperature of "Pd$_4$Te". The peritectoid formation temperature of "Pd$_4$Te" was reported as 723°C, which is probably the eutectoid decomposition temperature of Pd$_3$Te. Disordered W-type, high-temperature Pd$_3$Te was reported. The temperature range of existence of Pd$_3$Te is 785 to 727°C, and its composition is about 24.3 at.% Te. In more cursory works, Pd$_3$Te was recognized as the high-temperature modification of Pd$_{20}$Te$_7$. The transition temperature between Pd$_3$Te and Pd$_{20}$Te$_7$ was found between 700 and 750°C or at 745°C, which is understandable in view of the assessed diagram, which includes several transitions in this temperature range. The melting point was found at 777 ± 13°C, in agreement with the assessed peritectic temperature. A thermal effect at 885°C assigned as the melting point of Pd$_{20}$Te$_7$ is shown as the liquidus temperature. The congruent melting point of Pd$_8$Te$_3$ is 905 ± 5°C (905, 910, and 900°C). The eutectoid decomposition temperature is 563 or 562°C. Based on thermal effect data, it was considered that Pd$_8$Te$_3$ undergoes polymorphic transformations at 680 and 270°C. These temperatures probably correspond to phase boundaries of Pd$_8$Te$_5$ and Pd$_{20}$Te$_7$. The stoichiometry of Pd$_7$Te$_3$ is accepted tentatively from the observation of the monoclinic structure of this phase below 470°C. Evidence of two high-temperature polymorphs of Pd$_7$Te$_3$, with another transformation temperature at 595°C, however, was probably misinterpreted from Pd$_9$Te$_4$. The homogeneity range of Pd$_7$Te$_3$ is from 29 to 30 at.% Te. "Pd$_{2.5}$Te" (28.6 at.% Te) was observed below 495°C and existing up to 30 at.% Te. Likewise, "δ" was observed below 500°C and between about 27.5 and 30 at.% Te. The same stoichiometry of "Pd$_5$Te$_2$" found earlier may have been something else, because it was reportedly stable up to 760°C. The peritectic melting point of "high-temperature" Pd$_7$Te$_3$ observed at 830°C is likely to be a liquidus temperature. Pd$_9$Te$_4$ was found, and its peritectic melting point was reported to be 610 or 605°C. The "Pd$_2$Te" reported as melting at 590°C was most likely Pd$_9$Te$_4$. The eutectoid decomposition temperature is shown at 472°C, averaging 474 and 468 ± 3°C. A claimed polymorphic transformation at 460°C must have been the eutectoid decomposition.

associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: The purpose of the present work was to study the Cu2O - CuO part of the Cu - O phase diagram along the liquidus line. Available data for coordinates of the liquid in the eutectic equilibrium, L ⇌ Cu2O + CuO, are in significant disagreement. Therefore, measurements were carried out in the interval of oxygen pressures from 1 × 10^-3 up to 11 MPa. This interval covers regions on both sides of the eutectic point. The results of measurements of the liquidus line in coordinates x and T are given in the figure. As is shown in the figure, the congruent melting point of CuO was calculated in several theoretical studies, and the results of these predictions are in disagreement. Our experimental data have proved that the listed estimations failed in the case of the melts with a high oxygen content. For this reason, we have considered it useful to estimate the CuO congruent melting point position with the help of the present experimental results. The calculations were based on minimization of the sum-of-squares discrepancies between model and experimental coordinates of the liquidus line. The best results were obtained with the fourth degree polynomial: Q0 = 15,968.748, Q1 = -85,332.883, Q2 = 199,727.695, Q3 = -213,775.658, and Q4 = 91,630.561, if the Gibbs melting energy of CuO is expressed by the following equation: G_CuO^liq - G_CuO^sol = 54,705.827 - 32.475T - 0.176T ln T. The gaseous equation of state recommended in the monograph of [1981Syt] was used for calculation of oxygen pressure from the oxygen standard Gibbs energy. The above model parameters led to the following characteristics of CuO congruent melting: Tm = 1620 K at P_O2 ≈ 1000 MPa. However, it is necessary to note that the equation of state of gaseous oxygen was not experimentally checked at T > 1200 K, and thus, the value of 1000 MPa is only an estimation. In contrast to previous studies, the present approximation for the liquidus line takes into account experimental results for oxygen pressures higher than 0.1 MPa. The present data confirm the reliability of the results of [1921Rob] and improve on them. Results indicated that congruent melting of CuO is not expected below 1600 K and oxygen pressures below 10 MPa. However, one must recognize that results of modeling are very questionable for the oxygen-rich portion of the diagram (the scatter of calculated values on the right side of the figure speaks for itself). The problem of an adequate model choice for the system under consideration still remains to be solved.

associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: The assessed K-Se phase diagram is presented in Fig. 1. Special points of the assessed phase diagram are listed in Table 1. Data defining the phase diagram are available in three studies. Data points reproduced in Fig. 1 were read off diagrams in the three articles. The data are limited to the range 37 to 100 at.% Se. The general features of the phase diagram from zero to 55 at.% Se are uncertain because of poor data or absence of any information. Analogously to other alkali-S and alkali-Se systems, the K-side eutectic is presumed to coincide practically with the melting point of pure K, with a steep liquidus at low Se contents. The melting point of K2Se presumably congruent, has not been reported. As in the analogous systems with S, it is presumed to lie between those of Na2Se and Rb2Se. An approximate melting point may thus be estimated at 900 ± 200°C. The thermal analysis data for compositions between K2Se and K2Se2 are very scattered. It is not clear whether K2Se2 melts congruently or incongruity. X-ray diffractograms of six alloys between K2Se and K2Se2 were interpreted to suggest that K2Se may take up Se into solid solution, with a stoichiometry range possibly extending as far as 37.5 at.% Se (Fig. 1). In the assessed phase diagram, Fig. 1, a melting point of 460°C was tentatively assigned to K2Se2. The monotectic temperature was found to lie 0.5°C below the melting point of Se. The critical temperature was determined quite accurately as 310°C. The composition limits of the two-liquid region at the monotectic, determined by quenching of liquid samples followed by analysis by atomic absorption, were 87.5 and 99.0 at.% Se. The K-rich limit was independently verified as 87.7 at.% Se from monotectic heat measurements. However, on the assumption of a monotectic temperature 0.5°C below the melting point of Se and zero solubility of K in solid Se, the Se-rich monotectic liquid composition, calculated thermodynamically from the enthalpy of fusion of Se, is above 99.8 at.% Se. For the monotectic composition to be at 99.0 at.% Se, a monotectic temperature 3°C below the melting point of Se is required if it is assumed that solid solubility is negligible. Alternatively, if the monotectic is 0.5°C below the melting point, then solid solubility of nearly 1.0 at.% K in Se at the monotectic temperature is required. Given the nonmetallic nature of Se, such a large solid solubility of K seems unlikely. Because the measurements of the monotectic temperature are more precise than the measurements of the liquid composition, a monotectic liquid composition of 99.8 at.% Se is tentatively shown in the assessed phase diagram.

In the assessed Pd-Si phase diagram, the phase boundaries and the reaction temperatures are based on experimental work and on the thermodynamic calculations described in the present evaluation. Boundaries selected from the modeling calculations are depicted in the assessed diagram as dashed lines. The equilibrium solid phases present in the Pd-Si system are: (1) the terminal solid solutions, (Pd) and (Si); (2) the equiatomic phase PdSi, which melts congruently at $972^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and is an equilibrium phase between 972 and $824^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$; (3) the phase $\mathrm{Pd}_2\mathrm{Si}$, which melts congruently at $1331^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and has a composition range of 33.0 to 34.2 at.% Si at room temperature; (4) the phase $\mathrm{Pd}_2\mathrm{Si}'$, which is a low-temperature polymorph of $\mathrm{Pd}_2\mathrm{Si}$ ($T < 1090^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$); (5) the peritectically forming phase $\mathrm{Pd}_3\mathrm{Si}$; (6) the peritectically forming phase $\mathrm{Pd}_9\mathrm{Si}_2$; and (7) the phase $\mathrm{Pd}_5\mathrm{Si}$, which melts congruently at $818^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. Special points of the assessed diagram are listed in Table 1.

$\mathbf{Pd}_2\mathbf{Si} / \mathbf{L}$ Boundary. The $\mathrm{Pd}_2\mathrm{Si} / \mathrm{L}$ boundary data are shown in the figure. It was found that $\mathrm{Pd}_3\mathrm{Si}$ is a peritectically forming phase, and it was proposed that the $\mathrm{Pd}_2\mathrm{Si} / \mathrm{L}$ boundary extends to $\sim 23$ at.% Si at $1045^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. Other data indicate that the $\mathrm{Pd}_2\mathrm{Si} / \mathrm{L}$ boundary extends to $\sim 26$ at.% Si at $1050^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and that $\mathrm{Pd}_3\mathrm{Si}$ melts congruently. The generally lower liquidus temperatures reported are probably the result of their higher cooling rates, and hence most likely represent a slight undercooling of the liquid. There is a substantial difference between the congruent melting temperature of $\mathrm{Pd}_2\mathrm{Si}$ reported as 1331 °C and as 1394 °C. The values reported by earlier workers show similar discrepancies.

The $\mathrm{Pd}_2\mathrm{Si} / \mathrm{L}$ boundary for alloys with Si content greater than 33 at.% was determined from liquidus data shown in the figure, which extend to 51 at.% Si at $901^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, and the phase $\mathrm{PdSi}$ is formed from a peritectic reaction, $\mathrm{L} + \mathrm{Pd}_2\mathrm{Si} \leftrightarrow \mathrm{PdSi}$. The variation of Gibbs energy of $\mathrm{Pd}_2\mathrm{Si}$ with respect to temperature can be calculated using the Pd-rich and Si-rich $\mathrm{Pd}_2\mathrm{Si} / \mathrm{L}$ boundaries. The variation of the Gibbs energy with temperature and thus the liquidus data appear to be inaccurate for the following reasons: - At about $1050^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, the values of the Gibbs energy of $\mathrm{Pd_2Si}$ calculated from the Pd-rich and the Si-rich boundaries differ by $\sim 900\mathrm{J}$, and the difference becomes larger if the variation of the Gibbs energy with temperature is extrapolated to lower temperatures. Because $\mathrm{Pd}_2\mathrm{Si}$ is a nearly stoichiometric phase with only a small homogeneity range (33.0 to 34.2 at.% Si), the values of the Gibbs energy calculated from the Pd-rich and the Si-rich boundaries should be nearly equal at a given temperature; this is not the situation when the reported liquidus data are used.

PdSi/L Boundary. Significant discrepancies exist in the liquidus data reported by different investigators for alloy compositions near 50 at.% Si. PdSi was found by some to melt congruently at 990 °C, while others established the congruent melting temperature at $\sim 1090^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. Results showing that PdSi forms via a peritectic reaction are not accepted in the present evaluation for the reasons discussed above. Recently, the PdSi/L phase boundary was reexamined; thermal analysis data indicate that PdSi melts congruently at $905 \pm 2^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. PdSi is shown to be a congruently melting phase in the assessed phase diagram. The congruent melting temperature is $972^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. This value was estimated using the Gibbs energy of PdSi calculated from the eutectic reaction at $875^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ ($L \leftrightarrow \mathrm{Pd}_{2}\mathrm{Si}^{\prime} + \mathrm{PdSi}$) and at $892^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ [L $\leftrightarrow \mathrm{PdSi} + (\mathrm{Si})$]. The reaction temperature and liquid phase composition ($\sim 52$ at.% Si) for the second reaction are taken from prior work. Selected phase boundary data points are listed in Table 2.

- To have the Si-rich $\mathrm{Pd_2Si / L}$ boundary extend to 51 at.$\%$ Si at $901^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, the Gibbs energy of $\mathrm{Pd}_2\mathrm{Si}$ would have to decrease rapidly with decreasing temperatures. As a consequence, when this variation of Gibbs energy is extrapolated to temperatures below $901^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, it yields values of the Gibbs energy of $\mathbf{Pd}_2\mathbf{Si}$ that are too low to maintain the phase equilibria in the composition range 0 to 33 at.% Si. Hence, the Si-rich $\mathbf{Pd}_2\mathbf{Si} / \mathbf{L}$ phase boundary is incompatible with the phase boundaries and equilibria in the composition range 0 to 33 at.% Si.

The solubility of Al in $(\alpha Zr)$ was studied by [54Mcp] (metallography) and [70Tiw] (lattice parameters). The results of these authors are plotted in Fig. 2. The results of [54Mcp] and [70Tiw] agree around $850^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. However, below this temperature, [70Tiw] found that Al is significantly more soluble in $(\alpha Zr)$ than indicated by [54Mcp] (see Fig. 2). The reasons for this discrepancy are not clear. Nevertheless, since we estimate that the contamination levels with interstitial impurities in the samples of [70Tiw] are lower than those of [54Mcp] samples, we accept the results of [70Tiw]. The $(\alpha Zr)/[(\alpha Zr) + \mathbf{Zr}_3\mathbf{Al}]$ boundary can be described by the semi-empirical expression:

$$
\ln \left[ X _ {\mathrm {A l}} (1 - X _ {\mathrm {A l}}) ^ {3} \right] = 1. 8 8 8 8 - 5 4 2 8. 7 T ^ {- 1}
$$

where $T$ is in kelvin and $X_{\mathrm{Al}}$ indicates mole fraction. The values we adopt for the temperature of the peritectoid reaction $(\beta Zr) + Zr_3\mathrm{Al} \leftrightarrow (\alpha Zr)$, $940 \pm 10\mathrm{K}$, and the composition of $(\alpha Zr)$ at this reaction, $10.5 \pm 0.5$ at.% Al, agree with [54Mcp].
No experimental information exists concerning the shape of the two-phase $(\alpha + \beta)$ field except for some results presented by [54Mcp]. However, these results are particularly affected by contamination as demonstrated by the width of the $\alpha \leftrightarrow \beta$ transition $(\sim 20^{\circ}\mathrm{C})$ observed by [54Mcp] even in the case of their pure $\mathbf{Zr}$ metal. The experimental data of [54Mcp] are plotted in Fig. 2 as superimposed on the tentative $(\alpha + \beta)$ boundaries indicated in Fig. 1. These boundaries were drawn primarily to be consistent with the assessed temperature and $(\alpha Zr)$ composition at the peritectoid reaction $(\beta Zr) + Zr_{3}Al \leftrightarrow (\alpha Zr)$ as well as with the van't Hoff relation with the value $3888\mathrm{J / mol}$ for the latent heat of the $\alpha \leftrightarrow \beta$ transformation in pure $\mathbf{Zr}$ [76Alc]. Hence, the composition obtained for $(\beta Zr)$ at the peritectoid reaction is 8.1 at.% Al.
The $(\beta \mathrm{Zr}) / [(\beta \mathrm{Zr}) + \mathrm{Zr}_3\mathrm{Al}]$, $(\beta \mathrm{Zr}) / [(\beta \mathrm{Zr}) + \mathrm{Zr}_2\mathrm{Al}]$ and $(\beta \mathrm{Zr}) / [(\beta \mathrm{Zr}) + \mathrm{Zr}_5\mathrm{Al}_3]$ boundaries were investigated by [54Mcp] (metallography). Results from these authors are plotted in Fig. 2 as superimposed on the boundaries given in Fig. 1. The assessed $(\beta \mathrm{Zr}) / [(\beta \mathrm{Zr}) + \mathrm{Zr}_2\mathrm{Al}]$ boundary can be described by the semi-empirical expression:

$$
\ln \left[ X _ {\mathrm {A l}} \left(1 - X _ {\mathrm {A l}}\right) ^ {2} \right] = - 0. 3 4 3 3 - 2 5 2 6 T ^ {- 1}
$$

where $T$ is in kelvin and $X_{\mathrm{Al}}$ is again the mole fraction. The solubility of Al in $(\beta Zr)$ at the eutectic reaction $\mathbf{L} \leftrightarrow (\beta Zr) + Zr_5\mathrm{Al}_3$ was estimated by [54Mcp] to be approximately 26 at.% The $(\beta Zr) / [(BZr) + Zr_2Al]$ and $(\beta Zr) / [(BZr) + Zr_5Al_3]$ boundaries were also investigated by [75Sch] (metallography) using commercial Zr-Al alloys, and their results are inconsistent with those of [54Mcp].
Consistent with the observations of [54Mcp] (metallography) and [76Sch] (metallography, microhardness), the temperature of the peritectoid reaction $(\beta Zr) + Zr_{2}Al \leftrightarrow Zr_{3}Al$ is assessed to be 988 $\pm 12^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ (see Fig. 2). For the composition of $(\beta Zr)$ at this reaction, we adopt the value 12.5 at.% Al from the numerical expression given above for the $(\beta Zr) / [(Zr + Zr_{2}Al]$ boundary.
The existence of this phase was reported by [54Mcp] (metallography) who also estimated the temperature of the peritectoid reaction $(\beta \mathrm{Zr}) + \mathrm{Zr}_{5}\mathrm{Al}_{3} \leftrightarrow \mathrm{Zr}_{2}\mathrm{Al}$ to be within the limits 1200 to $1300^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ (see Fig. 2); the value adopted in Fig. 1 is $1250 \pm 40^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. For the composition of $(\beta \mathrm{Zr})$ at this reaction we take the value 22.5 at.% Al from the expression given above for the $(\beta \mathrm{Zr}) /[(\beta \mathrm{Zr}) + \mathrm{Zr}_{2}\mathrm{Al}]$ boundary.

associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: The Al-Mo system is of a complex type, and a variety of phases are reported as being stable. The diagram presented here (Fig. 1, Table 1) differs in a number of aspects from [80Bre] and is based on a review of original data and thermodynamic calculations. A review of the literature shows that the peritectic at $700^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ is associated with the formation of $\mathrm{Al}_{12}\mathrm{Mo}$ and the peritectic at $735^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ with $\mathrm{Al}_5\mathrm{Mo}$. It is noted that there is no evidence from other sources to corroborate the existence of the $\mathrm{Al}_6\mathrm{Mo}$ phase, and there is experimental evidence that $\mathrm{Al}_{12}\mathrm{Mo}$ forms by peritectic reaction from $\mathrm{Al}_5\mathrm{Mo}$. In addition, the equilibrium stability of $\mathrm{Al}_6\mathrm{Mo}$ has been questioned in recent work on an 11 at.% Mo alloy, who observed only $\mathrm{Al}_{12}\mathrm{Mo}$ and a new rhombohedral phase that is structurally related to $\mathrm{Al}_5\mathrm{Mo}$. In the diagram accepted here (Fig. 1), $\mathrm{Al}_6\mathrm{Mo}$ and the hypothetical reaction at $800^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ have been removed. $\mathrm{Al}_{17}\mathrm{Mo}_4$ and $\mathrm{Al}_{22}\mathrm{Mo}_5$ coexisted with at least three other phases; they therefore cannot by unambiguously identified as equilibrium phases and have not been included in the present diagram (Fig. 1). Based on the composition of the Al-rich liquidus, which is well established up to $1000^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, and the solid solubility measurements of Mo in Al, the most Al-rich reaction is a peritectic between the Al solid solution and $\mathrm{Al}_{12}\mathrm{Mo}$.
