The maximum solubility of O at 400 $^\circ \mathrm{C}$ shown in Fig. 1 is that given by [61Hol], 28.6 at.% This value is compatible with the experimental observations of [54Dom], [71Dub1], and [71Dub2], which indicate that at low temperatures, the solubility limit of O in $(\alpha \mathbf{Zr})$ should be placed somewhere between 28.4 and 30 at.%. The O distribution in the sublattice of the octahedral holes can be: (1) disordered, in the case of high temperatures and/or low O content, for which we keep the designation $(\alpha \mathrm{Zr})$; (2) partially ordered, in the case of intermediate temperatures and high O content, denoted by $(\alpha^{\prime}\mathrm{Zr})$ after [74Hir1]; and (3) highly ordered, which corresponds to a series of low-temperature, composition-dependent stacking variants of O atom layers normal to the $c$ axis of the cph structure, denoted generically $(\alpha^{\prime \prime}\mathrm{Zr})$ after [74Hir1] and [76Ara]. [76Ara] pointed out that with increasing O content, it is not clear whether the changes between the various low-temperature stacking variants occur continuously or discontinuously. It seems reasonable to speculate that the O arrangement within the sublattice of octahedral holes should resolve at low enough temperatures into a series of completely ordered compounds. Therefore, in the present evaluation, we accept the discontinuous alternative for $(\alpha^{\prime \prime}\mathrm{Zr})$, in the specific (nevertheless, arbitrary) way suggested by [76Ara] and reproduced here in Fig. 3. We would like to stress that this part of the Zr-O phase diagram in Fig. 1 is not only provisional, but also quite speculative. [74Hir2] (high-temperature neutron diffraction, see also [72Hir]) and [76Ara] (electrical resistivity and calorimetry) determined a transformation diagram for $(\alpha \mathrm{Zr})$, $(\alpha^{\prime}\mathrm{Zr})$, and $(\alpha^{\prime\prime}\mathrm{Zr})$. [74Hir2] worked at three compositions, and their main results may be summarized as follows: with increasing temperature, at the composition 23.1 at.% O, the Zr-O alloy undergoes a disordering process from $(\alpha^{\prime\prime}\mathrm{Zr})$ to $(\alpha \mathrm{Zr})$ at $\sim 450~^\circ \mathrm{C}$. At 25 and 29.1 at.% O, the alloy becomes disordered, changing first from $(\alpha^{\prime\prime}\mathrm{Zr})$ to $(\alpha^{\prime}\mathrm{Zr})$ at $T_{1}$, and subsequently from $(\alpha^{\prime}\mathrm{Zr})$ to $(\alpha \mathrm{Zr})$ at $T_{2}$. $T_{1}$ and $T_{2}$ are $\sim 450$ and $\sim 630^\circ C$ for the 25 at.% O alloy, and $\sim 500$ and $\sim 1050^\circ C$ for the 29.1 at.% O alloy, respectively. [74Hir2] emphasized that the disordering of $(\alpha^{\prime}\mathrm{Zr})$ appears nearly a second-order transition. [76Ara] worked in the range 13.8 to 28.6 at.% O, confirming the results of [74Hir2]. The results of [74Hir2] and [76Ara] are plotted in Fig. 3, superimposed on the diagram given in Fig. 1. In Fig. 3 we have also plotted experimental data of [71Dub1] and [71Dub2] (X-rays and metallography, 5 to 30 at.% O) and [74Has] (X-rays and neutron diffraction, 28.2 at.% O). The results of these authors appear to be in good agreement with those of [74Hir2] and [76Ara]. Earlier experimental results by [73Cla] (electrical resistivity, 12 to 29 at.% O) on the order-disorder transitions of O in cph Zr were judged by [74Hir2] to be consistent with their own.

associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: According to Fig. 2, the measurements on the equilibrated ternary alloys are in very good agreement with the results obtained from the diffusion couples. Figure 2 presents the isothermal section at $1000^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$; this has been constructed from microprobe analyses on quenched samples as well as from diffusion couple experiments. The main features of the isothermal section at $1000^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ are the large solubility of aluminum in $\beta \mathrm{Ti}$, FeTi, and $\mathrm{Fe_2Ti}$. The solubility range of Al in $\mathrm{Fe_2Ti}$ extends up to 47.5 at $\%$ thus crossing the existence domain of the $\tau_{2}$ phase and splitting it into two islands. As for the isothermal section at $800^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, the $\tau_{2}$ phase is cubic at high Ti contents and tetragonal at low Ti levels. Therefore the lower island is denoted as $\tau_{2}^{*}$. The tetragonality could clearly be verified at low Ti levels by additional lines appearing in the x-ray diffractograms. For compositions close to the upper closing part of the $\tau_{2}^{*}$-island, the tetragonality is small, and the $\tau_{2}^{*}$ phase could be observed only in multiphase alloys. In those cases, the intensity of the extra lines was too small to allow a determination of the tetragonality. In this isothermal section, many of the three-phase triangles are very narrow. These triangles could not be fixed quantitatively because none of the investigated compositions was inside those triangles. Their position and size had to be estimated in order to comply with the rules for phase boundaries and phase equilibria in isothermal sections. These three-phase triangles are represented in Fig. 2 by filled rather than shaded areas. From the binary phases of the Fe-Al system, the $\alpha$-solid solution exhibits the largest solubility for titanium with 25 at.% Ti at about 25 at.% Al. In accordance with former investigators, we found that the addition of titanium stabilizes the ordered polymorphs of the $\alpha$-solid solution. Preliminary results from a detailed transmission electron microscopic (TEM) investigation suggest that the $L2_{1}$ structure is stabilized above $1000^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ by the addition of titanium. The stability ranges of the different bcc polymorphs were not established during the course of this investigation, and therefore tentative composition ranges are given by broken lines. The solubility for titanium in the three intermetallic phases in the Fe-Al system is 1.8 at.% in $\mathrm{Al}_{2}\mathrm{Fe}$, about 2.5 at.% in $\mathrm{Al}_{5}\mathrm{Fe}_{2}$ and 6.5 at.% in $\mathrm{Al}_{3}\mathrm{Fe}$. associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: Some phase diagrams show all the intermediate phases present within the diagram as having vanishing solubility at $0\mathrm{K}$ (for example, Ta-H in the figure). The reasoning for this is that, according to the third law of thermodynamics, the entropy term is zero at $0\mathrm{K}$ and only perfectly ordered states are permissible. However, a perfectly ordered state with a specific composition is not the only permissible state for alloy systems. As long as the enthalpy of mixing of a phase is negative in at least some composition range, the Gibbs energy of mixing always becomes negative in the same range as the temperature approaches $0\mathrm{K}$ because the contribution to the Gibbs energy from the entropy term also approaches 0. Hence, a continuous phase field can exist to $0\mathrm{K}$. The unlikely occurrence of a zero-width phase field at $0\mathrm{K}$ may be considered with reference to the figure. The composition of the Ta-rich boundary of the $\eta$ phase is determined by the Gibbs energy relationship between the $\eta$ and $\beta$ phases. The composition of the H-rich boundary of $\eta$ is determined by the Gibbs energy relationship between the $\eta$ and $\zeta$ phases. There is no reason why the boundaries should intersect at $0\mathrm{K}$. The same applies of course to the other phases in the figure.

The liquidus data of [72Uga] beyond 46 at.% As are applicable only under constrained conditions, because pure As sublimes at $603^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. As such, these data were rejected, and the proposed phase relationships in the As-rich region are sketched schematically in Fig. 3. The Cu-As system is characterized by two terminal eutectics— $\mathrm{L} \leftrightarrow (\mathrm{Cu}) + \gamma$ and $\mathrm{L} \leftrightarrow \delta + (\varepsilon \mathrm{As})$. The proposed equilibrium diagram for the Cu-As system follows the essential features of [Hansen] and [Elliott], with certain revisions based on more recent experimental investigations. The phases accepted are: (1) the liquid, I; (2) the fcc terminal solid solution, (Cu), with a maximum solid solubility of 6.83 at.% As at the eutectic temperature of $685^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$; (3) Curich cph $\beta$ (A3, Mg type), forming peritectoidally from (Cu) and $\gamma'$ at $325^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$; (4) hexagonal $\gamma$ ( $D0_{18}$ , Na3As type), forming congruently from the liquid at 26.25 at.% As and $827^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$; (5) hexagonal $\gamma'$ (Cu3As type), existing over the maximum composition range of $\sim 25.5$ to 27.8 at.% As and undergoing an allotropic transformation to hexagonal $\gamma$ at temperatures between 450 and $475^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$; (6) cubic $\delta$ ( $D03$ , BiF2 type), forming peritectically from L and $\gamma$ at $709^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and $\sim 29$ at.% As and undergoing an allotropic transformation to orthorhombic $\delta'$ at $\sim 380^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$; (7) orthorhombic $\delta'$ ( $\mathrm{Cu5As2}$ type), existing over the limited temperature range 300 to $380^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and decomposing eutectoidally into $\gamma'$ and ( $\alpha\mathrm{As}$ ) at $300^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and $\sim 29$ at.% As; and (8) pure As phases ( $\alpha\mathrm{As}$ ) and ( $\varepsilon\mathrm{As}$ ), with no reported solid solubility of Cu. (Pure As is dimorphic; rhombohedral ( $\alpha\mathrm{As}$ ) is stable at lower temperatures, and high-temperature orthorhombic ( $\varepsilon\mathrm{As}$ ) is stable above 448 °C.) The (Cu) solidus was determined by [57Hum] from metallographic examination of samples quenched after annealing at various temperatures. Because there have been no other determinations of the (Cu) solidus, the accepted boundary is from [57Hum]. The solid solubility of As in (Cu) has been investigated by metallography [10Ben, 27Han, 34Hum], electrical resistivity [13Pus], and lattice parameter measurements [37Mer, 39Owe, 40Owe, 49Owe]. [49Hum] indicated that the measurements of [27Han] and [34Hum] are erroneous because of insufficient annealing periods. The lattice parameter measurements of [37Mer] indicate a linear decrease in solubility from 6.8 at.% As at $680^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ to 6.4 at.% As at $300^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. [40Owe] reported a discontinuous decrease in solubility at $\sim 380^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. More recent investigations confirm this discontinuity to be associated with the peritectoid formation of Cu-rich $\beta$ , not a result of a polymorphic transition in $\gamma$ (or Cu3As), as was interpreted in the review of [Hansen]. Solubility data of [37Mer], [40Owe], and [49Owe] show good agreement and blend in with the room temperature solubility value of [13Pus]. The maximum homogeneity range of $\delta$ and $\delta^{\prime}$ is accepted provisionally as extending from the Cu5As2 composition to the Cu19As8 composition in this review. The proposed phase relationships for this phase are based tentatively on the data of [68Juz], [71Lie], and [72Uga], although further investigations definitely are required in this region.

associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: Figure 1 shows a provisional equilibrium phase diagram for the Zr-Cr system, including the following phases: the bcc terminal solid solution, (Cr), in which Zr has a maximum solubility of less than 0.6 at.% Zr at 1592°C. The phase diagram in Fig. 1 differs from previous versions, because it includes details of the relationships among αZrCr2, βZrCr2, and γZrCr2. The assessed temperature and (βZr) composition for the eutectoid reaction are 836°C and 1.65 at.% Cr. The boundaries of the [(αZr) + (βZr)] two-phase region in Fig. 1 are consistent with the 863°C temperature for the α ⇌ β equilibrium in pure Zr and with the assessed temperature and (βZr) composition for the eutectoid reaction (βZr) ⇌ (αZr) + αZrCr2. The (βZr)/[(βZr) + αZrCr2] boundary in Fig. 1 is based on the metallographic results of [53Dom] and [69Rum] and can be represented by: ln (at.% Cr) = 5.609 - 5665 T^-1, where T is in K. This boundary also agrees with the results of [67Geb], who used metallographic techniques to establish that a 12 at.% Cr alloy is in the [(βZr) + αZrCr2] two-phase field at 1300°C. The congruent αZrCr2 ⇌ βZrCr2 transformation, indicated in Fig. 1 at 1592°C and 67 at.% Cr, is somewhat uncertain and is proposed as a compromise between the experimental results of [73Pet] and [74Nem]. Finally, the experimental information concerning the (βZrCr2 + γZrCr2) two-phase region is incomplete; consequently, this part of Fig. 1 is rather speculative. The [(αZr) + (βZr)] two-phase field and the (βZr)/(βZr) + αZrCr2 boundary portion of the assessed phase diagram is based on the metallographic work of [53Dom] and [69Rum]. The melting points of Zr and Cr are 1855 and 1863°C, respectively. The assessed eutectic temperature and composition, 1332°C and ~22 at.% Cr, for the reaction L ⇌ (βZr) + αZrCr2 are taken from [73Pet], because the Zr and Cr metals used were of higher purity than in the other studies. The liquidus appears to be reasonably well determined for compositions between about 60 and 90 at.% Cr. The congruent melting of γZrCr2 occurs at 66.7 at.% Cr and 1673°C, and the assessed eutectic temperature and composition for the reaction L ⇌ βZrCr2 + (Cr) are 1592°C and ~82 at.% Cr. The assessed (Cr) liquidus and solidus were evaluated by applying a similar procedure as for the [(βZr) + L] field. To apply the van't Hoff relation, the value 20500 J/mol was used for the heat of fusion of pure Cr.

associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: Experimental data for the region from 0 to 10 at.% Fe are shown in Fig. 2. The liquidus boundaries of the Be-Fe phase diagram were investigated by [16Oes], [29Wev], [48Gor], [48Tei], [60Gel], and [82Jon]. Generally, the trends of the liquidus in the Be-rich region observed by [48Gor], [60Gel] (results of heating cycle are preferred for consistency with the assessed melting point of β Be), and [82Jon] agree with [48Tei]. Impurities in Be appear to have caused the scatter in temperature. [48Tei] conducted X-ray experiments on quenched specimens, which indicated that an 8 at.% Fe alloy is single phase at 1025 and 950°C, and an 8.3 at.% Fe alloy is single phase at 950°C. [82Jon] found that an 8 at.% Fe alloy is two-phase at 827°C. [79Ald] assigned this phase the stoichiometry Be7Fe based on the crystal structure data obtained by [70Joh], but showed the compound at 8 at.% Fe. The homogeneity range of ε has not been clarified. [48Tei] estimated the maximum transition temperature of ε as ~1175 or 1188°C (different in different diagrams) from the trend of the δ/[ε + δ] boundary extrapolated to 8 at.% Fe. The δ phase covers the composition range from ~7 to 18 at.% Fe. The δ ↔ (αBe) + ε eutectoid reaction temperature, determined by thermal analysis [48Gor, 60Gel, 82Jon] and by a metallographic method (1020 to 1050°C) [65Ham], agree well.

associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: Together with the measurements along the CaO:MgO = 1:1 central line, the isoplethal map for the cubic phase lattice parameter was calculated, Fig. 3. As to the coprecipitation tie lines for these samples, they were easily drawn on the dopant-rich side, i.e., pure MgO is precipitated with the cubic phase. On the zirconia-rich side, however, only approximate tie lines were given since the other end of the tie lines are not well clarified due to the tetragonal solid solution phase. The tie lines corresponding to the sample bulk compositions are also illustrated in Fig. 3. Four isotherms of the cubic phase area determined by the isoplethal map are also shown in Fig. 3. The phase boundaries determined by these samples at both 1773 and 1683 K show that a two-phase region of (CaZrO3 + cubic), or at lower temperatures (Ca6Zr19O44 + cubic), exists. Dotted lines are given in Fig. 3 indicating the approximate positions of these phase boundaries. In work by Hellmann and Stubican and Longo and Podda, this two-phase region was ignored, and because of this, a much larger single cubic phase field was shown in their presentations. In the Hellmann and Stubican experiments, two contradictory points were determined with the inaccurate technique described earlier. One gives a concave shape and the other a convex shape of the phase boundary. However, they neglected the second point, which according to the present experiments, is correct. The abandoned phase boundary composition, 79.8 mol% ZrO2 / 15.2 mol% CaO / 5 mol% MgO at 1693 K, agrees well with the present 1683 K result and is also given in Fig. 3 by an asterisk. Great difficulties were found in fitting the 1523 K phase diagram. The three-phase region, which should cover at least the compositions of X(CaO + MgO) = 0.10, 0.12, 0.14, 0.15, 0.16, and possibly even 0.18, was found only to cover 0.10, 0.12, 0.14, and perhaps 0.16 samples. One possible explanation for this reduced three-phase region is, as discussed for the 1373 K ZrO2-CaO samples, the formation of the metastable cubic phase below the pseudoeutectoid temperature. The ternary samples were all prepared with zirconia powder plus calcium carbonate and magnesium nitrate. The oxide powder is perhaps not fine enough, and 1523 K temperature may also be too low to reach the chemical equilibrium in a reasonably short period of time. In order to get a better understanding of the phenomenon, two groups of samples were prepared: the samples directly heated at 1523 K for 325 hours and the samples heated at 1773 K for 330 hours before annealing at 1523 K for 805 hours. Unfortunately, all these samples showed the same tendency. The phase boundary, or rather the sharp corner, in Fig. 3 was fixed by assuming that the lattice parameter keeps constant between X(CaO + MgO) = 0.10 and 0.18. The position of the tie lines that link the cubic and the tetragonal phases are not known. Thus the boundary calculated from the isoplethal map (Fig. 3) has a larger uncertainty than other points. The tie lines are only at a small angle to the lattice parameter contours. Any small error in lattice parameter measurement will be magnified in the final phase boundary position. The equilibrium cubic phase composition of the three-phase region is at the sharp corner where two cubic phase boundaries join together. This disagrees with the works of Longo and Podda and Hellmann and Stubican in which no sign of such sharp corners were shown in their diagrams.

associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: Figure 7 shows a projection of the liquidus surface for the ternary system. The symbols shown in the figure correspond to those in the reaction scheme. The liquidus surface defines two sets of eutectic-peritectic valleys. The univariant line starting from the eutectic point $\mathbf{e}_1$ of the Fe-U system moves to the peritectic point $\mathfrak{p}_2$ of the Fe-Pu system. The other univariant line starting from the peritectic point $\mathfrak{p}_1$ of the Fe-U system meets two univariant lines from the eutectic point $\mathbf{e}_2$ and a metatectic point $\mathrm{mt}_1$ of the Fe-Pu system on a ternary eutectic point $\mathrm{E}_1$ . At the intersection point $\mathrm{E}_1$ , the liquid becomes triply saturated and a ternary eutectic occurs: $\mathrm{L} \leftrightarrows \mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{Pu}, \mathrm{U})_6 + \eta + \delta \mathrm{Pu}$ . The temperature of the $\mathrm{E}_1$ reaction is estimated to be $394^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and the composition of the ternary eutectic liquid is similar to that of the eutectic point $\mathbf{e}_2$ in the Fe-Pu system.

associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: The assessed phase diagram is based on thermodynamic optimization calculations using enthalpy of mixing and phase boundary data. This calculation provides an upper bound on the critical temperature because it uses a classical model for the Gibbs energies and predicts classical critical exponents that are known to be incorrect. The calculated miscibility gap has been adjusted near the critical point to give a more nearly correct exponent for the phase boundaries. We, therefore, rely primarily on emf data for the miscibility gap together with the direct sampling data of [52Cam] for temperatures $800^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and below. The phase boundary was arrived at by two steps: first, a thermodynamic analysis was performed, to be described below. The calculated critical temperature is $902^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. This temperature must be higher than the true critical temperature because the classical Gibbs energy model gives an exponent of 0.5 rather than 0.31 for the phase boundaries in the critical region. Below $T_{c}$, an exponent of 0.31 is nearly approximated by the calculation over a wide temperature range. Next, a "calculated" critical point of $875 \pm 5^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ was arrived at by extrapolating the noncritical region to $c_{\mathrm{L1}} - c_{\mathrm{L2}} = 0$. In-Rich Alloys. Below $300^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, the solubility of Al in the In-rich liquid is less than 0.2 at.% [47Val, 52Cam]. Reported temperatures of the reaction $\mathbf{L} \rightarrow (\mathrm{In}) + (\mathrm{Al})$ range between 155 and $156.3^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ [46Rau, 47Val, 48Kle, 48Dav, 49Pog, 52Cam]. The eutectic temperature in Fig. 1 is $156^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. Data on the (Al) liquidus between the monotectic and eutectic temperatures were reported by [66Mas], emf; [65Pre], DTA; [52Cam], quenching. There is no serious discrepancy among these determinations. The data are well represented by the present thermodynamic calculations, which have been used to draw the liquidus in Fig. 1. In our thermodynamic calculations, we found that we could easily reproduce a monotectic temperature between 635 and $639^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, but that the monotectic composition was a more sensitive test of the accuracy of the Gibbs energies. The monotectic composition was, therefore, heavily weighted among the experimental data. The calculated monotectic point lies at 4.96 at.% In and $638^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. The liquidus lies between the data of [52Cam] and [46Rau], within $6^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ of the [46Rau] data and $3^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ of the [52Cam] data. The calculated critical point is (37.5 at.% In, $902^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$). The calculated monotectic point is (4.96 at.% In, $638^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$), and the composition of the second liquid at the monotectic temperature is 88.5 at.% In. As discussed above, the calculated critical temperature should overshoot the true critical temperature, and corrections to the phase boundaries can be made by extrapolation into the critical region.

associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: The assessed Pb-Se phase diagram, Fig. 1, is based on the present evaluators' modeling and calculations. An intermediate phase, PbSe, with a narrow composition range of stability, forms at 50 at.% Se. In the Pb-PbSe region, a eutectic reaction occurs near pure Pb. In the PbSe-Se region, a liquid miscibility gap, a monotectic reaction, and a eutectic reaction exist. The melting points of Pb and Se are 327.502 and $221^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, respectively. The liquidus in the Pb-Se system was determined by [07Pel], [08Fri], [55Noz], [56Pel], [61Sei], [66Sei], [66Mil], and [74Sch2]. The calculated liquidus shown in Fig. 1 is in fairly good agreement with the experimental data. The Pb-Se phase diagram was calculated assuming that the PbSe phase is a line compound. Agreement between the calculated and experimental phase diagram is good. The assessed phase diagram (Fig. 1) is based on the calculated phase equilibrium. The liquidus curve in the Pb-PbSe region has an inflection point (Fig. 1) that indicates a metastable liquid miscibility gap at lower temperatures. This miscibility gap was calculated based on the thermodynamic model described in the next section and is shown as a dashed line in Fig. 1. It has not been confirmed experimentally.

associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: The assessed Na-S phase diagram is shown in Fig. 1. Special points of this diagram are listed in Table 1 along with estimated error limits. In order to avoid undue clutter, only selected data are shown in Fig. 1. Plots of equilibrium $S_{2}$ pressure over the melt are also shown on Fig. 1 (see "Thermodynamics"). The results of [14Fri] and [17Tho] are very scattered and are not shown on Fig. 1. However, the diagrams proposed by these authors are in reasonable concordance with later authors. Data obtained by hot-stage microscopy by [74Col] are generally of low quality, as acknowledged later by the authors [76Col], and are not plotted on Fig. 1. No data are available for compositions below 33.3 at.% S. This part of the diagram in Fig. 1 is thus based upon analogy with other alkali-S and alkali-Se systems. A region of liquid immiscibility has been observed in the K-S system [97San], and it is likely that such a region also appears in the Na-S system. An analysis of all the results (up to 1976) was performed [76Teg] in order to obtain the optimized iso- $P_{\mathrm{S}_2}$ curves shown on Fig. 1. (Note that these are plots of $P_{\mathrm{S}_2}$ and not of total sulfur pressure. The total sulfur pressure data were converted to $P_{\mathrm{S}_2}$ values by [76Teg] using the known equilibrium constants among the $S_{n}$ gaseous species.) The data for Na and S activities in the melt have been modeled [76Teg, 83Cle] on the assumption that polyanions $S_{n}^{2-}$ ( $n = 2$ to 8) exist in the melt. The sharply peaked liquidus of $\mathrm{Na}_{2}\mathrm{S}$ at its melting point is indicative of a sharp minimum in the Gibbs energy of the liquid at this composition.

associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: The binary Ti-V phase diagram is based on [87Mur1]. At high temperatures, the $( eta \mathrm{Ti})$ and (V) phase form a continuous series of bcc solid solution. Below $850^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, the miscibility gap is present in the $ eta$ phase giving rise to a monotectoid reaction, $( eta \mathrm{Ti}) \leftrightarrow (\alpha \mathrm{Ti}) + (\mathrm{V})$. In former assessments the $ eta / [ eta + (\alpha \mathrm{Ti})]$ boundaries were shown as a single curve. A recent study showed that the reported miscibility gap in the $ eta$ phase was possibly due to the oxygen impurity and that neither a miscibility gap nor a stable monotectoid was likely to occur in the binary Ti-V system, consistent with the former assessments. However, the miscibility gap was not observed in Ti-50V alloys of lower oxygen concentrations (<0.095 wt.%).

associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: A phase diagram for the system is shown with an enlarged section in Fig. 2. Except for the $\delta \rightarrow \gamma \rightarrow \gamma^{\prime}$ region, the features of this diagram have been taken from the work of Schober, most of which has been confirmed by other investigations. The diagram as proposed by Schober showed an alteration of single-phase regions and two-phase regions in accord with the phase rule; this implies that all phase transitions are first order. Although it seems clear that the $\alpha \rightarrow \beta$ transformation is first order, it is most likely that the $\delta \rightarrow \gamma$ and $\gamma -\gamma^{\prime}$ transformations are higher order, with the $\gamma$ phase being a superstructure of the $\delta$ phase and blending smoothly with it through an incommensurate region. Entin et al. observed that $\gamma$ undergoes further ordering at lower temperatures. With regard to the $\alpha \rightarrow \zeta \rightarrow \delta$ transitions, there is also some uncertainty. The early heat capacity measurements of Voronel et al. showed a single broad peak, which they interpreted as a second-order transition with a critical temperature of $232.8\mathrm{K}$. However, a temperature of $234\mathrm{K}(-39^{\circ}\mathrm{C})$ was found by Schober to be associated with the peritectoidal reaction, $\alpha +\delta \rightleftharpoons \zeta$, and Pesch et al. have recently used electron microscopy and diffraction to produce strong evidence that a distinguishable two-phase region exists between the $\alpha$ and $\zeta$ phases, though they were unable to unequivocally identify a two-phase region between the $\zeta$ and $\delta$ phases. The Schober version of the diagram in the $\alpha \rightarrow \zeta \rightarrow \delta$ region is shown in Fig. 2 because his data were accumulated with high purity V that was deuterated in bulk to minimize contamination and to facilitate homogeneity. $\mathbf{VD}_{1 - \kappa}$ Phase. A phase, $\delta$ in Fig. 2, exists over a wide composition and temperature range on the D-deficient side of stoichiometric VD. Many investigators have associated the appearance of this phase with eutectoidal decomposition of the $\alpha$ phase near $210\mathrm{K}$ at a composition near $\mathrm{VD}_{-0.8}$, and at least one investigation suggested that the $\alpha \rightarrow \delta$ transition is an order-disorder transformation of higher order. Extensive evidence exists, however, to indicate that the equilibria are more nearly as shown in Fig. 2, with a $\zeta$ phase existing over a narrow temperature range between the $\alpha$ and $\delta$ phases. Evidence for the existence of a two-phase field between the $\alpha$ and $\zeta$ phases implies that these two phases are related by a first-order transformation. It is still conceivable, of course, that the $\zeta$ and $\delta$ phases are related by a higher-order transformation, but if this is true it would be difficult to account for all of the four horizontal arrests that Schober has reported at 211, 217, 234, and $241\mathrm{K}$ $(-62, -56, -39,$ and $-32^{\circ}\mathrm{C})$. Whether or not the composition range of the $\delta$ extends at lower temperatures to include equiatomic stoichiometry is still uncertain. $\zeta$ Phase. During DTA measurements on alloys in the central portion of the V-D system, Schober observed transitions at 211 and $234\mathrm{K}$ $(-62$ and $-39^{\circ}\mathrm{C})$ that he associated with the extremal temperature range of stability of an intermediate phase. This is shown as the $\zeta$ phase in Fig. 2. Schober associated an additional transition near $217\mathrm{K}$ $(-56^{\circ}\mathrm{C})$ with eutectoidal dissociation of the $\alpha$ phase to form $\beta$ and $\zeta$ phases. Supporting evidence for the existence of the $\zeta$ phase was available in earlier publications of specific heat measurements and of nuclear magnetic resonance measurements. Included in the specific heat data was one curve in the composition range of interest; this was a curve of specific heat versus temperature for a 42 at.% D alloy that showed a broad peak spanning the range 190 to $225\mathrm{K}$, with two well-resolved maxima—one at $\sim 210\mathrm{K}$ and another at $\sim 220\mathrm{K}$. Similarly, the nuclear magnetic resonance data showed a distinguishably different resonance for an intermediate phase associated with transitions at 206 and $220\mathrm{K}$. Subsequent transmission electron microscopic investigations with alloy compositions in the range of 43 to 46 at.% D showed an unequivocal difference in domain structure above and below $\sim 211\mathrm{K}$. It was reported that heating through $\sim 211\mathrm{K}$ caused the coarse domain structure of the $\delta$ phase to be replaced by a fine domain structure, and further heating caused this fine structure to disappear and to be replaced by a structure representative of the $\alpha$ phase. The later investigation yielded strong evidence for a two-phase field between the $\alpha$ and $\zeta$ phases. It also should be noted that the DTA arrests at $234\mathrm{K}$ $(-39^{\circ}\mathrm{C})$, which Schober associated with the peritectoidal dissociation of the $\zeta$ phase, are in close correspondence with the temperature of $232.8\mathrm{K}$, which Voronel et al. postulated as the order-disorder transformation for $\delta \rightarrow \alpha$. Schober additionally found DTA arrests near $241\mathrm{K}$ $(-32^{\circ}\mathrm{C})$ for several alloys at compositions more rich in D, and these were associated with the peritectoidal decomposition of the $\delta$ phase. The observation of four different arrest temperatures, three of which are supported by independent investigations, provides support for the $\alpha \rightarrow \zeta \rightarrow \delta$ equilibria shown in Fig. 2.

associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: The results for the Ni-Al-Ta system are depicted in Fig. 11(a) and (b) in the form of the $\gamma$ -liquidus and solidus isothermal lines. Solidus isothermal lines should extend to the maximum terminal solid solubility of the $\gamma$ phase. This maximum solid solubility is shown by a dashed line in Fig. 11(b). It is obvious that the $\gamma$ -liquidus and solidus isothermal lines all show similar compositional dependencies of the same general shape. Though no previous data have been reported on the solidus projections of the Ni-Al-Ta system, data have previously been reported for the liquidus surface by [1986Wil]. The intercepts of the [1986Wil] isotherms at both the Ni-Al and Ni-Ta binary limits are in good accord with the intercepts of the present investigation. However, the isothermal contours for both liquidus and solidus in the ternary region from the present results extend away from the Ni corner, while the contours of the liquidus from the [1986Wil] investigation extend toward the Ni corner of the diagram. The present results are in qualitative agreement with our results for the Ni-Al-V system. So also is the stabilization of the $\gamma$ phase by small additions of Al evident in the Ni-Al-Nb system, but the effect appears to be less pronounced than in the Ni-Al-V system. The terminus of a monovariant line near 4 at.% Ta, noted with regard to Fig. 10(a), may be responsible for a minimum in the partition coefficient of Al between liquid and $\gamma$ phases. This composition of about 4 at.% of Ta is where a pseudobinary eutectic reaction is expected.

SnS and $\mathrm{SnS}_2$ melt congruently, whereas $\mathrm{Sn}_2\mathrm{S}_3$ melts peritectically to a liquid and $\mathrm{SnS}_2$. There are two liquid miscibility gaps, one in the Sn-SnS region, and one in the $\mathrm{SnS}_2$-S region. The three eutectics are in the Sn-rich corner, between SnS and $\mathrm{Sn}_2\mathrm{S}_3$, and in the S-rich corner. All three intermediate phases undergo several phase transformations in the solid state. Figure 1 gives the assessed Sn-S phase diagram.
Liquidus. The melting points of Sn and S are 231.9681 and $115.22^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, respectively. The Sn-S liquidus was determined by [06Pel], [09Bil], [43And], [61Alb1], [66Kar], and [69Moh]. [43And] also determined the liquid miscibility gap in the Sn-SnS region. The data are shown in Fig. 1.
Solid Solubilities. The mutual solid solubilities of Sn and S are negligible and have not been determined accurately. S in the solid state exists in two allotropic forms. $\alpha \mathrm{S}$ is stable up to $95.5^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$, where it transforms to $\beta \mathrm{S}$. $\beta \mathrm{S}$ melts at $115.22^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: To discuss the effect of temperature on the coherent equilibrium, we adopt the value $G^{\mathrm{el}} = 1$ kJ per mole of substitutional atoms as in the previous investigation. Figure 2 shows the two-phase coherent equilibrium boundaries (solid lines) and turning points (dashed and dot-dashed lines), with the ordinary Fe-C equilibrium and its extension to lower temperatures superimposed. The dashed line represents the locus of vanishing first and second derivatives, and the dot-dashed lines represent the turning points at $f = 0$ or $f = 1$. The dotted line is the $T_{0}$ line, where the two phases have the same Gibbs energy. Figure 2 shows that the dashed and dot-dashed lines extend into the $\gamma$ one-phase field, which means that thermodynamically the coherent mixture of the two phases could be metastable in the stable $\gamma$ one-phase field. In Fig. 2 the symbols denote the starting temperatures of formation of Widmanstätten ferrite evaluated experimentally. It looks encouraging since the model used in the present study is a very simple one. However, it has been realized that the mismatch between fcc and bcc Fe is rather large, and the estimated elastic energy, by assuming fully coherent interface, is much higher than 1 kJ/mol. In reality, much of the elastic energy is relaxed by the formation of dislocations. From the calculations in the Fe-Mn and Fe-C systems, it can already be seen that at $600^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, the $\gamma$ one-phase state is above its stability limit with respect to the two-phase coherent equilibrium. Thus the $\gamma$ one-phase state is stable or metastable at all compositions in the coherent equilibrium at $600^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$.

evidence.diagram_type: Figure 2 shows boundaries (solid lines) and turning points (dashed and dot-dashed lines); ordinary Fe-C equilibrium superimposed
evidence.phase_regions_boundaries: two-phase coherent equilibrium boundaries; T0 line; γ one-phase field; stability limit

associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: The Bi-O phase diagram at 1 bar total pressure as calculated from the present optimized description is shown in the figure together with the experimental data on the solubility limits of the liquid phase. The oxygen solubility limit in the bismuth-rich liquid has been investigated by several authors using chemical analysis and electrochemical techniques. These results are shown in the figure. Griffith et al. measured the oxygen content in samples equilibrated between 673 and $1023\mathrm{K}$ from $\mathrm{CO - CO_2}$ gas equilibrium analysis. Isecke et al. derived the oxygen solubility limit between 950 and $1473\mathrm{K}$ from a series of electromotive force (emf) measurements performed at constant oxygen content. At $1273\mathrm{K}$, they analyzed samples taken from the melt as described above and found the value $x_{\mathrm{O}} = 0.024$, which is in good agreement with the results obtained from emf measurements. Hahn and Stevenson determined it between 1073 and $1223\mathrm{K}$ using coulometric titration. The oxygen solubility limit has finally been derived from measurements of the oxygen diffusivity in the bismuth-rich liquid by Fitzner and Heshmatpour and Stevenson using potentiostatic titration techniques. The contradiction appearing between these studies is discussed in the optimization procedure. The activity values measured by Hahn and Stevenson are considerably larger, and the obtained solubility limit, as seen in the figure, is much lower than in the other studies. Contradictory results are found for the activity of oxygen in the Bi-rich liquid and the related solubility limit. A relatively good agreement exists between most measurements. The other results lead to smaller values for the oxygen solubility limit and larger values for the activity of oxygen. A better fit of these latter data leads to an increase of the miscibility gap and brings further contradictions with phase diagram data by increasing the value of the critical point and shifting the bismuth solubility limit towards lower bismuth contents. The results, on the other side, can be well fitted together with the phase diagram data at higher oxygen content. The data of Hahn and Stevenson and Heshmatpour and Stevenson were thus discarded, and the thermodynamic properties of the Bi-rich liquid were optimized from the remaining data. The solubility of U and Pu in Cd in the U-Pu-Cd ternary system was preliminarily calculated. In the two binary subsystems, U-Cd and Pu-Cd, the Cd-richest compound is the $\mathrm{Cd}_{11}\mathrm{M}$ type. In the first calculation, ideal mixing between U and Pu was assumed for the U-Pu site of the $\mathrm{Cd}_{11}\mathrm{M}$-type compound. Since the decomposition temperatures of the $\mathrm{Cd}_{11}\mathrm{M}$-type compound are 748 and $669\mathrm{K}$ for the U-Cd and Pu-Cd binary subsystems, respectively, the calculations were carried out at 668 and $718\mathrm{K}$. These temperatures correspond to the conditions that both $\mathrm{Cd}_{11}\mathrm{U}$ and $\mathrm{Cd}_{11}\mathrm{Pu}$ exist at $668\mathrm{K}$ and that only $\mathrm{Cd}_{11}\mathrm{U}$ exists at $718\mathrm{K}$. $$
S L _ {\mathrm {M}} ^ {\text {t e r n a r y}} = X _ {\mathrm {M}} \cdot S L _ {\mathrm {M}} ^ {\text {b i n a r y}} \tag {Eq2}
$$

where $\mathrm{SL}_{\mathrm{M}}^{\mathrm{ternary}}$ and $\mathrm{SL}_{\mathrm{M}}^{\mathrm{binary}}$ are the terminal solubility limits of M in ternary and binary systems, respectively; and $X_{\mathrm{M}}$ indicates the mole fraction in solute. The boundary between the single-phase liquid region, $L$, and the two-phase region, $L + \mathrm{Cd}_{11}\mathrm{M}$, resembles that at 668 K. Figure 10 shows the stable and metastable miscibility gaps of the liquid phase in the Fe-Cu-X system, where different types of miscibility gaps of liquid phase appear in the Fe-Cu-X system. It can be seen from Fig. 10(a) and (b) that the tie-lines in the Fe-Cu-Cr, and Fe-Cu-V systems lie along the Cu-FeCr, and Cu-FeV directions. This can be qualitatively explained as being due to the enthalpy of mixing in the binary systems. According to the semi-empirical values of mixing enthalpies of the liquid, the following relations are obtained:

$$
\Delta \mathrm {H} _ {\mathrm {C u F e}} (+ 5 3) > \Delta \mathrm {H} _ {\mathrm {C u C r}} (+ 5 1) > \Delta \mathrm {H} _ {\mathrm {F e C r}} (- 6) (\mathrm {k J / m o l})
$$

$$
\Delta \mathrm {H} _ {\mathrm {C u F e}} (+ 5 3) > \Delta \mathrm {H} _ {\mathrm {C u V}} (+ 2 1) > \Delta \mathrm {H} _ {\mathrm {F e V}} (- 2 9) (\mathrm {k J / m o l})
$$

Because repulsion forces exist between Cu and Fe, Cr, and V and attractive forces exist between Fe and Cr, and V, the tie-lines radiate from the Cu corner to the Fe-Cr or Fe-V sides. On the other hand, the tie-lines in the Fe-Cu-Si system lie along the CuSi-FeSi direction, as shown in Fig. 10(c). In this case, the mixing enthalpies of the liquid are as follows:

$$
\Delta \mathrm {H} _ {\mathrm {C u F e}} (+ 5 3) > > \Delta \mathrm {H} _ {\mathrm {C u S i}} (- 4 0) > \Delta \mathrm {H} _ {\mathrm {F e S i}} (- 7 5) (\mathrm {k J / m o l})
$$

Equation 3 was solved by the Newton-Raphson method at different temperatures, and the results are shown in the figure. The liquidus compositions calculated in this work are in good agreement with the reported measured data. Raoult's law has been assumed for the solvent in the RE-rich liquid solution. A simultaneous solution of Eq 3 and 4 for T and X_Ta gives eutectic temperature and composition, respectively. The eutectic temperature and composition accepted are $240^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and 12 wt.% Sb and 4.0 wt.% Sn, as in Fig. 3 and 4. It is suggested that the reaction $\mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{U}_1} + \mathrm{SbSn}(\mathrm{HT}) \rightleftharpoons$ $\mathrm{SbSn(LT)} + (\mathrm{Sb})$ occurs at a temperature between 325 and $320^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. The $325^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ upper limit for $\mathrm{U}_1$ is defined by the binary peritectic reaction $\mathfrak{p}_2$ $(\mathrm{L} + \mathrm{SbSn}(\mathrm{HT}) \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{SbSn(LT)})$ and the $320^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ lower limit by the binary eutectoid reaction, $\mathrm{SbSn}(\mathrm{HT}) \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{SbSn(LT)} + (\mathrm{Sb})$. It should be noted that the monovariant curve $\mathfrak{p}_2\mathrm{U}_1$ must closely approach the $320^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ isotherm (Fig. 3), and therefore, the composition of $\mathrm{U}_1$ can be estimated as being slightly richer in $\mathrm{Sb}$ than the point at which the $320^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ isotherm intersects the monovariant curve $\mathfrak{p}_1\mathbb{E}$. It is suggested that $\mathrm{U}_1$ lies at a composition of 31 wt.% $\mathrm{Sb}$ and 22 wt.% $\mathrm{Sn}$. From $\mathrm{U}_1$, the liquid separates into $(\mathrm{Sb}) + \mathrm{SbSn(LT)}$, until solidification ends at the ternary eutectic point $\mathbf{E}$. As shown in Fig. 3, the liquidus surface is composed of five areas representing the primary crystallization of the four Sb-Sn solid solutions: (Sb), SbSn(HT), SbSn(LT), and (Sn) occurring in the binary Sb-Sn system, and (Pb). Considering the internal boundaries of these areas, monovariant curves $\mathbf{e}_1\mathbf{E}$ and $\mathbf{e}_2\mathbf{E}$ represent the eutectic separations of (Pb) and (Sb) and of (Pb) and SbSn(LT), respectively. Along $\mathfrak{p}_1\mathbf{U}_1$, the peritectic reaction, $(\mathrm{Sb}) + \mathrm{L} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{SbSn}(\mathrm{HT})$, occurs; along $\mathfrak{p}_2\mathbf{U}_1$, the peritectic reaction, $\mathrm{L} + \mathrm{SbSn}(\mathrm{HT}) \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{SbSn}(\mathrm{LT})$, occurs; along $\mathrm{U}_1\mathbf{E}$, the eutectic separation of (Sb) and SbSn(LT) occurs; along $\mathfrak{p}_3\mathbf{U}_2$, the peritectic reaction, SbSn(LT) + $\mathrm{L} \rightleftharpoons (\mathrm{Sn})$, occurs. Eutectic separations of (Pb) and SbSn(LT) and of (Pb) and (Sn) occur, respectively, along the monovariant curves $\mathbf{e}_2\mathbf{U}_2$ and $\mathbf{U}_2\mathbf{e}_3$.

associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: For the $2 < X < 3$ portion of the $T - X$ diagram, containing the $\eta$ phases, which is presented on a larger scale in Fig. 3, we have relied entirely on the XRD data published by [87Bor] and [89Bor]. The larger scale of Fig. 3 allows for more detail of boundary uncertainties to be shown, as well as information on temperatures of cubic-to-tetragonal transformations determined prior to the work of [87Bor] and [89Bor]. This portion of the $T - X$ diagram represents a complex situation for which, as has been noted by [89Bor], an adequate description of a number of aspects is still not available. The data presented by [87Bor] and [89Bor] seem to offer the most comprehensive description, presently available, of the structural changes occurring in this region of the phase diagram and provide a hope that a background description is now available for correlating the various pieces of information on structural and thermal transitions. In selecting the boundaries of the $\eta_{1}$ and $\eta_{2}$ phase regions as provided by the work of [87Bor] and [89Bor], we have adopted the simplest choice and have used only data from one source to keep this choice simple. These phase boundaries are based on XRD determinations which are responsive only to the arrangement of the metallic Ce atoms. Neutron diffraction (ND) studies, responsive also to the presence of the hydrogens, tend to support the locations of these boundaries, in the main, but there are still some discrepancies which require further work for their resolution. [89Bor] also published proposed phase boundaries based on DSC measurements, the major features of which support the phase boundaries we have quoted from the XRD measurements of [89Bor]. In particular they support the general outline of the phase boundaries for the two regions with tetragonal structures and the existence of the mixed phase miscibility regions. Earlier measurements by [84Bas] used differential thermal analysis (DTA) to locate phase boundaries in the same region ( $2 < X < 3$ ) of the Ce-H phase diagram. While DTA is not as useful as DSC where small heats of transformation are involved, these DTA measurements did, nonetheless, obtain a phase boundary (shown as a dot-dash curve in Fig. 3) which corresponds fairly closely with the outline of the $\eta_{1}$ phase and its associated miscibility gaps as determined by [89Bor]. From their interpretations of their DTA measurements, [84Bas] were also aware that they were encountering mixed phase regions associated with the occurrence of ordered phases. One such region identified by [84Bas], is rather similar to that on the low $X$ side of the $\eta_{1}$ phase, our labelling $\varepsilon + \eta_{1}$ , but another involves a mixture of two ordered phases which has no equivalent in the phase boundary scheme we have taken from [89Bor]. In suggesting a second order phase, [84Bas] have located it well inside the $\eta_{1} + \varepsilon$ region on the high $X$ side of the $\eta_{1}$ phase field, in terms of our labelling, and well removed from the location of the second ordered phase (our $\eta_{2}$ ). A likely but not necessarily sole cause for this discrepancy, could be the greater purity of the Ce used by [89Bor]. [91Aro] has also proposed a structural phase diagram for the temperature range up to $\sim 400\mathrm{K}$ , which shows an outline of a tetragonal distortion of the cubic phase fairly close, near the apex, to the outer envelope of the $\eta_{1}$ phase and its miscibility gaps as determined by [87Bor] and [89Bor] and displayed in Fig. 3. Otherwise, the [91Aro] diagram does not have much in common with the phase diagram proposed by [87Bor] and [89Bor]. Thus the XRD determination by [89Bor] of the boundaries for the $\eta$ phases is consistent in a number of respects with earlier work and also provides the single most comprehensive statement of the form and extent of those boundaries. Although [84Ohk] searched for plateaus in the Ce-H isotherms corresponding to those found earlier in their laboratory for the Sm-H system, they did not search at low enough temperatures to cover the $\eta$ phase fields shown in Fig. 1 and 3. The lowest isotherm data available in the literature for the $\mathrm{CeH}_X$ system were measured at $100^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ [55Mul] and as an examination of Fig. 1 and 3 shows, this isotherm would be just about at the peak of the phase field we have designated as $\eta_{1}$ , based on the determinations of [87Bor] and [89Bor]. It is thus unlikely that this isotherm would show any possible effect due the presence of the $\eta_{1}$ phase field unless the density of experimental points was very much higher than that available from the work of [55Mul]. Because of this recent change in the "terms of reference" for making structure determinations with Ce-H samples, we have divided the presentation of structural information between Table 2 and Fig. 3. In Fig. 3 we show the boundaries of the phases we have labelled $\eta_{1}$ and $\eta_{2}$ . These denote two phase fields consisting of tetragonal distortions of the cubic lattice found, over a large area of the phase diagram, for temperatures above $\sim 100^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and $X > 2$ (67 at. $\%$ H). These boundaries are based on 600 measurements of the lattice constants and determinations of the related crystal structures and have been taken directly from the presentation given by [89Bor]. The dashed lines attributed to [89Bor] in Fig. 3 represent the less well determined boundaries based on the XRD data of [89Bor]. Tabulations of data from their 600 XRD measurements have not been included in the [89Bor] paper, so that the form of Fig. 3, together with the more detailed plotting of the occurrence of tetragonal structures shown in the plot of Fig. 6 in [89Bor], give the only generally available account of their XRD measurements on $\mathrm{CeH}_X$ ( $2 \leq X < 3$ ) (67 to 75 at. $\%$ H) with samples of high metallic purity and adequately characterized hydrogen concentration. To give some indication of the relationship between the form of the boundaries shown in Fig. 3 and some earlier determinations of the onset of tetragonality, we have added to Fig. 3 the $T-X$ coordinates of those cubic-to-tetragonal transitions which have been reported from laboratories other than that of [89Bor]. The solid points plotted in Fig. 3 are for XRD data and are the coordinates of transition points; they do not correspond to particular entries in Table 2. It can be seen that there is a rough consistency between the solid points and the $\eta$ phase fields, with their associated miscibility gaps, but there are too few points to give any useful suggestion of the existence of the boundaries as determined from the measurements of [89Bor]. We have supplemented the experimental information described above and plotted in Fig. 3, with a construction showing two areas outlined by shading. The bounding curves of these areas give simple representations of boundary curves for the $\eta_{1}$ and $\eta_{2}$ phases which satisfy the conditions for such boundaries, if the $\eta_{1}/\varepsilon$ and $\eta_{2}/\varepsilon$ transitions are congruent at $X \cong 2.38$ and $X \cong 2.74$ respectively; that is, that the outer ( $\varepsilon$ -phase) and the inner ( $\eta_{1}$ - and $\eta_{2}$ -phase) boundaries meet at an extremum. The designations of phase fields given in the first column of Table 2 are made on the basis of the phase boundaries delineated in Fig. 1 and 3 and do not, necessarily, correspond to the designations given by the authors who provided the source data. There is an internal discrepancy between the [87Kal] representation of the extent of this straight line and the lower H concentration boundary of the $\eta_{1}$ phase field as shown in Fig. 3, a boundary we have drawn with scrupulous attention to the manner in which it was represented in Fig. 6 of [89Bor]. The representation of this boundary by dashed lines on the lower concentration side, presumably indicates some uncertainty as to its course. One possibility for the path of this boundary is suggested by the form of the boundary for the tetragonality of the $\mathrm{CeH}_X$ lattice, as shown in Fig. 7 of [89Bor], over the same range of $X$ values ( $\sim 2.3 < X < \sim 2.5$ ). Only further work on the details of the tetragonal distortion in this range of $X$ values can resolve this matter. As can be seen from an examination of Table 2 and, to some extent, from Fig. 3, the $\varepsilon$ -phase, with its cubic fluorite structure exists down to temperatures of a few K for a small range of $X$ values below $X = 3$ . However, from the work of [89Con], the observations of the presence of a cubic structure must be carefully specified in terms of the diffracting radiation used to make the determination. For example, [89Con] found that ND showed the existence of a tetragonal distortion for a $\mathrm{CeD}_{2.64}$ sample at $-123^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , in a location on the phase diagram for which XRD showed only a cubic structure (this point is marked as an open circle in Fig. 3). Thus it would appear that the Ce atoms were arranged with cubic (fcc) symmetry, while only the deuteriums underwent the displacements which gave the tetragonal distortion record seen with ND. For the $\varepsilon$ phase field at $X$ values approaching 3, [89Con] have also shown that noncubic, as well as cubic reflections can appear in both XRD and ND patterns. The location in the $\varepsilon$ phase field of the occurrence of this type of diffraction pattern, is shown by an open circle with an attached downward pointing arrow. The arrow is used to indicate that the mix of cubic and noncubic reflections was observed down to a temperature of $15\mathrm{K}$ $(-258^{\circ}\mathrm{C})$ . Attempts to identify the superstructures involved in these diffraction patterns have so far not been successful [89Con] but considerable effort was devoted to excluding the possibility that the presence of impurities in the Ce-H alloys was responsible for the observations. In the case of the [84Ohk] measurements however, the temperatures involved are considerably higher than the highest observed temperature of the $\eta_1$ phase field [87Bor, 89Bor] (see Fig. 3, and the sections "Equilibrium Diagram" and "Crystal Structures and Lattice Parameters"), so that the observed anomalous behavior of $-\Delta H$ and $-\Delta S$ is unlikely to be explained by such complexities.

The chemistry of these phases was measured using EMPA. The three corners of this triangle were established using the EMPA data, and are shown by Xs in Fig. 3(a). The compositions of the three phases observed were Nb-11Ti-0.7Si for the $(\mathrm{Nb},\mathrm{Ti},\mathrm{Si})$, Nb-26Ti-24Si for the $(\mathrm{Nb},\mathrm{Ti})_{3}\mathrm{Si}$ and Nb-19Ti-36Si for the $\mathrm{Nb(Ti)_5Si_3}$. The Si concentrations of the silicides were slightly lean of the stoichiometric compositions.
The Nb-15Ti-10Si composition reported by Subramanian et al. possessed $(\mathrm{Nb},\mathrm{Ti},\mathrm{Si})$ and $(\mathrm{Nb},\mathrm{Ti})_{3}\mathrm{Si}$, and the phase field was drawn considering these data. The data presented here are almost consistent with the Nb-15Ti-10Si data of Subramanian et al. but not the Nb-10Ti-10Si data because they reported that the latter contained $(\mathrm{Nb},\mathrm{Ti},\mathrm{Si})$, $(\mathrm{Nb},\mathrm{Ti})_{3}\mathrm{Si}$, and $\mathrm{Nb}(\mathrm{Ti})_{5}\mathrm{Si}_{3}$ and the Nb-10Ti-10Si is outside the three-phase triangle shown in Fig. 3(a). The data of Subramanian et al. are shown by the solid diamonds in Fig. 3(a).
No compositions were examined from this phase field or the $\mathrm{L} + (\mathrm{Nb},\mathrm{Ti})_3\mathrm{Si} + (\mathrm{Nb},\mathrm{Ti},\mathrm{Si})$ phase field. The phase fields shown in Fig. 3(a) are therefore estimates. It is difficult to obtain reliable data from these regions because of the steep nature of the liquidus surface, and the difficulties that liquid in the microstructure generates on postheat treatment cooling.
Two compositions from this phase field were examined: Nb-3Ti-16Si and Nb-9Ti-16Si. The microstructure of the Nb-3Ti-16Si was similar to that observed at $1500^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. It contained large-scale primary metal dendrites, a eutectic of $(\mathrm{Nb},\mathrm{Ti},\mathrm{Si})$ and $(\mathrm{Nb},\mathrm{Ti})_3\mathrm{Si}$ and a fine-scale eutectoid of $(\mathrm{Nb},\mathrm{Ti},\mathrm{Si})$ and $\mathrm{Nb}(\mathrm{Ti})_5\mathrm{Si}_3$. In the isothermal section shown in Fig. 3(c), the Nb-9Ti-16Si composition was considered to be close to the phase boundary between this two-phase field and the $(\mathrm{Nb},\mathrm{Ti},\mathrm{Si}) - (\mathrm{Nb},\mathrm{Ti})_3\mathrm{Si} - \mathrm{Nb}(\mathrm{Ti})_5\mathrm{Si}_3$ three-phase field. Although the eutectoid transformation was not complete in the Nb-3Ti-16Si, it was considered that given sufficient time, it would have proceeded to completion. A small amount of silicide precipitation was also observed in the metal dendrites.
Electron beam microprobe analysis data of the Nb-9Ti-16Si composition are shown for the $(\mathrm{Nb},\mathrm{Ti},\mathrm{Si})$ and the $\mathrm{Nb(Ti)_5Si_3}$; these analyses place the solvus lines and provide an estimate of the Nb-rich corners of the $(\mathrm{Nb},\mathrm{Ti},\mathrm{Si})$-(Nb,Ti)Si-Nb(Ti)Si triangle. The EMPA data are shown as Xs in Fig. 3(c).

associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: The up-to-date information available for the binary RE-Mg systems has been summarized in the figure. The figure shows the diagrams formed with the trivalent lanthanides. Y has been added in the series and included among the lanthanides in a position corresponding to the average values of its atomic properties. This subdivision into two groups of the RE-Mg systems may be conveniently related to two different, well-defined, alloying behaviors. In each group (bearing in mind that the data are taken from various sources in literature), we note a gradual and smooth property variation as a function of atomic properties, such as the atomic radius. In the figure, we note a progressive variation in the number of compounds and in the stoichiometries of the phases richest in Mg from 12:1, 17:2, 41:5 to 24:5; this may be related to the correlation between the decrease of the atomic radius ratio $\mathrm{r}_{\mathrm{RE}} / \mathrm{r}_{\mathrm{Mg}}$ and the decrease of the coordination number of $\mathrm{Mg}$ around RE with the coordination number dropping from CN20 for the $\mathrm{ThMn}_{12}$-type structure of RE of low atomic number to reach CN16 for RE of high atomic number. More complex, possibly metastable, situations have often been reported for the Mg-rich alloys. In the figure, finally, we notice the variation of the melting behavior of the different phases, which could possibly also be related to the progressive change of the rare earth melting point. In particular, we notice the melting behavior of the $\mathrm{REMg}_3$ phases: many of them melt near $800^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. Their congruent or incongruent behavior, however, may be related to the trend of the liquidus curve descending from the rare earth melting point. associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: Consider the isobaric and isothermal addition of some carbon to an Fe-C alloy in an original state of $\alpha +\gamma$. The $\alpha/\gamma$ interface is sometimes rather immobile, and we can imagine that a new state of higher but uniform $\mu_{\mathrm{C}}$ is established before the $\alpha \rightarrow \gamma$ phase transformation occurs. When it finally occurs, $\mu_{\mathrm{C}}$ will decrease, and the original value will eventually be reestablished. The arrows on the abscissa in the figure illustrate that the system returns to the old two-phase equilibrium; the only difference is a change in the relative amounts of the two phases. This is in accordance with Le Chatelier's principle, but it is as trivial as the two cases illustrated in Fig. 3. Instead, consider a ternary alloy under isobaric and isothermal conditions. It is originally in an $\alpha + \gamma$ state represented by a tie-line in the figure. If carbon were added without a phase transformation, both phases would move horizontally, and if the diffusivity of carbon is high enough in comparison with the dimension of the specimen, they will have the same $\mu_{\mathrm{C}}$. In the figure, this is indicated by drawing the isoactivity (equipotential) line for C connected to another tie-line. The original alloy composition is indicated with an "x," and a third arrow shows how it has changed.

associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: Au in Au-Ta alloys behaves as a highly volatile element because of the large difference in the melting points of Au and Ta (1064.43 and $3020^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, respectively). Therefore, the composition of Au-Ta specimens is difficult to maintain during heat treatments, especially in the Aurich range. This seems to be the cause of the differences reported for the composition ranges of the three intermediate phases existing in this system. The homogeneity ranges reported by Raub, Beeskow, and Menzel were always richer in Au than those of Camacho. The reason for this disagreement seems to result from the difference in the estimated composition of specimens. The values are nominal compositions before alloying. Apart from the differences in homogeneity ranges, further disagreements were found for each phase. Figure 2 shows a schematic diagram derived solely from the experimental work of [61Rau]. According to the lattice parameter and microscopic work by [61Rau], the maximum solubility of Ta in (Au) is about 11 at.% at $1000^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. An alloy of 12.9 at.% Ta quenched from $1000^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ showed evidence of a liquid phase. Hence, a eutectic reaction is expected at about $1000^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. The AuTa compound having no appreciable solubility range and occurring at compositions in excess of 50 at.% Ta, according to [61Rau], is likely to be the same as the $\mathrm{Au}_2\mathrm{Ta}_3$ phase. [61Rau] also postulated the existence of a transition in AuTa alloy from microscopic observations. [61Rau] found no solubility range in the $\sigma$ phase $(\mathrm{AuTa}_2)$. Considering the volatility of Au, the nominal $\mathrm{AuTa}_3$ phase reported by [61Rau] may be identical to the $\mathrm{AuTa}_5$ phase. No homogeneity range was detected by [61Rau]. The results of X-ray observations made on specimens quenched from various temperatures [61Rau] suggested that the phase they reported as $\mathrm{AuTa}_3$ may not be stable above $\sim 1100^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$.

associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration:
The assessed equilibrium phase diagram of the Mg-Si system, as displayed in Fig. 1 and Table 1, consists of: (1) L, the liquid; (2) (Mg), the terminal Mg solid solution with a maximum solid solubility of 0.003 at.% Si; (3) Mg2Si, the stoichiometric intermetallic compound; and (4) (Si), the terminal Si solid solution with negligible solid solubility of Mg.
In the assessed phase diagram, the (Mg) liquidus curve has been taken from [40Ray], and the liquidus curve for the rest of the diagram has been based on selected data of [68Gef] and [77Sch].
Eutectic Reactions. There are two eutectic reactions in this system: (1) L ⇌ (Mg) + Mg2Si; and (2) L ⇌ Mg2Si + (Si). The composition of the eutectic point on the Mg-rich side at 3.48 at.% Si, as reported by [09Vog], is significantly higher than the 1.19 to 1.74 at.% Si deduced from metallographic analysis by [09Leb]. Thermal analysis of [40Ray] placed this eutectic point at 637.6 °C and 1.16 at.% Si. These data are in very good agreement with the recently published data, 1.3 at.% Si by [77Sch], and with those reported by [09Leb], [27Sch], and [37Got]. The Mg-rich eutectic point of 1.16 at.% Si and 637.6 °C determined by [40Ray] has been selected for the assessed phase diagram (Fig. 1).
The extrapolated hypoeutectic and hypereutectic liquidus curves of [77Sch], as shown in their diagram, dictate that the eutectic composition be in the range of 52.4 to 52.67 at.% Si, differing from the 54.14 at.% Si value they designated as the eutectic composition. It appears that the estimation of the eutectic composition from the solidification time of the eutectic portion of the hypoeutectic and hypereutectic alloys tends to be inaccurate. Calculation of the Mg-Si phase diagram in the present evaluation also indicates that the eutectic is at 53.0 at.% Si and 947 ± 0.5 °C, near the eutectic temperature and composition reported by [68Gef]. Therefore, in the assessed Mg-Si phase diagram of Fig. 1, the Si-rich eutectic point has been taken from [68Gef].
Mg2Si Compound. The congruently melting, stoichiometric Mg2Si is the only stable compound in the Mg-Si system. Magnesium silicide, Mg2Si, is a semiconductor (n type) with a forbidden gap of 0.78 eV at 0 K. [09Vog] reported two different melting points for this compound, 1090 and 1102 °C, corresponding to the low- (92.3 wt.% Si) and high-purity (99.2 wt.% Si) Si used in the preparation of the alloys. Both of these temperatures are higher than the 1070 °C reported by [26Woh] and the temperatures reported by other investigators. [68Gef] and [77Sch] reported 1085 and 1078 °C, respectively. The calculation of [81Dor] placed the melting point of Mg2Si at 1080 to 1082 °C. The value of 1085 °C, selected for the assessed Mg-Si phase diagram (Fig. 1), has been taken from [68Gef]. This is in agreement with 1087.0 °C that has been calculated by the present evaluators. Moreover, [68Gef] used +99.99% Mg and 99.999% Si in their experiments; these are the highest purity starting materials used in the various investigations of the Mg-Si phase diagram.

associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: Despite the technical importance of the Cr-H system, the available information concerning the phase diagram is limited and not very reliable. Based on the few investigations that were carried out in the Cr-rich region, the partial phase diagrams shown in Fig. 1 and 2 were constructed. The occurrence of three intermediate hydride phases—CrH, $\mathrm{CrH}_2$, and $\mathrm{CrH}_3$—was reported in the literature, but the existence of $\mathrm{CrH}_3$ is doubtful. The hydrides are stable only at elevated $\mathrm{H}_2$ pressures, but they can be retained in a metastable state under ambient conditions for limited times. The problems associated with high-pressure studies and the occurrence of nonequilibrium states make it difficult to establish a reliable Cr-H phase diagram. The Cr used in most investigations was obtained by electrodeposition from aqueous $\mathrm{CrO}_3$ solutions; very few investigators reported the purity of the Cr. The liquidus and solidus curves (Fig. 1) are based on the data of [81Sha]. They were drawn to match the isobars in the liquid and solid states. Because the melting temperature of Cr reported by [81Sha] $(1773^{\circ}\mathrm{C})$ is $90^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ lower than the adopted value of 1863 ${}^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ [Melt], the temperatures of both curves were raised by $90^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. The isobar $P(\mathrm{H}_2) = 1$ bar in the liquid state is described by Eq 1: $$\log (\text {at.} \% \mathrm {H}) = 1.970 - 5330 / T (\mathrm {K}) \tag{Eq1}$$ The isobar $P(\mathrm{H}_2) = 1$ bar in the solid state (Fig. 1) was obtained by extrapolation of the solubility curve (Eq 2, below) to higher temperatures. Analogous to that for the liquid state, the $P(\mathrm{H}_2) = 100$ bar isobar in the solid state is calculated from the 1-bar curve, with validity of Sieverts' law assumed.

associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: The structural details of the phases included in the assessed Au-Cu phase diagram are summarized in Table 1. Liquidus and solidus boundaries established by [62Ben] (Table 2), who used cooling and heating curves $(\sim 2$ to 3 $^\circ\mathrm{C / min})$ , are accepted in the assessed diagram. The assessed liquidus boundaries differ little from the early work of [00Rob]. The decrease in the melting temperature of Cu with additions of Au (up to 3.3 at.%) determined by [1897Hey] is also consistent with the presently accepted liquidus. The liquidus boundary in [Hansen] was based on [34Bro1] and [35Bro] (Table 2), whose minimum liquidus temperature is about $20^\circ{}C$ lower than the presently assessed value. The liquidus and solidus temperatures reported by [34Bro1] in the composition ranges near the pure elements were higher than the presently assessed temperatures. The liquidus in the assessed diagram can also be derived from the present thermodynamic assessment, which is consistent with the reported thermodynamic quantities. The solidus temperatures of [62Ben] are lower than the calculated values (maximum difference $\sim 10^\circ\mathrm{C}$ ) in the composition range $\sim 80$ to 90 at.% Cu, where the actual thermodynamic properties may be slightly different from the model properties. The accepted $\mathbf{AuCu}_3(\mathbf{I})$ phase boundaries are based primarily on the electrical resistivity and X-ray studies by [55Rhi]. The $\mathrm{AuCu_3(I)}$ phase is stable over wide composition limits on both sides of the stoichiometric point. It forms from the disordered phase by a congruent transformation at the stoichiometric composition and at Au-rich limits by a eutectoid transformation. The congruent and eutectoid temperatures at 390 and $284^\circ\mathrm{C}$ , respectively, and the eutectoid composition at 36 at.% Au are accepted from [55Rhi] as being the most precise. Most of the presently assessed phase boundaries are based on the isothermal change in the electrical resistivity measured by [55Rhi], [59Hir], and [59Kor]. From the trend of the $[(Au)+Au_{3}Cu]/Au_{3}Cu$ phase boundary and the $(Au)+AuCu \rightarrow Au_{3}Cu$ reaction at $\sim 240^\circ\mathrm{C}$ , the Cu-rich limit of the ordered $\mathrm{Au}_{3}\mathrm{Cu}$ phase is about 38.5 at.% Cu, in agreement with the value reported by [64Tot], rather than 35 at.% Cu reported earlier by [31Gru], [32Leb], and [55Rhi]. Neither electrical resistivity [36Joh] nor the superlattice line intensity attain a maximum at 25 at.% Cu. Thus, the $\mathrm{Au}_{3}\mathrm{Cu}$ phase is not symmetrical near the stoichiometric composition. The assessed diagram is primarily based on [55Rhi], [57Pia], and [59Pia1] for the high-temperature boundaries and on [57Pia] for the $\mathrm{AuCu(II)} \rightleftarrows \mathrm{AuCu(I)}$ boundaries, for which [55Rhi] did not present any data. The $\mathrm{AuCu(D)}\rightleftharpoons$ AuCu(II) transformation temperature is accepted as 410 $\pm 2^\circ\mathrm{C}$ . The $\mathrm{AuCu(II)}\rightleftharpoons$ AuCu(I) temperature is accepted as $385\pm 2^\circ\mathrm{C}$ . The accepted phase diagram in the region of the two-phase field between $\mathrm{AuCu}_3$ and $\mathrm{AuCu(I)}$ , from 34 to 37 at. $\%$ Au, and the associated eutectoid decomposition of the fcc solid solution is based on [31Gru] and [55Rhi].

associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: The calculated phase diagram is shown in Fig. 12. The experimentally assessed diagram from [88Rog] was used in this work as the basis for the thermodynamic modeling, [88Rog] preferring the phase diagram established by [65Rud1] to the version by [71Por]. The phase diagram from [65Rud1] is basically consistent with the version accepted by [90Mas], except for minor changes concerning the accepted melting temperatures of zirconium-free hafnium at $2231^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ ([65Rud1] at $2218^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$) and of boron at $2092^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ ([65Rud1] at $\sim 2100^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$) as well as the accepted $\alpha/\beta$ transformation temperature of Hf at $1743^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ ([65Rud1] at $\sim 1800^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$). Both compounds, HfB and $\mathrm{HfB}_2$, were claimed to form at stoichiometric compositions with a homogeneous range less than 1 to 2 at. $\%$ B. The solubility of B in $\alpha$ Hf at low temperatures is minimal (< 0.5 at. $\%$ B) but increases with temperature, resulting in a peritectoid decomposition of the $\alpha$ Hf solid solution into $\beta$ Hf + HfB at 1800 $\pm 15^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. From the increase in the lattice parameters of $\alpha$ Hf with respect to the pure metal, an interstitial type of solution is suggested. The solubility of B in $\beta$ Hf at the temperature of the $\beta$ Hf + HfB eutectic was found to be less than 2 at. $\%$ B; for the solubility of Hf in $\beta$ B an estimate of 1 at. $\%$ Hf was reported at the temperature of the $\mathrm{HfB}_2 + \beta$ B eutectic [65Rud1]. A quite satisfactory agreement is obtained when the calculated invariant equilibrium data are compared with the selected experimental values from [65Rud1]. Temperatures agree very well within a few degrees, and compositions correspond within the given invariances. As can be seen in the figure, a large difference exists between the calculated liquidus boundaries and the experimental temperatures determined by [65Rud1] using the Pirani melting-point technique. These liquidus temperatures can only be regarded as estimations, particularly because of the lack of suitable crucible materials for the aggressive melts at elevated temperatures. Secondly, the Pirani melting-point technique is virtually incapable of providing reliable liquidus data due to both gradual loss of the mechanical strength of the sample specimen during measurement and loss of the black body measuring hole when filled with melt.

The Lugscheider-Ettmayer investigation involved X-ray diffraction at temperature with polycrystalline samples of fixed composition. Patterns were taken from nine different alloys with compositions between 56.5 and 97.5 at.% Mn inclusive and with temperatures ranging up to $1020^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. Cu Kα radiation was employed so that differences between contributions of V species and Mn species to the diffraction peaks were unresolvable. The oxygen content of the starting materials was high, with 0.2 at.% O in Mn and 0.4 at.% O in V. Diffraction specimens were protected by static atmospheres of either $\mathrm{H}_{2}$ or He; $\mathrm{H}_{2}$ was inferred to be inert because comparable results were obtained in those cases where duplicate runs were made with the same alloy under different atmospheres. A partial diagram based on the Lugscheider-Ettmayer work is shown in Fig. 3. Because this partial diagram is based on only nine alloy compositions and a restricted temperature range, some latitude was exercised with the dashed lines, both to emphasize the requisite existence by the phase rule of alternating one-phase and two-phase fields and to extrapolate above $1020^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. In comparison with Fig. 1, this version of the diagram contains two additional phases, $\alpha'$ and $\beta'$, that have been categorized respectively as $\chi$ and $\pi$-type phases. These phases belong to a crystallographic family which includes the $\alpha$-Mn, $\beta$-Mn, and $\sigma$ phases. Actually, with Cu Kα radiation, $\alpha'$ was not structurally distinguishable from $\alpha$, nor $\beta'$ from $\beta$; rather, the new phases were postulated on the bases of trends in the lattice parameters as functions of temperature and/or composition. Additionally, Lugscheider and Ettmayer found an 86 at.% Mn alloy to be two-phase throughout the temperature range of investigation, which implies a Mn-rich terminus for the $\sigma$ phase of $< 86$ at.% Mn. For compositions greater than 85 at.% Mn, there is ambiguity because of conflicting data. Both proposed versions of the phase relationships in the Mn-rich region are equivocal, and it remains for some additional definitive data to resolve the situation.

Based on boundary line extremes, the extents in both $x$ and $y$ dimensions were determined for a given surface. A bounding rectangle was constructed that would envelop each surface in the projection of the $x - y$ plane. An array of points were assigned and distributed evenly throughout the rectangle. A search subroutine for each point was used to determine whether a particular point fell within the phase field. The algorithm for determining the phase field in which a point fell involved searching for phase boundaries and triangle edges that most closely surrounded the point and had a common compound embedded in their tags. When the point fell within the chosen phase field, the temperature of the point was determined using Eq 1, and the triplet was stored in an array to be sent to 3DGT. When the point fell outside of the phase field, it was relocated to one of the side boundaries, its temperature was calculated on that basis, and this revised triplet was then stored. $$

Equation 3 has three real solutions instead of a single value of $X_{\mathrm{Ta}}$ above a certain temperature for each system. The minimum temperature at which Eq 3 has three solutions corresponds to the monotectic temperature of the system. The two $X_{\mathrm{Ta}}$ values out of the three solutions at the monotectic temperature will be common corresponding to the monotectic composition, and the third value represents the RE-rich liquidus composition at this temperature. The Clausius-Clapeyron equation representing the liquidus curve for equilibrium between a pure solid RE and a liquid solution of Ta in the RE can be given as:
