associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: An extrapolation of the liquidus of $\mathbf{RbTl}_3$ above its peritectic melting point in the binary Rb-Tl diagram requires a very abrupt change of curvature above the peritectic temperature. The liquidus temperature of $\mathbf{RbTl}_3$ must fall below that of $\mathbf{RbTl}_2$ above the peritectic temperature (to avoid the $E$-type error), and the liquidus of $\mathbf{RbTl}_3$ must have a peak at the composition of $\mathbf{RbTl}_3$ when extrapolated. As a result, the needed curvature change becomes very pronounced only near the peritectic temperature. In the above example, if an ideal liquid is assumed, the required numerical free energy change for the Gibbs energy of $\mathrm{RbTl}_3$ (with respect to liquid Rb and liquid Tl) is $-3660 + 2.063T$ J/mol above the peritectic temperature and $-1420 - 2.139T$ J/mol below the peritectic temperature. The change from one form of the Gibbs energy function to the other form in a narrow temperature range appears to be unjustified and unreasonable. Thus, in the Rb-Tl case, the form of the $\mathrm{RbTl}_2$ liquidus is most likely in error.

associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: Isothermal sections presented in the figure are based on literature data and on the experimental data obtained in the present work in accordance with the accepted binary systems. The isothermal section at $1250^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ is based on the work of [1989Kha2]. However, for consistency with the new Al-Ti binary, the phase equilibria involving $(\alpha \mathrm{Ti})$ were introduced. We have to acknowledge that [1989Kha2] introduced equilibria involving $\mathrm{RuAl_2}$, although they were not in agreement with the binary Al-Ru diagram known at that time. But these data now perfectly comply with the Al-Ru binary accepted throughout this work. The homogeneity region of the $\tau_{1}$ phase is assumed to be the same as at solidus temperatures. The extension of the $\tau_{2}$ single-phase field is compatible with the trend of its decrease with decreasing temperature as seen in samples annealed at $1100^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and lower. Decreasing the temperature from $1250^{\circ}\mathrm{C} - 1100^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ results in the phase equilibria changing due to the appearance of $\mathrm{Ti}_{3}\mathrm{Al}\left(\alpha_{2}\right)$, which results in a strongly decreasing aluminum content in $(\alpha \mathrm{Ti})$ and $(\beta \mathrm{Ti})$. The isothermal section at $1100^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ reveals two three-phase equilibria $(p)$ $\beta +\alpha +\alpha_{2}$ and $(q)$ $\beta +\alpha_{2} + \mathrm{TiAl}(\gamma)$, which were not observed at $1250^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. These equilibria are the product of an invariant equilibrium, $\alpha +\gamma = \beta +\alpha_{2}$ (U14), which is connected to the binary eutectoid reaction $\alpha = \gamma +\alpha_{2}$ at $1114^{\circ}\mathrm{C},$ and to the three-phase region $\alpha +\beta +\gamma$ at $1250^{\circ}\mathrm{C}.$ The alternative reaction $(\alpha +\gamma +\beta = \alpha_{2})$ was rejected because it would suggest a significant solubility of Ru in $\alpha_{2}$ for which there is no evidence from the experimental data. Phase relations in the region $\tau_{2}\mathrm{-RuAl_2}\mathrm{-Ru_{4}Al_{13}}\mathrm{-TiAl_{3}}$ change from the two-phase equilibrium $\mathrm{TiAl_3} + \mathrm{RuAl_2}$ towards the equilibrium $\tau_{2} + \mathrm{Ru}_{4}\mathrm{Al}_{13}$. This fact is revealed from combined x-ray, SEM, and EMPA data for samples in the as-cast state and those annealed at $1100^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. $\tau_{2}$ was found to be perfectly homogenized, in contrast to as-cast conditions, and it forms equilibria with $\tau_{1}$ and $\mathrm{RuAl_2}$. The general tendency in the change of the $(\beta \mathrm{Ti})$ homogeneity region on lowering of temperature can be seen from a comparison of the isothermal sections at $1100^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and $1050^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ after [1989Kha2]. Only one inconsistency in the $1050^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ isothermal section of [1989Kha2] has to be noted—the homogeneity region of $(\beta \mathrm{Ti})$ meets the Al-Ti diagram two times in disagreement with the binary system. Therefore, phase equilibria for the Al-rich part of $(\beta \mathrm{Ti})$ have to be read as in the isothermal section at $1100^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. From comparison of the proposed sections at 1100 and $950^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, one can see a significant change in the phase relations concerning the $\tau_{2}$-phase. A rather extended single $\tau_{2}$-phase field, observed at higher temperatures, reduces to a point at $950^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, and this phase refrains from forming equilibria with $\tau_{1}$. Furthermore, the structural transformation from bcc $\beta \mathrm{Ti}$ to CsCl-type (denoted as $\beta^{\prime}\mathrm{Ti}$) was included in the isothermal sections at $1250^{\circ}$ and $1100^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ by dotted lines following the data of Khataee et al. associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: A composite Efimov-Savitskii diagram is shown in Fig. 1 by dashed lines. According to Savitskii et al., the materials that produced the phase relationships of this dashed diagram were electrolytic Cu and 99.7 wt.% pure V; specific impurities in the V are listed as 0.17 wt.% C, 0.02 wt.% N, 0.1 wt.% O, and other impurities not more than 0.05 wt.% Because of differences in gram atomic weights, this means that the total interstitial impurities, C, N and O, in the V were present at a combined level of 1.1 to 1.2 at.% This also appears to be the situation for the V-Cu system, although the qualitative features of the Efimov-Savitskii diagram appear to be reliable. These qualitative features include quite limited terminal solubility on the Cu-rich side, peritectic melting of the Cu-rich terminal solution, and a monotectic reaction at elevated temperatures. The experimental points of Allibert and Driole are plotted as triangles in Fig. 1, and, at temperatures above 1100 °C, the solid lines in the figure represent their derived diagram. It may be noted that the Allibert-Driole diagram is in reasonable accord with the Efimov-Savitskii diagram with regard to liquidus compositions in the temperature range 1150 to 1400 °C. Above 1400 °C, the liquidus compositions diverge appreciably. Although the Allibert-Driole diagram also indicates a monotectic reaction, it is at significantly higher temperature with significantly different compositions for the two liquids in equilibrium, and the associated miscibility gap is much smaller with a lower critical temperature. In the V-rich region, the Allibert-Driole diagram shows the terminal solubility of Cu in V at any given temperature to be roughly one-half as great as indicated in the Efimov-Savitskii diagram. Attributing the differences between the two diagrams to differences in purity of the V of the two investigations is consistent with the observations because the impurities should be highly diluted and have least effect in the Cu-rich region where the experimental agreement is best, and should be less diluted and have more effect at higher V concentrations where divergence occurs. On the basis of purity, it must be concluded that even though portions of the Allibert-Driole diagram are extrapolated with a model based upon regular solutions, this diagram is more likely to represent the pure binary V-Cu system. All reports indicate that the terminal solubility of V in Cu is quite small. Savitskii et al. report peritectic melting of the Cu-rich terminal solution at 1120 °C at a composition of X_Cu = 0.992 in equilibrium with a liquidus of X_Cu = 0.966. They further report that, with decreasing temperature, the Cu-rich solvus becomes more Cu-rich, reaching a composition near X_Cu = 0.999 at room temperature. A detailed set of Cu-rich solvus data is provided by Eicke and Hahlbohm and is based primarily upon electrical resistivity values as a function of quench temperature, but with confirmation also by other electrical measurements. The Eicke and Hahlbohm data are given in Table 1 and are included in Fig. 1 and 2. It must be emphasized that the variations among these three reports involve differences in solvus compositions of the order of tenths of an atomic percent, so there is little question that the terminal solubility of V in Cu is quite limited. However, both because of compatibility with liquidus data and for thermodynamic reasons, the data of Eicke and Hahlbohm are preferred. Compatibility between the solvus and solidus values is evident from the positions of the experimental points on the solidus and liquidus lines in Fig. 1; the slope discontinuity that is requisite at the peritectic temperature is, on the scale of the figure, unlikely to be large enough to be visually discernible or to invalidate a smooth interpolation between solidus and solvus points. If one uses the values of Savitskii et al. of X_Cu = 0.992 for the solvus and X_Cu = 0.996 for the liquidus at the peritectic reaction, a Clausius-Clapeyron approximation predicts a peritectic temperature ~5 °C above the melting point of Cu, or 1088 °C rather than the 1120 °C of the Savitskii report. A peritectic reaction temperature only a few degrees above the melting point of Cu is also supported by the experimental results of McHugh and of Stevens. McHugh found cooling curves for V-Cu alloys to exhibit thermal arrests at 1085 °C, two degrees above the thermal arrest of pure Cu. Stevens also made thermal analyses and his data include twenty-four points from ten alloy compositions. The values show a rather wide scatter, but deletion of statistically aberrant points yields 1088 ± 3 °C for the peritectic temperature. McHugh's value of 1085 °C, within the uncertainty of the Stevens result, has been selected for the accompanying diagram because, first, a Clausius-Clapeyron approximation with the extrapolated compositions shown in Fig. 2 indicates a melting point elevation of ~2 °C and, second, thermodynamic functions for the formation of the three phases are compatible at 1085 °C.

Using the results of the quantitative phase analysis and the lever rule, the authors have determined the tie-lines and tie-triangles as well as the single-phase boundaries in the solid-state equilibria region, as depicted in the figure. Various two- and three-phase fields could be identified, surrounding two ternary compounds $(\tau, \zeta)$ and the liquid. In the Fe-rich corner, the extended two-phase fields $[\alpha + \tau]$, $[\zeta + \tau]$, $[\mathrm{Fe}_{17}\mathrm{Gd}_2 + \tau]$, and $[\mathrm{Fe}_{23}\mathrm{Gd}_6 + \tau]$ are separated by small three-phase fields $[\alpha + \tau + \zeta]$, $[\zeta + \tau + \mathrm{Fe}_{17}\mathrm{Gd}_2]$, and $[\mathrm{Fe}_{17}\mathrm{Gd}_2 + \tau + \mathrm{Fe}_{23}\mathrm{Gd}_6]$. On the (Mo) side $\tau$ phase coexists with (Mo) terminal solid solution and also forms extended two-phase fields with the intermetallic compounds R and $\mu$. The liquid phase is characterized by the largest two- and three-phase fields coexisting in equilibrium with $\mathrm{Fe}_{23}\mathrm{Gd}_6$, $\tau$, (Mo), and Gd phases. Some multiphase regions shown are only suggestions because no alloys of corresponding compositions were prepared; such is the case for the equilibria $\alpha - \gamma - \zeta$, $\gamma - \zeta - \mathrm{Fe}_{17}\mathrm{Gd}_2$, $\mathrm{Fe}_{17}\mathrm{Gd}_2 - \mathrm{Fe}_{23}\mathrm{Gd}_6$, R-$\tau - \mu$, and (Mo)-L-Gd. To combine the predicted phase regions into an isothermal section, a number of instructions based on Gibbs phase rule were used. Additional experimental work would be required in appropriate composition ranges for a more accurate determination of tie-lines and tie-triangles. The scale used in the figure does not allow the displaying of all the phase relations in detail. The ternary phase $\tau$ with the $\mathrm{ThMn}_{12}$-type structure exhibits a broad homogeneity range. Three samples were found to contain only this phase. It was also identified in all the multiphase samples investigated; these were used to determine the appropriate phase boundary. Taking into account the location of the pertinent alloys in the phase diagram, the unit-cell parameters of several compositions at the boundary of the single-phase field $\tau$ could be estimated. It should be pointed out that the homogeneity region of the $\tau$ phase is much more sensitive to Mo content than to Gd content. Another ternary phase $(\zeta)$ with a monoclinic unit cell probably has a very narrow, if any, homogeneity range. It was identified only in two three-phase samples together with $\alpha$Fe and $\tau$ phases. However, in view of the structural relations to the $\mathrm{ThMn}_{12}$ and $\mathrm{Th}_2\mathrm{Zn}_{17}$ types, some variation of Mo content cannot be excluded. The maximum solubility (up to 5 at.% Mo) was found for $\mathrm{Fe}_{17}\mathrm{Gd}_2$ phase. The terminal solutions of the Fe-Mo binary phase diagram were found to contain negligible amounts of Gd.

associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: The most undeniable effect of a magnetic transition on phase boundaries is a change in solubility of a second phase, observed in many systems. It occurs whenever the Curie temperature intersects a transus line, and not only does the effect coincide with the Curie temperature, but also its magnitude is proportional to the degree of magnetization involved. This is well demonstrated by looking at the effect of cobalt additions on the solubility of other solutes (Fig. 2). With so many magnetic effects occurring in iron-base alloys, one might well ask why cobalt-base alloys, with their much higher Curie temperature, are not prone to similar variations. The answer seems to be that as far as solubility changes of precipitates are concerned the effect is obviously there, but as far as effects on the fcc/cph equilibrium in cobalt-base alloys are concerned, these are not to be expected because the magnetic properties of the two cobalt allotropes are very similar (remember that it is the relative magnetic properties that count).

evidence.materials_system: cobalt-base alloys; iron-base alloys; cobalt additions
evidence.phase_regions_boundaries: phase boundaries; transus line; solubility of a second phase; fcc/cph equilibrium

For modeling of individual phases, the sublattice concept was applied. Among Ti-Al-X systems, $X = \mathrm{Nb}$ and Cr systems were assessed using Thermo-Calc with the modified database of Saunders, but there is little information for the $X = \mathrm{Mo}$ system. For the Ti-Al-Mo calculation, only the interactions of Al-(Ti,Mo) are considered for $\alpha$ and $\beta$ phases, and these were optimized so that the calculated boundaries match experimental observation. The interaction is simplified because the Ti-Mo binary system shows a wide region of solid solution, with the interactions of Al-(Ti,Mo) being expected to play an important role in the Ti-Al-Mo ternary system. Initial values of the interactions of Al-(Ti,Mo) for calculation were estimated on the basis of the Ti-Al-Cr and Ti-Al-Nb systems. The results for the Ti-Mo-Al calculation are shown at $1573\mathrm{K}$. The phase equilibrium of this system can be discussed using the figure and earlier reported studies. One clear feature of this system $(X = \mathrm{Mo})$ compared to other Ti-Al-X $(X = \mathrm{Cr},\mathrm{Nb})$ systems is a low-solubility limit of the transition metal, Mo, in both $\alpha$ and $\gamma$ phases. This feature is consistent with the earlier reports, though the solubility limit is a little lower in this study than that found by Nakamura et al. The other interesting feature is the shift of $\alpha +\beta +\gamma$ three-phase region between at 1473 and $1573\mathrm{K}$; it shifts to the Al side as temperature increases, and this feature is consistent with the Nakamura report. From the composite results, it can be concluded that Mo is a strong "$\beta$ stabilizer," particularly in a compositional region around $\mathrm{Ti / Al} = 1$. associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: A provisional temperature-composition phase diagram for the Zr-Sn system is given in Fig. 1. The equilibrium phases indicated are: (A15), stable up to the peritectoid $(\beta \mathrm{Zr}) + \mathrm{Zr}_{5}\mathrm{Sn}_{3} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{Zr}_{4}\mathrm{Sn}$ decomposition temperature at $1327^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. The fcc diamond-type modification of Sn $(\alpha \mathrm{Sn})$ is stable below $13^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. This phase is not indicated in Fig. 1. No experimental data exist for the solubility of Zr in $(\alpha \mathrm{Sn})$, but we suppose it to be practically null. The Zr-Sn phase diagram in Fig. 1 is based primarily on the results of the careful and comprehensive experimental work (mainly micrographic analysis) of McPherson and Hansen. Generally speaking, the diagram in Fig. 1 is considered to be rather uncertain regarding most of the liquidus as well as the entire region between about 30 and 50 at.% Sn. Recently, the results obtained by McPherson and Hansen were essentially confirmed by Arias et al., who performed metallographic observations, electrical resistivity measurements (cooling and heating), and electron probe microanalysis on samples isothermally equilibrated for long periods of time (540 h at $950^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ up to 4000 h at $700^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$). For temperatures above $600^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, the $(\alpha \mathrm{Zr}) / (\alpha \mathrm{Zr}) + \mathrm{Zr}_4\mathrm{Sn}$ boundary in Fig. 1 is based on the work of McPherson and Hansen, because of the good qualitative agreement existing between McPherson-Hansen and Sperner, and the recent confirmation by Arias et al. of McPherson-Hansen quantitative results. Below $600^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, the results of Sperner are accepted here. Early work by Salokhin showed a solubility of Sn in $(\alpha \mathrm{Zr})$ of about 2 at.% at $700^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, in good agreement with Fig. 1. Regarding the values for the $(\alpha Zr) / (\alpha Zr) + Zr_4Sn$ boundary given in Fig. 1, above $750^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ they were obtained from a numerical calculation based on the provisional thermodynamic quantities given in the section under "Thermodynamic Considerations", whereas below $700^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ such values result from fitting the combined data of McPherson-Hansen and Sperner by means of the expression: $$\ln X _ {\mathrm {S n}} = 0. 4 0 4 - 4 1 9 0 T ^ {- 1}$$ where $T$ is in kelvins. The $(\alpha + \beta)$ region was investigated by McPherson and Hansen with the same experimental techniques they used for the $(\alpha \mathrm{Zr}) / (\alpha \mathrm{Zr}) + \mathrm{Zr}_4\mathrm{Sn}$ boundary. For the most part, the results of McPherson and Hansen were corroborated by Arias et al. by means of metallographic observations and electrical resistivity measurements. The $(\alpha + \beta)$ boundaries in Fig. 1 result from a numerical calculation based on the tentative thermodynamic functions given in the section under "Thermodynamic Considerations". The temperature accepted here for the $\alpha / \beta$ transition in pure Zr is $863^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. The $(\beta Zr) / (\beta Zr) + Zr_4Sn$ and $(\beta Zr) / (\beta Zr) + Zr_5Sn_3$ boundaries given in Fig. 1 have been calculated using the tentative thermodynamic quantities given in the section under "Thermodynamic Considerations". The computed solubility of Sn in $(\beta \mathrm{Zr})$ is 17.0 at.% at the eutectic reaction $\mathrm{L} \rightleftharpoons (\beta \mathrm{Zr}) + \mathrm{Zr}_{5} \mathrm{Sn}_{3}$ (1592 °C), 11.8 at.% at the peritectoid $(\beta \mathrm{Zr}) + \mathrm{Zr}_{5} \mathrm{Sn}_{3} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{Zr}_{4} \mathrm{Sn}$ (1327 °C), and 4.9 at.% at the peritectoid $(\beta \mathrm{Zr}) + \mathrm{Zr}_{4} \mathrm{Sn} \rightleftharpoons (\alpha \mathrm{Zr})$ (982 °C). Other compounds of composition between 33 and 44 at.% Sn also were reported. These additional compounds have not been included in Fig. 1 because either we think that they are essentially the same $\mathrm{Zr}_{5}\mathrm{Sn}_{3}$ phase mentioned above or they have been discarded because excessive contamination of the samples with interstitial impurities is suspected. However, we are bound to ascribe a significant uncertainty to the phase diagram in Fig. 1 for the composition range between approximately 30 to 50 at.% Sn. Nowotny examined alloys between 25 and 55 at.% Sn by means of X-rays. They reported a compound in the composition interval $0.33 < X_{\mathrm{Sn}} < 0.38$ with the hexagonal $\mathrm{Mn}_{5}\mathrm{Si}_{3}$-type structure. In view of the high content (3.3 at.%) of interstitial impurities (C, N, and O) in the original Zr used by Nowotny, and considering that the thermodynamic stability of the $\mathrm{Zr}_{5}\mathrm{Sn}_{3}$ phase is probably significantly enhanced by these impurities, we decided not to include this result by Nowotny in Fig. 1. Grant et al. performed X-ray analysis of samples quenched after annealing for two months at $900^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, working in the range 28 to 41 at.% Sn. These authors observed two compounds, one at $X_{\mathrm{Sn}} = 0.33$ and the other at $X_{\mathrm{Sn}} = 0.39$ ($\pm \sim 0.01$). Both compounds have the hexagonal $\mathrm{Mn}_{5}\mathrm{Si}_{3}$ type structure, and the symbols $\mathrm{Zr}_{5}\mathrm{Sn}_{3}^{\prime}$ and $\mathrm{Zr}_{5}\mathrm{Sn}_{3}^{\prime \prime}$ were used by Grant et al. to designate the compounds of low and high Sn content, respectively. Grant et al. reported that $\mathrm{Zr}_{5}\mathrm{Sn}_{3}^{\prime}$ coexisted in equilibrium with $\mathrm{Zr}_{5}\mathrm{Sn}_{3}^{\prime \prime}$. Probably, $\mathrm{Zr}_{5}\mathrm{Sn}_{3}^{\prime \prime}$ is the same $\mathrm{Zr}_{5}\mathrm{Sn}_{3}$ phase proposed by McPherson and Hansen and accepted here; however, the observed two-phase field, $\mathrm{Zr}_{5}\mathrm{Sn}_{3}^{\prime} + \mathrm{Zr}_{5}\mathrm{Sn}_{3}^{\prime \prime}$, suggests the existence of a miscibility gap within an intermediate $\mathrm{Zr}_{5}\mathrm{Sn}_{3}$ phase, which would now occupy an overall composition width of at least 6 at.% Sn. No sign of this eventual feature of the Zr-Sn phase diagram seems to appear in the metallographic observations of McPherson and Hansen. Noting also that the corresponding $\mathrm{Hf}_{5}\mathrm{Sn}_{3}$ phase in the Hf-Sn system was evaluated to be only a line compound, we finally have decided not to include $\mathrm{Zr}_{5}\mathrm{Sn}_{3}^{\prime}$ in the provisional phase diagram presented in Fig. 1. We speculate that the results of Grant et al. may have been due to inhomogeneities in the overall composition of their samples. This difficulty found in preparing alloys of high Sn content was pointed out by Salokhin. Rosstutta et al. reported the compound $\mathrm{Zr}_{5}\mathrm{Sn}_{4}$ with the hexagonal $\mathrm{Ti}_{5}\mathrm{Ga}_{4}$-type structure, which is somewhat similar to that of $\mathrm{Zr}_{5}\mathrm{Sn}_{3}$. No information is available on the interstitial impurity content of the original $\mathrm{Zr}$ used by Rosstutta et al. Provisionally, considering that further experimental confirmation of the $\mathrm{Zr}_{5}\mathrm{Sn}_{4}$ phase is advisable, we have not included it in Fig. 1. The $(\beta \mathrm{Zr}) / (\beta \mathrm{Zr}) + \mathrm{L}$ boundary in Fig. 1 was evaluated using 17.0 at.% for the Sn content of $(\beta \mathrm{Zr})$ at the eutectic temperature, the melting point of pure Zr, and the results due to McPherson and Hansen of the micrographic examination and incipient melting determinations at two intermediate compositions between 0 and 17 at.% Sn. The values for this boundary were obtained from a numerical calculation based on the provisional thermodynamic functions given in the section entitled "Thermodynamic Considerations". In view of the lack of experimental data, these functions also were used to compute the liquidus in Fig. 1 for $X_{\mathrm{Sn}} \leqslant 0.20$. The slope for the $\mathrm{L} / (\mathrm{L} + \mathrm{Zr}_5\mathrm{Sn}_3)$ boundary at the $\mathbf{L} \rightleftarrows (\beta \mathbf{Zr}) + \mathbf{Zr}_{6} \mathbf{Sn}_{3}$ eutectic reaction was determined to be $28.2^{\circ} \mathrm{C} / \text { at. } \% \mathrm{Sn}$. For $X_{\mathrm{Sn}} > 0.20$ the liquidus in Fig. 1 follows closely the tentative liquidus indicated by McPherson and Hansen. The only relatively safe points in this part of the liquidus are: $X_{\mathrm{Sn}} \cong 0.40$ and $1988^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ for the congruent melting of the compound $\mathrm{Zr}_{6}\mathrm{Sn}_{3}$, $X_{\mathrm{Sn}} = 0.79$ and $1142^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ for the liquid entering the peritectic reaction, $\mathrm{Zr}_{5}\mathrm{Sn}_{3} + \mathrm{L} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{ZrSn}_{2}$ (values obtained by McPherson and Hansen by means of metallographic examination of samples quenched from the melt), and the melting point of Sn. It is not known whether there is a eutectic or peritectic reaction involving the L, $(\beta \mathrm{Sn})$, and $\mathrm{ZrSn}_{2}$ phases. The solubility of Sn in $(\alpha \mathrm{Zr})$ between 700 and $900^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ was also studied by Sperner by means of X-ray lattice parameter determinations in heat treated (300 h at $900^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ up to $1600\mathrm{h}$ at $700^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$) and quenched alloys. The results obtained are fairly consistent with the value for the composition of $(\alpha \mathrm{Zr})$ at the peritectoid reaction given by McPherson and Hansen. However, at lower temperatures, Sperner found that Sn is somewhat more soluble in $(\alpha \mathrm{Zr})$ than indicated by McPherson and Hansen. This discrepancy between McPherson-Hansen and Sperner was tentatively attributed by Carlson to the presence of impurities, coming either from the source materials and/or from contamination, in their respective alloys. This comment made by Carlson is relevant because, for example, the Zr-Sn alloys have a high affinity for gaseous oxygen and low levels of iron, an impurity that is normally present in Zr, which significantly modify the binary phase diagram making the Zr-Sn alloys display a ternary character.

This report is dubious because no subsequent investigation has identified any intermediate phase in this system. Despite the numerous and extensive investigations of the BiHg system and its apparent simplicity, the liquidus line of the equilibrium diagram is not precisely defined although almost 150 experimental points have been reported. All data are listed in Table 1, but to avoid confusion, only representative and contrasting values are shown in Fig. 1. Liquidus data were accumulated in several different ways. Thermal analyses, chemical analyses of the saturated amalgam filtrate, measurements of the electromotive force (emf) of amalgam cells, estimation of the solubility from changes in resistivity versus amalgam composition, and calorimetric titration of heterogeneous Bi amalgams with Hg were used. The results of [1892Hey] were corrected for the Bi melting point difference because only Bi-rich alloys were investigated. associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: The assessed Ti-H phase diagram is shown in the figure, which is a section of a $P - T - X$ surface in the $P - X$ plane, where $P$ is pressure in Pa, $T$ is temperature in K and ${}^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , and $X$ is the hydrogen concentration, expressed as $X = \mathrm{H / Ti}$ (the atomic ratio). Two presentations are necessary for a hydrogen-metal system, because the equilibrium pressure of the hydrogen surrounding the metal is always a significant thermodynamic variable, in contrast to most situations involving metallic alloys. The participation of hydrogen in the various phases of alloy systems is the best available example of hydrogen acting as a metal. The composite phase diagram is of the eutectoid type, and consists of the following phases: (1) cph $\alpha$ ; (2) bcc $\beta$ ; 3) two interstitial solid solutions of hydrogen based on the allotropic $\alpha$ and $\beta$ forms of pure Ti; (4) $\delta$ , a fcc hydride; (5) $\varepsilon$ , a tetragonally distorted fcc or fct hydride with axial ratio $c / a < 1$ ; and (6) $\gamma$ , a metastable fct hy dride with $c / a > 1$ . Above the eutectoid temperature, the stability ranges of the $\alpha$ , $\beta$ , and $\delta$ phases are delineated by temperature-composition values obtained from a composite set of isotherms. The figure shows a simplified version. More reliable characterization of Ti-H alloys (concentration, impurities, etc.) is needed in future work. In the $\beta +\delta$ region, data from different authors for the solubility limits of the $\beta$ phase (i.e., $\beta /(\beta +\delta)$ boundary) are in good agreement, but differences exist for the $(\beta +\delta) / \delta$ boundary. The boundary drawn lies at much lower H concentration than those of other studies. However, the data points delineating the isotherm lines are rather sparse, leaving the composition at which the isotherms leave the two-phase region ill defined. The boundary points were obtained from considerably more experimental data, and they are probably more reliable. Using these data, the $\beta / (\beta + \delta)$ and $(\beta + \delta) / \delta$ boundaries were drawn to achieve maximum conformity with other data. Below the eutectoid temperature, the limit of H solubility in the $\alpha$ phase was delineated, using results from ER measurements and metallographic observation. In XRD patterns taken at $\sim 20^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , the $\delta$ phase was first detected at $X =$ approximately 0.17 ( $\sim 15$ at.% H). The effect of pressure on the phase relationships of the Ti-H system was analyzed, using data from previous compilations. Postulated phase diagrams are available for pressures of 0.5 and $1\mathrm{kPa}$ and for pressures of 0.1 and $100\mathrm{kPa}$ and $10\mathrm{MPa}$ . However, the results for $10\mathrm{MPa}$ should be considered with caution, because they were based on data which deviate considerably from the figure. The phase rule requires that $\Delta_{\mathrm{H}}H$ and $P_{\mathrm{equi}}$ retain constant values throughout a mixed phase region. It can be seen that $\Delta_{\mathrm{H}}H$ does not satisfy this condition for the $\alpha + \beta$ two-phase region, whereas $P_{\mathrm{equi}}$ does satisfy it for the same two-phase region. Above $X = 0.33$ , the dependence of $\Delta_{\mathrm{H}}H$ on composition is even more pronounced, and the origin of these discrepancies was hypothesized. The $\alpha / (\alpha + \beta)$ boundary is retrograde, based on $P-T-X$ measurements. These results were presented in a small $T-X$ diagram; however, the purity of the materials used was not reported. Below $500^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , the results modified the straight-line extrapolation of this boundary to $x = 0.086$ (7.9 at.% H) at $300^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , which was proposed and is generally accepted. The uncertainty about impurity levels leaves the difference between these two sets of results unresolved at the present time. Of all the boundaries of the $\delta$ phase, the boundary corresponding to the second-order transformation has been studied the most extensively and is the most well defined. Data that this boundary is based on were obtained from heat capacity, ER, and XRD measurements. The $\delta$ phase was investigated up to $X = 1.85$ $(P_{\mathrm{equi}} = 90650\mathrm{Pa})$ .

associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: To facilitate an explanation of some terminology used here and to offer a perspective on our measurements, a phase diagram is shown in the figure. In such a diagram, it is commonly understood that the hydrostatic pressure is fixed at some value greater than the vapor pressure, so there is no vapor phase present. This corresponds to the system being confined in a piston-cylinder arrangement. Another equally valid phase diagram is one for which the pressure is the vapor pressure of the system, which varies with composition as well as temperature. This corresponds to the system being held in an initially evacuated, rigid-wall container, and the situation that essentially holds in the present experiments and in many of the previous studies. A vapor phase is always present, and the two-phase fields of the constant pressure view become three-phase fields. Partial pressures for compositions and temperatures within such three-phase fields are said to lie on three-phase curves. Thus, the partial pressure of $\mathrm{Se}_2$ over 54 at.% Se at $940\mathrm{K}$ would give one point on a $\mathrm{Se}_2$ three-phase curve for In-rich $\mathrm{In}_2\mathrm{Se}_3(\mathrm{s})$ . The complete three-phase curve would be generated from compositions within the three-phase fields on either side of the sesquiselenide homogeneity range. It would be a parabol-like loop whose apex would be at the congruent melting point of the sesquiselenide. Se-saturated $\mathrm{In}_2\mathrm{Se}_3(\mathrm{s})$ , a Se-rich liquid, and vapor except possibly for a temperature interval near $1000\mathrm{K}$ . The critical temperature at which liquid immiscibility disappears was calculated as $1905\mathrm{K}$ by the parameters used in the present work. As indicated from typical metal composition of MTP (Fe, 6 to 20 mass% Cu, 4 to 10 mass% Si), most of the metal composition range in MTP is on the solid-liquid $(\alpha$ or $\gamma) + (\mathrm{L}_1$ or $\mathrm{L}_2))$ or liquid-liquid $(\mathrm{L}_1 + \mathrm{L}_2)$ two-phase region or liquid-liquid-solid $(\mathrm{L}_1 + \mathrm{L}_2 + \alpha$ or $\gamma)$ three-phase region at the typical operating temperature of MTP, 1523 to 1623 K. A part of the metal composition range would still lie on the two-phase region such as $\mathrm{L}_1 + \mathrm{L}_2$ range even at higher temperature such as $1723\mathrm{K}$ . However, the liquid miscibility gap shrinks significantly with higher temperature. As it was found in the present work that an Fe-rich melt was in equilibrium with almost pure liquid Cu, the activity of Cu in two-liquid area is high and close to unity. They also found that an Fe-rich Fe-Cu-Si solid solution was in equilibrium with almost pure liquid Cu; this is very close to the present authors' findings. Solubility of Cu in the $\tau$ phase was found to be negligibly small. Unfortunately, the microstructure of the two-liquid matrix was too fine to detect each composition by EPMA; thus the average composition of two liquid phases in the $\tau +\mathrm{L}_1 + \mathrm{L}_2$ three-phase region is plotted with open squares. From experimental findings, it was demonstrated that composition regions of miscibility gap for liquid alloys, of solid Fe + liquid and of liquid + t two-phase regions are larger than expected from the phase diagram proposed by Chang et al.

associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: The location of the phases participating in the reaction $\mathrm{L}+$ gas $\leftrightarrow \delta +(\mathrm{Ni})$ at $5\mathrm{Pa}(U_1^{\prime})$ become obvious in the isothermal section at $1353^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, just $2^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ above $U_{1}^{\prime}$ . The intersection of the tie lines $\mathbf{L}+$ gas and $\delta +(\mathrm{Ni})$ at $U_{1}^{\prime}$ indicate the overall composition expected after complete transformation of $\mathbf{L}+$ gas into a eutectic type $\delta +(\mathrm{Ni})$ microstructure: it is $87.93\mathrm{Ni - }10.75\mathrm{Ti - }1.32\mathrm{N}$ (at.%) or $90.64\mathrm{Ni - }9.03\mathrm{Ti - }0.33\mathrm{N}$ (wt.%). This compares reasonably well to the composition $88.2\mathrm{Ni - }10.2\mathrm{Ti - }1.6\mathrm{N}$ (wt.%) found in the eutectic microstructure of a $87\mathrm{Ni - }13\mathrm{TiN}$ (wt.%) sample, considering the uncertainty induced by the gas pressure and the difficulties in determining the N-content. After sintering at $1500^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ in vacuum, a reaction between Ni and TiN and a eutectic microstructure of $\delta + (\mathrm{Ni})$ was observed. This can be clearly understood from the calculated phase diagrams. One starts with the isothermal reaction at $1500^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and $5\mathrm{Pa}$. Initially, Ti will be dissolved in liquid Ni and N gas will be liberated. The molten binder phase is the liquid of the three-phase equilibrium $\mathbf{L} + \mathbf{gas} + \delta$. It contains 14.8 at.% Ti and 0.0031 at.% N. Upon cooling L shifts toward $U_{1}^{\prime}$ and the first solid solution (Ni) appears. In the experiments of Fukuhara et al., the liquid must have had access to the gas phase, possibly entrapped in some porosity formed by the initial reaction. As long as $\mathbf{L} + \mathbf{gas}$ can react, the eutectic-like $\delta + (\mathrm{Ni})$ structure can be formed in $U_{1}^{\prime}$ . Even with an excess amount of gas, this solidification will be complete. These conditions must be assumed for experiments of Binder et al., who did not observe the eutectic structure in their samples, not even for the one with the same composition of 60 wt.% TiN, sintered also at 1500 °C. The difference was in the Ar atmosphere used. If it is assumed that the initially evolved N₂ at 1500 °C was carried away by the Ar, possibly compounded by a larger open porosity of the sample, the solidification of the molten binder with 14.8Ti-0.0031N (at.%) overruns the U₁ reaction and precipitates virtually no δ-nitride, as discussed above. This results in the observed "noneutectic" microstructure. Another key result of the thermodynamic calculation is the huge amount of Ni in the gas phase in the $\mathrm{L} + \mathrm{gas} + \delta$ equilibrium if the temperature is high or the pressure is low. This relates to an increasing Ti content of the almost binary Ni-Ti liquid phase. At $5\mathrm{Pa}$ and $1353^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ the gas is still almost pure $\mathbf{N}_2$. At $1500^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ an appreciable amount of 6.1 at. $\%$ Ni is in the gas phase. Above $1650^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ there is more Ni than N in the gas and at $1800^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ the gas composition is $77\mathrm{Ni}-23\mathrm{Ti}-0.001\mathrm{N}$ (at. $\%$ ). The practical consequence is that a substantial amount of Ni will be lost to the gas phase if sintering is done at high temperature or low pressure. This explains the diminishing amount of binder phase observed in the samples sintered at $1800^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ in pure Ar at 0.35 bar. Another practical consequence is the shift of liquid phase composition to higher Ti-content. The subsequent solidification of Ti-enriched liquid explains why longer sintering times result in the formation of more Ti-rich intermetallics in addition to $\theta \mathrm{TiNi}_3$ , $\beta_{2}\mathrm{TiNi}$ or even $\kappa \mathrm{Ti}_{2}\mathrm{NiN}_{x}$. At the lower pressure of $5\mathrm{Pa}$ the equilibria with the gas phase are considerably extended, as given by the dashed lines for $\mathbf{L} + \delta +$ gas and $\mathbf{L}+$ $(\mathrm{Ni}) +$ gas, which intersect in point $U_{1}^{\prime}:\mathbf{L} + \mathbf{gas}\leftrightarrow (\mathbf{Ni}) + \delta .$ The difference in melting temperatures of TiN + Ni powder mixtures is due to the fact that the corresponding four-phase reaction $\mathrm{L} + \mathrm{gas} \leftrightarrow (\mathrm{Ni}) + \delta$ depends strongly on pressure. In the vacuum apparatus described by Fukuhara et al. the pressure was measured far away from the sample. The local pressure around the vaporizing sample should have been higher than the reading of the vacuum meter, $0.05\mathrm{Pa}$ . It might be reasonable to assume a local pressure of about $5\mathrm{Pa}$ . This corresponds to $1351^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ for reaction $U_{1}^{\prime}(5\mathrm{Pa})$, and corresponds well with the measured $1353^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ . Using this assumption on the local pressure, all the related data can be quantitatively understood from the thermodynamic model. In essence, virtually all of the N found in the reaction products $\delta + (\mathrm{Ni})$ stems from the gas phase and not from the liquid; the reaction $\mathrm{L} + \mathrm{gas}\leftrightarrow (\mathrm{Ni}) + \delta$ is not of eutectic type but of transition type.

associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: An important feature is the composition of the alloy-rich end points of the three-phase triangles. These are plotted as functions of temperature in the binary Al-Ca phase diagram. The regions between dashed lines thus represent alloys that are in equilibrium with the same oxide. In this system, there are experimental data by Srikanth et al. available at $1373\mathrm{K}$ , but unfortunately there are large discrepancies between experimental and calculated data as shown by the first two columns in the table. A major part of these discrepancies can be traced back to the current description of the Al-Ca system. In the third column of the table, the data of Srikanth et al. for the $\mathrm{Al_2O_3 - CaO}$ system are used together with the current description of the Al-Ca system. The results are slightly better but still not good. The interaction in the Al-Ca liquid is described by four linearly temperature-dependent parameters, which at $1373\mathrm{K}$ and $X_{\mathrm{Ca}} = 0.2$ is equivalent to a regular interaction of $-44\mathrm{kJ / mol}$ . If instead a regular interaction of $-67\mathrm{kJ / mol}$ is used together with the Srikanth et al. data, the results in the fourth column of the table are obtained. These give a fairly good representation of the experimental data, but it is obvious that a regular interaction in the Al-Ca liquid is not quite sufficient. However, for the present purpose, it might suffice. In the last column, a regular interaction of $-74\mathrm{kJ / mol}$ is used together with the present description of the $\mathrm{Al_2O_3 - CaO}$ system, and the results are similar to the previous ones. It is obvious that data of this type are very sensitive to the thermodynamics of both the alloy and the oxide system, and thus they provide very valuable information. To make full use of such data, the alloy and the oxide system should be optimized together, which is quite possible with current software. The above calculation was made by combining assessments of the Al-Ca, $\mathrm{Al}_{2}\mathrm{O}_{3}$ -CaO, Al-O (as described in paragraph 3.1), and Ca-O systems, and the same combination was also used to calculate an isothermal section at $1500\mathrm{K}$. $\mathbf{Zr}$ is an important minor alloying addition to Al-based alloys, and therefore the Al-rich side of the diagram up to $1000^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ is accurately known. Solubilities of $\mathbf{Zr}$ in both liquid and solid Al were definitively determined. Solid (Al) forms from the liquid by the peritectic reaction $\mathrm{L} + \mathrm{ZrAl}_3 \leftrightarrow (\mathrm{Al})$ at $660.8^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ . The maximum solubility of $\mathrm{Zr}$ in solid (Al) is 0.083 at.%; the composition of the liquid in the peritectic equilibrium is 0.033 at.% Zr. The present thermodynamic calculations verify the validity of the dilute limit approximation for the Al liquidus and solvus up to $1000^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , as suggested by the linear relationship between the logarithm of the solubility and $1 / T$ in K. 
Solid solubilities were also reported; parametric methods based on microhardness data were used to determine the solvus compositions. The reported solubilities from these studies are somewhat higher than the selected values. The data are compared with the assessed boundaries. 
With an electrochemical technique, the activity of Al at $850^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ in Al-rich liquid alloys was measured. The solubility limit of $\mathbf{Zr}$ in liquid Al proposed at this temperature is $\sim 1.3$ at. $\%$ Zr which is much larger than the assessed value of 0.2 at. $\%$ Zr. Therefore, the validity of the results obtained are questioned and not further considered in this evaluation. 
These two results are clearly inconsistent. The lower solubility is preferred because fewer questionable assumptions are required to interpret a measurement made at temperature. The coherent $\mathsf{mZrAl}_3$ solvus was modeled thermodynamically as part of this work. Although very different approaches were taken to the problem, the results agree reasonably well with each other and with the measurement. Details of the calculations and suggested critical experiments are discussed in the section "Thermodynamics" of this evaluation. 
The calculated metastable phase boundaries are shown. The calculated solvus is somewhat higher in $\mathrm{Zr}$ than the value taken from the work, but much lower than the value reported. Finally the calculated metastable peritectic reaction occurs at $661.3^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , with liquid and solid compositions of 0.09 and 0.21 at.% $\mathrm{Zr}$ respectively. This phase could not be quenched. Because of the similarity in phase diagrams, it is tempting to assume that $\beta 1$ is part of $\beta$ , separated by an order-disorder transformation, by analogy with the Be-Cu system, or that $\beta 1$ is disordered bcc, similar to the $(\alpha \mathrm{Fe})$ phase in the Be-Fe phase diagram. There is general agreement regarding the main features of the Zr-Hf phase diagram. In the liquid phase (L), there is complete miscibility. In the solid state, there exist: $(a)$ a high-temperature bcc $(\beta)$ phase, and $(b)$ a low-temperature cph $(\alpha)$ phase. Both phases extend from 0 to $100\%$ Hf. Ordering reactions have not been reported in the solid state. The $\alpha \rightleftarrows \beta$ and $\beta \rightleftarrows \mathbf{L}$ equilibrium transformations are incongruent for every alloy composition. It is normally accepted that the phase diagram of the Zr-Hf system corresponds to the situation of nearly ideal solutions. 
The Two-Phase $(\alpha + \beta)$ Field. The temperatures accepted here for the $\alpha/\beta$ equilibrium in pure Zr and pure Hf are $863^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and $1743^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, respectively. The $(\alpha + \beta)$ boundaries shown in the figure are a compromise between the indicated allotropic transformation temperatures of the pure metals and the alloy experimental data. These data are not sufficient to establish approximate experimental values for the temperature width, $\Delta \theta$ , of the $(\alpha + \beta)$ region; hence, it is provisionally accepted here that this compromise must render a value for $\Delta \theta$ at 50 at.% Hf very close to that corresponding to the situation of ideal mixing between $\mathbf{Zr}$ and Hf. This condition on $\Delta \theta$ can be conveniently satisfied by using, as done here, expressions cubic in temperature for the composition of the $(\alpha + \beta)$ boundaries, subject to van't Hoff's relation. The resulting numerical expressions for the $\alpha / (\alpha + \beta)$ and $\beta / (\alpha + \beta)$ boundaries, which we consider to give the best possible fit to the combined experimental data under the indicated constraints, are given below. A check on this simple construction of the $(\alpha + \beta)$ region, based on the theoretical work, is mentioned at the end of the section on thermodynamic considerations. At this point, it should also be noted that the errors we ascribe to the $(\alpha + \beta)$ region in the figure are important (see text below). 
The $\alpha / (\alpha + \beta)$ curve in the figure can be represented by the equation:

$$
\begin{array}{l} \text {a t .} \\ + 3. 9 7 4 \times 1 0 ^ {- 8} (T - 8 6 3) ^ {3} \quad (T \text {i n} ^ {\circ} C) \\ \end{array}
$$

These numerical expressions conform with the van't Hoff's equation, in which the values for the heats of the $\alpha \rightarrow \beta$ transformations in pure Zr and pure Hf are assumed to be 930 cal/mol and 1400 cal/mol, respectively. Work in the range 0 to 43 at.% Hf determined the $\alpha \rightleftharpoons \beta$ transformation by differential thermal analysis. The temperature width suggested for the $(\alpha + \beta)$ region is negligible and definitely narrower than that of the figure. This can be attributed to insufficient sensitivity of the experimental technique used to determine this region. Measurements of the electrical resistance vs. raising temperature of Hf-rich alloys containing up to 18 at.% Zr were made. Based on this work, the value of $7.2^{\circ}\mathrm{C} / \mathrm{at.}\%$ Zr was adopted for the lowering of the $\alpha \rightarrow \beta$ (heating) transformation temperature of pure Hf upon alloying with Zr. This value is consistent with the figure, where the average slope of the $(\alpha + \beta)$ boundaries at pure Hf is $-7.39^{\circ}\mathrm{C}/$ at.% Zr. Using thermal analysis and working with alloys up to 6.5 at.% Zr, the (mean) value $-11.2^{\circ}\mathrm{C} / \mathrm{at.}\%$ Zr was obtained for the lowering of the $\beta \rightarrow \alpha$ (cooling) transformation temperature, a value that seems too negative to be directly related to the $(\alpha + \beta)$ stable-equilibrium region (this deviation could be due to the inadequacy of the experimental technique itself). 
It is necessary to remark that a considerable uncertainty still exists regarding the shape (width) of the provisional $(\alpha + \beta)$ region indicated in the figure. This is related to the uncertainty we must ascribe to the value $1400~\mathrm{cal / mol}$ used here for the heat of the $\alpha \rightarrow \beta$ transformation in pure Hf $(\Delta H_{\mathrm{Hf}}^{\alpha \rightarrow \beta})$ . This value, which is based essentially on only one experimental determination, was recently recommended as the most probable value of $\Delta H_{\mathrm{Hf}}^{\alpha \rightarrow \beta}$ ; however, this value would be definitely too low to be used in an otherwise successful thermodynamic modeling of the Hf-Mo phase diagram. Thus, although keeping the $1400~\mathrm{cal / mol}$ as the most probable value of $\Delta H_{\mathrm{Hf}}^{\alpha \rightarrow \beta}$ , we propose here to bracket this quantity between 1260 and 3080 cal/mol, the upper limit being the value necessitated in the synthesis of the Hf-Mo phase diagram. The uncertainty in the $(\alpha + \beta)$ region, associated with this bracketing, is graphically represented for the equiatomic composition. 
The solidus curve indicated in the figure has been adjusted to the values determined by optical measurements. The numerical description of the solidus in the figure is given by:

$$
\begin{array}{l} \mathrm{at.}\% \mathrm{Hf} = 3.774\times 10^{-1}(T - 1855) - 2.279 \\ \times 1 0 ^ {- 4} (T - 1 8 5 5) ^ {2} \\ - 1. 8 1 7 \times 1 0 ^ {- 7} (T - 1 8 5 5) ^ {3} \quad (T \text {i n} ^ {\circ} \mathrm {C}) \\ \end{array}
$$

which is also in general agreement with the incipient melting data and the evaluated solidus. 
The liquidus shown in the figure is represented by:

$$
\begin{array}{l} \mathrm {a t .} \% \mathrm {H f} = 3.274 \times 10 ^ {- 1} (T - 1855) - 1.007 \\ \times 1 0 ^ {- 4} (T - 1 8 5 5) ^ {2} \\ - 1. 6 6 5 \times 1 0 ^ {- 7} (T - 1 8 5 5) ^ {3} \quad (T \text {i n} ^ {\circ} \mathrm {C}) \\ \end{array}
$$

This construction of the $(\beta + \mathrm{L})$ boundaries is rather similar to that made above for the situation of the $(\alpha + \beta)$ boundaries. Accordingly, the fact that the liquidus proposed here agrees well with the corresponding data (we consider that the existing small differences are within the uncertainty produced by the stated error in the estimation of the heats of melting of Zr and Hf, plus the experimental errors themselves) suggests that the width $\Delta \theta$ of the $(\beta + \mathbf{L})$ region at 50 at.% Hf should be very close to the width calculated for the instance of ideal mixing between Zr and Hf. This proved to be true (see also the comment on $\Delta \theta$ of the $(\beta + \mathbf{L})$ field at the end of the section on thermodynamic considerations). For completeness, let us mention that the evaluated liquidus curve lies about $35^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ higher in temperature at the equiatomic composition than that of the figure. 
The $(\alpha + \beta)$ region was studied by means of metallographic examination of heat treated (800 to $1800^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ ) and quenched specimens. On quenching from $(\alpha + \beta)$ , it was possible to observe a typical microstructure showing transformed $\beta$ plus isothermal $\alpha$ . It was remarked that there was no evidence of any retention of the high-temperature bcc $(\beta)$ phase upon quenching, but that this was not corroborated by X-ray analysis. The obtained results were judged to be in substantial agreement with previous data but, nevertheless, a much wider $(\alpha + \beta)$ region was suggested. Work on the ternary Zr-Hf-O system gave results that are consistent with those for Zr-Hf. It was also shown that oxygen quickly stabilizes the $\alpha$ phase. For completeness, data obtained by differential thermal analysis also appear to deviate toward higher temperatures and, in the instance of the Hf-rich alloys, they are not considered to be compatible with the $\alpha/\beta$ equilibrium temperature of pure Hf accepted here.

associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: A liquidus with a strongly asymmetric form is unlikely, because an abrupt change in the composition dependence of the Gibbs energy of the liquid phase would be required at the composition of the compound without any obvious reasons. This situation may be illustrated with reference to the Au-U system. In the phase diagram shown in the figure, the proposed liquidus of $\mathrm{Au}_3\mathrm{U}$ is strongly asymmetric and a rather abrupt change of slope is required below $1216^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ to avoid the $E$ -type error. Accordingly, the validity of this liquidus was questioned and other possible diagrams were proposed. However, the problem of asymmetry of the liquidus between $\mathrm{Au}_{51}\mathrm{U}_{14}$ and $\mathrm{Au}_2\mathrm{U}$ remains. The present authors speculate that the $\mathbf{L} \leftrightarrow \mathbf{A u}_{51}\mathbf{U}_{14} + \mathbf{A u}_2\mathbf{U}$ eutectic composition may actually be located closer to $\mathrm{Au}_{51}\mathrm{U}_{14}$ , as shown with the dot-dashed lines.

associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: The calculated liquidus surface of the Ti-Hf-B system is presented. The agreement with the experimental results is quite good. A better comparison between the calculated and experimentally established composition and temperature dependence of the metal-rich eutectic trough and the peritectic melting of the monoboride solid solutions is provided. The calculated temperature dependence of the eutectic trough deviates from the experiments, but when better reproduction of the measurements was attempted, the appearance of a minimum in the temperature dependence of the peritectic melting of the monoboride solid solution could not be prevented. The experimentally established liquidus surface of the Ti-Hf-B system is given. The location of the metal-rich eutectic trough extending from the titanium side to the hafnium side was determined by metallographic and melting point examinations of alloys with 10 and 25 at.% B. The measured incipient melting points and boron content at the eutectic trough as a function of hafnium exchange are shown. The curve fitted through several incipient melting points ascends smoothly from the titanium to the hafnium side and does not pass through a maximum or minimum. The measured melting points of the monoboride solid solutions as a function of hafnium exchange are shown. The peritectic temperatures for the hafnium-rich monoborides were uncertain, because even after $300\mathrm{h}$ heat treatment at $1450^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ the alloys did not attain complete equilibrium. Because the measured peritectic temperatures of the titanium-rich monoboride solid solutions drop rapidly from 2190 to about $2100^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , which is nearly the peritectic temperature of pure HfB, it was assumed that further peritectic temperatures toward the hafnium side will not change very drastically. The relatively low melting points of the two hafnium-rich alloys were attributed to the presence of an unreacted metal-diboride mixture. The curve fitted through the melting point measurements descends smoothly from the titanium to the hafnium side and does not pass through a minimum in the hafnium-rich region. Some difficulties were also encountered in the determination of the melting maximum of the diboride solid solutions. Because the vapor pressure of boron is relatively high at these temperatures, it was not possible to accurately predetermine the final composition of the samples. Due to the narrow homogeneous range, the melting points drop sharply on either side of the maximum melting composition. Therefore, the maximum melting points, corresponding to about 66 at.% B, could only be estimated, although a large number of boron-rich alloys were measured. Although no experimental examination of the boron-rich eutectic trough between the diboride solid solutions and boron was performed, a continuous decrease in temperature from $2080^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ at the titanium side to $2065^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ at the hafnium side was estimated.

associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: Details for the Au-rich region are shown in the figure. The phases included in the assessed diagram are: (1) the liquid, L; (2) the fcc Au terminal solid solution, (Au), with a maximum solubility of 32.5 at.% Cd in (Au) at $627^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ ; (3) the phases $\alpha_{1}, \alpha_{2}$ , and a series of long-period superlattices in the composition range between $\alpha_{1}$ and $\alpha_{2}$ ; (4) the CsCl-type $\beta$ phase, with several forms of martensitic modifications at low temperatures; (5) a succession of related phases, $\delta$ , $\delta'$ , and $\delta''$ , at temperatures above approximately $305^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ ; (6) the $\mathrm{Au}_{3}\mathrm{Cd}_{5}$ phase, below $340^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ ; (7) the $\varepsilon$ phase, with a possible martensitic transformation at $\sim 270^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ ; (8) the closely related $\eta$ and $\eta'$ phases; and (9) the cph Cd terminal solid solution, (Cd), with a maximum solubility of 3.5 at.% Au in (Cd) at $309^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ . Au Terminal Solid Solution, (Au). The (Au) solidus boundary is based on a thermodynamic assessment by Filby and Pratt, which is in agreement with the experimental values of Rivlin, Hume-Rothery, and Rader. The $(\mathrm{Au}) / [(A u) + \alpha_{2}]$ and $(\mathrm{Au}) / [(A u) + \alpha_{1}]$ solvus boundaries were determined by Owen and Roberts and by Hirabayashi and Ogawa. $\alpha_{1}$ Phase. The $(\mathrm{Au}) + \alpha_{2} \rightleftharpoons \alpha_{1}$ peritectoid reaction was reported to occur at $425^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ from lattice parameter measurements, and at $415^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ from thermal measurements. Subsequently, Rivlin, Hume-Rothery, and Rader considered that the thermal effect at $412^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ observed by Hirabayashi and Ogawa, also corresponded to the above reaction. The order-disorder like transition at $422^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ in a 25 at.% Cd alloy is apparently the result of a peritectoid reaction. The form of the $[(A u) + \alpha_{1}] / \alpha_{1}$ boundary remains controversial. X-ray studies show this boundary to pass through $\sim 24$ at.% Cd at $250^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ or 20 at.% Cd at $300^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ . The $(\mathrm{Au}) + \alpha_{2} \rightleftharpoons \alpha_{1}$ peritectoid temperature at $412^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and the phase boundary of the $\alpha_{1}$ phase on the Au-rich side have been based tentatively on the results of Hirabayashi and Ogawa. A transition (reported to be an order-disorder type) was found in a 25 at.% Cd thin film sample at $300^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , more than $100^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ lower than the corresponding reaction temperature in bulk materials. $\alpha_{2}$ Phase. According to Rivlin, Hume-Rothery, and Rader, the $\mathrm{L} + (\mathrm{Au}) \rightleftharpoons \alpha_{2}$ peritectic temperature and the $\mathrm{L} \rightleftharpoons \alpha_{2} + \beta$ eutectic temperature are 627 and $626.6^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , respectively. The lattice parameter measurements of Owen and Roberts suggested the form of the $[(A u) + \alpha_{2}] / \alpha_{2}$ phase boundary. The $\alpha_{2} / [\alpha_{2} + \beta]$ boundary is also from the work of Owen and Roberts. Massalski placed the Cd-rich side of the $\alpha_{2}$ phase boundary at $439^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , in agreement with Owen and Roberts. $\pmb{\beta}$ Phase. The $\beta$ liquidus and solidus were examined by many investigators. Earlier reports on the $(\mathbf{L} + \beta)$ two-phase field, in the composition region of less than $\sim 50$ at.% Cd, indicated wider temperature ranges between the liquidus and solidus $(\sim 10^{\circ}\mathrm{C})$ than the more recent reports $(\sim 1^{\circ}\mathrm{C})$ . The results of Komarek and Stummerer have been accepted tentatively. The results of Rivlin, Hume-Rothery, and Rader and Wasilewski are not in agreement with Komarek and Stummerer when compared in detail. The data of Wasilewski suggested the existence of two L $\neq \beta$ congruent points at $\sim 47.5$ and $\sim 50.5$ at.% Cd, which is unlikely from the thermodynamic point of view. The volatility of Cd in this temperature range $(\sim 630^{\circ}\mathrm{C})$ makes the experimental work particularly difficult.

At $\approx 1355\mathrm{K}$ and under oxygen pressure of about $\sim 0.05$ MPa, the eutectic point is observed in the system. This corresponds to equilibrium between solid $\mathrm{Cu_2O}$ , $\mathrm{CuO}$ , and liquid, whose oxygen mole fraction is $\sim 0.39$ . The concentration of oxygen in the liquid phase of the system $\mathrm{Cu - O}$ depends on oxygen pressure and increases with increasing $P_{\mathrm{O_2}}$ . Phase equilibria along the liquidus line of the melt with the high concentrations of oxygen have not yet been adequately investigated. Until now, the only paper wherein experimental data were reported for oxygen pressures greater than $0.1\mathrm{MPa} (\approx 1$ atm) is that of Roberts and Smyth. Later, theoretical assessments produced results that agreed with the data only for oxygen pressures $< 0.1\mathrm{MPa} (\approx 1$ atm). At higher oxygen pressure, the theoretical results disagreed. The liquidus line observed under oxygen pressures lower than 1 atm corresponds to the interval The first exothermic event was caused by precipitation of solid CuO occurring at intersection of the sector $\mathbf{EB}$ of the liquidus line at point $\pmb{D}$ . The temperature of this exothermic event was in close agreement with the temperature of the endothermic effect observed during heating and depended on oxygen pressure in the same way. For oxygen pressures higher than the pressure at the eutectic point, the liquidus data were fit to the equation

$$
\ln P _ {\mathrm {O} 2} (\mathrm {M P a}) = - 6 5, 0 0 3 / T + 4 4. 9 8 2
$$

The second exothermic effect was associated with passage through the eutectic temperature and did not depend on oxygen pressure. A rapid cooling rate could induce some degree of supercooling. If cooling should be stopped just after the crossing of the liquidus line and the sample be held at constant $T$ , the liquid phase should gradually be oxidized to solid CuO stoichiometry (these changes are shown by the arrow). However, during DTA measurements, the heating (cooling) rate has to be constant, and pauses for achievement of equilibrium state are undesirable; therefore, in our DTA experiments, the metastable liquid phase could exist down or even slightly below the eutectic temperature. The standard procedure for deriving partial thermodynamic functions from integral functions yields

$$
\begin{array}{l} \overline {{G _ {\mathrm {C u O}} ^ {\mathrm {l i q}}}} = G _ {\mathrm {C u O}} ^ {\mathrm {l i q}} + \mathrm {R T} \ln x \\ + \sum_ {k = 0} ^ {n} (k + 1) x ^ {k} (1 - x) ^ {2} Q _ {k}, \\ \end{array}
$$

$$
\begin{array}{l} \overline {{G _ {\mathrm {C u} _ {2} \mathrm {O}} ^ {\mathrm {l i q}}}} = G _ {\mathrm {C u} _ {2} \mathrm {O}} ^ {\mathrm {l i q}} + R T \ln (1 - x) \\ + \sum_ {k = 0} ^ {n} x ^ {k + 1} ((k + 1) x - k) Q _ {k} \\ \end{array}
$$

where $\overline{G_{\mathrm{CuO}}^{\mathrm{lig}}}$ and $\overline{G_{\mathrm{Cu_2O}}^{\mathrm{lig}}}$ are partial molar Gibbs energies of liquid $\mathrm{CuO}$ and $\mathrm{Cu}_{2}\mathrm{O}$ , respectively. At a point $C$ of the liquidus line, the liquid with composition $\mathrm{Cu}_{2 - x}\mathrm{O}$ is in equilibrium with solid $\mathrm{Cu_2O}$ and gaseous oxygen:

$$
\frac {2 - x}{2} \mathrm {C u} _ {2} \mathrm {O} ^ {\text {s o l}} + \frac {x}{4} \mathrm {O} _ {2} ^ {\text {g a s}} = \mathrm {C u} _ {2 - x} \mathrm {O} ^ {\text {m i x}}
$$

and, therefore,

$$
\begin{array}{l} G ^ {\text {m i x}} - \frac {2 - x}{2} G _ {\mathrm {C u} _ {2} \mathrm {O}} ^ {\text {s o l}} - \frac {x}{4} G _ {\bar {O} _ {2}} ^ {\text {g a s}} = x \overline {{G _ {\mathrm {C u O}} ^ {\text {l i q}}}} \\ + (1 - x) \overline {{G _ {\mathrm {C u} _ {2} \mathrm {O}} ^ {\mathrm {l i q}}}} - \frac {2 - x}{2} G _ {\mathrm {C u} _ {2} \mathrm {O}} ^ {\text {s o l}} - \frac {x}{4} G _ {\mathrm {O} _ {2}} ^ {\text {g a s}} = 0 \\ \end{array}
$$

Similar reasoning for the right branch $\mathbf{EB}$ results in the following equations:

$$
\begin{array}{l} F _ {E B} (x, T) = G _ {\mathrm {C u O}} ^ {\mathrm {l i q}} - G _ {\mathrm {C u O}} ^ {\mathrm {s o l}} + R T \ln x \\ + \sum_ {k = 0} ^ {n} (k + 1) x ^ {k} (1 - x) ^ {2} Q _ {k} = 0 \\ \end{array}
$$

$$
\begin{array}{l} G _ {\mathrm {O} _ {2}} ^ {\text {g a s}} = 4 G _ {\mathrm {C u O}} ^ {\text {s o l}} - 2 \mathrm {R T} \ln (1 - x) \\ - 2 \sum_ {k = 0} ^ {n} x ^ {k} (k x - (n - 1)) Q _ {k} - 2 G _ {\mathrm {C u} _ {2} \mathrm {O}} ^ {\mathrm {l i q}} \\ \end{array}
$$

At the eutectic point $\pmb{E}$ , both groups of equations (obtained for sectors $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{E}$ and $\mathbf{EB}$ ) are valid. In addition, for reaction $4\mathrm{CuO} = 2\mathrm{Cu}_{2}\mathrm{O} + \mathrm{O}_{2}$ between solid phases at this point, we can write

$$
G _ {\mathrm {O} _ {2}} ^ {\text {g a s}} = 4 G _ {\mathrm {C u O}} ^ {\mathrm {l i q}} - 2 G _ {\mathrm {C u} _ {2} \mathrm {O}} ^ {\text {s o l}}
$$

associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: Ternary alloys of 23 compositions were prepared from these master alloys by arc melting with a nonconsumable tungsten electrode on a water-cooled Cu hearth under an argon atmosphere (pressure $\sim80\mathrm{kPa}$ ) that had previously been gettered by melting Ti for $3\mathrm{min}$ . Experimental results form the basis for construction of the phase diagram as projections of solidus, liquidus surfaces, and melting (crystallization) diagrams, reaction scheme, and a number of vertical sections. Ternary compounds are absent in the system. Chromium carbides are confirmed to be in equilibria with (Ni) and (Cr) solid-solution phases to form two- and three-phase regions on the solidus surface. Comparison of structures for as-cast alloys and alloys annealed at subsolidus temperatures shows that annealing produces integration of structure with thin-phase boundaries, which verifies the attainment of equilibrium. X-ray diffraction patterns of annealed samples contain narrow reflections and are split into doublets at high angles by $\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2}$ resolution. Because the annealing temperatures were very close to the solidus, the authors considered the microstructures and XRD patterns to be representative of the state on the solidus surface. The metal content ratios of phases coexisting in three-phase equilibria at the solidus were determined by EPMA. The combination of EPMA, XRD, and metallographic data, and solidus temperatures allowed the determination of the positions of the three-phase boundaries and their phase compositions. One can see that the terminal solid solutions of (fcc Ni) and (bcc Cr) have ranges of homogeneity greater than any of the other solid phases. The apex coordinates of tie triangles on the solidus surface are presented. One can see that there is a wide two-phase region $(\mathrm{Ni}) + (\mathrm{Cr}_7\mathrm{C}_3)$ . The solidus temperature for the $(\mathrm{Ni}) + (\mathrm{Cr}_7\mathrm{C}_3)$ mixture increases from $1316^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ at the boundary with the three-phase region $(\mathrm{Ni}) + (\mathrm{Cr}_{23}\mathrm{C}_6) + (\mathrm{Cr}_7\mathrm{C}_3)$ to the maximum at $1324^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and then begins to decrease, reaching the value $1255^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ at the boundary with the three-phase region $(\mathrm{Ni}) + (\mathrm{Cr}_7\mathrm{C}_3) + (\mathrm{Cr}_3\mathrm{C}_2)$ . As this maximum is rather weak, additional DTA experiments were carried out to detect its exact location. Two two-phase alloys containing 10 at.% C and slightly different concentrations of Ni and Cr were simultaneously placed on the measuring block. One was used as a sample, the other as a standard and vice versa in the second experiment. The results of both experiments were in agreement; the more refractory alloy gave the thermal effect of melting at higher temperature. By gradually varying Cr concentration in these experiments, it was found that the maximum melting temperature is characteristic of the $\mathrm{Cr}_{40}\mathrm{Ni}_{50}\mathrm{C}_{10}$ alloy with a value of $1324 \pm 6^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ according to the Pirani-Alterthum method. The six fields of primary crystallization are evidently connected with the six phases found on the solidus surface. The saddle point $e_5$ corresponds to the maximum tem perature of the two-phase $(\mathrm{Ni}) + (\mathrm{Cr}_7\mathrm{C}_3)$ ruled solidus surface. The final phase composition of the material depends on the ratio of the carbide ingredients and Ni in the starting mixture, as can be seen from the Cr-Ni-C phase diagram. This problem was discussed in detail, recommending sintering the desired material as a mixture of the carbides containing $13.2\mathrm{mass}\%$ C with $15\mathrm{mass}\%$ Ni. Nevertheless, it seems quite safe to divide the ternary Cr-Ni-C diagram into two partial subsystems, $\mathrm{Cr - Cr_7C_3 - (Cr_{0.93}Ni_{0.07})_7}$ $\mathrm{C_3 - Cr_{29.5}Ni_{69}C_{1.5} - Ni}$ and $\mathrm{C - Cr_7C_3 - (Cr_{0.93}Ni_{0.07})_7C_3 - Cr_{29.5}Ni_{69}}$ $\mathrm{C_{1.5} - Ni}$ . The solidus temperatures of both subsystems decrease as the configuration point of the composition moves from the quasi-binary section or from the boundary systems inward. Since the liquid phase in the quenched alloys did not show a constant composition in an EDX analysis, an indirect method had to be used to determine the liquidus line. After all the quenched alloys had been classified by optical observation of the microstructure, the liquidus line was interpolated between the closest pairs of alloys with coexisting solid and liquid phases and liquid phase only. The composition of the liquid phase in equilibrium was then estimated by extrapolating the tie-line connecting the overall composition of the alloy and the composition of the solid phase to the intersection with the liquidus line. The isothermal sections of the phase diagram based on this experimental data at 800 and $1000^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , respectively, are shown. These phases are also present in the Al-Mn-Ni system and show considerable similarities in their ranges of composition. At 800 $^\circ \mathrm{C}$ , an additional phase appears, extending from the $\gamma \mathrm{GaNi}$ (NiAs type) into the ternary. This phase does not exist in the Al-analogue system. associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: Typical cooling transformation characteristics can be summarized in the figure, using Fe-Mn alloys as an example. In the low-cooling-rate range (<1000 °C/s for Fe-1.22 at.% Mn al loy), the higher the cooling rate the lower the transformation-start temperature, i.e. the further away from equilibrium, as shown in the figure. Above a certain critical cooling rate $(\sim 1000^{\circ}\mathrm{C / s}$ for Fe-1.22 at. $\%$ Mn), the transformation temperature becomes independent of the cooling rate and several plateaus appear in the $\mathbf{T}_{\mathfrak{t}}$ -T diagram. These plateaus (stages) signify the formation of various metastable phases, and they indicate that each kind of metastable phase possesses its own transformation-start temperature, which is independent of the cooling rate. When the results of several investigations are put together, as shown in the figure, distinct transformation-start temperatures $(\mathbf{M}_{\mathbf{a}},\mathbf{B}_{\mathbf{s}},$ and $\mathbf{M}_{\mathbf{s}})$ for various metastable phases (massive ferrite, bainitic ferrite, lath martensite, and twinned martensite) are evident. If the cooling or heating rate is high enough to initiate a metastable phase transformation, then the $\mathbf{M}_{\mathbf{s}}$ data will have relatively less scatter because the $\mathbf{M}_{\mathbf{s}}$ for metastable phase transformation is independent of cooling rate, as shown in the figure for Fe-Mn alloys. It is clear that each metastable phase has its own $\mathbf{T}_{\mathbf{s}}$ , which is independent of $\dot{\mathbf{T}}$ . Correspondingly, the $\mathbf{T}_{\mathbf{t}}$ - $\dot{\mathbf{T}}$ diagrams display staged kinetics, i.e. several plateaus, each for a specific metastable phase. This staged kinetics is found to be a general behavior of the cooling transformations, although different alloys may have a different metastable phase sequence. It is clear that each kind of metastable phase (massive ferrite, bainitic ferrite, lath martensite, and twinned martensite) has its own transformation-start temperature. Without such an analysis, the widely scattered “ $\mathbf{M}_{\mathrm{s}}$ ” points cannot be rationalized.

A further argument to improve the Ti-rich portion of the isothermal section at $950^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ concerns the curvature of the homogeneity regions of $(\beta \mathrm{Ti})$ in the two-phase equilibrium with $(\alpha \mathrm{Ti})$ and $\alpha_{2}$ , which is strongly concave at $1100^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , but appears as convex in the isothermal section at $950^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ . The new version of the isothermal section at $950^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ includes a modified section. From comparison of the proposed sections at 1100 and $950^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , one can see a significant change in the phase relations concerning the $\tau_{2}$ -phase. This difference arises due to decomposition of this phase on the Al-poor side of its solid solution revealing fine microstructures, with overall compositions corresponding to the single-phase regions of the $\tau_{2}$ -phase at higher temperatures. A rather extended single $\tau_{2}$ -phase field, observed at higher temperatures, reduces to a point at $950^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , and this phase refrains from forming equilibria with $\tau_{1}$ . Invariant equilibria $\mathrm{U}_{16}$ and $\mathrm{U}_{18}$ prompted such change of the phase relations in this portion of the diagram. Invariant equilibria concerning the polymorphic transformation of binary $\mathrm{TiAl}_3$ are not included. The isothermal section at $800^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ disagrees (1) with the compositions of the solid phases in the Al-Ti binary system, and (2) with the extent of the two-phase region, $\alpha_{2} + \delta$ , within the isothermal section for $770^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ . On the other hand, both groups of authors agree on the compositions of the $\beta$ and $\delta$ -phases in three-phase equilibria involving $\alpha_{2}$ . Our experimental data provided the information lacking in the Al-rich portion of the diagram, and a corresponding section is presented. Phase equilibria for the $800^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ section differ from those at $950^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ due to (1) a significant decrease of the homogeneity region of $\beta$ Ti and (2) the appearance of $\mathrm{Ti}_{3}\mathrm{Al}_{5}$ . The latter phase was not observed in the current study, probably, due to slow formation kinetics. Equilibria involving this phase are included to comply with the accepted Al-Ti binary. No significant changes are assumed to appear in the TiRu-Ru $_4$ Al $_{13}$ -TiAl $_3$ portion of Al-Ru-Ti diagram on lowering the temperature from $800^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ . The decrease of the homogeneity regions of $\beta \mathrm{Ti}$ triggers the disappearance of phase fields $(p)$ $\beta +\alpha +\alpha_{2}$ and $(w)$ $\beta +\alpha_{2} + \delta$ . The Ru content of the $\tau_{1}$ -phase holds for the entire homogeneity region extending from 36.7-50.8 at.% Al and equals about 23.5 at.% Ru. These data agree with the Ru content in the G-phase, as defined by various authors at 24.2 at.%, 25 at.%, and 19-28 at.%. Based on an uncertainty in the determination of the Ru content on Ru-rich and Ru-poor sides of the $\tau_{1}$ -phase, this phase boundary is presented in dashed lines. There are no contradictions on the Al content in the Al-rich part of the $\tau_{1}$ -phase. Values from 50-52 at.% Al at $800^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ are reported in fair accord with 52 at.% Al established at $1250^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ . Composition of the Ti-rich side of the $\tau_{1}$ -phase is uncertain: a content of 33 at.% Al is reported, a value of 36 at.% Al can be read from the $800^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ isothermal section, and aluminum contents of about 38 at.% at $770^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and 40 at.% at $1250^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ are claimed. The homogeneity region of the $\tau_{1}$ phase is assumed to be the same as at solidus temperatures. The extension of the $\tau_{2}$ single-phase field is compatible with the trend of its decrease with decreasing temperature as seen in samples annealed at $1100^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and lower. Additional corrections due to literature data were made to comply with thermodynamic rules for proper connection of phase regions and for a smooth change of phase boundaries with temperature. Phase equilibria that derive from the proposed solidus surface and reaction scheme were introduced. Dashed lines mark phase equilibria still uncertain.
