The corresponding calculated phase diagram is shown in the figure. As a further simplification, a regular solution model

$$
\Delta_ {\text {m i x}} G ^ {\text {e x}} (\mathrm {L}) = X (1 - X) (- 1 4 \quad 1 1 5) \mathrm {J} / \mathrm {m o l} 
$$

was derived here by retaining the peritectic point of the (Au) liquidus at 43 at. $\%$ Pb and $434^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ . The difference in the $\mathbf{L} / [\mathbf{L} + (\mathbf{Au})]$ liquidus boundary compositions calculated from these two models is within experimental uncertainty. In the case of Au-Pb, the enthalpy of mixing of the liquid phase was known experimentally (although with substantial uncertainty). Therefore, the enthalpy term of $\Delta_{\mathrm{mix}}G^{\mathrm{ex}}(\mathbf{L})$ could not be chosen arbitrarily. For example, the subregular solution model requires a minimum value of $-3529\mathrm{J / mol}$ for $\Delta_{\mathrm{mix}}G^{\mathrm{ex}}(\mathbf{L})$ at 50 at. $\%$ Pb, which is too exothermic a value in comparison with all experimental data. The general difference is accounted for by the excess entropy of mixing term. However, this example suggests that if no experimental data were available for the enthalpy or the entropy of mixing in a given system, the excess entropy of mixing term might be ignored as far as the calculated phase diagram is concerned. In fact, the assumption of a zero excess entropy of mixing is often more realistic than the values obtained by optimization of relatively inaccurate thermodynamic and phase diagram data. The enthalpy of mixing of the Au-Pb liquid alloys provides another example. Because the enthalpy of mixing values, measured at different temperatures, differ significantly, it could be assumed that the temperature dependence of the enthalpy of mixing is substantial and should be accounted for via a suitable expression. However, the appearance of the temperature dependence is far too complex, and modeling using only a limited number of parameters is not possible. Fortunately, in most such cases the temperature dependence of the enthalpy and of the excess entropy of mixing can be assumed to be rather small, or zero, at least at higher temperatures. (If they are not zero, the specific heat of mixing would have to be considered.) Most likely, much, if not all, of the measured data are not particularly accurate.

For example, the authors confirmed the eutectic reaction on the Al side (reported at $654^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and 0.75 at.% Sr). The melting point of $\mathrm{Al_4Sr}$ was given as $1025^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , the peritectic reaction of formation of $\mathrm{Al_2Sr}$ at $920^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , and "AlSr" (instead of the "Al $_2$ Sr $_3$ ") at $664^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ . The confirmation of the results in subsequent publications has lead to the adoption of most of the features of their diagram. However, the temperature of the eutectic reaction on the Al side—(654 °C) was taken from subsequent publications. The composition of the eutectic point was estimated on the basis of the properties of Al: $T_{\mathrm{fus}} = 660.45^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , $\Delta_{\mathrm{fus}}H = 10.7\mathrm{kJ / mol}$ , and the assumption that the Al activity coefficient in liquid alloys with up to 1 at.% Sr is equal to 1. The figure shows that the estimated position of the eutectic point at about 1 at.% Sr does not contradict the data of previous works. Therefore, the position of the calculated L/[L + (Al)] boundary is accepted, rather than the experimental result of previous works. The assessed Al-Sr phase diagram consists of: the liquid, L; the fcc terminal solid solution, (Al), with a small solubility of Sr; the bcc terminal solid solution, $(\beta \mathrm{Sr})$ , with a small solubility of Al; the fcc terminal solid solution, $(\alpha \mathrm{Sr})$ , with a small solubility of Al; and three intermetallic phases— $\mathrm{Al}_{2}\mathrm{Sr}$ , $\mathrm{Al}_{4}\mathrm{Sr}$ , and $\mathrm{Al}_{7}\mathrm{Sr}_{8}$ . The phase designated herein as $\mathrm{Al}_{7}\mathrm{Sr}_{8}$ has also been reported as “ $\mathrm{AlSr}$ ” and “ $\mathrm{Al}_{2}\mathrm{Sr}_{3}$ ” by several investigators. Three compounds were reported— $\mathrm{Al_4Sr}$ , $\mathrm{Al_2Sr}$ , and “ $\mathrm{Al_2Sr_3}$ ” The first melts congruently at $1040^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and the second and the third decompose by peritectic reactions at 936 and $666^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , respectively. “ $\mathrm{Al_2Sr_3}$ ” and $(\beta \mathrm{Sr})$ form a eutectic reaction at 81.75 at.% Sr and $590^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ ; no information was given about a eutectic reaction between (Al) and $\mathrm{Al_4Sr}$ ; except a line drawn at $660^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ . The temperatures of the peritectic reactions of formation of $\mathrm{Al_2Sr}$ and $\mathrm{Al_7Sr_8}$ and the temperature of the congruent melting of $\mathrm{Al_4Sr}$ were adopted from previous works. It should be noted that none of the above investigations mentioned the allotropic transformation in Sr at $547^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , which should influence the shape of the phase diagram. This transformation is included in the phase diagram as a dashed line. Did not observe any solubility of Sr in (Al). They concluded that $\mathrm{Al_4Sr}$ possesses a homogeneity range from about 15 to 25.7 at.% Sr at $700^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , and that "AlSr" dissolves some Sr. The solubility in the intermetallic phases was not confirmed in subsequent publications.

Because this phase is in the center of glass forming range, and the experimental results of Lundin et al. involving this phase have not been confirmed, no further attempt was made to improve this part of the calculated phase diagram. The calculated isothermal sections of the Ga-In-Sb phase diagram at selected temperatures are shown. The overall agreement between Ga-In-Sb phase diagrams calculated in the present work and previous experimental data is generally very satisfactory. The Ga-In-Sb phase diagram was previously calculated by Gratton and Woolley, Miki et al., Blom and Plaskett, Szapiro, Liao et al., and Brebrick et al. Miki et al. also used the regular solution model for the liquid phase and a complicated modified delta lattice parameter (MDLP) model for the solid compound, obtaining good agreement with the liquidus data and with the tie-line data. associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: The assessed phase diagram is shown in Fig. 1. Due to the speculative nature of much of the diagram, no table of special points is given. Liquidus points were measured by thermal analysis under argon in the range 0 to 58 at.% Li in graphitized corundum crucibles and in the range 95.5 to 100 at.% Li in Fe crucibles. No suitable container material was found for intermediate compositions. Ge of $99.99\%$ purity was used. The purity of the Li was not given. However, its melting point was $186^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, which is not in good agreement with the presently accepted value of $180.6^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. Samples were apparently analyzed after the experiments in order to determine the compositions. These authors report observing the two compounds $\mathrm{Ge}_5\mathrm{Li}_{22}$ and $\mathrm{GeLi}_3$ microscopically. The limiting liquidus slope in Fig. 1 at 0 at.% Li was calculated thermodynamically from the enthalpy of fusion of Ge under the assumption of negligible solubility of Li in solid Ge. Agreement with these results is reasonable. Thermal analysis was used to obtain liquidus points at 66.7, 75, and 80 at.% Li as shown on Fig. 1. As well, a thermal arrest was observed at $525^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ at 66.7 at.% Li. The composition at 80 at.% Li was also studied by thermal analysis on samples prepared from 99.9% Li and spectroscopically pure Ge. Cooling was started at $946^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. The first thermal effect was noticed at $690^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. Subsequent thermal arrests were observed at 667, 655, and $567^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. The results shown in Fig. 1 diverge greatly. A second thermal arrest in the range 90 to 100 at.% Li was observed as shown in Fig. 1. These authors interpreted this as evidence of a phase transformation. These thermal arrests fall very close to the liquidus of [81Dad] who failed to detect any evidence of such a transformation. It may be that the "phase transformation" was actually the liquidus and that their points at higher temperatures were caused by impurities. (As discussed above, their Li seems to have been of low purity.) Several compounds have been reported in this system, but their temperatures of fusion and transformation are, for the most part, unknown. The assessed diagram drawn in Fig. 1 is highly speculative, and is one possible interpretation of the available data. Coulometric titration between a Li-Ge electrode and a Li-Al electrode with a molten salt electrolyte was carried out between 360 and $440^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. Five plateaus were observed. These were identified with the following five compounds: GeLi, $\mathrm{Ge}_4\mathrm{Li}_9$, $\mathrm{Ge}_5\mathrm{Li}_{16}$, $\mathrm{Ge}_4\mathrm{Li}_{15}$, and $\mathrm{Ge}_5\mathrm{Li}_{22}$. GeLi was prepared by fusion at $750^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ or $650^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, followed by slow cooling, and its crystal structure was determined in single-crystal x-ray studies. Its presence at $400^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ was observed by coulometric titration, and its existence at $500^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ was confirmed, converted to a high-pressure form at this temperature. If the liquidus and eutectic data are correct, GeLi must decompose in a peritectoid reaction between 500 and $525^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, or it must melt, either congruently or incongruently, at a temperature close to $525^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. In Fig. 1, peritectic melting at $528^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ is shown, but only as a possibility. $\mathrm{Ge}_4\mathrm{Li}_9$ was prepared by fusion at $1000^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ followed by slow cooling, and its crystal structure was determined in single-crystal studies. From the meager liquidus data, it is tentatively postulated in Fig. 1 that this compound melts congruently.

Below $1000^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ the experimental data points of Fig. 1 are scattered within a narrow region and the phase boundaries can be identified with a reasonable degree of certainty. associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: The Mg-Th phase diagram constructed after evaluation of the literature is shown in the figure. [58Yam] placed the eutectic point at 7.05 at.% Th and $582^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. The solid phases in the eutectic structure were determined to be $(\mathbf{Mg})$ with 0.49 at.% Th, and an intermediate phase, with 16.5 at.% Th. The composition of the intermediate phase was determined by quantitative metallography, from which the authors assigned the formula "Mg5Th." Sturkey, Gladyshevskii et al., and [Elliott] showed the results of X-ray and thermal analysis of [58Yam] are consistent with a compound of the formula $\mathbf{Mg}_{23}\mathbf{Th}_6$ prototype of $\mathbf{Mn}_{23}\mathbf{Th}_6$. Hence, [60Stu] and [Elliott] placed the intermediate phase of the eutectic structure at 20.68 at.% Th corresponding to $\mathbf{Mg}_{23}\mathbf{Th}_6$, which for simplicity [60Stu] designated as $\mathbf{Mg}_4\mathbf{Th}$. Contrary to the above investigations, [63Pet] reported that the intermediate phase of the eutectic structure is $\mathbf{Mg}_2\mathbf{Th}$. There is lack of experimental data in the literature to resolve unequivocally the dispute over the intermediate phase of the eutectic structure and the mechanism of its formation. In the assessed Mg-Th diagram, the eutectic reaction is shown according to the results of [58Yam], as will be elucidated in the following sections. Jones and Nash and Yamamoto and Rostoker determined the liquidus temperature in the composition ranges from 0 to 6 at.% Th and 0 to 20 at.% Th, respectively. The liquid exhibits a miscibility gap. The oxygen solubility limit in the bismuth-rich liquid has been investigated by several authors using chemical analysis and electrochemical techniques. These results are shown in Fig. 1 and 2. Griffith et al. measured the oxygen content in samples equilibrated between 673 and $1023\mathrm{K}$ from $\mathrm{CO - CO_2}$ gas equilibrium analysis. Isecke et al. derived the oxygen solubility limit between 950 and $1473\mathrm{K}$ from a series of electromotive force (emf) measurements performed at constant oxygen content. At $1273\mathrm{K}$, they analyzed samples taken from the melt as described above and found the value $x_{\mathrm{O}} = 0.024$, which is in good agreement with the results obtained from emf measurements. Hahn and Stevenson determined it between 1073 and $1223\mathrm{K}$ using coulometric titration. The oxygen solubility limit has finally been derived from measurements of the oxygen diffusivity in the bismuth-rich liquid by Fitzner and Heshmatpour and Stevenson using potentiostatic titration techniques. The contradiction appearing between these studies is discussed in the optimization procedure. Most phase diagram, electrochemical, and calorimetric measurements are quantitatively well reproduced by the calculated values. The calculated phase diagram at 1 bar total pressure is shown in Fig. 1 and compared with experimental data.

associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: The phase diagram in the region 34 to 38 at.% In is proposed on the basis of the work of [72Jai] and may need further revisions. The more recently published data of [72Jai] drastically revised the phase relationships in the “η” phase field for temperatures below ~480 °C. According to [72Jai], the region ~33 to 38 at.% In comprises five different phases, which the authors labelled as “C,” “B,” “A,” “A,” and “h,” where the “h,” “A,” and “A,” phases occupy the “η” region proposed by [34Wei]. According to [72Jai], the “h” (or Cu₂₋ₓIn) is stable between 440 and 660 °C. Between 350 and 480 °C and in the composition range 35.5 to 37.8 at.% In, “A” (or Cu₇In₄) is stable, and between 300 and 450 °C in alloys between 35.4 and 37.8 at.% In, “A” exists. At temperatures below 389 °C, “B” was reported to exist in the composition range 35.6 to 37.2 at.% In. Finally, "C" was shown to form peritectoidally below 350 °C and in the composition range between 34.1 and 35.2 at.% In, although its formation was not observed by thermal analysis. Moreover, the equilibrium between "B" and "C" was not established clearly in metallographic studies. The limiting composition of "h" corresponds to ~33 at.% In at the peritectic temperature of 667 °C. Figure 4 shows the homogeneity ranges determined for the various phases by [72Jai] from DTA and metallographic investigations. Furthermore, results of X-ray investigations by [72Jai] are consistent with the homogeneity regions shown in Fig. 4.

associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: Fig. 1 shows the most likely equilibrium diagram based on currently available information, but further partial amendments at various points may be necessary. The equilibrium phases are (1) the liquid, L; (2) the fcc terminal solid solution, (Au), with a maximum solid solubility of 33.5 at.% Zn in (Au); (3) the cph terminal solid solution, (Zn), with about 7.5 at.% solid solubility of Au in (Zn); (4) four intermediate phases, $\alpha 3$, $\alpha 1$, $\alpha^{\prime}2$, and $\alpha 2$, in the composition range between 10 and 30 at.% Zn, with poorly defined phase boundaries; (5) the intermetallic compound Au5Zn3, forming peritectoidally at about $300^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$; (6) the CsCl-type $\beta^{\prime}$ phase, with a maximum solubility range between 38 and 57 at.% Zn, associated by a martensitic transformation to the $\beta 1$ phase at very low temperatures ($<100\mathrm{K}$); (7) the $\delta$ phase at about 56 at.% Zn, forming peritectoidally at $180^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$; (8) three intermediate phases, $\gamma$, $\gamma 2$, and $\gamma 3$, in the composition range between 63 and 83 at.% Zn, with not well established phase boundaries; and (8) the $\varepsilon$ phase, stable below $490^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ in the composition range between $-84$ and 89 at.% Zn with an allotropic variation, $\varepsilon^{\prime}$, below $-175^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. The $\mathrm{L} / [\mathrm{L} + (\mathrm{Au})]$ and $[\mathbf{L} + (\mathbf{A}\mathbf{u})] / (\mathbf{A}\mathbf{u})$ boundaries in the assessed phase diagram are based on the present thermodynamic calculations. The assessed phase diagram is a combined product of data points from various sources and which allows for some uncertainty in each set of data. Many critical points in Fig. 1 are subject to further modifications. The assessed boundaries in Fig. 1 are based primarily on the data of [06Vog] and [70Yaz]. The $\mathrm{L} \leftrightarrow (\mathrm{Au}) + \beta'$ eutectic temperature was estimated to be $683^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. The (Au)/[(Au) + $\beta'$] solvus boundary in Fig. 1 is based on the results of [71Pem] and [73Ald]. Thus the maximum solubility of Zn in (Au) is estimated to be 33.5 at.% at $683^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. The (Au)/[(Au) + $\alpha1$] and (Au)/[(Au) + $\alpha3$] solvus boundaries in Fig. 1 are based on the results of [58Wil] and [60Iwa]. The $\alpha_{3}$ phase was found in addition to $\alpha_{1}$ and $\alpha_{2}$ in the range of the ideal composition of 20 at.% Zn (see Fig. 1). The eutectoid reaction $(\mathrm{Au}) \leftrightarrow \alpha_{3} + \alpha_{1}$ at $260^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ for the $\alpha_{3}$ phase formation proposed by [58Wil] was modified by [60Iwa] to $(\mathrm{Au}) + \alpha_{1} \leftrightarrow \alpha_{3}$ peritectoid reaction at $300^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. The latter reaction is accepted in Fig. 1. The $(\mathrm{Au}) / \alpha 1$ and the $\alpha 1 / \alpha 2$ transformation temperatures are tentatively shown in Fig. 1 at 420 and $270^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, respectively. The coexistence of two phases, $\alpha_{1}$ and $\alpha_{2}$, between $204^{\circ}C$ and $274^{\circ}C$, reported by [59Fei] does not conform with the present assessment. The $\alpha 2$ phase was found to consist of two separate phases, $\mathrm{Au3Zn[R_1]}$ and $\mathrm{Au3Zn[R2]}$ ($\alpha^{\prime}2$ and $\alpha^{\prime}2$ in Fig. 1). The $\alpha 1 + \alpha 2\leftrightarrow \alpha^{\prime}2$ peritectoid temperature is about $215^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. The $\alpha 1\leftrightarrow \alpha 2 + \mathrm{Au5Zn3}$ reaction was not confirmed; this feature is not shown in Fig. 1. The $\mathrm{L} \leftrightarrow \beta^{\prime}$ congruent melting temperature: the result of [70Yaz] (751 °C) has been accepted in Fig. 1 for consistency with the liquidus curve in this composition range. The composition of the congruent point may be at 48.5 at.% Zn, slightly off the equiatomic composition, as estimated from the trend of the solidus curve. The $[(Au) + \beta^{\prime}] / \beta^{\prime}$ and $\beta^{\prime} / \beta^{\prime} + \gamma]$ boundaries in Fig. 1 have been drawn using the results of [71Pem], [73Ald], and [79Pea]. Other boundaries of the $\beta^{\prime}$ phase ($[\alpha_{1} + \beta^{\prime}] / \beta^{\prime}$, Au5Zn3 / [Au5Zn3 + $\beta^{\prime}$], and $\beta^{\prime} / [\beta^{\prime} + \delta]$) are not well defined. The present estimation (Fig. 1) is based (roughly) on the results of [40Age] at room temperature. The homogeneity range of the $\beta^{\prime}$ phase at about $100\mathrm{K}$ (at which temperature martensitic transformations take place) is likely to be very narrow. Figure 1 indicates only the beginning of the martensitic transformation temperatures on cooling $(\mathbf{M}_{\mathbf{s}})$ in the composition range between 49 and 51 at.% Zn. From the $\mathrm{L / [L + \beta^{\prime}]}$ liquidus, $\mathrm{L / [L + \gamma]}$ liquidus, and $[\beta^{\prime} + \gamma] / \gamma$ solvus trends, the present diagram shows the peritectic reaction at $654^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ (Fig.1). The most conspicuous differences are the absence of the $\gamma 1$ phase, and the presence of the $\gamma 3$ phase (Fig. 1). The assessed diagram (Fig. 1) differs from that of [79Pea], who assumed that the results of [23Sol] were basically acceptable outside of their investigation range; the present diagram is based on the work of [06Vog] for the same range. There are slight disagreements in the details of the phase relationships between the results of the high-temperature X-ray investigations and those obtained in quenched alloys by [79Pea]. They have been averaged in Fig. 1. The homogeneity range of the $\gamma$ phase at room temperature is accepted from [79Pea]. The homogeneity range of the $\gamma 2$ phase was reported as $75 \pm 0.5$ at.% Zn by [25Wes] and as $75.5 \pm 0.5$ at.% Zn by [79Pea], in good agreement. The latter is shown in Fig. 1. The homogeneity range of the $\gamma 3$ phase is not well established, but according to the X-ray observations of [79Pea] it is likely to be very narrow at low temperatures ($\sim$ room temperature). The $\varepsilon$ phase was reported as AuZng, forming at $490^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ by [06Vog]. This temperature is accepted in Fig. 1. Considerable solubility range was found by [25Wes], [62Mas], and [79Pea] (Fig. 1). In addition to the $\varepsilon$ phase, [79Pea] found the allotropic phase $\varepsilon'$, in the region 84 to 86 at.% Zn and at a temperature between 160 and 189 °C. The homogeneity range (between 84 and 89 at.% Zn at room temperature) reported by [25Wes] is in good agreement with the $\varepsilon + \varepsilon'$ phase field in the assessed phase diagram. The calculated phase boundaries according to the present model seem to represent the scattered experimental data points (Fig. 1), but they are by no means conclusive.

associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: In the Fe-base alloys with C, one could be interested in keeping the activity of C constant. With Fig. 19 it was already demonstrated that an activity axis should not be used together with a molar axis involving variations in $T$. On the other hand, an activity could be used together with $T$ itself. The reason is that phase equilibria at different $T$ cannot interfere because they become separated in the $T$ direction. Thus, one can get a true phase diagram by sectioning at a constant activity if $T$ is used as one of the axes. An example is given in Fig. 28. On the other hand, when selecting the other axis one must remember that the activity is used as a variable although it is not seen. One should thus consult the last column in Table 2. It contains $\mu_{f} / T$, which represents the activity of $i$. The activity of $i$ can thus be used as an axis or it can be kept constant, but it is necessary that component $i$ is not included in the $j$ components used to define the size of the system.

evidence.materials_system: Fe-base alloys with C
evidence.diagram_type: phase diagram by sectioning at a constant activity if T is used as one of the axes; activity axis ... molar axis

associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration:
The assessed equilibrium diagram in Fig. 1 is based mainly on the extensive thermal analysis, electrical resistivity, and dilatometric studies of [32Gru]. The limited thermal analysis results of [10Mas], also shown on Fig. 1, are in fair agreement. Agreement with the earlier work is reasonable for the liquidus on the Cd-rich side. However, the maximum in the liquidus/solidus was found to occur at 40 rather than 50 at.% Li. The liquidus and solidus on the Li-rich side differ from the earlier work by up to $50^{\circ}$.
In the diagram presented by [32Gru], an additional "β" phase between (Cd) and Cd3Li was proposed, with a two-phase region approximately as shown by the dotted lines on Fig. 1, a peritectic at $328^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, and a eutectoid involving (Cd), β, and Cd3Li at $80^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. However, the X-ray studies of [68Far] showed that the (Cd) phase extends at least to 22 at.% Li at $150^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. Therefore, it seems most likely that the "β" phase does not exist.
The existence of a separate Cd3Li phase is supported by the X-ray studies of [35Zin] and [33Bar, 34Bar], although the two studies disagree about the structure. The stoichiometry Cd3Li is based on the observation of the peak in the 2-phase region at $370^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ at 25 at.% Li as well as a peak in the electrical resistivity at this composition [32Gru]. The proposed boundaries of the two-phase $(\mathrm{Cd}) + \mathrm{Cd3Li}$ shown on Fig. 1, however, are not consistent with the results of [68Far] which, as mentioned above, show single-phase (Cd) extending to at least 22 at.% Li at $150^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$.
The existence of Li3Cd with an fcc crystal structure was confirmed by X-ray studies by both [35Zin] and [34Bar]. However, the entire phase diagram in Fig. 1 above 65 at.% Li is taken solely from the work of [32Gru]. In view of the discrepancies (noted above) between this study and more recent studies in the high-Li concentration ranges, the high-Li concentration region also should be re-examined.
The assessed Cd-Li equilibrium diagram is shown in Fig. 1, and special points on the diagram are listed in Table 1. Melting points of the elements are from [83Cha]. Figure 1 is based mainly on the extensive thermal analysis, electrical resistivity, and dilatometric measurements of [32Gru]. Alloys were prepared with Li of $99\%$ purity containing $0.6\%$ K and $0.15\%$ Na in Fe crucibles under argon. The thermal analysis experiments were also carried out in Fe crucibles under argon. Apparently, the alloys were not analyzed after the experiments to check for possible compositional changes. Liquidus points were obtained using cooling curves, whereas solidus points were found by heating curves. The samples for the resistivity and dilatometric studies were annealed at high temperature and slowly cooled in glass tubes. This may have caused some contamination due to attack of the glass by Li. All of the dilatometric and most of the resistivity points shown on Fig. 1 were obtained from the changes of slopes of resistivity vs temperature or dilatation vs temperature curves measured at heating rates of approximately 0.5 to $1.0^{\circ}\mathrm{C / min}$. The resistivity points delineating the Cd3Li + LiCd two-phase region were obtained from the slope changes of isothermal resistivity vs composition plots.
Earlier thermal analysis results [10Mas] are in reasonable agreement with the diagram of [32Gru], as can be seen in Fig. 1. Because of the high price of Li in 1910, these measurements were made on samples containing only 2 to $5\mathrm{g}$ of Li.
The liquidus/solidus of [32Gru] (Fig. 1) passes through a maximum at 50 at.% Li and $549^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. The liquidus measurements from the two studies for alloys with less than 30 at.% Li agree within about 10 $\mathrm{^\circ C}$. However, for alloys with higher Li contents, the liquidus and solidus lines, while having the same general shape, differ by up to $50^{\circ}C$. A possible explanation for the discrepancy could be Cd or Li losses by volatilization or by oxidation during the experiments. The maximum occurs above the phase field of the compound LiCd, which has been reported [56Sch2] to have the B32 NaTl structure up to $518^{\circ}C$ and which therefore would be expected to have its maximum thermodynamic stability near the stoichiometric 50 at.% composition. This supports a liquidus/solidus maximum near 50 at.%
From their resistivity and dilatometric studies, [32Gru] reported a " $\beta$ " phase between (Cd) and Cd3Li with the two-phase $(\mathrm{Cd}) + \beta$ region approximately as shown by the dotted lines on Fig. 1. A peritectic reaction was proposed at $328^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. However, as can be seen from an examination of the experimental points in Fig. 1, there is no firm evidence of an invariant plateau at this temperature. A eutectoid reaction involving (Cd), $\beta$, and Cd3Li at $80^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ was also proposed. Isothermal plots of resistivity vs composition [32Gru] at 100, 200, and $300^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ appear to change slope at the boundaries of the proposed two-phase region.
An alloy containing 23.1 at.% Li was found by [35Zin] to have disordered cph structure with $c / a = 1.586$. This may be the $\varepsilon$ phase in the Cd-Li system. However, [33Bar] attributed a bcc structure to this phase and maintained that this was correct [34Bar], despite criticism by [34Zin]. Isothermal electrical resistivity vs composition curves [32Gru] at 100, 200, 300, and 350 °C showed sharp peaks at 25 at.% Li, but at 400 °C no peak was observed. The two-phase region above the Cd3Li field in Fig. 1 also passes through a maximum near 25 at.% at 370 °C.
The two-phase $(\mathrm{Cd}) + \mathrm{Cd3Li}$ region, shown as dashed lines in Fig. 1, is not consistent with the aforementioned results of [68Far], which show single-phase (Cd) up to at least 22 at.% Li at $150^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$.
A powder diagram at 76.5 at.% Li was indexed by [35Zin] as disordered fcc. This was also observed by [34Bar]. However, [34Bar] claimed that his sample was annealed at $300^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and mentioned that $\mathrm{Li_3Cd}$ decomposes into LiCd and Li. Both these statements appear contrary to the diagram of [32Gru] (Fig. 1).
The LiCd phase is well established as having the NaTl (B32) structure at room temperature and at 50 at.% Li [34Bar, 35Zin, 52Sch2]. [56Sch2] reports the same structure up to $518^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ at 50 at% Li. Earlier results by [34Bar] indicating the NaTl structure at room temperature but a different structure at elevated temperatures were discounted by [35Zin] and [56Sch2] because of the lack of any supporting phase diagram evidence.

associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: In the Hg-S system, the intermediate phase HgS is formed at ~50 at.% S. It exists in three allotropic forms (αHgS, βHgS, and γHgS), and it melts congruently at 820 °C. Hg₂S is formed in chemical reactions, but not in a direct alloying. There are two liquid miscibility gaps and two monotectic reactions, i.e., one each in the Hg-HgS and HgS-S regions of the phase diagram. The two eutectic reactions close to pure Hg and pure S are essentially degenerate. The assessed Hg-S phase diagram is based partially on our modeling and calculations. [78Pot] observed a third allotropic form (γHgS) at higher temperatures and found that all three forms of HgS (α, β, and γ) dissolve excess S under equilibrium conditions. The stability range of αHgS, βHgS, and γHgS and the related equilibria shown in the figure are based essentially on the work of [78Pot]. Table 1 gives αHgS → βHgS, βHgS → γHgS temperatures, and the congruent melting point of γHgS reported by various investigators, along with the assessed values, 51.1 at.% S and 820 °C.

associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: One eutectic invariant exists at $180.3 \pm 0.1^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. Figure 2 shows the detail of the eutectic region. In thermal analysis experiments, [76Hub] observed eutectic arrests at $180.24 \pm 0.03^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, in good agreement with [75Yon]. However, these authors measured a melting point of pure Li of 180.49 $^\circ\mathrm{C}$, which is $0.11^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ below the accepted value. Figure 2 shows liquidus points measured by [76Hub]. High purity Li gettered with Zr and Y was used. Successive additions of small amounts of $\mathrm{N}_2$ gas $(\sim 1\mathrm{ml})$ were metered in and were assumed to dissolve completely in the molten Li. Details of the metering technique were not given, nor was it indicated why complete dissolution of the N could be assumed. Liquidus temperatures were subsequently measured by thermal analysis. A liquidus drawn through the points of [76Hub] in Fig. 2 would be very curved, with a nearly horizontal limiting slope at 0 at. $\%$ N. Thermodynamically, this is extremely unlikely.

associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: The assessed Ga-Hg phase diagram is virtually the same as originally constructed by [60Pre] and recently confirmed by [90Gub]. The equilibrium phases in the Ga-Hg system are: (1) the liquid, L, with a miscibility gap $(\mathrm{L}_1 + \mathrm{L}_2)$ between 26.7 and $203.5^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ ; (2) the orthorhombic terminal solution (Ga) with small solubility of Hg; and (3) the rhombohedral terminal solid solution (Hg) with low solubility of Ga. Table 1 lists the special points of the assessed Ga-Hg phase diagram. No compounds were reported in the temperature range that has been investigated. The critical point estimated from thermal analysis [60Pre, 90Gub] is about $1^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ higher than that from precise resistivity measurements [71Sch1, 71Sch2, 84Tsc] or that from neutron absorption [72Dab]. The selection of critical temperature at $203.5^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ seems to be the best compromise among the results of all techniques. [71Sch1], [72Dab], and [84Tsc] pointed out that the liquidus line of [60Pre] should be slightly modified near the critical region. This was corroborated by [90Gub], who found more shallow slopes of the liquidus on both sides of the critical point. As can be seen, no temperature dependence on the heat of mixing for the liquid was assumed and calculated monotectic and other miscibility gap points are reproduced within the error of experiments.

associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: The condensed phases in the Cr-Te system are: (1) liquid with a probable miscibility gap; (2) solid phase, bcc $(\mathrm{Cr})$; (3) solid phase, hexagonal $(\mathrm{Te})$; (4) NiAs-like intermediate phases between 52.4 and 62.0 at.% Te; and (5) at least one polytelluride phase, $\mathrm{CrTe}_3$ (monoclinic), between 70 and 75 at.% Te. Existence of two other polytellurides, "$\mathrm{Cr}_2\mathrm{Te}_5$" and "$\mathrm{CrTe}_{4-y}$" is not yet confirmed. In the assessed results, the NiAs-like phases are divided into high-, intermediate-, and low-temperature regions. The high-temperature region containing only the disordered $\mathrm{Cr}_{1-x}\mathrm{Te}$ phase is speculative. At intermediate temperatures, the phase field is separated into $\mathrm{Cr}_3\mathrm{Te}_4$-h (hexagonal-monoclinic), $\mathrm{Cr}_5\mathrm{Te}_8$-m (monoclinic), and $\mathrm{Cr}_5\mathrm{Te}_8$-tr (trigonal). At low temperatures, the phases are $\mathrm{Cr}_3\mathrm{Te}_4$-l (monoclinic), $\mathrm{Cr}_2\mathrm{Te}_3$ (trigonal), $\mathrm{Cr}_5\mathrm{Te}_8$-m (monoclinic), and $\mathrm{Cr}_5\mathrm{Te}_8$-tr (trigonal). An assessed Cr-Te phase diagram at standard atmospheric pressure, which is consistent with current experimental evidence, is shown in Fig. 1. The diagram is principally based on the investigations of [79Gun] and [83Ips]. The estimated eutectic composition of 10 at.% Te conforms to the limiting slope calculated for Cr metal. The phase diagram in Fig. 1 has been constructed to accommodate the fact that the supposed solidus and the liquidus show a gap of $\sim 30^\circ\mathrm{C}$ at the maximum, and shows an order-disorder type transition from $\mathrm{Cr}_3\mathrm{Te}_4$-h to $\mathrm{Cr}_{1-x}\mathrm{Te}$ at $1252^\circ\mathrm{C}$ but this seems inconsistent with invariant reactions at three temperatures. The features of the diagram include an invariant eutectoid reaction at $1204^\circ\mathrm{C}$, congruent transition points at $1283^\circ\mathrm{C}$ (melting) and $1252^\circ\mathrm{C}$ at 55 at.% Te, as well as an assumed eutectoid reaction at $450^\circ\mathrm{C}$. On the Te side, two phases that are stable below $480^\circ\mathrm{C}$ are assigned formulas, "$\mathrm{Cr}_2\mathrm{Te}_5$" and $\mathrm{CrTe}_3$, both with very narrow to negligible homogeneity ranges. A value of 98 at.% Te is assigned to the eutectic composition from the limiting slope of pure Te. The highly disordered NiAs structure is speculated to form by an order-disorder reaction from $\mathrm{Cr}_3\mathrm{Te}_4$-h beginning near $1252^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and 55 at.% Te. On the Cr-rich side, it extends to 52.4 at.% Te and forms by a metatectic reaction between (Cr) and liquid. At $1204^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and at 52.2 at.% Te it is believed to form from liquid plus $\mathrm{Cr}_3\mathrm{Te}_4$-h. On the Te-rich side, the disordered structure starts ordering somewhere above $800^\circ\mathrm{C}$ giving rise to the monoclinic and trigonal modifications, again with transformations believed to be higher order. The Te-rich limit of the hexagonal structure is represented in Fig. 1 as a vertical dotted line at 53.5 at.% Te. Beyond this composition the structure is monoclinic. The liquidus, solidus, and $\alpha / (\alpha + \beta)$ boundary as presented in Fig. 1 do not differ greatly from previous evaluations. The $\beta / (\alpha + \beta)$ boundary is significantly different from the versions of previous compilations, and therefore the estimated thermodynamic parameters for all three phases differ from the values based on earlier evaluations. Hence, the solidus and liquidus of Fig. 1 are calculated curves. The maximum solubility of Nb in $\alpha -\mathrm{Ti}$ is taken to be 2.0 to 2.5 at.% Nb at a temperature between 600 and $650^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. The data point on the $\alpha /(\alpha + \beta)$ boundary is located at 2.25 at.% Nb and $625^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. The phase boundary in Fig. 1 is the result of thermodynamic calculation in which the $\alpha$ phase was modeled as a regular solution (see "Thermodynamics"). The calculated value of the maximum solubility is 2 at.% Nb and the calculated $\alpha / (\alpha + \beta)$ boundary is considered an adequate representation of the experimental data. The same discrepancy has been found in other $\beta$-stabilizing systems (e.g., Ti-Cr) by investigators who have compared the results of the conventional and rapid quenching techniques. Because rapid quenching techniques have been shown to give the best representation of equilibrium, the evaluated phase boundary is based on the work of [66BRO]. However, the data of [66BRO] produce difficulties for thermodynamic optimization calculations. The calculations suggest that while the shape of the boundary is correct the temperatures are too low. It is not clear why this is so. Therefore, the $\beta / (\alpha + \beta)$ boundary in Fig. 1 is drawn as a dashed line. The diagram of Fig. 1 is the result of a regular solution calculation. The free energies of all three phases are represented as:

$$
\begin{array}{r l} G ^ {i} & = F _ {\mathrm {T i}} ^ {i} (1 - x) + F _ {\mathrm {N b}} ^ {i} x + R T (x \ln x + (1 - x) \ln (1 - x)) + \\ & B ^ {i} x (1 - x) \end{array}
$$

where $i$ designates the phase, $x$, the atom fraction of $\mathrm{Nb}$; $F^i$, the lattice stability parameters; and $B^i$, the regular solution interaction parameter. More recently, [74Uga] performed DTA of Si-As alloys in the temperature range 760 to 1100 °C. The liquidus points were determined from the heating curves obtained at a heating rate of 6 to 7 °C/min, whereas the eutectic and peritectic temperatures were found from the cooling curves obtained at a cooling rate of 1.5 to 2 °C/min. The temperatures were reported to be accurate within ±5 °C. The results of [41Kle] and [74Uga], reproduced in Fig. 1, agree fairly well. The main discrepancy is in the eutectic temperature at the As-rich side of the diagram: 786 °C according to [41Kle], compared with 797 °C of [74Uga]. The data of [74Uga] were re-evaluated by [81Uga] using vapor pressure measurements performed in the composition range 25 to 80 at.% As by a static manometric method. The accuracy of the pressure measurements was believed to be ±0.01 bar for pressures up to 1 bar, and ±0.1 bar for pressures above 1 bar. As evident from the T-X projection, the characteristic temperatures in the system are higher than those of [41Kle] and [74Uga] by up to 33 °C (for the peritectic temperature). The discrepancy might be due to the insufficiently slow cooling rate used for thermal analysis experiments by [41Kle] and [74Uga]. Assuming this, the present evaluators have accepted the critical points coordinates reported by [81Uga] (Fig. 1). The solidus and solvus, reproduced in Fig. 1 and 3, are adopted from [60Tru] and [71San], respectively. Sandhu; the measurements were performed by a static method in the temperature range 800 to 1009 °C, and the samples were analyzed by radiotracer and chemical methods. The P-T-X diagram in Fig. 2 implies an extrapolated sublimation point of As at about 40 bar and 820 °C. The present evaluators have calculated the sublimation temperature at 30 and 40 bar as 810 and 831 °C, respectively.

associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: The program begins with the standard two-dimensional, top-view projection ternary diagram, as shown in Fig. 1. This figure displays the digitized compounds (circles), the joins between them (blue on the screen), phase boundaries (red on the screen), and the temperature isotherms for each primary phase field (grey on the screen). A template of compound names and temperatures is superimposed. The net result is a diagram visually the same as Plate No. 1, with the exceptions indicated in the Introduction. The screen display also shows a key defining the different types of lines as well as the chemical composition of mineral names. The main program, written in Microsoft Visual Basic 3.0 for Windows, input the revised digitized data and stored the compound names, data, and tags as arrays. These data then were replotted on the two-dimensional view (Fig. 1) with lines extending from point to point where the points were spaced closely enough to give the impression of smooth curves. The blue joins were determined on the basis of compatibility triangles, which in turn were based on calculations from boundary tags. The text overlay of compound names, formulas, and temperatures was created via an included program module containing this information for this specific phase diagram. Although writing and locating standard text in a chosen font style, size, etc., was straightforward in Visual Basic, writing chemical formulas with subscripts and temperatures on angles to follow isotherm lines was more involved. Subscripts were created by breaking each text string up letter by letter and looking for subscript flags (e.g. the underline in the formula Al_2O_3). The text was then printed to the screen one letter at a time, offsetting the subscript characters. Although Visual Basic is not capable of writing text strings on an angle, Windows itself can. Visual Basic allows access to Windows functions via calls to subroutines referred to as the Windows API (application program interface). Thus the angular text was written by this indirect method. There are two ways to transfer from the two-dimensional view window to the three-dimensional rendering. If a location within the diagram is clicked, a three-dimensional rendering of just the surfaces germane to cooling of the chosen composition will be shown. associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: Metallography and XRD patterns lead one to the conclusion that the alloys 52.5Sc-40C, 27Sc-46C, 21Sc-44C, 15Sc-45C, 35Sc-38C, and 16.3Sc-38.5C (all in at.%) are single-phase with the NaCl-type structure. An assumption of the existence of this continuity was made by Novotny and Auer-Welsbach taking into account the high mutual solubility of the phases. The existence of a continuous solid solution across the system was proposed also by Velikanova et al. It is based on the fact that the difference between cubic carbide lattice parameters of $9\%$ is less than the limiting value established for d-transition IV to VI group metal carbides. However, taking into consideration the particular position of Sc in the Periodic Table, this possibility needed experimental verification and was later confirmed experimentally in our research work. Using modified δ phase lattice parameters we constructed isoparametric lines for (Sc, Ti)C solid solution. The intersection points of the rays $\mathrm{Ti} / (\mathrm{Ti} + \mathrm{Sc})_{1 - x}$ for δ phase by EPMA data for three-phase alloys $\delta +\mu +\mathrm{C}$ and $\delta +\mu +\rho$ with the isoparametric lines corresponding to the lattice parameter of δ phase in given phase ranges defining the compositions at the C-rich limit of the δ phase locates the δ phase corner of the tietriangles on the solidus. The tie-lines position in the $\beta +\delta$ range has been established by the EPMA, DTA, and XRD data. The tie-line inclinations indicate that the δ phase is enriched with Ti in comparison with the metal phase. Thus, thermodynamic stability of Ti carbide is higher than that of Sc carbide. There is a minimum in the solidus tie-lines surface at about $1300^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ in the $\beta +\delta$ range. It corresponds to an extreme shape of solidus and liquidus curves of the Ti-Sc binary system. The compositions of phases existing at this temperature are: for $\delta ,14\mathrm{Sc - }37.5\mathrm{C},$ and for $\beta ,49.5\mathrm{Sc - 1C}$. associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: Control of the kinetics of galvannealing of steel can be understood by examination of phase equilibria in the Fe-Al-Zn system. A schematic representation of the equilibria in this system at $450^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ is shown in Fig. 12, in which the eight white areas are single-phase fields, and the seven shaded triangles are three-phase equilibria. The Fe-Al binary system contains four intermetallic phases, three of which can contain significant concentrations of zinc, and the binary system Fe-Zn contains three intermetallic phases, all of which are capable of dissolving aluminum. The liquidus composition in binary Zn-Al occurs at 16 wt.% Al, and Fe has a very small solubility in the liquid Zn-Al alloys at $450^\circ\mathrm{C}$. When a thin layer of pure liquid zinc is placed on an iron (steel) surface at $450^\circ\mathrm{C}$, Fe dissolves in the liquid, and saturation occurs at an iron content of 0.029 wt.% At this point, the $\zeta$ phase of composition $a$ in Fig. 12 nucleates at the solid-liquid interface and begins to grow into the layer of liquid zinc. During this growth, the concentration of iron in the $\zeta$ phase at the $\zeta$-steel interface increases, and when the composition reaches $b$, the $\delta_{1}$ phase of composition $c$ nucleates and begins to grow into the $\zeta$ phase. Given enough time, the composition of the $\delta_{1}$ phase in contact with the steel moves to the point $d$, and the $\Gamma$ phase nucleates and begins to grow into the $\delta_{1}$. Thus, during the galvannealing of steel, all three intermetallics can be present in the galvannealed layer. Also, when the advancing layer of $\zeta$ phase consumes the liquid zinc, it in turn is then consumed by the advancing $\delta_{1}$ phase. The reactions that occur during galvannealing are extremely rapid and over-galvannealing can occur during the time required to run the zinc-coated steel strip through the galvannealing furnace. Consequently, the galvannealing reactions are inhibited by adding Al to the liquid zinc. Figure 12 shows that the liquid zinc phase, which is doubly saturated with $\mathrm{Fe}_2\mathrm{Al}_5$ and $\delta_{1}$, contains 0.11 wt.% Al, and the liquid zinc phase, which is doubly saturated with $\delta_{1}$ and $\zeta$, contains 0.07 wt.% Al. Thus, if the zinc used for galvannealing contains slightly more than 0.11 wt.% Al, the phase that first nucleates on the steel, as a result of dissolution of Fe in the melt, is $\mathrm{Fe}_2\mathrm{Al}_5$. Growth of this layer causes a decrease in the Al content of the liquid, and when the weight percentage of Al has been decreased to 0.07, the melt is in equilibrium with both $\delta_{1}$ and $\mathrm{Fe}_2\mathrm{Al}_5$. Further decrease in the aluminum content of the melt moves the system into the liquid-$\delta_{1}$ two-phase region, which causes the nucleation and growth of $\delta_{1}$ on the steel and the dissolution of $\mathrm{Fe}_2\mathrm{Al}_5$. The rate of growth of the initial $\mathrm{Fe}_2\mathrm{Al}_5$ layer is significantly lower than the rate of growth of the $\delta_{1}$ layer, and hence the initial time period during which the $\mathrm{Fe}_2\mathrm{Al}_5$ grows can be considered to be an incubation period, the length of which is determined by the initial concentration of Al in the liquid zinc.

associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: Fig. 1 shows a comparison of the well-known low-carbon section of the binary Fe-C equilibrium phase diagram (light dashed line) and the corresponding diagram calculated for ternary Fe-C-Mn (bold solid line). As indicated in this figure, addition of manganese shifts the $\gamma/\gamma + \alpha$ phase boundary to lower temperatures and decreases the size of the $\alpha$ single-phase field. The eutectoid reaction $\gamma \Leftrightarrow \alpha +$ cementite in binary Fe-C is represented by the straight line $(h)$. Addition of manganese adds one degree of freedom to the system and allows for the existence of a three-phase field $\gamma + \alpha +$ cementite (between lines $(e)$ and $(f)$). The equilibrium phase diagrams reveal much of the information necessary for a treatment of possible phase transformation reactions in the alloying system under consideration. Depending on the location of the start and end points of a reaction in the phase diagram, information on the reaction products and possible intermediate reaction paths can be derived. It must be emphasized, however, that a phase diagram can only represent the thermodynamic limits for phase transformations. Whether any such transformation reaction actually occurs depends on kinetic constraints such as the availability of potential nucleation sites or sufficient driving force for nucleation and for the maintenance of the phase boundary movement.

associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: The experimental phase boundary data related to the ordered $\mathrm{Au}_{3}\mathrm{Cu}$ phase have been reported as various values by different investigators, presumably because of the difficulty in attaining a full equilibrium state at low transformation temperatures $(<240^{\circ}\mathrm{C})$. Other portions of Fig. 3 are only tentative. The Cu concentration at the Au-rich limit of the ordered $\mathrm{Au}_{3}\mathrm{Cu}$ phase decreases as the temperature is lowered. However, the observed trend is controversial. An X-ray diffraction study of a 22 at.% Cu alloy, heat treated at $160^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, showed no indication of an ordered $\mathrm{Au}_{3}\mathrm{Cu}$ phase [57Bat]. On the other hand, electron diffraction patterns obtained by [59Oku] and [64Tot] indicated the existence of this phase in an alloy containing 9 at.% Cu. Thermal arrest temperatures on heating at a rather high rate $(8^{\circ}\mathrm{C / min})$ measured by [71Lut] are not likely to correspond to an equilibrium state, but the occurrence of a reaction involving the $\mathrm{Au}_{3}\mathrm{Cu}$ phase is indicated at lower Cu concentration than expected from [57Bat]. From the trend of the $[(Au)+Au_{3}Cu]/Au_{3}Cu$ phase boundary and the $(Au)+AuCu \rightarrow Au_{3}Cu$ reaction at $\sim 240^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, the Cu-rich limit of the ordered $\mathrm{Au}_{3}\mathrm{Cu}$ phase is about 38.5 at.% Cu, in agreement with the value reported by [64Tot], rather than 35 at.% Cu reported earlier by [31Gru], [32Leb], and [55Rhi]. Neither electrical resistivity [36Joh] nor the superlattice line intensity attain a maximum at 25 at.% Cu. Thus, the $\mathrm{Au}_{3}\mathrm{Cu}$ phase is not symmetrical near the stoichiometric composition.

The liquidus and solidus separations of Fig. 1 are based primarily on those predicted by the measured thermodynamic parameters in the liquid and fcc phases, with the assessed boundary location giving greatest weight to the measurements of the liquidus. Due to the sluggishness of the $(\gamma \mathrm{Fe},\mathrm{Ni})\rightarrow (\alpha \mathrm{Fe})$ and $(\alpha \mathrm{Fe})\rightarrow (\gamma \mathrm{Fe},\mathrm{Ni})$ phase transformations below $800^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, the $(\alpha \mathrm{Fe}) / (\gamma \mathrm{Fe},\mathrm{Ni})$ equilibrium boundaries are difficult to determine. These results, along with those of [69Sta], demonstrated clearly the retrograde solubility of Ni in $(\alpha \mathrm{Fe})$. The data of [49Owe], [49Jon], [65Gol], and [80Rom] agree fairly well at $500^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and above. The boundaries shown in Fig. 1 were constructed using these data, giving greatest weight to the results of [80Rom]. Figure 6 compares the cluster variation calculations of [84Yam] for the ordering reactions with the assessed diagram of Fig. 1. The FeNi and $\mathrm{Fe}_3\mathrm{Ni}$ ordered structures are not shown on the diagram of Fig. 1. Although still an open question, it is probable that these ordered phases are metastable or unstable structures reached in alloys in which the sluggish $(\gamma \mathrm{Fe,Ni})\rightarrow (\alpha \mathrm{Fe}) + \mathrm{FeNi}_3$ eutectoid reaction has been suppressed. associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: The experimentally determined Co-Pr-B (Co-rich) isothermal section at $1000^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ is shown in Fig. 5. The binary and ternary $\mathrm{Pr - Co - B}$ intermetallics were found to be true line compounds (no detectable solid solubility). This result is in agreement with the results obtained by other researchers, and it was confirmed by obtaining XRD patterns from several out-of-stoichiometry alloys, which contained these intermetallics. In the case of the $\mathrm{Pr}_2\mathrm{Co}_{14}\mathrm{B}$ intermetallic compound, the lattice parameters determined for such out-of-stoichiometry alloys were the same as those determined for the stoichiometric compound itself ( $a = 0.866\mathrm{nm}$ and $c = 1.190\mathrm{nm}$ ) within the experimental error of $\pm 0.001\mathrm{nm}$ . In addition, the Curie temperature of the $\mathrm{Pr}_2\mathrm{Co}_{14}\mathrm{B}$ compound present in the out-of-stoichiometry alloys was the same ( $T_{\mathrm{C}} = 715^\circ\mathrm{C}$ ) as the Curie temperature obtained for the single-phase stoichiometric compound within the experimental error of $\pm 3^\circ\mathrm{C}$ . The lattice parameters and Curie temperature are generally sensitive to changes in the chemical composition. Since no such changes were observed, it was concluded that no appreciable solid solubility exists in the $\mathrm{Pr}_2\mathrm{Co}_{14}\mathrm{B}$ intermetallic compound. Similar experiments have confirmed that all of the $\mathrm{Pr - Co - B}$ ternary intermetallics that were examined $(\mathrm{Pr}_2\mathrm{Co}_{14}\mathrm{B},\mathrm{Pr}\mathrm{Co}_4\mathrm{B},$ $\mathrm{PrCo_{12}B_6}$ $\mathrm{Pr}_3\mathrm{Co}_{11}\mathrm{B}_4$ , and $\mathrm{Pr}_2\mathrm{Co}_7\mathrm{B}_3)$ have no appreciable solid solubility. In addition to the fact that the binary and ternary $\mathrm{Pr - Co - B}$ (Co-rich) intermetallics are true line compounds, it was also found that no liquid exists in equilibrium with the $\mathrm{Pr}_2\mathrm{Co}_{14}\mathrm{B}$ phase below $1000^\circ\mathrm{C}$ (only solid phases). Therefore, in the isothermal section shown in Fig. 5, the single-phase fields are represented by points (the composition of the intermetallics), the two-phase fields by straight lines (lines linking the compositions of two intermetallics), and the three-phase fields by triangles. These triangles are "compatibility triangles," and their three sides are Alkemade lines. Liquid phase exists in the vicinity of the $\mathrm{PrCo_2}$ binary intermetallic only. The $\mathrm{Pr}_2\mathrm{Co}_{14}\mathrm{B}$ intermetallic is involved in five compatibility triangles with $\alpha \mathrm{Co}$ , $\mathrm{Pr}_2\mathrm{Co}_{17}$ , $\mathrm{PrCo}_5$ , $\mathrm{PrCo}_4\mathrm{B}$ , and $\mathrm{PrCo}_{12}\mathrm{B}_6$ , respectively as shown in Fig. 5. The microstructures of five isothermally heat treated alloys ( $\mathrm{I}_1$ , $\mathrm{I}_2$ , $\mathrm{I}_3$ , $\mathrm{I}_4$ , and $\mathrm{I}_5$ ), whose compositions (Fig. 5) fall inside some of these compatibility triangles, are shown in Fig. 10 through 14. Each of the microstructures shown in these figures is accompanied by the corresponding TMA curve. The TMA curve of the alloy confirms the chemical compositions of the phases present in the alloy. This is indicated by the occurrence of the Curie temperatures corresponding to these phases. For example, Fig. 10 shows the microstructure of alloy $\mathrm{I}_1$ of composition $\mathrm{Pr}_9\mathrm{Co}_{89}\mathrm{B}_2$ , which was isothermally heat treated at $1000^\circ\mathrm{C}$ . The TMA curve (Fig. 10b) suggests that alloy $\mathrm{I}_1$ consists of three phases: $\mathrm{Pr}_2\mathrm{Co}_{14}\mathrm{B}$ ( $T_{\mathrm{C}} = 715^\circ\mathrm{C}$ ), $\mathrm{Pr}_2\mathrm{Co}_{17}$ ( $T_{\mathrm{C}} = 904^\circ\mathrm{C}$ ), and $\alpha \mathrm{Co}$ ( $T_{\mathrm{C}} = 1127^\circ\mathrm{C}$ ). The $T_{\mathrm{C}}$ of $\alpha \mathrm{Co}$ is not evident in the TMA curve because the maximum temperature that the instrument could reach was only $1050^\circ\mathrm{C}$ . However, the nonzero value of the magnetization at the maximum temperature of measurement was taken as evidence of the existence of Co. This is because there is no compound in the $\mathrm{Co}-\mathrm{Pr}-\mathrm{B}$ system, other than $\alpha \mathrm{Co}$ , that has Curie temperature higher than that of $\mathrm{Pr}_2\mathrm{Co}_{17}$ ( $T_{\mathrm{C}} = 904^\circ\mathrm{C}$ ). The three phases ( $\mathrm{Pr}_2\mathrm{Co}_{14}\mathrm{B}$ , $\mathrm{Pr}_2\mathrm{Co}_{17}$ , $\alpha \mathrm{Co}$ ) identified by the TMA are also shown in the microstructure of the alloy shown in Fig. 10a. The composition of alloy $\mathrm{I}_1$ falls inside the compatibility triangle comprised of the $\mathrm{Pr}_2\mathrm{Co}_{14}\mathrm{B},\mathrm{Pr}_2\mathrm{Co}_{17}$ , and $\alpha \mathrm{Co}$ phases. Therefore, following the solidification under equilibrium conditions, one expects to find the above three phases present in the alloy. The final composition of $\mathrm{Pr}_2\mathrm{Co}_{14}$B-based sintered magnets was found to be located very close to the $\mathrm{Pr}_2\mathrm{Co}_{14}\mathrm{B - PrCo_4B}$ Alkemade line (see Fig. 5). Depending on the side of the Alkemade line of which the overall magnet composition is located, one can observe the presence of traces of either $\mathrm{PrCo_5}$ or $\mathrm{PrCo_{12}B_6}$ phases. It is very possible that if one chooses the final composition of the sintered magnets to be located on the $\mathrm{Pr}_2\mathrm{Co}_{14}\mathrm{B - PrCo_{12}B_6}$ Alkemade line, the resulting intrinsic coercivity of the magnets will be maximized. This is because the secondary $\mathrm{PrCo_{12}B_6}$ phase is nonmagnetic and will effectively isolate the magnetic $\mathrm{Pr}_2\mathrm{Co}_{14}\mathrm{B}$ grains. In the case of the $\mathrm{Pr}_2\mathrm{Co}_{14}\mathrm{B}$ -based rapidly quenched magnets, the secondary phases are the $\mathrm{PrCo_4B}$ and traces of $\mathrm{PrCo_{12}B_6}$ . In this case, the composition of the magnets was located inside the compatibility triangle involving the $\mathrm{PrCo_{12}B_6}$ and not the $\mathrm{PrCo_5}$ phase (left side of the $\mathrm{Pr}_2\mathrm{Co}_{14}\mathrm{B - PrCo_4B}$ Alkemade line). According to the present Co-Pr-B phase diagram, we concluded that the presence of $\mathrm{PrCo_2}$ is highly improbable. We believe that the observed reflections are due to the presence of the $\mathrm{PrCo_4B}$ phase. This is also supported by the fact that $\mathrm{PrCo_4B}$ is a very stable phase and forms a pseudobinary eutectic together with $\mathrm{Pr}_2\mathrm{Co}_{14}\mathrm{B}$ . The microstructures and corresponding TMA curves (Fig. 11-14) of the alloys heat treated isothermally at $1000^\circ\mathrm{C} - \mathrm{I}_{2}$ $(\mathrm{Pr}_{6}\mathrm{Co}_{85}\mathrm{B}_{9})$ $\mathbf{I}_3$ $(\mathrm{Pr}_{5.45}\mathrm{Co}_{64.55}\mathrm{B}_{30})$ $\mathbf{I}_4$ $(\mathrm{Pr}_{15}\mathrm{Co}_{82}\mathrm{B}_3)$ , and $\mathbf{I}_5$ $(\mathrm{Pr}_{12.5}\mathrm{Co}_{83.5}\mathrm{B}_4)$ can be interpreted in a similar manner by considering the compatibility triangles inside which these alloy compositions are located.

associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: The assessed Li-Sr equilibrium phase diagram is shown in Fig. 1. The solid lines on the diagram are taken directly from the results of the same group of investigators, who performed differential thermal analysis and both low- and high-temperature X-ray analysis. Their investigation was part of an overall project that included the systems Ba-Sr, Mg-Sr, Ca-Sr, Li-Ba, Ca-Sr, Ba-Mg, Ca-Mg, Ba-Al, Ca-Li, Ba-Na, and Sr-Na. There are no other reported measurements of the Li-Sr phase diagram. Transition points of the elements on Fig. 1 are from [83Cha] except for the melting point of Sr, which is taken from [Melt]. This value originates from [66Pet]. The dashed lines in Fig. 1 represent important modifications that have been made to the diagram of [62Wan2]. The LiSr8 and LiSr7 structures are reported in Table 1, but are not indicated in Fig. 1 because there is some evidence that at least one of these solids may be the hydride $\mathrm{SrH_2}$, which has an orthorhombic lattice and a slightly distorted cph structure of the metal atoms. The dashed liquidus lines in Fig. 1 were calculated from thermodynamic principles using selected experimental data from the lower regions of the liquidus lines of Fig. 2 and the assumption of negligible solid solubility of Li in $(\alpha \mathrm{Sr})$ and $(\beta \mathrm{Sr})$. The experimental details presented by [60Wan], [62Wan1], and [62Wan2] were sometimes unclear. The results of the phase diagram measurements were given in the form of diagrams such as the one shown in Fig. 2. There were no tables or diagrams of the compositions and temperature arrests. The experimental results and the phase diagram of [62Wan1] show three allotropes of Sr: a low-temperature fcc form transforming into an intermediate cph structure at $232^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, which transforms to a high-temperature bcc form at $620^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. Other authors have reported the existence of the intermediate cph structure of Sr. However, it has been shown by [66Pet] that this phase is most likely a binary hydride. It is now generally accepted that pure Sr has only two allotropes: a low-temperature fcc form that transforms into the higher temperature bcc form at $547^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. The liquidus, eutectic, peritectic, and solidus lines were determined by differential thermal analysis. Samples, initially at every 2 at.% were heated to $800^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ in thin-walled Fe crucibles under dry argon and stirred with an Fe thermocouple. Cooling rates were in the order of 1 to $5^{\circ}\mathrm{C / min}$, and transitions measured for both heating and cooling experiments were generally within 1 to $2^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ reproducibility. Samples taken every 1 at.% were used in the range 80 to 100 at.% Sr. There are no reported thermodynamic data in the binary system. The ratio of atomic radii $r_{\mathrm{Sr}} / r_{\mathrm{Li}}$ is 1.38. This would suggest negligible solid solubility. From the phase diagram of [62Wan1], the limiting slope of the liquidus line on the Sr side is estimated to be 11.7 K/at.% Li. Assuming Sr obeys Raoult's law in the liquid, a limiting liquidus slope of 11.3 K/at.% Li can be calculated from the temperature and enthalpy of fusion if no solid solubility exists. Hence, the liquidus data of [62Wan1] indicate little solid solubility on the Sr side. This disagrees with the reported solidus lines in Fig. 2. The limiting liquidus slope on the Li side is not well defined in Fig. 2. However, it is unlikely that the solid solubility is as high as 2 at.% Sr, as shown in Fig. 2.

associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: The corresponding $P - X$ diagram for Sc-H is presented in Fig. 2. The only information available on the solubility of $\mathbf{H}$ in Sc is contained in the equilibrium isotherm measurements of [60Bec], [65Lie], and [66Sta]. Some earlier measurements by [60Mcg] showed significant departures from what was, for the most part, a large degree of agreement evident between the isotherms of [60Bec], [65Lie] and [66Sta] and therefore the [60Mcg] data have not been included in the construction of the figure. Only [65Lie] tested their experimental H solubility data for compliance with Sievert's law. Their conclusion was that for $X = 0.1$ (9.1 at.% H), the isotherms up to a temperature of $900^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ obey Sievert's law (i.e., $\sqrt{P} = kX$ , where $P$ is the equilibrium isotherm pressure and $k$ is a constant). The density of available experimental points used in making this test of Sievert's law is not very high, so that the criteria of applicability could possibly be altered with further measurements at pressures in the region of $10^{3}\mathrm{Pa}$ and below. None of the sets of available isotherm data provide many experimental points in this range of pressures. The measurements of [65Lie] provide most of the available isotherm data and the majority of their measurements were produced during H absorption. They did, however, carry out desorption measurements on two isotherms which traversed the $[(a\mathrm{Sc}) + \delta ]$ mixed phase region and these indicated little or no hysteresis. The possibility of hysteresis was explored in more detail by [66Sta], for an 800 $^\circ \mathrm{C}$ isotherm, and in less detail for one at $900^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ . The $800^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ isotherm shows an absence of hysteresis to within the experimental uncertainty of the pressure measurements $(\pm 1\mu \mathrm{m};$ i.e., $0.133\mathrm{Pa})$ and the temperature control $(\pm 0.5^{\circ}\mathrm{C})$ . We have given preference to the determination of the $[(a\mathrm{Sc}) + \delta ] / \delta$ coexistence boundary by [66Sta] because, to locate it, he used a differential plot of change of equilibrium pressure with composition for each of the isotherms and also, because for the 800 $^\circ \mathrm{C}$ isotherm, for example, the density of experimental points is much higher than for the isotherm plots of [65Lie]. The [66Sta] estimate of the location of this coexistence boundary is significantly shifted to higher $X$ values, compared with that given by [65Lie]. There is satisfactory agreement between the determinations of the $(a\mathrm{Sc}) / [(a\mathrm{Sc}) + \delta ]$ coexistence boundary by [65Lie] and [66Sta] as can be seen in the figure. associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: Solid Solubility of Cr in Cu. The solid solubility of Cr in Cu was studied by several authors. Wide discrepancy is present among these results, as shown in the figure. The solid solubility of Cu in Cr is known to be negligibly small below the eutectic temperature. Also the solid solubility of Cr in Cu is observed to be less than 1 at.%. Thus, the equilibrium solubility of Cr in the terminal solid solution based on Cu, $\mathbf{X}_{\mathrm{Cr}}^{\mathrm{(Cu)}}$, can be approximated by the equation: $\ln X _ {\mathrm {C r}} ^ {\left(\mathrm {C u}\right)} = ^ {\mathrm {E}} \Delta \bar {S} _ {\mathrm {C r}} ^ {\left(\mathrm {C u}\right)} / R - \Delta \bar {H} _ {\mathrm {C r}} ^ {\left(\mathrm {C u}\right)} / R T$, where $\Delta \overline{H}_{\mathrm{Cr}}^{(\mathrm{Cu})}$ is the change in enthalpy when 1 mol of Cr with the bcc structure dissolves in Cu to make a dilute solution, (Cu), with the fcc structure, and ${}^{\mathrm {E}}\Delta \widetilde{S}_{\mathrm{Cr}}^{(\mathrm{Cu})}$ is the relative partial molar excess entropy of Cr between the (Cr) and (Cu) phases. Although the data of [57Doi1] do not extend to temperatures as low as those of others, the good linear fit of the results even at temperatures where the rest show deviations, indicate a closer approach to equilibrium in these alloys. The alloys were also made carefully by vacuum melting, using reasonably high-purity material, and were studied by electrical resistivity and microscopy. Therefore, the results of [57Doi1] were used to draw the terminal solubility limits of Cu in the figure. These indicate a much lower level of solubility of Cr in Cu at lower temperatures than considered previously. The equation of the extrapolated line from the data of [57Doi1] is: $X _ {C r} ^ {(C u)} = 2 4 8 4 0 \exp (- 1 1 4 8 8 0 / R T)$, where $R$ is in $\mathbf{J} / \mathbf{mol} \cdot \mathbf{K}$. This equation can be used to calculate the solubility values at (low) temperatures where experimental results are suspect due to lack of equilibrium.

associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: The assessed Zr-Rh phase diagram is based primarily on the work of [64Ram], [65Zeg], [78Ere1], [78Ere2], [80Ere], [83Ere], [88Jor1], and [88Jor2]. Table 1 summarizes the three-phase equilibria and congruent transformations in the Zr-Rh phase diagram, as it is drawn in Fig. 1. The eutectoid reaction $(\beta \mathrm{Zr}) \leftrightarrow (\alpha \mathrm{Zr}) + \mathrm{Zr}_2\mathrm{Rh}$ was studied by [65Zeg], [78Ere2], and [88Jor1]. Using metallography, [65Zeg] found that the maximum solubility of Rh in $(\alpha \mathrm{Zr})$ is less than $0.1\%$ at the temperature of the eutectoid reaction. This is shown in Fig. 1. The boundaries of the $(\alpha \mathrm{Zr}) + (\beta \mathrm{Zr})$ two-phase region in Fig. 1 are consistent with the temperature of $863^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ for the $\alpha \leftrightarrow \beta$ transformation in pure Zr [Melt] and with the assessed temperature and $(\alpha Zr)$ and $(\beta Zr)$ compositions for the eutectoid reaction $(\beta Zr) \leftrightarrow (\alpha Zr) + Zr_2Rh$. The $(\beta Zr) / (\beta Zr) + Zr_2Rh$ boundary was studied by [65Zeg], [78Ere2], [80Ere], and [88Jor1] using metallographic and X-ray techniques. Reasonable agreement exists among the results of these authors, and this was the basis for the corresponding curve in Fig. 1. The eutectic reaction $\mathbf{L} \leftrightarrow (\beta \mathrm{Zr}) + \mathrm{Zr}_2\mathrm{Rh}$ was studied by [65Zeg], [78Ere2], [79Dre], [80Ere], [88Jor1], and [88Jor2]. Figure 1 employs values consistent with the more recent and detailed works by [80Ere], [88Jor1], and [88Jor2]. The melting point of pure $\mathrm{Zr}$ is $1855^{\circ}C$ [Melt]. There is only limited information on the $(\beta \mathrm{Zr}) + \mathrm{L}$ two-phase field. The results reported by [65Zeg], [79Dre], [80Ere], and [88Jor1] on the $(\beta \mathrm{Zr}) / (\beta \mathrm{Zr}) + \mathrm{L}$ boundary are not in agreement. In Fig. 1 we provisionally adopted the values given by [88Jor1] because these authors used several different compositions covering the whole $(\beta \mathrm{Zr})$ composition range. The existence of this intermediate phase with $\mathrm{Al}_{2}\mathrm{Cu}$-type structure was well established by [64Ram] (X-rays), [65Zeg] (X-rays, metallography), [78Ere2] and [80Ere] (X-rays, metallography), and [88Jor1] (X-rays, metallography, electron microprobe). [80Ere] (metallography, thermal analysis) and [88Jor1] (thermal analysis) determined the temperature of the peritectic reaction $\mathbf{L} + \beta \mathrm{ZrRh} \leftrightarrow \mathrm{Zr}_2\mathrm{Rh}$ to be $1160\pm 10$ and $1175\pm 5^{\circ}\mathrm{C},$ respectively. The corresponding value adopted in Fig. 1 is $1170\pm 10^{\circ}\mathrm{C}.$ The composition of L at this reaction is taken to be $\sim 29$ at.% Rh in agreement with [79Dre] and [88Jor1]. According to [88Jor1], there is no experimental indication of nonstoichiometry in this phase; consequently, it is shown as a line compound in Fig. 1. This intermediate phase was studied using X-rays by [64Ram], by means of thermal analysis, metallography, and X-rays by [78Ere1], [80Ere], and [83Ere], and by the same techniques plus electron microprobe analysis by [88Jor1]. The joint results of these authors demonstrated that ZrRh forms congruently at $1910 \pm 25^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and has a wide range of asymmetric nonstoichiometry that corresponds to Rh contents in excess of 50 at.$\%$ (see Fig. 1). The Zr-rich phase limit was confirmed to be temperature independent at 50 at.$\%$ Rh by [88Jor1]. At 1780 $^\circ \mathrm{C}$, the temperature of the peritectic reaction $\beta \mathrm{ZrRh} + \mathrm{L} \leftrightarrow \mathrm{Zr}_{3}\mathrm{Rh}_{5}$, the composition of $\beta \mathrm{ZrRh}$ varies from 50 to $\sim 62$ at.$\%$ Rh [80Ere, 83Ere, 88Jor1]. The $\beta \mathrm{ZrRh} + \mathrm{L}$ two-phase region in Fig. 1 is based on [88Jor1] and [88Jor2] (thermal analysis). With thermal analysis and X-rays, [80Ere] observed that $\beta \mathrm{ZrRh}$ (CsCl-type structure) transformed to $\gamma \mathrm{ZrRh}$ (bcc disordered) by means of an order-disorder reaction with a critical temperature of around $1455^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. However, this phase transformation of $\beta \mathrm{ZrRh}$ to $\gamma \mathrm{ZrRh}$ was not found by [88Jor1] who indicated that the $\beta \mathrm{ZrRh}$ phase is stable up to its melting. We think this important experimental discrepancy regarding the existence of $\gamma \mathrm{ZrRh}$ is due to the different levels of unrecorded interstitial contamination in the respective samples used by [80Ere] and [88Jor1]. The results of [88Jor1] are probably more trustworthy because these authors had more modern experimental procedures available to them, and therefore we have not included $\gamma \mathrm{ZrRh}$ in Fig. 1. The eutectoid decomposition $\beta \mathrm{ZrRh} \leftrightarrow \mathrm{Zr}_3\mathrm{Rh}_4 + \mathrm{Zr}_3\mathrm{Rh}_5$ at $1550^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and $\sim 59$ at.$\%$ Rh, shown in Fig. 1, was observed by [88Jor1]. However, this decomposition was not reported by [80Ere] who instead found the monotectoid reaction $\gamma \mathrm{ZrRh} \leftrightarrow \gamma \mathrm{ZrRh} + \mathrm{Zr}_3\mathrm{Rh}_5$ at practically the same temperature and composition values. The $\beta \mathrm{ZrRh} / \beta \mathrm{ZrRh} + \mathrm{Zr}_3\mathrm{Rh}_4$ phase boundary in Fig. 1 is a composite of the results reported by [80Ere] and [88Jor1]. The crystal structure of $\alpha \mathrm{ZrRh}$ is possibly orthorhombic [88Jor1]. The composition dependence of the equilibrium temperature for the reaction $\beta \mathrm{ZrRh} \leftrightarrow \alpha \mathrm{ZrRh}$ is very uncertain. [67Wan] (single-crystal X-ray diffraction) determined that at the stoichiometric composition, $\beta \mathrm{ZrRh}$ transforms martensitically to $\alpha \mathrm{ZrRh}$ with $\mathbf{M}_{\mathrm{s}} = 380^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. According to this author, the structure of $\alpha \mathrm{ZrRh}$ should be monoclinic. [78Ere1] (thermal analysis) suggested $\mathbf{M}_{\mathrm{s}} = 450^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ with a monoclinic structure for $\alpha \mathrm{ZrRh}$. According to [78Ere1] and [88Jor1], stoichiometric $\alpha \mathrm{ZrRh}$ reverts on heating to $\beta \mathrm{ZrRh}$ at approximately 610 and $670^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, respectively. A tentative curve is shown in Fig. 1 which is intended to represent the $T_{0}$ temperature (equal Gibbs energies) for $\alpha \mathrm{ZrRh}$ and $\beta \mathrm{ZrRh}$. The decrease of $T_{0}$ with increasing Rh contents is consistent with the observations of [80Ere], [83Ere], and [88Jor1]. The existence of this intermediate phase was reported by [64Ram], [80Ere], [83Ere], [88Jor1], and [88Jor2]. [64Ram] tentatively suggested a cubic $\mathrm{Fe}_3\mathrm{W}_3\mathrm{C}$-type structure for this phase, whereas [80Ere] reported a structure with tetragonal symmetry. Another important discrepancy exists between [80Ere, 83Ere] and [88Jor1, 88Jor2]; this is the mode of formation of $\mathrm{Zr}_3\mathrm{Rh}_4$. Using thermal analysis and metallography [80Ere], [83Ere] concluded that $\mathrm{Zr}_3\mathrm{Rh}_4$ would form through the peritectoid reaction $\gamma \mathrm{ZrRh} + \mathrm{Zr}_3\mathrm{Rh}_5 \leftrightarrow \mathrm{Zr}_3\mathrm{Rh}_4$ at $1480^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. However, [88Jor1] and [88Jor2] proposed the congruent reaction $\beta \mathrm{ZrRh} \leftrightarrow \mathrm{Zr}_3\mathrm{Rh}_4$ at $1660^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. We think, however, that each of the results obtained by [80Ere, 83Ere] and [88Jor1, 88Jor2] is indeed correct, and each could be interpreted if the actual interstitial contamination levels of the respective samples had been recorded and taken into account. Nevertheless, in Fig. 1 we reproduced the more recent results due to [88Jor1]. The existence of this intermediate phase was first reported by [59Dwi] (X-rays) who determined its crystal structure to be $\mathrm{AuCu}_3$ type. This result was confirmed by [64Ram], [80Ere], [85Kue], and [88Jor1]. [80Ere] (thermal analysis, metallography) and [88Jor1] (thermal analysis) determined that $\mathrm{ZrRh}_3$ forms congruently at stoichiometric composition at $1880 \pm 15$ and $1920 \pm 10^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, respectively. The value adopted in Fig. 1 is $1900 \pm 20^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. According to [80Ere], $\mathrm{ZrRh}_{3}$ has a range of nonstoichiometry of $\sim 7$ at.$\%$ Rh at $1650^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and of $\sim 9$ at.$\%$ Rh at $1715^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. On the other hand, [88Jor1] indicated a range of $\sim 12$ at.$\%$ Rh at around $1730^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. The eutectic reaction $\mathrm{L} \leftrightarrow \mathrm{Zr}_{3}\mathrm{Rh}_{5} + \mathrm{ZrRh}_{3}$ was studied by [74Ere] and [80Ere] (metallography, thermal analysis, incipient melting) who found for this reaction a temperature of $1720 \pm 15^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ with $\mathrm{L}$ and $\mathrm{ZrRh}_{3}$ compositions of 66 and 73 at.$\%$ Rh, respectively.
