associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: Recently, major progress was made by Chuang et al. They showed the interplay of the chemical and magnetic contributions to the stability of phase equilibria of Fe-Ni alloys. They calculated the Fe-Ni phase diagram by taking into account the magnetic effect on the Gibbs free energy. The magnetic contribution is large enough to change the free energy curve in a system that shows rapidly changing Curie temperature versus composition. Based on thermodynamic calculations, Chuang et al. introduced a tricritical point at $462^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and $48.8\mathrm{wt.\%}$ Ni as shown in Fig. 2. In addition, a miscibility gap of the fcc phase, as well as an associated spinodal, and the formation of a monotectoid equilibrium at $389^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ were predicted for the Fe-Ni alloy system at low temperatures. The $\alpha$ and $\gamma'$ phases are in equilibrium at low temperatures. Since Chuang et al. used the Kubaschewski phase diagram to establish the thermodynamic functions that they needed for the calculation, their phase diagram is basically the same as that of Kubaschewski except for the tricritical point, the miscibility gap, the $\alpha + \gamma_{2}$ two-phase field, and the monotectoid reaction. The major difference from previous phase diagrams is the presence of the $\gamma''$ (FeNi) phase field in the Reuter et al. diagram; in the Chuang et al. diagram there is no $\gamma''$ single-phase field. Instead, at $\sim 50$ wt.% Ni, an $\alpha + \gamma'$ ( $\mathrm{Ni}_3\mathrm{Fe}$ ) two-phase field is predicted. The boundaries of the miscibility gap and the spinodal decomposition area determined by Reuter et al. are wider than those predicted by Chuang et al. Spinodal boundaries were also calculated by Chuang et al. and are shown as lines with cross hatching in Fig. 2. Evidence supporting the existence of a miscibility gap in the Fe-Ni system and in a similar system, Fe-Pd, can be found in the literature. A major discrepancy between the Chuang et al. phase diagram and the Reuter et al. phase diagram is whether the $\gamma''$ (FeNi) field is an equilibrium phase. The tricritical point is based on the rapid change in Curie temperature $(T_{\mathrm{C}})$ with Ni content and the resultant magnetic contributions to the Gibbs free energy of the fcc $\gamma$ phase. Below the tricritical point, the fcc $\gamma$ phase splits into the low-Ni $\gamma_{1}$ paramagnetic and the high-Ni ferromagnetic $\gamma_{2}$ phases. The tricritical point was also accepted by Reuter et al. in constructing the Fe-Ni phase diagram. The $\alpha / (\alpha + \gamma)$ and $(\alpha + \gamma) / \gamma$ phase boundaries in the Chuang et al. and Reuter et al. phase diagrams agree reasonably well with previous data based on measurements of Fe-Ni alloys by Romig and Goldstein. As discussed in the Introduction, Chuang et al. constructed the Fe-Ni phase diagram by using thermodynamic calculations. A tricritical point introduced at 462 $^\circ \mathrm{C}$ and 48.8 wt.% Ni associated with a miscibility gap results in the formation of a monotectoid reaction at $389^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. The solubility limit of Ni in $\gamma$ calculated by Chuang et al. fits within the error range given by Romig and Goldstein and Zhang et al. Therefore, at the temperature of the monotectoid reaction, the solubility limits of Ni in $\alpha$ and $\gamma$ calculated by Chuang et al. are accepted in the new phase diagram. The $\alpha / (\alpha + \gamma_{2})$ boundary is defined by the experimental data of Romig and Goldstein and the calculated boundary of Chuang et al. The composition of the $\gamma^{\prime \prime}$ (FeNi) phase is coincident with the dashed line that defines the high-Ni side of the miscibility gap.

Figure 9a presents a phase diagram near the $\mathrm{Ni}_3\mathrm{Al}$ compound showing the data points presented in the previous study with one additional liquidus point determined here at $23.5\%$ Al. The eutectic composition, 1, was determined by extrapolation of the two liquidus lines, giving a value of $24.5\%$ Al. It has been shown here that this eutectic was actually a metastable $\beta + \gamma$ eutectic and not the equilibrium eutectic indicated in Fig. 9a. In this study, a direct measure of eutectic compositions was made. Interestingly, the equilibrium eutectic structure occurred only after macrosegregation in both the hypoeutectic and hypereutectic alloys, while the nominal eutectic composition alloy of $24.5\%$ Al alloy produced the metastable eutectic with a measured composition of $24.5\%$ Al. It appears likely that the eutectic structures found in the hypereutectic alloys both had off-eutectic compositions because the compositions scale with the target compositions. However, both hypoeutectic alloys gave the same eutectic composition of $24.6\%$ Al; therefore, this value will be taken as the equilibrium eutectic composition. Using the slope of $S_4 = 14^{\circ}\mathrm{C} / \%$ (from Ref. 4), the $1\%$ Al difference in the equilibrium and metastable eutectics allow one to estimate that the equilibrium eutectic must lie $1.4^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ above the metastable eutectic. This result is shown on Fig. 9b, where the $1.4^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ difference is shown as $\Delta T_2$.

Because the spacing of the eutectic alloys was unusually large in this system, it was possible to do EPMA upon the $\gamma^\prime$ component of the equilibrium eutectic without interference from the neighboring $\beta$ phase. To minimize beam spreading, the analysis was done at a beam voltage of $5\mathrm{kV}$. Three equilibrium eutectic samples were analyzed using a $\gamma^\prime$ standard that had been analyzed by wet chemical analysis. The composition of the $\gamma^\prime$ in the equilibrium eutectic was found to be $23.813\pm 0.133$ (54 data points). Based on this analysis, the composition of point 2 in Fig. 9a was taken as $23.8\%$ Al, as shown in Fig. 9b.

The diffusion analysis describes the decomposition of the metastable eutectic; therefore, the compositions $C_1$ to $C_4$ of the analysis are the compositions at the metastable eutectic temperature. Compositions 3 and 4 of Fig. 9a were evaluated previously as 21.3 and $28.2\%$ Al, respectively. In the previous study, composition 4 was evaluated at the metastable eutectic temperature. Because the temperature of composition 4 must be raised $\approx 1.4^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ to the equilibrium eutectic, it is now estimated as $28.1\%$ Al. Extrapolating down the small $\Delta T$'s to the metastable eutectic temperature, $C_1$ and $C_4$ are estimated as 21.5 and $28.0\%$ Al, respectively. The composition $C_3$ was evaluated from the $\gamma'$ eutectic composition of $23.8\%$ Al by estimating the slope S2 with a straight line between the 23.8 value and the two lower-temperature data points for this phase boundary shown in Fig. 9a. The slope S2 was taken as 30 $^{\circ}\mathrm{C} / \%$, giving $C_3 = 23.85$.

The experiment of Fig. 2 was further examined for evaluation of composition points 2 and 5 shown in Fig. 9a. The phase diagram of Fig. 9a predicts that if no undercooling occurs before the onset and termination of the $\gamma'$ phase, its composition should rise from the point 5 composition to the point 2 composition. Both the onset and termination compositions of the $\gamma'$ phase in Fig. 2 were measured on two neighboring thin sections cut from the rods, giving values of onset composition equals $23.6 \pm 0.1\%$ Al and terminal composition equals $23.8 \pm 0.1\%$ Al, where the deviations are averages over the two sections. The termination composition agrees very well with the value of 23.8 measured on the $\gamma'$ component of the equilibrium eutectic and indicates that little supercooling had occurred when the $\gamma'$ growth was terminated by formation of the eutectic structure. If it is also assumed that little supercooling occurred before formation of the $\gamma^\prime$ phase, then the composition of point 5 may be taken as the onset composition of $23.6\%$ Al, as was done in Fig. 9b.

One can evaluate the temperature difference $\Delta T$ shown on Fig. 9b by estimating the slope $S1$ with a straight line from 23.6 to the two lower data points for this phase boundary shown on Fig. 9a. Using an upper bound value for $S1$ of $45^{\circ}\mathrm{C} / \%$, the values for $\Delta T = 2.3^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and $\Delta T1 = 0.9^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ shown in Fig. 9b were obtained. Using lower values for $S1$ produces smaller values of $\Delta T$, which indicates that $\Delta T1$ is quite small. This technique of evaluating $\Delta T1$ is very approximate, however, because it is very sensitive to the differences in the compositions 23.6 and $C_2$. Although the $\Delta T$ values are consistent with the composition data, they should be regarded as only rough estimates. Previous experiments by Bremer et al. using DTA analysis estimated the $\Delta T1$ value as $3^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. One would only need to change the composition of 23.6 in Fig. 9b to $23.65\%$ Al to agree with the $3^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ value.

Conventional coupled eutectic growth theory requires the solid liquid growth temperature to be undercooled below the equilibrium eutectic temperature a small amount. As shown in Fig. 9b, the metastable eutectic temperature is estimated to be only $1.4^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ lower than the equilibrium eutectic temperature. If the undercooling required to grow the equilibrium eutectic at a given rate is larger than that of the metastable eutectic by this amount, then the metastable eutectic growth front temperature would lie at higher values than the equilibrium temperature and would lead the equilibrium growth front, and could crowd it out, particularly at the faster growth rate of $61~\mu \mathrm{m / s}$. If this were true, then it appears that this condition must be composition dependent since the metastable eutectic only appears at the composition of 24.4 to $24.5\%$ Al.

associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: Most recently, Reuter et al. proposed the Fe-Ni phase diagram as shown in Fig. 3. The Fe-rich portion of the diagram was determined by investigating the microstructure and chemical composition of the metallic phases in iron meteorites. Meteoritic metal is basically an Fe-Ni alloy containing from 5 to 60 wt.% Ni with small amounts (<1 wt.%) of Co, P, S, and C. Because meteorites have cooled slowly over millions of years (1 to 1000 million years) in their asteroidal bodies, meteoritic metal contains a characteristic structure that cannot be completely duplicated in the laboratory due to the slow diffusion process at low temperatures. This characteristic structure is formed by a series of phase transformations that occur at low temperatures. Therefore, meteorites are useful as indicators of the low-temperature phase transformations that occur in Fe-Ni alloys. The microstructure and chemical composition of the metallic phases in meteorites can be used to construct the stable and metastable phase boundaries below ~400 °C in the Fe-Ni phase diagram. The major difference from previous phase diagrams is the presence of the γ'' (FeNi) phase field. The FeNi phase is present in this version of the diagram as a stable phase and joins the γ phase congruently at 462 °C and 47 at.% Ni. The critical ordering temperature of the ordered FeNi phase is 320 °C. The FeNi phase field was extended to the disordered γ phase field because no α/Ni3Fe equilibrium was observed in iron meteorites at that time. The boundaries of the miscibility gap and the spinodal decomposition area were determined from the phase compositions of the metallic phases in iron meteorites and from high voltage electron microscope in situ irradiation experiments. These phase boundaries are wider than those predicted by Chuang et al. The tricritical point was also accepted by Reuter et al. in constructing the Fe-Ni phase diagram as shown in Fig. 3. A major discrepancy between the Chuang et al. phase diagram and the Reuter et al. phase diagram is whether the γ'' (FeNi) field is an equilibrium phase. In the Chuang et al. phase diagram, there is no γ'' single-phase field. Instead, at ~50 wt.% Ni, an α + γ' (Ni3Fe) two-phase field is predicted. However, the results of many investigations, including studies of meteorites and studies using irradiation to enhance the diffusion rates, show that the γ'' (L10 ordered FeNi) phase exists chemically, structurally, and microscopically. By studying metallic phases in meteorites, Reuter et al. did not observe the α/γ' equilibrium and thus concluded that the γ'' phase was present as a stable phase and that the α and γ'' phases are in equilibrium at low temperatures. Therefore the γ'' phase field was included in the Reuter et al. phase diagram as an equilibrium phase. With the Reuter et al. phase diagram, in which γ'' is a stable phase, there is no way to have the high-Ni γ' phase in contact with the α phase. This high Ni content at the α/γ' interface cannot be explained with the Reuter et al. phase diagram. The α / (α + γ) and (α + γ) / γ phase boundaries in the Chuang et al. and Reuter et al. phase diagrams agree reasonably well with previous data based on measurements of Fe-Ni alloys by Romig and Goldstein. The cloudy zone structure in meteorites is formed by a spinodal decomposition process. Therefore, Reuter et al. modified the low-temperature portion of the miscibility gap and spinodal boundaries of the Chuang et al. phase diagram based on the AEM results obtained from meteorites. The Ni content of 9.0 wt.% is lower than that of 11.7 wt.% observed by Reuter et al. Consequently, the γ1 + γ2 miscibility gap is somewhat wider than that in the Reuter et al. phase diagram, especially at the low-Ni end. This discrepancy is due to the fact that the x-ray spatial resolution of the VG HB501 AEM used in this study for the measurement of α2 in the honeycomb region is much better than that of the EM400T AEM used by Reuter et al. (2 nm versus 30 to ~50 nm). In this study, the high-Ni spinodal boundary is 46.8 wt.% Ni, which is consistent with the observation of Reuter et al. Since the meteorites investigated in this study contain only the OTR and the CZ, the low-Ni spinodal boundary, 28 wt.% Ni, determined by Reuter et al. at the CT-2/CZ boundary for iron meteorites is used in the new phase diagram. In addition, the low-Ni spinodal boundary at temperatures higher than ~200 °C was determined by Reuter et al. using an electron irradiation experiment. Although the γ1 + γ2 miscibility gap is somewhat wider than that in the Reuter et al. phase diagram, the spinodal region is unchanged. The critical ordering temperature of FeNi is 320 °C at 52 wt.% Ni. This ordering temperature was first determined by Paulevé et al. using neutron irradiation and electrical resistivity measurements of Fe-Ni alloys and was recently confirmed by Reuter et al. using 1 MeV electron irradiation.

associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: The equilibrium phase diagram of Fe-Ru is shown in Fig. 1. The $\mathbf{L} + \varepsilon \rightarrow \gamma$ peritectic, at $1590 \pm 20^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, was reported by [59Obr]. The $\mathbf{L} + \gamma \rightarrow \delta$ peritectic, at $1541 \pm 5^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, was studied by [58Gib]. Due to the sluggishness and the diffusionless nature of the $\gamma \rightleftarrows \alpha$ and $\gamma \rightleftarrows \varepsilon$ transitions at low temperature, the $\gamma \rightarrow \alpha + \varepsilon$ eutectoid temperature and the phase boundaries at low temperature are highly uncertain. Also, no data are available on the $\mathbf{L} / \varepsilon$ phase boundaries. The most reliable data on the Fe-Ru system are the thermal analysis measurements of [58Gib] on Fe-rich alloys at temperatures between about 1380 and $1560^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. The temperatures reported by [58Gib] have been adjusted to agree with a value of $1538^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ on IPTS-68 for the melting point of pure Fe. ([58Gib] obtained $1534^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, to which $2^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ of the difference may be attributed to the temperature scale and $2^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ to impurities and other uncertainties.) Using the thermodynamic model described below, an optimized fit to the adjusted data of [58Gib] yields a peritectic temperature of $1540.8^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ with $\mathbf{L}$, $\alpha$, and $\gamma$ compositions of 5.6, 5.7, and 6.3 at.% Ru, respectively. Data on the $\gamma/\varepsilon$ equilibrium were provided by [59Obr], [60Rau], and [68Ste]. The tie line at $1327^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ (0.21 to 0.36 at.% Ru) determined by [68Ste] using vapor pressure activity measurements was taken into account, as was their value of the Fe activity (0.75 in the $\gamma + \varepsilon$ region at $1327^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$), although the latter was given a low weight. [59Obr] measured the peritectic reaction for $\mathbf{L} + \varepsilon$ as $1590^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and gave an approximate composition of 36 at.% Ru in the $\varepsilon$ phase at that temperature. The X-ray and metallographic investigations of [60Rau] provide several valid data points for the $(\alpha + \varepsilon) \rightarrow \varepsilon$ boundary ( $\sim 32$ at.% at $1300^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, $\sim 30$ at.% at $1100^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, and $\sim 23$ at.% at $700^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$). The boundaries shown in Fig. 1 represent the results of an optimized fit to these data using a thermodynamic model as discussed below. The regular solution parameters above provided a satisfactory fit to the input data with two exceptions: (1) the predicted $\mathbf{L} + \varepsilon \rightarrow \gamma$ peritectic was $20\mathrm{K}$ below the reported value of [59Obr], and (2) the width of the $(\gamma + \varepsilon)$ two-phase region was larger than reported by [60Raul]. Although the reliability of the existing data might allow such a deviation, it was felt that, lacking further evidence, the model should be extended to be more in accord with the [59Obr] and [60Rau] data. Therefore, a subregular term was added to the liquid, a slight temperature dependence was added to the $\gamma$ regular solution interaction, and the $G_{\mathrm{Fe}}^{\mathrm{cph}}, G_{\mathrm{Ru}}^{\mathrm{bcc}}$, and $G_{\mathrm{Ru}}^{\mathrm{fcc}}$ lattice stabilities were adjusted slightly (in no instance by more than $10\%$). These adjustments cannot be made in a unique way on the basis of existing data but, as can be seen in Fig. 1, the resulting model of Table 3 does provide an assessment that will represent the currently available data on this system. Thus, the calculated diagram is provisionally accepted as the equilibrium diagram for this system. Note that, to obtain the best agreement with the data of [58Gib], the $\mathrm{L} + \gamma \rightarrow \alpha$ peritectic temperature and compositions were no longer entered as data but were calculated from the optimized parameters obtained using their data points. Additional data, especially on the $\mathrm{L} + \varepsilon \rightarrow \gamma$ peritectic and the $(\varepsilon + \gamma)$ two-phase region would greatly aid in better defining this diagram. Combining this with the $\gamma/\varepsilon$ equilibrium shifts the eutectoid temperature to a much higher value $(\sim 650^{\circ}\mathrm{C})$ than that given by [60Rau] $(\sim 500^{\circ}\mathrm{C})$. Because of a lack of true equilibrium studies, a very high uncertainty must be placed on this eutectoid temperature.

As seen in Fig. 2, the $\alpha / \alpha + \delta$ phase boundaries of [49Owe] and [53Jon] are in essential agreement with one another, but show higher solubility than those of [34Wei] and [40Hum1]. Moreover, the data of [53Jon] show a change of slope in the $\alpha$ phase boundary at $470^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. More recent differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) measurements in a two-phase $\alpha + \delta$ alloy of eutectoid composition by [78Kir] showed a discontinuity at $447^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. This could be related to the change of slope observed in the $\alpha$ solubility curve, although there is a temperature difference of $23^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ between the two reported temperatures. Similarly, heat capacity measurements by [81Wal] for an $\alpha + \delta$ alloy with 20 at.% In showed a steep increase in heat capacity above $427^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. The data of [53Jon], [78Kir], and [81Wal] therefore seem to suggest that there is a solid-state transformation in the temperature range between 427 and $470^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. However, [88Cla] maintain that above and below $470^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, the intermetallic in equilibrium with (Cu) was always the $\delta (\mathrm{Cu}_7\mathrm{In}_3)$ phase. These authors did not observe any other compound in the $\alpha + \delta$ two-phase field below $574^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. The maximum solid solubility is accepted as 10.9 at.% In at the eutectoid temperature of $574^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, and the solubility at the peritectic temperature of $710^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ is accepted as 10.05 at.% In. The $\beta/\beta + \mathrm{L}$ solidus was determined by [34Wei] from thermal analysis of alloys between 18 and 25 at.% In. However, the $\alpha + \beta/\beta$, $\beta/\beta + \gamma$, and $\beta/\beta + \delta$ phase boundaries of [34Wei] were not determined precisely. On the Cu-rich side, the limiting composition of $\beta$ was determined by [40Hum1] to be 18.05 at.% In at the peritectic temperature of $\sim 710^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, in contrast to a value of 18.2 at.% In reported by [34Wei] at 715 °C. However, [34Wei] indicated the eutectoid composition to be stoichiometric at 20 at.% In, so that this phase was given the formula $\mathrm{Cu_4In}$. On the other hand, [40Hum1] regarded $\beta$ to be slightly off-stoichiometric toward the In-rich side. They determined the eutectoid composition to be 20.15 at.% In, on the basis of metallographic examination of alloys with 19.98 at.% In and 20.99 at.% In. On the In-rich side, [40Hum1] placed the limiting composition at 24.5 at.% In at the eutectic temperature of 676 °C whereas the measurements of [34Wei] indicated this composition to be 23.8 at.% In at 679 °C. Moreover, [40Hum1] pointed out that the composition of $\beta$ on the In-rich side does not extend to 25 at.% In, which is the stoichiometric composition for the formula $\mathrm{Cu_3In}$. On this basis, [40Hum2] indicated that $\beta$ is based on a true 3:2 electron compound, wherein the phase boundaries are displaced from 25 at.% In toward the Cu-rich side because of size factor considerations. associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: The equilibrium diagram for the Cu-Cr system is of the eutectic type with a flat liquidus and complete miscibility in the liquid state, see Fig. 1. In contrast, the diagram proposed hitherto shows a miscibility gap in the liquid that is based on antiquated and debatable experimental evidence. The solid solution fields have restricted width. A metastable phase based on fcc Cr is most likely present. Calculations made in this review based on the experimental phase diagram and thermodynamic results confirm that the miscibility gap in the liquid lies immediately below the equilibrium liquidus and not above it. The provisionally accepted diagram, presented in Fig. 1, therefore, is shown to be of the eutectic type with a nearly flat liquidus in the midcomposition range. Further experimental work is needed to verify this interpretation. The Cu-rich portion of the liquidus in equilibrium with the (Cr) solid solution was determined by thermal analysis and by partial solute dissolution techniques. The latter method was based on the isothermal equilibration of the liquid alloy and the partially dissolved Cr metal in a known charge of Cr and Cu. The composition of the liquidus was determined from the amount of undissolved Cr remaining in the (rapidly) solidified sample by its selective dissolution. The results indicated a liquidus richer in Cu than that obtained by thermal analysis. The interaction parameters thus computed from the phase diagram when applied to higher temperatures indicated that the two-phase equilibria between the liquid and the (Cr) phase persisted over the entire composition range up to pure Cr (Fig. 1). The resultant liquidus is nearly flat in the middle but does not show a miscibility gap. The initial slope of the liquidus at the Cr end of the diagram was calculated by the Clausius-Clapeyron equation from the freezing point depression at 1% dilution level, assuming negligible solubility of Cu in Cr. The resultant value is approximately -22.7 °C per at.% Cu. The accepted liquidus is drawn based on the data of the partial solute dissolution technique and the activity determinations. The slope of the liquidus was made to conform with the foregoing limiting slope at the Cr end.

Figure 4 shows an extension of available data to develop the general character of the quasi-ternary diagram. This extension was a melting diagram. Construction of this diagram was accomplished in the following way. First, the melting minimum at the $1380^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ eutectic in the $\mathrm{LaPO_4 - Ba_2P_2O_7}$ subsystem (point $\mathbf{e}_3$) was extrapolated through the $1000^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ liquid minimum (point a) of the $\mathrm{LaPO_4 - Ba_3P_4O_{13}}$ isopleth. Liquidus data from the $\mathrm{Ba}_2\mathrm{P}_2\mathrm{O}_7\mathrm{-Ba}(\mathrm{PO}_3)_2$ and $\mathrm{LaPO_4 - }$ $\mathrm{Ba}(\mathrm{PO}_3)_2$ subsystems were used to establish contours for determining temperatures along this line. Then, noting that the quasi-ternary peritectic reaction is:

$$
\mathrm {L} + \mathrm {B a} _ {2} \mathrm {P} _ {2} \mathrm {O} _ {7} \leftrightarrow \mathrm {L a P O} _ {4} + \beta \mathrm {B a} _ {3} \mathrm {P} _ {4} \mathrm {O} _ {1 3}
$$

a line from $\mathrm{Ba}_2\mathrm{P}_2\mathrm{O}_7$ through the invariant point of the $\mathbf{L}+$ $\mathrm{Ba}_2\mathrm{P}_2\mathrm{O}_7$ two-phase field (point b) was extended to intersect the melting curve at $890^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ (point P). This intersection defines the liquid composition in the equilibrium reaction at $890^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. Extension of the line beyond the intersection shows the direction in which the liquid composition will shift as temperature is lowered below $890^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$.
Beyond the point P toward the $\mathrm{LaPO_4 - Ba(PO_3)_2}$ side, $\mathrm{Ba}_2\mathrm{P}_2\mathrm{O}_7$ is no longer present as an equilibrium phase, and further reduction in temperature results in the composition of solidifying liquid moving toward the $\mathrm{LaPO_4 - Ba_2P_2O_7}$ side of the system. Liquid will cease to exist as an equilibrium phase in the system at temperatures below the ternary eutectic:

$$
\mathrm {L} \leftrightarrow \mathrm {L a P O} _ {4} + \alpha \mathrm {B a} _ {3} \mathrm {P} _ {4} \mathrm {O} _ {1 3} + \mathrm {B a} (\mathrm {P O} _ {3}) _ {2}
$$

at the point E where this postperitectic solidification line meets the melting depressions (lines $\mathbf{e}_1\mathbf{E}$ and $\mathbf{e}_2\mathbf{E}$) of the 825 $^\circ \mathrm{C}$ eutectic (point $\mathbf{e}_1$) in the $\mathrm{LaPO_4 - Ba(PO_3)_2}$ subsystem and the $840^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ eutectic (point $\mathbf{e}_2$) in the $\mathrm{Ba}_2\mathrm{P}_2\mathrm{O}_7\mathrm{-Ba}(\mathrm{PO}_3)_2$ subsystem. This triple junction is indicated to occur near $812^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$.
Knowledge of the phase equilibria in the three subsystems that bound the $\mathrm{LaPO_4 - Ba_2P_2O_7 - Ba(PO_3)_2}$ system places constraints on the quasi-ternary equilibria. To determine how the equilibria in the contributory subsystems extend into the quasi-ternary system, samples were prepared at selected compositions through the isopleth between $\mathrm{Ba}_3\mathrm{P}_4\mathrm{O}_{13}$ and $\mathrm{LaPO_4}$. These samples were prepared by sintering mixtures of the two phases at $800^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ for $5\mathrm{h}$. Crushed samples were then examined by both DTA and XRD.

associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: The assessed Li-Sr equilibrium phase diagram is shown in Fig. 1. The solid lines on the diagram are taken directly from the results of the same group of investigators, who performed differential thermal analysis and both low- and high-temperature X-ray analysis. Their investigation was part of an overall project that included the systems Ba-Sr, Mg-Sr, Ca-Sr, Li-Ba, Ca-Sr, Ba-Mg, Ca-Mg, Ba-Al, Ca-Li, Ba-Na, and Sr-Na. There are no other reported measurements of the Li-Sr phase diagram. Transition points of the elements on Fig. 1 are from [83Cha] except for the melting point of Sr, which is taken from [Melt]. This value originates from [66Pet]. The dashed lines in Fig. 1 represent important modifications that have been made to the diagram of [62Wan2]. The LiSr8 and LiSr7 structures are reported in Table 1, but are not indicated in Fig. 1 because there is some evidence that at least one of these solids may be the hydride $\mathrm{SrH_2}$, which has an orthorhombic lattice and a slightly distorted cph structure of the metal atoms. The dashed liquidus lines in Fig. 1 were calculated from thermodynamic principles using selected experimental data from the lower regions of the liquidus lines of Fig. 2 and the assumption of negligible solid solubility of Li in $(\alpha \mathrm{Sr})$ and $(\beta \mathrm{Sr})$. The experimental details presented by [60Wan], [62Wan1], and [62Wan2] were sometimes unclear. The results of the phase diagram measurements were given in the form of diagrams such as the one shown in Fig. 2. There were no tables or diagrams of the compositions and temperature arrests. The experimental results and the phase diagram of [62Wan1] show three allotropes of Sr: a low-temperature fcc form transforming into an intermediate cph structure at $232^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, which transforms to a high-temperature bcc form at $620^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. Other authors have reported the existence of the intermediate cph structure of Sr. However, it has been shown by [66Pet] that this phase is most likely a binary hydride. It is now generally accepted that pure Sr has only two allotropes: a low-temperature fcc form that transforms into the higher temperature bcc form at $547^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. The liquidus, eutectic, peritectic, and solidus lines were determined by differential thermal analysis. Samples, initially at every 2 at.% were heated to $800^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ in thin-walled Fe crucibles under dry argon and stirred with an Fe thermocouple. Cooling rates were in the order of 1 to $5^{\circ}\mathrm{C / min}$, and transitions measured for both heating and cooling experiments were generally within 1 to $2^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ reproducibility. Samples taken every 1 at.% were used in the range 80 to 100 at.% Sr. There are no reported thermodynamic data in the binary system. The ratio of atomic radii $r_{\mathrm{Sr}} / r_{\mathrm{Li}}$ is 1.38. This would suggest negligible solid solubility. From the phase diagram of [62Wan1], the limiting slope of the liquidus line on the Sr side is estimated to be 11.7 K/at.% Li. Assuming Sr obeys Raoult's law in the liquid, a limiting liquidus slope of 11.3 K/at.% Li can be calculated from the temperature and enthalpy of fusion if no solid solubility exists. Hence, the liquidus data of [62Wan1] indicate little solid solubility on the Sr side. This disagrees with the reported solidus lines in Fig. 2. The limiting liquidus slope on the Li side is not well defined in Fig. 2. However, it is unlikely that the solid solubility is as high as 2 at.% Sr, as shown in Fig. 2.

associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: The experimentally revised phase diagram of $\mathrm{Cu - In}$ is shown in Fig. 2. Three aspects of this diagram differ from the assessed diagram by Subramanian and Laughlin. First, the compound $\mathrm{Cu}_{11}\mathrm{In}_9$ is stable to low temperatures instead of decomposing by an inverse peritectic reaction to $\eta$ and L at $157^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. Second, the "phase bundle" consisting of "h," "A," "A'," "B," and "C" has been removed in favor of the original $\eta' / \eta$ dimorphic phase, with minor phase boundary adjustments. Third, the temperature of the $\eta' + \mathrm{L} = \mathrm{Cu}_{11}\mathrm{In}_9$ peritectic isotherm has been lowered from $310^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ to $307 \pm 1^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, and the eutectic $\mathrm{L} = \mathrm{Cu}_{11}\mathrm{In}_9 + (\mathrm{In})$ has been raised from $153^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ to $154.5 \pm 1^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. In the following, we present evidence to support the proposed phase relationships given in Fig. 2. The results are in contrast to those for the Cu-rich alloys and are consistent with the proposed phase diagram in Fig. 2. The eutectic temperature is $154.5 \pm 1^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. The slightly lower temperature of $153^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ reported in the literature probably corresponds to the metastable $\mathbf{L} = \boldsymbol{\eta} + (\ln)$ eutectic isotherm. This result indicates that there is only one phase transition series within this region, supporting the original proposal of $\eta^{\prime} / \eta$ transition instead of the "phase bundle" proposed by Jain et al., and adopted by Subramanian and Laughlin. The reaction observed by Jain, et al. using DTA denoting the transition between "h" and "A" was never observed. For the In-rich alloys, the endothermic peak occurs at $307^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, the peritectic reaction $\eta' + \mathrm{L} = \mathrm{Cu}_{11}\mathrm{In}_9$. On the basis of these observations, the phase relationships involving the transformation of $\eta'/\eta$ are proposed as shown in Fig. 2. The existence of the "phase bundle" between 32.0 and 38.0 at.% In, originally proposed by Jain et al., and adopted by Subramanian and Laughlin, is not supported by our experimental measurements. On the basis of our DSC studies, we favor the originally proposed equilibria involving $\eta' / \eta$. The invariant equilibria are $\delta + \eta' = \eta$ on the Cu side, and $\eta' + L = Cu_{11}In_9$ and $\eta' = \eta + Cu_{11}In_9$, as shown in Fig. 2. These data led us to believe that the temperature for the $\eta^{\prime} = \eta + \mathrm{Cu}_{11}\mathrm{In}_9$ reaction is close to that for $\eta^{\prime} + \mathrm{L} = \mathrm{Cu}_{11}\mathrm{In}_9$. Although the peak for the former reaction could not be observed, it is probably a eutectoid isotherm with a very small enthalpy of reaction, located slightly below the peritectic reaction.

associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: Figure 1 represents the Al-Pb phase diagram, as taken from the compilation of [58Han]. The miscibility gap in the liquid state is known only in the region of the monotectic temperature. An alloy that is single-phase at high temperatures passes the miscibility gap on cooling. During this process both liquid phases—due to their different densities—separate into two layers, one above the other. Subsequently, both melts solidify to a regulus. Such a regulus has no value for technical applications. On passing through a miscibility gap, at first a finely dispersed precipitation occurs. In the gravity field of earth, the tiny droplets are rapidly transformed into layers, one above the other. The kinetics of this process consist of diffusion, convection, and movement by buoyancy caused by density differences. The lowering of the center of gravity caused by these processes results in a potential energy gain. Of course, this potential energy gain is dependent on the concentration. For the case of the Al-Pb system, the potential energy gain $\Delta A$ is plotted against the mass fraction: $\zeta_{\mathrm{Al}} = \frac{m_{\mathrm{Al}}}{m_{\mathrm{Al}} + m_{\mathrm{Pb}}}$.

For the group $T_{1}$, ranging from 905 to $947^{\circ}\mathbf{C}$, all the samples exhibiting this heat effect are plotted as solid triangles with the onset temperature in Fig. 9b and all the others as light triangles including binary Mo-Ga samples. Also shown is a suggested four-phase region L-GaAs-$\mathrm{Mo}_{5}\mathrm{As}_{4}$-$\mathrm{Mo}_{3}\mathrm{Ga}$. All the samples entering this region on heating from the equilibrium triangles L-GaAs-$\mathrm{Mo}_{3}\mathrm{Ga}$ or GaAs-$\mathrm{Mo}_{5}\mathrm{As}_{4}$-$\mathrm{Mo}_{3}\mathrm{Ga}$ will participate in this four-phase equilibrium while the other ones including the fringes will not, as seen from Fig. 9b. The following four phase reaction is therefore concluded:

$$
\mathrm {L} + \mathrm {M o} _ {5} \mathrm {A s} _ {4} \leftrightarrow \mathrm {G a A s} + \mathrm {M o} _ {3} \mathrm {G a}
$$

at $T_{1} = 912 \pm 10^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. The temperature of this nonvariant equilibrium should be constant for all samples. It is interesting to note that all samples in the triangle GaAs-Mo $_5$ As $_4$ -Mo $_3$ Ga exhibit the $T_{1}$-effect below $920^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. The higher temperatures up to $947^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ only occur in the other triangle L-GaAs-Mo $_3$ Ga. This is plausible, since upon heating, samples of the former triangle only have to produce a liquid phase, while those of the latter triangle have to nucleate the crystalline phase Mo $_5$ As $_4$. Being aware that the range 905 to $947^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ has been covered within seven min during heating, delays of this reaction are likely. Therefore, not the average of all $T_{1}$-effects (922°C) but only that of the GaAs-Mo $_5$ As $_4$ -Mo $_3$ Ga equilibrium samples (912°C) has been evaluated as the nonvariant four-phase temperature.
In a similar manner, the DTA signals of group $T_{2}$ (868 to $900^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$) are plotted in Fig. 9c together with the four-phase equilibrium region, which is interpreted as the peritectic formation of the ternary phase $\tau$:

$$
\mathrm {L} + \mathrm {M o} _ {3} \mathrm {G a} + \mathrm {G a A s} \leftrightarrow \tau
$$

at $T_{2} = 883 \pm 10^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. All the other DTA signals are smaller and not so conclusive. One reason is that the Ga-rich samples still contain nonequilibrium phase mixtures after annealing.
The seven samples exhibiting the high-temperature effect $T_{0}$ (average on heating $1167^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$) are located in the composition region of a four-phase reaction:

$$
\mathrm {L} + \mathrm {M o} _ {2} \mathrm {A s} _ {3} \leftrightarrow \mathrm {M o} _ {5} \mathrm {A s} _ {4} + \mathrm {G a A s}
$$

at $T_{0} = 1167 \pm 30^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, as depicted in Fig. 9a. The samples without that effect, also shown in Fig. 9a are only those with a maximum furnace temperature of at least $1250^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ since the sample temperature is always lagging behind that value in a DTA run. They confirm the validity of the proposed reaction with the exception of two samples in the $\mathrm{L} + \mathrm{Mo}_{5}\mathrm{As}_{4}$ field. It seems strange that the cooling peaks are above the heating peaks in the $T_{0}$ group. One might assume that the cooling peaks are related to the emerging three-phase equilibria $\mathrm{L} + \mathrm{Mo}_{2}\mathrm{As}_{3} + \mathrm{Mo}_{5}\mathrm{As}_{4}$ and $\mathrm{L} + \mathrm{Mo}_{2}\mathrm{As}_{3} + \mathrm{GaAs}$, which cover the four-phase onset temperature and vice versa.

associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: The proposed Ce-Pr phase diagram involves an $A$-type problem. Assuming that the trend of the $[(yCe) + ( eta Ce, \alpha Pr)] / ( eta Ce, \alpha Pr)$ solves is correct, its extrapolation to the Pr-rich side appears to cross the 100 at.% Pr line at $\sim 800^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. However, this requires a rather unlikely and abrupt change of slope in the latter solvus. Alternatively, if the latter solvus is correct, the former solvus must be modified so that it does not cross the 100 at.% Pr line at all when extrapolated smoothly. At any rate, either one or the other of the solvus boundaries appears to need revision. In many binary phase diagrams of intra-rare earth systems, quite often no two-phase fields are shown between the liquidus and the solidus in this diagram. This is mainly because the difference in the melting points of two elements is small and both the liquidus and the solidus are nearly horizontal. In addition, the separation between the two lines is essentially too small to be recorded graphically. Thus, although the absence of a two-phase field appears to be an $I$-type error, it may be simply due to a two-phase field with an unresolvable width.

The assessed equilibrium diagram is shown in Fig. 1. Melting points of the elements have been taken from [83Cha]. The boiling point of pure Cs is $669^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. The existence of one compound, $\mathrm{AuCs}$, with the CsCl structure, is definitely established. It is not clear whether this compound melts congruently or incongruity. The existence of the compound $\mathrm{Au}_{5}\mathrm{Cs}$ was proposed on the basis of thermal analysis results and by analogy with the compounds $\mathrm{Au}_{5}\mathrm{K}$ and $\mathrm{Au}_{5}\mathrm{Rb}$. No X-ray or other verification was reported. A phase of average composition $\mathrm{AuCs}_{0.77}$, reported in an early study, could not be found by [61Kie] and has not been reported subsequently. Data points from the thermal analysis experiments of [61Kie] are shown in Fig. 1. Very little description of the experimental procedures was given by [61Kie]. It is not stated whether thermal analysis points are from heating, or cooling, or both. No mention was made of the purity of the materials. No metallography was reported. DTA results of [81Kem] and thermal analysis results of [79Esc] and [81Som] are also shown in Fig. 1. Only a few compositions were studied, but these data are probably more reliable than those of [61Kie].
For Cs concentrations above 70 at.%, the liquidus curves reported by [61Kie] and [79Esc] and [81Som] differed markedly. The thermodynamic analysis discussed below (see "Thermodynamics") supports the data of [79Esc] and [81Som], and the liquidus has been drawn in Fig. 1 on this basis. Further support was given by [80Mar1], who reported that at 75 at.% Cs, Bragg reflections were observed during neutron diffraction studies at temperatures up to $90^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ above the liquidus reported by [61Kie]. Error bars of at least $50^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ should be placed on the assessed liquidus in Fig. 1 at Cs concentrations above 75 at%.
A eutectic reaction was reported at $27^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ by [61Kie]. Under the assumption of negligible solubility of Au in (Cs), a liquid composition of 99.6 at.% Cs at the eutectic temperature was calculated from the enthalpy of fusion and melting point of pure Cs $(28.39^{\circ}\mathrm{C})$. However, from the thermodynamically extrapolated liquidus in Fig. 1, a much lower solubility of Au in liquid Cs at this temperature is calculated, so that a eutectic temperature virtually identical to the melting point of Cs is predicted.
A eutectic reaction at approximately 42 at.% Cs and $580^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ was postulated, with the AuCs compound melting congruently at $590^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. This proposed liquidus is difficult to accept, first, because the nearly horizontal limiting liquidus slope at 100 at.% Au grossly violates the thermodynamic limiting slope equation, unless an impossibly large solid solubility of Cs in (Au) is postulated; and second, because the precipitous drop of the liquidus near 25 at.% Cs, followed by a nearly horizontal section from 30 to 50 at.% Cs, would require very unusual thermodynamic properties of the liquid phase. Recognizing the problem of the limiting slope, [81Som] proposed the existence of $\mathrm{Au}_4\mathrm{Cs}$, corresponding to $\mathrm{Au}_4\mathrm{K}$ and $\mathrm{Au}_4\mathrm{Rb}$, observed in the Au-K and Au-Rb systems. (The stoichiometry of these is now known to be $\mathrm{Au}_5\mathrm{K}$ and $\mathrm{Au}_5\mathrm{Rb}$.) $\mathrm{Au}_4\mathrm{Cs}$ was proposed to melt congruently near $1048^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. As evidence, the existence of two distinct thermal effects at 1048 and $1042^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and 5 and 12 at.% Cs were cited (presumably, liquidus and eutectic halts), whereas at 20 at.% Cs, only one arrest—at $1048^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$—was observed. In a series of DTA experiments, [81Kem] observed thermal effects at the points indicated in Fig. 1, supporting the proposal of $\mathrm{Au}_5\mathrm{Cs}$. No confirmatory X-ray or other evidence for this compound was reported. Much experimental difficulty was reported by [79Esc] in this region.
Pending verification, therefore, $\mathrm{Au}_{5}\mathrm{Cs}$, with a congruent melting point at $1070 \pm 20^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and a eutectic reaction at $1035 \pm 15^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, has been proposed in Fig. 1. The (Au) liquidus in Fig. 1 has been calculated from the thermodynamic limiting slope equation under the assumption of negligible solubility of Cs in (Au).
[81Kem] also reported a thermal effect at $990^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ (see Fig. 1), which he associated with an allotropic transformation of $\mathrm{Au}_{5}\mathrm{Cs}$. Thermal effects were also observed near $900^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ by [81Kem], as shown in Fig. 1. These were proposed to indicate a peritectic associated with another compound, such as $\mathrm{Au}_{2}\mathrm{Cs}$ (by analogy with $\mathrm{Au}_{2}\mathrm{Rb}$ and $\mathrm{Au}_{2}\mathrm{K}$). This needs to be verified.
Instead of the liquidus proposed by [61Kie], which drops rapidly near 25 at.% Cs, [81Kem] proposed that the actual liquidus is displaced to much higher Cs concentrations. This suggestion has been followed in the assessed diagram of Fig. 1. The liquidus drops very steeply to an invariant at $585 \pm 10^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. This may be a eutectic or a peritectic reaction, but in either case, the liquid composition at the invariant temperature lies close to the compound composition of 50 at.% Cs. This interpretation is supported by the thermodynamic analysis discussed below. Further support was given by [80Mar1], who reported that in their neutron diffraction studies at $640^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, they were unable to obtain homogeneous liquid specimens with Au content higher than 50 at%.
The AuCs-Cs Subsystem. This subsystem can be considered to be similar to other metal-molten salt systems: CsF-Cs, CsCl-Cs, and CsI-Cs. All three exhibit liquidus curves indicative of a tendency to immiscibility and positive deviations from ideality in the liquid state. When AuCs and Cs are mixed, positive excess enthalpies are observed, which results in the liquidus for this subsystem, as shown in Fig. 1. The positive deviations could arise from the different bonding characteristics of liquid Cs, which is metallic, and liquid AuCs, which is ionic.
In Fig. 1, the $\mathrm{Au}_{5}\mathrm{Cs}$ liquidus descends steeply as the concentration of Cs approaches 50 at.%; this construction is supported by the curve of $\Delta_{\mathrm{mix}}S$. As the Cs concentration increases toward 50 at.% the partial molar entropy of Au (given by the tangent intercept construction) increases to a large value. Therefore, the partial molar Gibbs energy of Au in the liquid alloy decreases rapidly in this region, yielding a steep liquidus.
If the proposed phase diagram in Fig. 1 is correct, the enthalpy of mixing points at $627^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ measured by [79Esc] and [81Som] at Cs concentrations below 50 at.% were obtained actually in a two-phase region, consisting of solid Au and a liquid with close to 50 at.% Cs.
For purposes of curve fitting and extrapolation, the liquidus drawn in Fig. 1 has been calculated with $\Delta_{\mathrm{mix}}H$ and $\Delta_{\mathrm{mix}}S$ given by the above model, and with the enthalpy of fusion of $\mathrm{Au}_{0.5}\mathrm{Cs}_{0.5}$ adjusted artificially to $13.4\mathrm{kJ / mol}$. With enthalpies of fusion of Au and Cs of 13.00 and $2.09\mathrm{kJ / mol}$, respectively, assumed to be temperature independent, the enthalpy of formation of solid $\mathrm{Au}_{0.5}\mathrm{Cs}_{0.5}$ from solid Au and Cs has been calculated as $47.5\mathrm{kJ / mol}$, which compares well with $44\pm 4\mathrm{kJ / mol}$ at $298\mathrm{K}$, reported by [79Esc] and [81Som] from calorimetric measurements.

associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: Cu-rich Solvus and Liquidus. All reports indicate that the terminal solubility of V in Cu is quite small. Savitskii et al. report peritectic melting of the Cu-rich terminal solution at $1120^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ at a composition of $X_{\mathrm{Cu}} = 0.992$ in equilibrium with a liquidus of $X_{\mathrm{Cu}} = 0.966$. They further report that, with decreasing temperature, the Cu-rich solvus becomes more Cu-rich, reaching a composition near $X_{\mathrm{Cu}} = 0.999$ at room temperature. To compare with the Savitskii report, Elliott has referred to an unpublished thesis by C.O. McHugh at Pennsylvania State University that indicates a composition of $X_{\mathrm{Cu}} > 0.9971$ for the limit of terminal solubility of V in Cu at $1000^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. A detailed set of Cu-rich solvus data is provided by Eicke and Hahlbohm and is based primarily upon electrical resistivity values as a function of quench temperature, but with confirmation also by other electrical measurements. The Eicke and Hahlbohm data are given in Table 1 and are included in the figure. It must be emphasized that the variations among these three reports involve differences in solvus compositions of the order of tenths of an atomic percent, so there is little question that the terminal solubility of V in Cu is quite limited. However, both because of compatibility with liquidus data and for thermodynamic reasons, the data of Eicke and Hahlbohm are preferred. Peritectic Melting Temperature. If one uses the values of Savitskii et al. of $X_{\mathrm{Cu}} = 0.992$ for the solvus and $X_{\mathrm{Cu}} = 0.996$ for the liquidus at the peritectic reaction, a Clausius-Clapeyron approximation predicts a peritectic temperature $\sim 5^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ above the melting point of Cu, or $1088^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ rather than the $1120^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ of the Savitskii report. A peritectic reaction temperature only a few degrees above the melting point of Cu is also supported by the experimental results of McHugh and of Stevens. McHugh found cooling curves for V-Cu alloys to exhibit thermal arrests at $1085^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, two degrees above the thermal arrest of pure Cu. associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: The temperatures accepted here for the α/β equilibrium in pure Zr and pure Hf are 863°C and 1743°C, respectively. The (α + β) boundaries shown in Fig. 1 are a compromise between the indicated allotropic transformation temperatures of the pure metals and the alloy experimental data. These data are not sufficient to establish approximate experimental values for the temperature width, Δθ, of the (α + β) region; hence, it is provisionally accepted here that this compromise must render a value for Δθ at 50 at.% Hf very close to that corresponding to the situation of ideal mixing between Zr and Hf. This condition on Δθ can be conveniently satisfied by using, as done here, expressions cubic in temperature for the composition of the (α + β) boundaries, subject to van't Hoff's relation. The resulting numerical expressions for the α/(α + β) and β/(α + β) boundaries, which we consider to give the best possible fit (see Fig. 2) to the combined experimental data under the indicated constraints, are given below. These numerical expressions conform with the van't Hoff's equation, in which the values for the heats of the α → β transformations in pure Zr and pure Hf are assumed to be 930 cal/mol and 1400 cal/mol, respectively. [57Hay] worked in the range 0 to 43 at.% Hf, determining the α ⇌ β transformation by differential thermal analysis. The temperature width suggested by [57Hay] for the (α + β) region (see Fig. 2) is negligible and definitely narrower than that of Fig. 1. This can be attributed to insufficient sensitivity of the experimental technique used to determine this region. [66Dom] studied the (α + β) region by means of metallographic examination of heat treated (800 to 1800°C) and quenched specimens. On quenching from (α + β), [66Dom] was able to observe a typical microstructure showing transformed β plus isothermal α. He remarked that there was no evidence of any retention of the high-temperature bcc (β) phase upon quenching, but that this was not corroborated by X-ray analysis. The obtained results were judged by [66Dom] to be in substantial agreement with those of [57Hay] but, nevertheless, [66Dom] suggested a much wider (α + β) region than that of [57Hay] (see Fig. 2). For completeness, Fig. 2 also shows data due to [66Har] obtained by differential thermal analysis; these data appear to deviate toward higher temperatures and, in the instance of the Hf-rich alloys, they are not considered to be compatible with the α/β equilibrium temperature of pure Hf accepted here. Possibly, the samples used in these experiments were contaminated with oxygen. It is necessary to remark that a considerable uncertainty still exists regarding the shape (width) of the provisional (α + β) region indicated in Fig. 1. This is related to the uncertainty we must ascribe to the value 1400 cal/mol used here for the heat of the α → β transformation in pure Hf (ΔH_Hf^{α → β}). This value, which is based essentially on only one experimental determination, was recently recommended as the most probable value of ΔH_Hf^{α → β}; however, this value would be definitely too low to be used in an otherwise successful thermodynamic modeling of the Hf-Mo phase diagram. Thus, although keeping the 1400 cal/mol as the most probable value of ΔH_Hf^{α → β}, we propose here to bracket this quantity between 1260 and 3080 cal/mol, the upper limit being the value necessitated in the synthesis of the Hf-Mo phase diagram. The uncertainty in the (α + β) region, associated with this bracketing, is graphically represented in Fig. 2 for the equiatomic composition.

The phase boundaries for the uranium-rich side of this system are presented in the figure, which is taken from [Hansen]. The figure is largely based on Fig. 1 and early data on the dissociation pressure of $\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{U}$. Other pertinent data are summarized by [Elliott] and [Shunk]. This figure represents the equilibrium phases and compositions under the equilibrium dissociation pressure of the hydride produced by the reaction:

$$
\mathrm {H} _ {3 - X} \mathrm {U} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm {U} (\text {s o l i d s o l u t i o n}) + \frac {3 - X}{2} \mathrm {H} _ {2}
$$

However, their data for higher temperatures showed a very rapid increase of the solubility of uranium in the hydride phase and their values of $-\ln X_{\mathrm{U}}$ fall far below the range indicated on the figure and were not plotted. Their isotherms also showed a much higher solubility of hydrogen in the uranium-rich phase than is indicated in the figure. The reason for the gross discrepancy in these data with the data of other investigators is not known.

Examination of the figure shows that the isotherms corresponding to the $\alpha \rightarrow \beta$ and $\beta \rightarrow \gamma$ transitions for uranium occur at the same temperatures. The same is true for the eutectic temperature of $1120^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. It may be expected that at the pressures indicated on the right side of the diagram given by [Hansen] that the transition temperatures for pure uranium would not be significantly affected. The increase in hydrogen content due to higher hydrogen pressures would be expected to lower the isotherms to some extent. However, the decrease in temperature with increase in hydrogen content is quite small; that is, the phase boundaries are nearly horizontal. Consequently, there would be only a small and perhaps insignificant decrease. The compositions in the figure were apparently calculated with the relation:

$$
X _ {\mathrm {H}} = \frac {1}{\gamma_ {\mathrm {H}}} P _ {\mathrm {H} _ {2}} ^ {1 / 2}
$$

which reduces to Sieverts law if $\gamma_{\mathbf{H}}$ is independent of composition:

$$
S = k P _ {\mathrm {H} _ {2}} ^ {1 / 2}
$$

The pressure indicated by [Hansen] for the higher temperatures are somewhat higher than values calculated from Eq 5. However, the values indicated in the figure are considered a good approximation. In any case, the lowering of the eutectic isotherm from 1120 to about $1050^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ is not realistic in view of present information. The actual melting temperature for $\mathbf{H}_3\mathbf{U}$ is not accurately known but could conceivably account for the incipient fusion indicated by [7].

The solubility of hydrogen in uranium as estimated from the pressure isotherms determined by [1] indicate a H/U ratio of 0.256 to 0.051 (0.108 to 0.022 wt.% H) in the temperature span 846 to $673^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, respectively. However, pressure isotherms by [7] indicate that the solubilities at 950 and $900^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ are 0.07 and 0.029 wt.% H, respectively. Without further information, a change in the figure does not appear to be justified.

It should not be construed that these results confirm the phase diagram but only that they are not grossly inconsistent. Thermal analysis of alloys with compositions in the two-phase regions at equilibrium hydrogen pressures would be very helpful in confirming the isotherms and in yielding additional evidence for the partial or incipient fusion of $\mathrm{H}_{3 - X}\mathrm{U}$ at $1050^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ reported by [7]. If partial fusion occurs at $1050^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ leading to equilibrium between a liquid phase, $\mathrm{H}_{3 - X}\mathrm{U}$, uranium solid solution and hydrogen, then this would require an isotherm terminating in a peritectic or eutectic reaction near the $\mathrm{H}_{3 - X}\mathrm{U}$ phase boundary. A two-liquid phase field instead of the liquid and $\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{U}$ phases above $1120^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ indicated in the figure would be required. A somewhat different interpretation is given by [24]. More information is needed on the actual melting temperature of $\mathbf{H}_3\mathbf{U}$ and the possible $1050^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ isotherm before these features can be incorporated in the phase diagram.

associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: The reported phase diagram of [62Wan1] is shown in Fig. 2. The results of the phase diagram measurements were given in the form of diagrams such as the one shown in Fig. 2. There were no tables or diagrams of the compositions and temperature arrests. The experimental results and the phase diagram of [62Wan1] show three allotropes of Sr: a low-temperature fcc form transforming into an intermediate cph structure at $232^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, which transforms to a high-temperature bcc form at $620^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. Other authors have reported the existence of the intermediate cph structure of Sr. However, it has been shown by [66Pet] that this phase is most likely a binary hydride. It is now generally accepted that pure Sr has only two allotropes: a low-temperature fcc form that transforms into the higher temperature bcc form at $547^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. The liquidus, eutectic, peritectic, and solidus lines in Fig. 2 were determined by differential thermal analysis. Samples, initially at every 2 at.% were heated to $800^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ in thin-walled Fe crucibles under dry argon and stirred with an Fe thermocouple. Cooling rates were in the order of 1 to $5^{\circ}\mathrm{C / min}$, and transitions measured for both heating and cooling experiments were generally within 1 to $2^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ reproducibility. Samples taken every 1 at.% were used in the range 80 to 100 at.% Sr. From the phase diagram of [62Wan1], the limiting slope of the liquidus line on the Sr side is estimated to be 11.7 K/at.% Li. Assuming Sr obeys Raoult's law in the liquid, a limiting liquidus slope of 11.3 K/at.% Li can be calculated from the temperature and enthalpy of fusion if no solid solubility exists. Hence, the liquidus data of [62Wan1] indicate little solid solubility on the Sr side. This disagrees with the reported solidus lines in Fig. 2. The limiting liquidus slope on the Li side is not well defined in Fig. 2. However, it is unlikely that the solid solubility is as high as 2 at.% Sr, as shown in Fig. 2. The dashed liquidus lines in Fig. 1 were calculated from thermodynamic principles using selected experimental data from the lower regions of the liquidus lines of Fig. 2 and the assumption of negligible solid solubility of Li in $(\alpha \mathrm{Sr})$ and $(\beta \mathrm{Sr})$.

The proposed phase diagram of the Na-Zn system is shown in Fig. 6. In Fig. 6, the Zn-rich liquidus at the syntectic temperature is only slightly more Zn rich than $\mathrm{NaZn_{13}}$. Data are inadequate to be sure whether $\mathrm{NaZn_{13}}$ and solid Zn form liquid by peritectic or by eutectic reaction. Crowther obtained a solubility of 0.8 at.% Zn, whereas in Fig. 6, a solubility of 11 at.% Zn in liquid Na is indicated at $548^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. If the solubility is as low as 0.8 at.% at $548^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, then it is unlikely that complete solubility at all compositions could be achieved at 820 °C, as shown in Fig. 6. The miscibility gap in Fig. 6 is nearly symmetrical with composition. This suggests the use of a regular-solution model for the liquid. Letting:

$$
G ^ {\mathrm {e x}} = \Delta H = X _ {\mathrm {N a}} X _ {\mathrm {Z n}} \times \omega
$$

where $S^{\mathrm{ex}} = 0$ and $\omega$ is composition and temperature independent, we can calculate $\omega = 2RT_{c}$, where $T_{c}$ is the critical temperature. If this is $820^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, as in Fig. 4, then $\omega = 18.2\mathrm{kJ}$. The entire miscibility gap can now be calculated. At $548^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, the calculated gap extends from 10 to 90 at. $\%$ Zn, in very good agreement with that reported in Fig. 6. Further, the activity coefficient of Na in pure Zn should then be:

$$
R T \ln \gamma_ {\mathrm {N a}} = 1 8. 2 \mathrm {k J}
$$

when

$$
X _ {\mathrm {N a}} = 0
$$
